chunks.title: Accessibility Statement
chunks.text:
Legal
Accessibility Statement
We want this site to work for every customer, including those using a screen reader, a keyboard, magnification or voice control.
Last updated: October 4, 2026
This document is written to be understood, not to hide anything in the fine print. It is general information about how TireDrop operates — it is not legal advice, and it does not replace the terms shown at checkout, your order confirmation, or any written agreement or invoice we give you. Where those are more specific, they govern. If something here is unclear or does not seem to match your situation, call (954) 773-1896 or use our contact form and ask. We would rather talk it through.

chunks.title: Accessibility Statement
chunks.text:
1. Our commitment
We are working to conform to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 at Level AA. That standard is our target for this site, and we treat it as a continuing obligation rather than a box to tick once.
This matters more, not less, for an online store: if the only way to buy a set of tires from us is through this website, the website has to work for everybody. As we add pages, product photography and features, we check them against the same standard.

chunks.title: Accessibility Statement
chunks.text:
2. What we have built in
Practical measures applied across the site include:
- Semantic headings and landmarks so screen readers can navigate the structure
- Keyboard access to every interactive control, with a visible focus indicator
- Labels tied to every form field, and error messages announced with the field they belong to
- Color combinations chosen for contrast, with color never used as the only way to convey meaning
- Text alternatives for meaningful images, and decorative graphics hidden from assistive technology
- Respect for the reduced-motion setting in your operating system
- Layouts that reflow on small screens and hold up when text is enlarged

chunks.title: Accessibility Statement
chunks.text:
3. Known limitations
Being honest about the gaps is part of the job. Content supplied by third parties — mapping, payment, carrier tracking and financing tools — is not fully under our control, and its accessibility depends on those providers. Product data comes from distributor catalogs, so a specification table may occasionally read awkwardly with a screen reader. Media added over time may briefly appear before captions or full descriptions are in place.
If you hit something that does not work, that is information we want. It is usually the fastest route to a fix.

chunks.title: Accessibility Statement
chunks.text:
4. Report a barrier
If any part of this site blocks you, call (954) 773-1896 during business hours and tell us what happened. It helps if you can mention the page, the browser or assistive technology you were using, and what you were trying to do — but call even if you cannot, and we will work it out together.
We aim to respond to accessibility reports promptly, and to tell you what we are doing about it rather than leave you guessing. If a fix will take time, we will find a way to get you what you needed in the meantime.

chunks.title: Accessibility Statement
chunks.text:
5. You can always just call
If the website is difficult for you to use for any reason, the phone is a full alternative, not a consolation prize. Call (954) 773-1896 and we will look up fitment, read you the options, take the order and arrange the shipping — the same order you would have placed online, placed by a person instead.
Locally, accessibility is not only a web issue either. If getting to the Sunrise shop is difficult, the mobile van covers our South Florida install area and can come to your home or workplace. Call and say what you need; we will work around it.

chunks.title: Crossing Alligator Alley: Tires, Spare and Fuel Plan
chunks.text:
Travel & Roadside
Crossing Alligator Alley: Tires, Spare and Fuel Plan
Driving Alligator Alley, I-75 across the Everglades: a tire and spare check before you go, fuel planning, and who to call if a tire goes.
The road with nothing on it
Alligator Alley is the stretch of I-75 that crosses the Everglades between Broward and Collier counties. FDOT describes it as running from the Everglades toll plaza in Broward to the Alligator Alley West toll plaza in Collier. It's the fastest way from Fort Lauderdale or Weston to Naples and the Gulf coast.
It's also a road with very little on it: long, straight, flat, with water and sawgrass on both sides, few exits, and very few services between the two ends. That's what makes the drive pleasant, and it's why a little preparation goes a long way.

chunks.title: Crossing Alligator Alley: Tires, Spare and Fuel Plan
chunks.text:
Before you leave: fuel and tires
Fill up first. Plan on leaving Weston, Fort Lauderdale or Naples with a full tank or a good charge. Along the crossing, the stop most drivers know is the Miccosukee Service Plaza at Exit 49, which sells fuel and has a store. Check its hours before relying on it, especially late at night.
Then the tires. A long crossing at highway speed, often in the afternoon heat, is exactly where an underinflated or worn tire shows itself. Take 15 minutes in the driveway:
- Pressure, cold, in all four tires and the spare, against the driver's door placard. USTMA defines cold as parked for at least three hours. Our guide to checking tire pressure shows how.
- Tread, in three grooves on each tire. Afternoon storms are common in the wet season, and standing water on a fast highway is where worn tread matters. Our post on why 4/32 matters in Florida rain explains the line.

chunks.title: Crossing Alligator Alley: Tires, Spare and Fuel Plan
chunks.text:
Before you leave: fuel and tires
- Sidewalls: no bulges, cuts or deep cracks.
- Anything in the tread: a nail or screw is far better found in your driveway than at mile marker 40.
Heat on the long straight
A summer crossing means hot pavement and an hour or more at steady highway speed. Tires warm up as they run, and USTMA says pressure rises about 1 to 2 psi for every 10°F of temperature change. So a gauge reading at the Exit 49 plaza will be higher than the cold reading you took at home.
That's normal. Don't let air out of a warm tire to match the placard; it will be low once it cools. What matters is that the cold pressure was right before you left. If one tire reads noticeably lower than the others, even warm, look for a nail or a leak before you carry on.

chunks.title: Crossing Alligator Alley: Tires, Spare and Fuel Plan
chunks.text:
Know your spare before the Alley
This is the most important check for this particular road. AAA says about 30 percent of new cars now come without a spare, carrying a sealant and inflator kit or run-flat tires instead. On a road with few exits, it matters a lot which one you have.
What's in your trunk
What it means out here
Full-size spare
The best case. Check its pressure and age.
Compact spare ("donut")
Gets you to a shop. Michelin says not to exceed 50 mph on one.
Sealant and inflator kit
Seals small punctures in the tread only. AAA says kits don't work on larger leaks or sidewall damage.
Run-flat tires
Limited distance at reduced speed; check your manual.
Nothing
A tow, and possibly a long one.
Our spare tire types guide explains each option, and our glovebox tire kit lists what to carry, including a gauge and an inflator.

chunks.title: Crossing Alligator Alley: Tires, Spare and Fuel Plan
chunks.text:
If a tire goes on the Alley
- Hold the wheel firmly and ease off the gas. Let the car slow down; don't brake hard.
- Get onto the shoulder, as far from the travel lanes as you can, on firm ground. Be careful near the canal edges.
- Hazard lights on. Florida's Move Over law, as FLHSMV describes it, now covers any vehicle stopped with its hazards flashing, a flat tire included. Approaching drivers must move over or slow to 20 mph below the limit.
- Dial *347.

chunks.title: Crossing Alligator Alley: Tires, Spare and Fuel Plan
chunks.text:
If a tire goes on the Alley
*347 reaches the Florida Highway Patrol and FDOT's Road Rangers, who FDOT says change flat tires, supply emergency fuel, jump-start cars and help clear disabled vehicles from the lanes, at no charge. FDOT District Four's Road Ranger guidelines include I-75 from the Miami-Dade County line to mile marker 50, west of the Alligator Alley toll plaza, with a patrol beat assigned to that stretch. The Collier County side falls under FDOT District One.
While you wait, FDOT's advice is to stay inside your vehicle once you're out of the flow of traffic. Keep water in the car; it's a hot place to sit.
One catch: Road Rangers change a flat with your spare. No spare, no tire change. If the car needs more than they can do, FDOT says FHP will contact a tow company at your expense.

chunks.title: Crossing Alligator Alley: Tires, Spare and Fuel Plan
chunks.text:
After the crossing
A donut or a sealed tire is a way to reach a tire shop, not to finish a road trip. At the far end:
- Have the tire inspected before driving on. A tread puncture can often be repaired from the inside; sidewall damage can't. Can My Tire Be Repaired? shows the limits.
- Tell the shop if you used sealant.
- Recheck the other tires cold the next morning.
For more on the roadside steps, our post on a flat tire on I-95 goes into detail.

chunks.title: Crossing Alligator Alley: Tires, Spare and Fuel Plan
chunks.text:
Coming home to Broward
If the crossing turned up a tire problem, we can help at the Broward end. In Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we install at our Sunrise shop, or our mobile van can come to you at home, including in Weston. Need new tires before the next trip? Shop by size or vehicle. Shipping is free to the 48 contiguous states and DC.
Key takeaways
- Alligator Alley is I-75 between the Everglades toll plaza in Broward and the Alligator Alley West toll plaza in Collier. Services along it are few.
- Fill the tank and check the tires before you leave Weston or Naples. Plan on one fuel stop, the Miccosukee Service Plaza at Exit 49.
- FDOT's District Four Road Ranger guidelines cover I-75 from the Miami-Dade line out to mile marker 50. Dial *347 for help.
- Know your spare. Road Rangers change flats with your spare; no spare means a tow, and a long one out here.

chunks.title: Crossing Alligator Alley: Tires, Spare and Fuel Plan
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- A compact spare or a sealant kit gets you to a shop at reduced speed. It isn't for finishing a long crossing.
Questions people ask
Is there a gas station on Alligator Alley?
There's one service plaza along the crossing: the Miccosukee Service Plaza at Exit 49, which sells fuel and has a convenience store. Check its hours before you go, and fill up in Weston, Fort Lauderdale or Naples so you don't depend on it.
What do I do if I get a flat on Alligator Alley?
Get off the travel lanes onto the shoulder, turn on your hazard lights and dial *347, which reaches the Florida Highway Patrol and FDOT's Road Rangers. FDOT's District Four guidelines have Road Rangers covering I-75 out to mile marker 50 west of the toll plaza. Stay in the car with your seat belt on while you wait, as FDOT advises.
Do Road Rangers patrol Alligator Alley?

chunks.title: Crossing Alligator Alley: Tires, Spare and Fuel Plan
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
FDOT District Four's Road Ranger guidelines include the I-75 corridor from the Miami-Dade County line to mile marker 50, west of the Alligator Alley toll plaza, with a beat dedicated to that stretch. The Collier County side is FDOT District One. Either way, *347 is the number to call.
How should I prepare my car for Alligator Alley?
Leave with a full tank or a good charge, tires set cold to the door placard pressure, tread you've measured, and a spare or repair kit you know how to use. Save *347 and your roadside assistance number, and carry water. There are few exits and services between the two ends.

chunks.title: Back-to-School Car Check for Broward Families
chunks.text:
Rain, Heat & Weather
Back-to-School Car Check for Broward Families
A back-to-school car checklist for Broward families and teen drivers: recalls by VIN, tire tread, age and pressure, and a 10-minute routine to teach.
The school-year car
For a lot of Broward families, the school year changes how the car gets used. More short trips, drop-off lines, after-school practice, and for some families, a teenager driving to school for the first time, often in a car that used to be a parent's.
Broward County Public Schools' 2026/27 year started on Monday, August 10, 2026. If you missed the August check, the school calendar gives you two more natural moments: winter break, December 21 to 31, 2026, and spring break, March 22 to 26, 2027. Pick one and put it on the family calendar.

chunks.title: Back-to-School Car Check for Broward Families
chunks.text:
Why it matters more with a new driver
NHTSA's teen driving page is blunt about the risk. Teen drivers have a higher rate of fatal crashes, it says, mainly because of immaturity, lack of skills and lack of experience. NHTSA counts 2,320 people killed in crashes involving a teen driver (ages 15 to 18) in 2024.
Most of what reduces that risk is behavior: seat belts, no phone, limited passengers, and practice. NHTSA notes that graduated driver licensing can reduce a teen's crash risk by as much as 50 percent, and reminds parents that you have more influence on your teen than you may think. A car in good shape is the part you can check in an afternoon.

chunks.title: Back-to-School Car Check for Broward Families
chunks.text:
Step 1: Open recalls, by VIN
Find the 17-character VIN on the lower left of the windshield, or on the registration or insurance card. Enter it on NHTSA's recall lookup . Searching by VIN tells you whether that specific vehicle needs a recall repair, and NHTSA says the dealer fixes the recalled part for free.
With a hand-me-down car, recall letters may have gone to a previous owner or an old address. Tires can be recalled too; our guide to tire recalls shows how to check them by the DOT number.

chunks.title: Back-to-School Car Check for Broward Families
chunks.text:
Step 2: Tread depth
NHTSA says tires should be replaced when the tread is worn to 2/32 of an inch, and suggests checking tread at least once a month when you check pressure. The quick version is the penny test: put Lincoln's head into a groove upside down, and if you can see the top of his head, replace the tires.
For South Florida's wet season, aim higher. AAA recommends replacing at 4/32; its testing found tires worn to that depth took an average of 87 feet longer to stop on wet pavement at highway speed than new tires. Our post on why 4/32 matters in Florida rain explains the numbers.

chunks.title: Back-to-School Car Check for Broward Families
chunks.text:
Step 3: Pressure, cold
Check pressure in the morning before driving, with a gauge, against the number on the driver's door placard, not the sidewall. FLHSMV's tire page says to check monthly with a gauge and always when the tires are cold. Include the spare; FLHSMV notes that even tires that aren't driven lose air.
Our guide to checking tire pressure walks through it.
Step 4: Age and condition
A first car often comes with tires nobody has thought about in years. Read the DOT date code on each sidewall; the last four digits are the week and year the tire was made. Our DOT date code guide shows where to look.
- FLHSMV says never to operate a vehicle on tires more than six years old.
- Michelin and Bridgestone recommend yearly inspections from five years and replacement at ten.
While you're there, look for bulges, cuts and cracks. FLHSMV suggests checking for damage weekly.

chunks.title: Back-to-School Car Check for Broward Families
chunks.text:
Step 5: Rotation and uneven wear
A school year adds a lot of miles: the morning run, practice, weekend games, the drive to a part-time job. FLHSMV's tire page says to rotate tires every 5,000 miles or as your vehicle's manufacturer requires, and USTMA recommends every 5,000 to 8,000 miles when the owner's manual gives no interval.
While you're measuring tread, compare the inside, center and outside grooves, and the front tires with the rear. Wear on one edge usually points to alignment; wear in the center or on both edges points to pressure. Either way, fixing the cause now saves the tires. Our rotation pattern tool shows the right pattern for your car.

chunks.title: Back-to-School Car Check for Broward Families
chunks.text:
Step 6: The rest of the walk-around
- Lights: headlights, brake lights and turn signals. Have someone stand behind the car.
- Wipers: streaking or chattering blades won't cope with an afternoon downpour.
- Brakes: squealing, grinding or a soft pedal means a visit to a shop.
- Dashboard: any warning light that stays on, including the TPMS light; our TPMS light guide explains it.
- The spare or kit: know where it is and how it works.

chunks.title: Back-to-School Car Check for Broward Families
chunks.text:
Teach the 10-minute check
The most useful thing you can hand a new driver isn't the car; it's the habit. Do this check together the first time, then have them do it once a month while you watch:
Check
Tool
Pass
Pressure, all four plus spare
Gauge, tires cold
Matches the door placard
Tread
Penny or tread gauge
4/32 or more in every groove
Sidewalls
Eyes
No bulges, cuts or deep cracks
DOT date
Eyes
Within the age guidance above
Lights
A helper
All working
Save *347 in their phone too. It reaches the Florida Highway Patrol, and our post on a flat tire on I-95 explains what to do while waiting.

chunks.title: Back-to-School Car Check for Broward Families
chunks.text:
If the check finds worn or old tires
Not sure? Do I Need Tires Yet? walks you through it. When it's time, shop by size or vehicle. In Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we install at our Sunrise shop, or our mobile van can come to your driveway. Shipping is free to the 48 contiguous states and DC.
Key takeaways
- Broward's 2026/27 school year began August 10, 2026. Winter break (December 21 to 31) and spring break (March 22 to 26, 2027) are good times to repeat the check.
- Run the car's VIN through NHTSA's recall lookup. Recall repairs are done by the dealer at no charge.
- Measure tread in three grooves. NHTSA says replace at 2/32 inch; AAA recommends 4/32 for wet roads.
- A hand-me-down car often has hand-me-down tires. Read the DOT date on every tire, and the spare.

chunks.title: Back-to-School Car Check for Broward Families
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- NHTSA reminds parents they have more influence on a teen driver than they may think. Teach the 10-minute check, then do it together monthly.
Questions people ask
What should I check on my car before school starts?
Start with open recalls, using the VIN on NHTSA's lookup. Then the tires: pressure set cold to the door placard, tread depth in three grooves, sidewalls for bulges, cuts or cracks, and the DOT date. Finish with lights, wipers and brakes. If a teen will drive the car, do the check with them so they learn it.
How do I check my car for recalls?
Find the 17-character VIN on the lower left of your windshield or on your registration, and enter it on NHTSA's recall lookup at nhtsa.gov/recalls. It tells you whether that specific vehicle has an open recall. NHTSA says you can contact your local dealership to have the recalled part fixed for free.

chunks.title: Back-to-School Car Check for Broward Families
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How much tread should my teen's tires have?
Tires are worn out at 2/32 inch, when the tread is level with the wear bars, and NHTSA says to replace them then. AAA recommends replacing at 4/32, because its testing found worn tires take much longer to stop on wet roads. With afternoon storms for half the year, 4/32 is the sensible line here.
How old can the tires on a used first car be?
Check the last four digits of the DOT code on each sidewall: the week and year the tire was made. FLHSMV's tire page says never to operate a vehicle on tires more than six years old. Michelin and Bridgestone recommend yearly inspections from five years and replacement at ten. Don't forget the spare.

chunks.title: Best Time to Buy Tires in South Florida, by Season
chunks.text:
Buying & Price
Best Time to Buy Tires in South Florida, by Season
The best time to buy tires in South Florida is before the season that tests them: rain, hurricanes and road trips. A tread and age calendar for the year.
The best time is before you need them
Search "best time to buy tires" and most answers are about store calendars. This isn't that kind of post. We're answering a different question: when should a South Florida driver replace tires so the new set is on the car before the conditions that test it?
Up north, the answer is tied to snow. Here, there's no winter-tire changeover. What Florida has instead is a long rainy season, a hurricane season that overlaps it, and a lot of highway miles. Time the tires to those.

chunks.title: Best Time to Buy Tires in South Florida, by Season
chunks.text:
Florida's tire calendar
Season
Dates
Why it matters for tires
Rainy season
May 15 to October 15 (NWS Miami)
Daily downpours test tread depth and wet grip
Hurricane season
June 1 to November 30
Evacuations, flooded streets, debris punctures
Holiday travel
Thanksgiving through New Year
Long trips on I-95 and the Turnpike
Dry season
Mid-October to mid-May
The calmest window to measure, shop and install
Notice the overlap. From June to October, rain and hurricane season run together. That makes spring the most useful time to take stock: measure in March or April, and if the tires won't last through the summer, replace them before mid-May.

chunks.title: Best Time to Buy Tires in South Florida, by Season
chunks.text:
Window 1: before the rainy season (March to early May)
Tread depth does its real work in the wet. In AAA's 2018 tests, tires worn to 4/32 of an inch took an average of 87 feet longer to stop on wet pavement than new ones. AAA recommends replacing at 4/32, before wet braking falls off that far.
A simple rule for spring:
- 6/32 or more: you're likely set for the summer.
- 5/32: borderline. Heavy summer driving could take you to 4/32 by August.
- 4/32 or less: replace before May 15.
Our post on why 4/32 matters more than 2/32 in Florida rain explains the numbers.

chunks.title: Best Time to Buy Tires in South Florida, by Season
chunks.text:
Window 2: before hurricane season (by June 1)
The Atlantic hurricane season officially runs June 1 to November 30. NOAA notes that the window covers the large majority of Atlantic storms, though storms can form outside it.
Why it matters for tires:
- Evacuations are long, loaded drives in rain and traffic. That's a bad time to find out a tire is past its prime.
- Shopping during a storm watch is harder. Everyone else is getting ready at the same time.
- After a storm, roads carry nails, roofing debris and standing water.
Our hurricane season tire check lists what to inspect, including the spare.

chunks.title: Best Time to Buy Tires in South Florida, by Season
chunks.text:
Window 3: before a road trip
Thanksgiving and year-end drives put hundreds of miles on tires in a weekend, often with a full car. Measure two or three weeks before you leave. That gives you time to order, ship and book an install without rushing. Our hurricane check covers the same pre-trip basics: pressure, tread, sidewalls and spare.
The window you can't pick: age
Some tires age out before they wear out, especially on cars that don't cover many miles. Bridgestone and Michelin both recommend a professional inspection every year once a tire is five years old, and replacement 10 years after the tire was made, even if the tread looks good. Your vehicle maker may set a shorter limit.
Florida's heat doesn't help. Our guide on Florida heat and tires explains why, and how old is too old shows how to read the DOT date code.

chunks.title: Best Time to Buy Tires in South Florida, by Season
chunks.text:
Two tires or four?
Timing often comes down to whether you need two tires now or four. If one axle is near 4/32 and the other still has plenty of tread, a matched pair can carry you to the next window. Tire makers recommend the new pair goes on the rear axle; our post on new tires on the front or back explains why. On all-wheel-drive vehicles, check your owner's manual first, because many call for all four to match.

chunks.title: Best Time to Buy Tires in South Florida, by Season
chunks.text:
Can you buy too early?
Yes, in one sense. A tire's clock starts at its DOT date, not the day it's mounted. Buying a set months ahead and leaving it in a hot garage uses up part of its life before it rolls. Buy when you're ready to install, and check the date code on the tires when they arrive.
Have these ready before you shop
Shopping goes faster, and ends with the right tire, when you know four things first:
- Your exact size, from the door placard on the driver's door pillar. Our Find My Tires tool can look it up by year, make and model.
- Your load index and speed rating, from the same placard. Replacements should match or exceed both.
- Your tread readings, lowest groove on each tire. They tell you whether you need two tires or four.
- How you drive: mostly highway, mostly city, lots of rain, regular towing or long trips. That narrows the tire type.

chunks.title: Best Time to Buy Tires in South Florida, by Season
chunks.text:
Have these ready before you shop
Leave yourself a few weeks. Ordering online means allowing time for shipping and an install appointment, and choosing calmly beats choosing on the side of the road. If you're installing in South Florida, you can ship the order free to our Sunrise shop or book our mobile van.
The worst time to buy
After a blowout, on a Sunday night, with a donut on the car. You take whatever fits and whatever's available, and you pay for the rush in choice.
The fix is a routine, not a calendar:
- Monthly: check pressure cold against the door placard.
- Every few months: measure tread in three grooves per tire.
- Each spring: decide whether the tires will last through October.
- Each year from five years old: have the tires inspected.

chunks.title: Best Time to Buy Tires in South Florida, by Season
chunks.text:
Your next step
Run your measurements through Do I Need Tires Yet?. If the answer is "soon," shop by size or vehicle and pick a date before your next season starts. Free shipping covers the 48 contiguous states and DC, and in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we install at our Sunrise shop or by mobile van.
Key takeaways
- Florida has no winter-tire cycle, so the right time is set by your tires' condition and the season ahead, not by a calendar month.
- The rainy season runs May 15 to October 15 (NWS Miami). Tires near 4/32 in spring should be replaced before it starts.
- Hurricane season runs June 1 to November 30. You don't want to be shopping for tires during an evacuation.
- Age counts too: Bridgestone and Michelin recommend a yearly inspection from five years old and replacement at 10.
- The worst time to buy is after a failure, when you take whatever fits today.

chunks.title: Best Time to Buy Tires in South Florida, by Season
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What is the best month to buy tires in Florida?
There isn't one month. Without a winter-tire changeover, the best time is before the season that will test your tires: before the rainy season starts on May 15, before hurricane season starts on June 1, or before a long road trip. Measure your tread and check the age a few weeks ahead so you can choose instead of rushing.
Should I replace my tires before hurricane season?
If they're near the end of their life, yes. Evacuation routes mean long drives in heavy rain, sometimes with a loaded car, and replacing tires during a storm watch is harder. If your tread is at or near 4/32, or your tires are approaching the age your vehicle or tire maker sets, replace them before June.
How do I know my tires need replacing soon?

chunks.title: Best Time to Buy Tires in South Florida, by Season
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Measure tread depth in three grooves per tire. AAA recommends replacing at 4/32 of an inch; NHTSA's line is 2/32. Check the DOT date code for age. Look for cracks, bulges or uneven wear. Any one of these can set the timing.
Can I buy tires too early?
Tires age from the day they're made, not the day they're mounted, so buying a set and storing it for a long time uses up some of its life. Buy when you're ready to install, and check the DOT date on the tires you receive.

chunks.title: Do Bigger Wheels Always Handle Better? Not Quite
chunks.text:
Myth-Busting
Do Bigger Wheels Always Handle Better? Not Quite
Plus size tires, pros and cons: bigger wheels sharpen steering, but makers list a harsher ride, more noise, longer braking and lower mileage or range.
The myth
Bigger wheels look great. Look at almost any performance car or upscale trim and the wheels get bigger as the price goes up, so it's natural to assume bigger wheels with thinner tires simply drive better.
They do drive differently. Whether that's better depends on what you want from the car, and on South Florida roads, the trade-offs are worth knowing before you spend money on a wheel upgrade.

chunks.title: Do Bigger Wheels Always Handle Better? Not Quite
chunks.text:
What "plus sizing" means
Plus sizing is moving to a larger wheel diameter while keeping the tire's overall height the same. To do that, the tire gets a lower aspect ratio, a shorter sidewall. For example, a car on 17-inch wheels going "plus one" moves to 18-inch wheels with a lower-profile tire, so the overall diameter barely changes.
That last part is the key rule. Bridgestone says replacement tires should always stay within 3 percent of the original diameter, so features like anti-lock brakes and stability control keep working as designed. See how a size change moves the speedometer here:
Compares a current and a new tire size by overall diameter, sidewall height and revolutions per mile, and shows what the speedometer reads at 30, 45, 60 and 70 mph. The common 3% diameter figure is a guideline, not a fitment approval, so have fitment confirmed before you order.

chunks.title: Do Bigger Wheels Always Handle Better? Not Quite
chunks.text:
What "plus sizing" means
Our guide to changing tire size covers diameter, load and speed rating in detail.
The part that's true: sharper steering
A shorter sidewall flexes less. Michelin describes it plainly: a taller sidewall absorbs road impacts more but flexes more in corners, while a lower-profile tire feels sharper in steering response but can be harsher over rough surfaces.
So if you want the car to react more crisply when you turn the wheel, plus sizing can deliver that. That's the kernel of truth in the myth.

chunks.title: Do Bigger Wheels Always Handle Better? Not Quite
chunks.text:
The trade-offs the myth leaves out
Bridgestone's own tire-size pages say that when the change is to larger diameter wheels, there may be trade-offs in the form of:
- Increased ride harshness
- Longer braking distances
- Reduced fuel mileage
Goodyear's advice on low-profile tires adds that steering feel, noise levels and driving comfort may all change. Here's how it adds up:
Trait
Original size
Plus size (bigger wheel, lower profile)
Steering response
Softer
Sharper
Ride over rough roads
More cushioned
Harsher
Noise
Usually lower
May increase
Braking distance
Baseline
May be longer, per Bridgestone
Fuel economy or EV range
Baseline
May drop
Cost to replace
Baseline
Often higher

chunks.title: Do Bigger Wheels Always Handle Better? Not Quite
chunks.text:
The EV example: same car, less range
Electric vehicles show the efficiency cost clearly, because the EPA rates range for each wheel option. On fueleconomy.gov, the 2026 Tesla Model Y Standard RWD is rated:
- 18-inch wheels: 138 MPGe, 321 miles of range
- 19-inch wheels: 131 MPGe, 303 miles of range
Same car, same battery, 18 fewer miles of rated range from a one-inch step up in wheel size. Gas cars feel the same physics as reduced fuel mileage, just without a range number on the dash.

chunks.title: Do Bigger Wheels Always Handle Better? Not Quite
chunks.text:
Florida roads: potholes, curbs and less cushion
Less sidewall means less rubber between a pothole edge and your wheel. AAA's 2022 pothole survey found 1 in 10 drivers had pothole damage bad enough to need a repair the year before, adding up to 26.5 billion dollars in repairs nationwide in 2021.
Between construction zones, parking-garage curbs and flooded streets hiding holes, South Florida gives low-profile tires plenty to hit. If you go bigger, keep pressure at the placard and slow down for broken pavement. Our post on hitting a curb or pothole covers the signs of damage afterward.

chunks.title: Do Bigger Wheels Always Handle Better? Not Quite
chunks.text:
If you still want bigger wheels, do it right
Plenty of drivers decide the look and the steering feel are worth it. That's a fair choice. Just make it carefully:
- Keep the overall diameter within 3 percent of the original, as Bridgestone advises. Our plus-size calculator checks it for you.
- Never go below the original load rating. Michelin notes that plus-sized tires aren't always interchangeable because of differences in load ratings, dimensions, clearance and rim size. Our guide to load index shows how to read it.
- Match the speed rating on your door placard or better.
- Get the wheel specs right: bolt pattern, offset and center bore. Our guide to wheel offset and backspacing explains why it matters.
- Mind staggered setups. Different sizes front and rear limit rotation; see our staggered tires guide.
- Check clearance at full steering lock and with the suspension compressed.

chunks.title: Do Bigger Wheels Always Handle Better? Not Quite
chunks.text:
What else changes when you swap wheels
New wheels bring a few jobs people forget to budget time for:
- TPMS sensors. Nearly all the TPMS-equipped cars in NHTSA's field study used direct systems, with a sensor inside each wheel, usually on the valve stem. New wheels need those sensors moved over or new ones fitted, then the system relearned. Our TPMS service handles both.
- Lug nuts and torque. Aftermarket wheels may need different lug nuts or hub rings, and every wheel should be torqued to the vehicle maker's spec.
- Balance. Every new wheel and tire pairing gets balanced. A vibration at highway speed after an upgrade usually points here first.
- The spare. Your spare won't match the new size. Check that it still clears the brakes and know its limits; our spare tire types guide explains them.

chunks.title: Do Bigger Wheels Always Handle Better? Not Quite
chunks.text:
Try before you buy
If you're on the fence, ride in a friend's car with the larger wheel option, or ask the dealer to let you drive the same model on both sizes. Pay attention on the roughest street you drive every day, not the smoothest highway. Then check the range or fuel economy ratings for each wheel size, if your model lists them, and decide whether the look and the steering feel are worth the difference.

chunks.title: Do Bigger Wheels Always Handle Better? Not Quite
chunks.text:
The verdict
Bigger wheels don't always handle better. They steer sharper, and they usually ride harder, often cost more to replace and give up some mileage or range. For a daily driver on South Florida pavement, the original size is often the better all-round choice. If you want the upgrade anyway, keep the diameter and load rating right.
Browse wheels or shop tires by size or vehicle. In Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we mount and install at our Sunrise shop or with our mobile van, including wheel installation. Shipping is free to the 48 contiguous states and DC.

chunks.title: Do Bigger Wheels Always Handle Better? Not Quite
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Bigger wheels with lower-profile tires do sharpen steering response, as Michelin describes.
- Bridgestone lists the trade-offs: increased ride harshness, longer braking distances and reduced fuel mileage.
- On a 2026 Model Y Standard, EPA range is 321 miles on 18-inch wheels and 303 on 19s, per fueleconomy.gov.
- Keep the overall diameter within 3 percent of the original, Bridgestone says, and never drop below the original load rating.
- In pothole country, less sidewall means less cushion between the road and your wheel.

chunks.title: Do Bigger Wheels Always Handle Better? Not Quite
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Do bigger wheels improve handling?
They can sharpen how the car responds to the steering wheel, because a lower-profile tire has a shorter sidewall that flexes less. Michelin describes a lower-profile tire as feeling sharper in steering response. But handling isn't only steering feel; grip, braking and how the tire copes with rough or wet roads all count too.
What are the downsides of plus sizing tires?
Bridgestone lists increased ride harshness, longer braking distances and reduced fuel mileage when the change is to larger diameter wheels. Goodyear adds that steering feel, noise and comfort may change with low-profile tires. Bigger wheels and tires often cost more to replace, too.
Will bigger wheels mess up my speedometer?

chunks.title: Do Bigger Wheels Always Handle Better? Not Quite
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Only if the tire's overall diameter changes. Michelin says altering the overall diameter affects speedometer accuracy, wheel-well clearance and potentially how ABS and stability control behave. Bridgestone says replacement tires should stay within 3 percent of the original diameter. A correct plus-size keeps the same overall height.
Do bigger wheels reduce EV range?
They can. On fueleconomy.gov, the 2026 Tesla Model Y Standard RWD is rated at 321 miles of range on 18-inch wheels and 303 miles on 19-inch wheels, 131 MPGe vs 138. Same car, same battery; the wheel and tire package makes the difference.

chunks.title: Where to Get Tires Installed After Buying Online: Broward
chunks.text:
Local Buying & Service
Where to Get Tires Installed After Buying Online: Broward
Where to get tires installed after buying online in Broward: free ship-to-store in Sunrise, a mobile van at home, and what to check when tires arrive.
By TireDrop Team, Extreme Tires, Sunrise FL·Published Sep 30, 2026·Updated Oct 1, 2026·5 min read
Four tires, one question
Ordering tires online is the easy part. Then comes the question every online buyer hits: who's going to put them on?
If you're in South Florida, TireDrop was built around that question. TireDrop is the online store of Extreme Tires, a tire and service shop at 7712 West Oakland Park Blvd in Sunrise. So the answer can be "the same people who sold them to you." The full details live on our installation page. This post is the practical version: which route fits you, and what to check before a single lug nut comes off.

chunks.title: Where to Get Tires Installed After Buying Online: Broward
chunks.text:
Route 1: Ship them to the shop in Sunrise
Choose ship-to-store at checkout and the order goes to Extreme Tires instead of your house.
How it works:
- It's free. Ship-to-store adds nothing to your total for shipping. You pay for the tires, and separately for installation when you come in.
- The shop calls you when the order is checked in and on the rack.
- You can book the fitting before the tires arrive. The shop matches the booking to the delivery and calls you to move it if the shipment runs late.
- Your old tires stay at the shop and get recycled.
What installation covers: dismounting and disposing of the old set, mounting and balancing the new one, new valve stems, torque to spec, and a TPMS reset where the vehicle has it. The shop confirms your total before any work starts.

chunks.title: Where to Get Tires Installed After Buying Online: Broward
chunks.text:
Route 1: Ship them to the shop in Sunrise
This route suits you if you'd rather not store four tires in a condo, or if the car needs anything else done while it's in the bay. Alignment, brakes and suspension work happen at the shop, not in a driveway.
Route 2: Have the van fit them where you park
Extreme Tires also runs mobile installation vans across Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties; the ZIP code where the car is parked decides it.
You can send the order free to the Sunrise shop and have the van bring it to you, or ship to your house and have the van fit them there. What the van needs:
- one standard parking space next to your car, with about ten feet of clearance on the work side
- a driveway, a flat stretch of street, an office lot or a jobsite area
- at a condo or apartment complex, the complex name and any gate code or call-up instructions when you book

chunks.title: Where to Get Tires Installed After Buying Online: Broward
chunks.text:
Route 2: Have the van fit them where you park
Mobile work covers installation, balancing, puncture repair, rotation and TPMS service. See the mobile service page for how booking works, and our post on mobile installation at a condo or office for gate codes and garage rules.
Route 3: Ship home and take them to a fitter
Outside the South Florida install area, this is the route. TireDrop ships free to addresses in the 48 contiguous states and DC, but installation is a South Florida service. Anywhere else, your order ships to you and you take it to an installer you trust.
Before you order, call that installer and ask two things: whether they fit tires the customer brings in, and what they charge to do it. Better to find out before four tires are sitting in your hallway. Our nationwide guide to getting online tires installed covers the full list of questions.

chunks.title: Where to Get Tires Installed After Buying Online: Broward
chunks.text:
Questions to ask any installer
Whether it's our shop or one near you in another state, the same short list saves surprises:
- Do you fit tires the customer brings in? Some shops do; some don't. Ask before you order.
- What's included in the price? Mounting, balancing, valve stems, TPMS work and disposal of the old tires are sometimes separate line items.
- How is TPMS handled? If your car has pressure sensors, ask whether a reset or relearn is part of the job.
- Are wheels torqued to the vehicle maker's spec? A torque wrench, not just an impact gun.
- Is tire registration handled? If not, plan to do it yourself (more on that below).
- How do you want to be told the tires have arrived? If you're shipping to the installer, agree on who calls whom.

chunks.title: Where to Get Tires Installed After Buying Online: Broward
chunks.text:
Questions to ask any installer
We don't quote arrival dates for shipments. For ship-to-store orders, the Sunrise shop calls you when the tires are checked in, so book the fitting and let the shop line it up.
Before anything gets mounted: the arrival check
Whichever route you choose, check the tires against your car before they go on. Five minutes now beats a second appointment later.
- Size. Match it to the Tire and Loading Information placard on your driver's door edge or door post, not just to the old tires.
- Load index and speed rating. USTMA's guidance is that replacement tires match the size, load-carrying capacity and speed rating on the vehicle placard, with a load index equal to or above what the placard requires.
- Same model on every position. Especially if you ordered in two batches.
- Shipping damage. Look along the beads and sidewalls for cuts or crushed spots.

chunks.title: Where to Get Tires Installed After Buying Online: Broward
chunks.text:
Before anything gets mounted: the arrival check
- Date codes. Find the four digits at the end of the DOT number on each tire. Per Goodyear, the first two are the week and the last two are the year, so 3224 would be week 32 of 2024.
Enter a date code here to see exactly how old a tire is:
Can't find the date? The full DOT number may be on only one sidewall. Our guide to reading the tire date code shows where to look.
If something doesn't match, raise it before mounting. Call (954) 773-1896 and ask.

chunks.title: Where to Get Tires Installed After Buying Online: Broward
chunks.text:
After the install: two small jobs
Keep the DOT numbers. Photograph the full DOT number on each tire, or ask the installer whether they can be noted on your invoice. That's what a recall lookup needs.
Register the tires. Federal rules under 49 CFR Part 574 set up a tire registration program so manufacturers can notify buyers if a tire is recalled. Ask your installer whether registration is handled for you. If not, register each tire with the manufacturer. You can also search tire recalls by brand and line on NHTSA's recall site at any time. Our recalls and registration guide walks through it.
Ready to order? Shop by size or vehicle, choose ship-to-store at checkout, and book the fitting that suits you on the install page.

chunks.title: Where to Get Tires Installed After Buying Online: Broward
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- In South Florida you have three routes: ship to the Sunrise shop, have a mobile van fit them where you park, or ship home and take them to a fitter.
- Ship-to-store is free, and the shop calls when your order is checked in.
- Before anything gets mounted, check size, load index and speed rating against your door placard, and read the DOT date codes.
- Keep one full DOT number per tire and register the tires with the manufacturer so recall notices reach you.
- Shipping is free to the 48 contiguous states and DC. Installation is South Florida only.

chunks.title: Where to Get Tires Installed After Buying Online: Broward
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Where can I get tires installed after buying them online?
In South Florida, TireDrop orders can ship free to Extreme Tires in Sunrise, where installation is charged per tire, or a mobile van can fit them at your home or office inside the local install area. Outside that area, your order ships to your address and you take the tires to an installer you trust.
Will a shop install tires I bought online somewhere else?
Extreme Tires fits customer-supplied tires the same way it fits its own. Book a tire installation and bring them in, or mention it when you book so the shop knows what to expect. For other shops, call and ask before you order.
What should I check when my tires arrive?

chunks.title: Where to Get Tires Installed After Buying Online: Broward
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Confirm the size, load index and speed rating match your vehicle placard, check that every tire is the same model, look for shipping damage and read the four-digit DOT date code on each tire. Do this before any tire is mounted.
Do I need to register tires I bought online?
Registration is how manufacturers reach you with a recall. Federal rules set up a tire registration program for exactly that reason. Ask your installer whether registration is handled; if not, register each tire with the manufacturer using its DOT number.

chunks.title: Buying Tires Online vs a Local Shop: Honest Trade-offs
chunks.text:
Buying & Price
Buying Tires Online vs a Local Shop: Honest Trade-offs
Buy tires online vs a local shop: where each is strong, how to compare the full installed cost, and the size, fitting and registration steps either way.
By TireDrop Team, Extreme Tires, Sunrise FL·Published Sep 30, 2026·Updated Sep 30, 2026·5 min read
Two good options, different strengths
We sell tires online and we fit them in a shop, so we see this question from both sides. The honest answer is that neither is always better. Each one is strong at different things, and the right choice depends on what you care about and where you live.
Here are the trade-offs, how to compare cost without being fooled by a tire-only price, and the steps that matter no matter where you buy.

chunks.title: Buying Tires Online vs a Local Shop: Honest Trade-offs
chunks.text:
Where buying online is strong
Choice. An online store isn't limited to what fits on one shop's racks. TireDrop, for example, ships from distributor warehouses, so the catalog isn't capped by what's in one building.
Comparing at your own pace. You can line up two or three tires and read the specs side by side: size, load index, speed rating and the UTQG grades for treadwear, traction and temperature. NHTSA's consumer guide explains that the UTQG grades are assigned by the tire makers themselves, so treat them as one input, not the verdict. TireDrop's compare tool shows each tire's full spec sheet.
Shipping to where it suits you. Home, work or an installer. TireDrop ships free to addresses in the 48 contiguous states and DC.
No pressure at the counter. You can research on a Sunday night and order when you're ready.

chunks.title: Buying Tires Online vs a Local Shop: Honest Trade-offs
chunks.text:
Where a local shop is strong
It sees your car. A technician can look at the old tires, spot the wear pattern, and tell you if it points to alignment or suspension. That's hard to do from a product page.
One visit. If the shop has your size on hand, buying and fitting can happen in the same stop. If not, it orders them and you come back.
One place to call. If something's wrong after the install, the shop that sold and fitted the tires is the single point of contact.
Local knowledge. A shop in your area knows the roads, the rain and the potholes on your commute.

chunks.title: Buying Tires Online vs a Local Shop: Honest Trade-offs
chunks.text:
The hybrid most people end up using
A lot of drivers now split the job: buy online, install locally. It works well if you plan the installation before you order.
In South Florida, that's how TireDrop is built. It's the online store of Extreme Tires in Sunrise, so you can:
- choose free ship-to-store at checkout and have the tires fitted at the Sunrise shop (installation is charged per tire), or
- have a mobile van fit them at your home or office inside the local install area.
Outside South Florida, the order ships to you and you take the tires to an installer you trust. Call that installer first and ask two things: whether they fit tires the customer brings in, and what they charge to do it. Our post on getting tires installed after buying online walks through each South Florida route, and our nationwide installation guide covers finding an installer anywhere else.

chunks.title: Buying Tires Online vs a Local Shop: Honest Trade-offs
chunks.text:
Get the size right before anything else
Online or local, the tires have to fit your car. USTMA's guidance is that replacement tires match the size, load index and speed rating on your vehicle placard, with a load index equal to or above what the placard requires. The placard is on the driver's door edge or door post.
Type the size from your placard or your current tires to see what each part means:
Our guide to reading tire size covers each segment in detail.

chunks.title: Buying Tires Online vs a Local Shop: Honest Trade-offs
chunks.text:
Compare the installed total, not the tire price
A tire-only price can make two options look further apart, or closer, than they are. Put both on the same footing by listing everything it takes to get the tires on the car:

About that last line: Florida law puts a $1 fee on each new tire sold at retail in the state, and it must be stated separately on the invoice (Fla. Stat. § 403.718). Seeing it as its own line is normal.

chunks.title: Buying Tires Online vs a Local Shop: Honest Trade-offs
chunks.text:
Compare the installed total, not the tire price
Ask each side for the full, installed number before you choose.
Timing
A shop that has your size in stock can often fit it on the spot. An online order needs shipping time, and the installation has to be arranged around delivery.
We don't print delivery promises. TireDrop's checkout shows a delivery estimate for your specific order once your address is in, because transit depends on which warehouse has your size. For ship-to-store orders, the Sunrise shop calls you when your tires are checked in, and you can book the fitting ahead of time.
If you need tires today because one just failed, that points to a local shop or a mobile service with your size on hand. If you're planning ahead, either route works.

chunks.title: Buying Tires Online vs a Local Shop: Honest Trade-offs
chunks.text:
After you buy, wherever you bought
Two small jobs protect you later, and they apply to both routes.
Keep the DOT numbers. Photograph the full DOT number on each tire, or ask for them on your invoice.
Make sure the tires are registered. Federal rules under 49 CFR 574.8 require independent tire sellers to give each buyer a registration form with the tire identification numbers already recorded, and tire makers that offer it also accept registration online. That's how a recall notice finds you. You can also search tire recalls on NHTSA's recall site at any time.

Ready to look? Shop by size or vehicle, compare a few options, and plan the fitting before you check out.

chunks.title: Buying Tires Online vs a Local Shop: Honest Trade-offs
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Online is strong on choice and on comparing specs at your own pace. A local shop is strong on seeing the car and handling it in one visit.
- Either way, the tires have to match your door placard's size, load index and speed rating.
- Compare the installed total, not the tire price: mounting, balancing, valve stems, TPMS work, disposal and Florida's $1-per-tire fee.
- Online orders need shipping time and a plan for who installs them. Settle that before you order.
- Keep the full DOT numbers and make sure the tires are registered, so recall notices can reach you.

chunks.title: Buying Tires Online vs a Local Shop: Honest Trade-offs
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Is it better to buy tires online or from a local shop?
It depends on what you value. Buying online gives you a wide choice and time to compare specs, but you need a plan for installation. A local shop can look at the car, check the wheels and alignment, and handle everything in one place. Many people now do both: order online and have a local installer fit them.
Can I buy tires online and have them installed locally?
Yes. Some shops fit tires customers bring in; call first and ask what they charge. In South Florida, TireDrop orders can ship free to Extreme Tires in Sunrise, where installation is charged per tire, or a mobile van can fit them where you park inside the local install area.
What should an installed tire price include?

chunks.title: Buying Tires Online vs a Local Shop: Honest Trade-offs
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Ask what's in it. Mounting, balancing, valve stems, TPMS reset or relearn, and disposal of the old tires are sometimes separate line items. In Florida, a $1 fee applies to each new tire sold at retail and must be listed separately on the invoice.
Do I need to register tires I bought online?
Registration is how manufacturers reach you if a tire is recalled. Federal rules require independent tire sellers to give buyers a registration form with the tire identification numbers filled in, and tire makers that offer it also take registration online. Ask whoever sells or installs your tires how it's handled.

chunks.title: Choosing Between Tire Brands Without the Hype
chunks.text:
Buying & Price
Choosing Between Tire Brands Without the Hype
Which tire brand is best? It depends on the tire, not the logo. How to compare brands using UTQG grades, independent tests, warranties and your placard.
The honest answer: it's the tire, not the logo
"Which tire brand is best?" is one of the most common questions in tire shopping. The honest answer is that it's the wrong unit of comparison.
Every major tire maker sells a range of lines: touring tires for quiet commutes, all-terrain tires for trucks, performance tires for grip, and value lines built to a price. Two tires with the same logo can be further apart than two tires from different makers built for the same job.
So instead of ranking brands (we don't), here's how to compare tires, using tools that work across any brand.

chunks.title: Choosing Between Tire Brands Without the Hype
chunks.text:
Step 1: The placard comes before the brand
Before brand matters at all, a tire has to fit. USTMA's guidance is to match the size, load-carrying capacity and speed rating your vehicle maker specifies on the door placard or in the owner's manual.
- Size must match your placard, or an approved alternative in your manual.
- Load index must be at or above the original. Never go below it.
- Speed rating should be at or above the original.
That filter alone removes a lot of choices, and it's the same for every brand. Our load and speed checker compares any tire against your placard.

chunks.title: Choosing Between Tire Brands Without the Hype
chunks.text:
Step 2: Pick the type for how you drive
Bridgestone's tire-type guide starts with your driving: mostly city and highway, performance, light off-road, or snow. In South Florida, snow drops off the list, which simplifies things.
Type
Built for
Trade-off
All-season (touring or standard)
Dry and wet roads, comfort, tread life
Less ultimate grip than performance tires
Summer or performance
Grip and handling in warm weather
Often noisier, firmer and faster-wearing
All-terrain
Pavement plus dirt and sand
More noise, often more weight
Highway (truck and SUV)
Long pavement miles, comfort
Less off-road traction
Choose the type first, then compare brands within it.

chunks.title: Choosing Between Tire Brands Without the Hype
chunks.text:
Step 3: Use UTQG grades, and know their limits
Most passenger tires carry three Uniform Tire Quality Grading marks, required by NHTSA:
- Treadwear is a number measured against a control tire graded 100. NHTSA's consumer guide notes the grades are assigned by the manufacturer based on its testing, so they're most useful for comparing tires within one brand, not across brands.
- Traction (AA, A, B or C) reflects straight-line braking on wet pavement. It doesn't measure cornering or hydroplaning.
- Temperature (A, B or C) reflects resistance to heat buildup at speed.
For a Florida driver, a higher traction grade is a useful signal for wet braking. Our UTQG guide explains each grade in more detail.

chunks.title: Choosing Between Tire Brands Without the Hype
chunks.text:
Step 4: Look at independent test results
UTQG is self-reported. Independent testing fills the gap. Consumer Reports, for example, buys tires and tests them for dry and wet braking, handling, hydroplaning resistance, noise, ride comfort, rolling resistance and tread life, using the same procedures for every brand.
When you read any test results, look at the categories that match your driving. A tire that wins in snow doesn't help much on I-95 in July. Wet braking and hydroplaning resistance matter most here.

chunks.title: Choosing Between Tire Brands Without the Hype
chunks.text:
Step 5: Read the warranty, not just the number
Many tires carry a treadwear warranty: the maker's mileage promise, with conditions. Those conditions usually include regular rotation, correct pressure and records to prove it. Tire makers publish their own terms; Goodyear's tread life warranty page is a typical example of how they're structured.
A mileage warranty is easier to compare across brands than a UTQG treadwear grade. Just compare like with like: the same tire type, the same size range, and the conditions behind the number.

chunks.title: Choosing Between Tire Brands Without the Hype
chunks.text:
What about premium vs budget?
Same-size tires can vary widely in what they cost. Our post on why same-size tires cost different amounts breaks it down: compound, construction, load rating, testing and warranty all play a part.
A practical way to decide:
- High mileage or lots of rain driving? Wet braking, hydroplaning resistance and tread life tend to matter most.
- Low mileage? Age may end the tire's life before tread does, so a long tread warranty matters less. See how long tires last.
- Any car: the placard specification is non-negotiable, whatever the price.

chunks.title: Choosing Between Tire Brands Without the Hype
chunks.text:
Marketing claims to read carefully
Tire marketing is full of words that sound like measurements. A few to slow down on:
- "Best" or "number one" with no test named. Ask: best at what, measured by whom?
- A mileage number without the conditions. Most treadwear warranties require rotation and records. Read the terms.
- Comparisons across brands using treadwear grades. NHTSA's guide notes the grade is assigned by each manufacturer, so it doesn't line up neatly between brands.
- Snow and ice results. Useful up north; much less relevant on I-95 in July.
- "Fits your vehicle" without the load index. A tire that matches the size but not the load rating isn't a match.
Plain criteria beat adjectives: the placard specification, the tire type, wet braking results, the warranty terms and the recall record.

chunks.title: Choosing Between Tire Brands Without the Hype
chunks.text:
Two checks that apply to every brand
- Recalls. NHTSA's recall site lists tire recalls by brand and line. After you buy, register your tires so the maker can reach you. Our guide to tire recalls and registration shows how.
- Matching. Tire makers recommend a matched set, and many AWD vehicles require the same brand and tread pattern on all four. Our myth check on replacing all four tires explains why.

chunks.title: Choosing Between Tire Brands Without the Hype
chunks.text:
Your next step
Find your size with Find My Tires, then shop by size and filter by type. When you've narrowed it to two or three, put them side by side in Compare and check the UTQG grades, load and speed ratings, and warranty.
Key takeaways
- Compare tire models, not brands. One maker's lineup can range from budget all-seasons to high-performance tires.
- Start with the placard: size, load index and speed rating must match before brand matters at all.
- UTQG grades help, with limits. NHTSA's treadwear grade is relative and assigned by the maker, so it's most useful within one brand.
- Independent testers such as Consumer Reports run wet braking, hydroplaning, noise and tread-life tests across brands.
- In South Florida, put wet braking and hydroplaning resistance near the top of your list.

chunks.title: Choosing Between Tire Brands Without the Hype
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Which tire brand is the best?
There isn't one answer, and we don't rank brands. Every major maker sells several lines, from budget to premium, built for different jobs. A better question is which tire model fits your size, load and speed rating, your driving and your climate. Compare models using UTQG grades, independent test results, the treadwear warranty and the tire type.
Are budget tires worth it?
They can be, if they match your placard's size, load index and speed rating and suit how you drive. Price differences often come from compound, construction, tread design, testing and warranty. If you drive a lot in the rain, compare wet braking and hydroplaning results before choosing on price alone.
Can I compare treadwear grades between brands?

chunks.title: Choosing Between Tire Brands Without the Hype
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Only loosely. NHTSA's UTQG treadwear grade is measured against a control tire, and each manufacturer assigns grades from its own testing, so comparisons are most reliable within one brand. The treadwear warranty in miles is often easier to compare, as long as you read its conditions.
Can I mix tire brands on my car?
It's best not to. Tire makers recommend a matched set, and many all-wheel-drive vehicles call for the same brand and tread pattern on all four. If you must replace only two, match the size, load index and speed rating, and follow your vehicle maker's guidance.

chunks.title: Why Your TPMS Light Comes On After a Florida Cold Front
chunks.text:
Rain, Heat & Weather
Why Your TPMS Light Comes On After a Florida Cold Front
TPMS light on after a South Florida cold front? A cool night drops tire pressure, but rarely 25% on its own. Here's the math and what to do that morning.
The 7 a.m. surprise
It's the first properly cool morning of the season. You grab a jacket you haven't worn since last winter, start the car, and there it is: the amber horseshoe with an exclamation point. The tire pressure light. By lunch it's gone. What happened?

chunks.title: Why Your TPMS Light Comes On After a Florida Cold Front
chunks.text:
The 7 a.m. surprise
South Florida's wet season ends in mid-October; the National Weather Service in Miami defines it as May 15 to October 15. After that come the dry months and the cold fronts that sweep down the peninsula. NWS notes that inland areas are the most likely to see freezing temperatures, mainly in the middle of January. NWS also notes that overnight temperatures rarely drop below freezing in South Florida, especially along the coasts. But a front doesn't need to bring a freeze to matter. In the 2024–25 winter, January was the coolest in 15 years, and Fort Lauderdale/Hollywood's lowest reading was 46°F, NWS Miami's winter summary says. After a summer of 90-degree afternoons, that's the coolest air your tires have felt in months.

chunks.title: Why Your TPMS Light Comes On After a Florida Cold Front
chunks.text:
What the cold does to the air in your tires
The air in a tire is a fixed amount of gas. Cool it and its pressure drops; warm it and the pressure rises. NHTSA's winter guidance says it simply: as the outside temperature drops, so does tire inflation pressure.
USTMA gives the size of the effect: inflation pressure goes up in warm weather and down in cold weather by one to two psi for every 10 degrees of temperature change. Try it with your own numbers:

chunks.title: Why Your TPMS Light Comes On After a Florida Cold Front
chunks.text:
The math: why the front usually isn't the whole story
Here's where it gets interesting. The federal standard for tire pressure monitoring, FMVSS No. 138, requires the warning when a tire is 25 percent or more below the vehicle maker's recommended cold pressure. Automakers can warn earlier, but that's the required line.
Take a car with a 35 psi door placard. Twenty-five percent below that is about 26 psi. Now an example, using USTMA's rule of thumb (the temperatures are illustrative, not a forecast):
Scenario
Starting pressure
Overnight drop of 30°F
Morning pressure

Set correctly to the placard

chunks.title: Why Your TPMS Light Comes On After a Florida Cold Front
chunks.text:
The math: why the front usually isn't the whole story
A correctly filled tire usually stays above the line even after a big temperature drop. The tires that trip the light are the ones that were already low. Maybe they were set on a hot afternoon, or they've been slowly losing air for weeks, which all tires do. The front didn't cause the problem. It revealed it.
NHTSA's own tire page says much the same: on cold mornings the TPMS light may come on briefly and then turn off, likely because of marginally low pressure that dips below the warning threshold overnight and rises again as the tires warm up.
That's the useful part: the cold-morning light is an early, free inspection. Take it seriously.

chunks.title: Why Your TPMS Light Comes On After a Florida Cold Front
chunks.text:
Why it goes off by lunchtime
As you drive, the tires flex and warm up, and the sun heats the pavement and the car. The pressure climbs back a few psi and crosses back over the warning line, so the light goes out.
The tire is no fuller than it was at 7 a.m. Tonight it will cool, and tomorrow morning the light will probably be back. Our TPMS light guide explains this and what a flashing light means.

chunks.title: Why Your TPMS Light Comes On After a Florida Cold Front
chunks.text:
What to do that morning
- Check all four with a gauge while they're cold. That's the morning, before you've driven more than a short distance. USTMA defines cold as parked for at least three hours.
- Fill to the door placard number, not the maximum on the sidewall. The placard is on the driver's door pillar.
- Check the spare too. It loses pressure just like the others.
- Note which tire was lowest. If the same one is low again in a week or two, look for a nail, a damaged valve or a leaking bead. A slow leak won't fix itself when it warms up.
- Don't let air out on a warm afternoon. The placard pressure is a cold pressure. A higher reading after driving is normal.
If you fill at a gas station after a drive, the tires are already warm. Add a little above what you'd normally set, then recheck cold the next morning. Our guide to tire pressure and temperature walks through it.

chunks.title: Why Your TPMS Light Comes On After a Florida Cold Front
chunks.text:
When it isn't the weather
Some signs point to something other than a cool morning:
- The light flashes for a minute or so at startup, then stays on. That's a system fault, often a sensor battery or a damaged sensor, not low pressure.
- One tire is far lower than the others, or drops again within days.
- The light stays on after you've filled all four to the placard and driven a few miles.
Our TPMS service diagnoses and replaces sensors, and a puncture can often be repaired; see Can My Tire Be Repaired?

chunks.title: Why Your TPMS Light Comes On After a Florida Cold Front
chunks.text:
Why a gauge beats waiting for the light
The cold-front light is a reminder that TPMS is built to catch a big pressure loss, not to keep your pressure right. A tire can run well below the placard all summer with the dash dark. Our post on whether you still need a tire gauge with TPMS covers what NHTSA found.
If the tires themselves are the problem
Tires that keep losing air may be worn, damaged or old. Shop by size or vehicle when it's time. In Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we install at our Sunrise shop or come to you with our mobile van. Shipping is free to the 48 contiguous states and DC.

chunks.title: Why Your TPMS Light Comes On After a Florida Cold Front
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- USTMA's rule of thumb: tire pressure drops 1 to 2 psi for every 10°F the temperature falls.
- The TPMS light must come on when a tire is 25 percent below the placard pressure. A cool front alone rarely takes a correctly filled tire that far.
- If the light comes on after a front, the tire was probably already low. The front just pushed it over the line.
- The light going off by lunchtime means the tire warmed up, not that it got its air back.
- Fix it that morning: check all four with a gauge while cold and fill to the door placard.

chunks.title: Why Your TPMS Light Comes On After a Florida Cold Front
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Why does my tire pressure light come on when it's cold?
Air in a tire loses pressure as it cools. USTMA puts it at about 1 to 2 psi for every 10°F drop. If a tire was already a bit under the placard pressure, a cool night can drop it past the point where the TPMS has to warn you, which the federal standard sets at 25 percent below the recommended cold pressure.
Why does the TPMS light go off after I drive for a while?
Driving and the afternoon sun warm the tires, and warm air reads higher, so a tire just under the warning line can climb back above it. The tire is still low when it cools again. Check it cold with a gauge and set it to the door placard number.
Should I add air when the TPMS light comes on in cold weather?

chunks.title: Why Your TPMS Light Comes On After a Florida Cold Front
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Yes, after checking with a gauge. Check all four tires while they're cold, before driving far, and fill them to the pressure on the driver's door placard. Then keep an eye on whether one tire drops again faster than the others, which points to a leak rather than the weather.
Do I need to let air out when it warms up again?
No. The placard pressure is a cold pressure. As long as you set it with cold tires, the higher reading on a warm afternoon is normal and expected. Never let air out of hot tires to bring the number down.

chunks.title: Hit a Curb or Pothole? Tire and Alignment Signs
chunks.text:
Local Buying & Service
Hit a Curb or Pothole? Tire and Alignment Signs
Hit a pothole or curb? The tire, wheel and alignment signs to check afterward, what can't be repaired, and when to stop driving on the tire.
That bang you felt
It happens in a second: a pothole in a lane closure on State Road 7, a curb in a tight parking garage turn, a lip at a construction zone you didn't see in the rain. The car keeps going and the noise fades, so most drivers forget about it.
The damage doesn't always show at once. Here's what to check right after, over the next few days, and what to do about each sign.

chunks.title: Hit a Curb or Pothole? Tire and Alignment Signs
chunks.text:
Why one hit matters
AAA puts it plainly: when a vehicle hits a pothole with any force, the tires, wheels and suspension take the brunt of the impact. In an AAA survey, one in 10 drivers said they'd had vehicle damage from a pothole that was bad enough to need a repair in the previous year.
A curb strike works the same way, just from the side. The tire is squeezed between the rim and a hard edge, and the sidewall is the thinnest, least protected part of the tire.

chunks.title: Hit a Curb or Pothole? Tire and Alignment Signs
chunks.text:
Right after: a two-minute look
When you can stop somewhere sensible, look at the tire that hit:
- The sidewall, both sides if you can. You're looking for a bulge or bubble, a cut, or a scuff that went deep.
- The rim edge. A bend or a crack in the lip of the wheel can leak air slowly.
- The tread. Check for a cut or anything stuck in it.
- The pressure. If you have a gauge, compare it with the other tires and the door placard.
A bulge is the sign to act on at once. Michelin says a sidewall bulge generally means the cords inside were damaged by a severe impact, such as a pothole or curb, and that a tire with a bulge must be replaced. Its advice is to put on the spare and have the tire inspected. Don't plan to drive on it until a convenient day.

chunks.title: Hit a Curb or Pothole? Tire and Alignment Signs
chunks.text:
Right after: a two-minute look
Not every mark is damage. Michelin describes small indentations (dips inward) in the sidewall as normal on radial tires. A dip is usually normal; a bump outward is not. If you're unsure which you have, have it looked at. Our guide to bubbles in the sidewall has pictures and more detail.
Over the next few days: what the car tells you
Some damage shows up as a change in how the car drives. AAA lists the signs worth acting on:
- The car pulls left or right. A hit can knock the wheels out of alignment and affect the steering. AAA says to have the alignment checked.
- The steering wheel sits off-center on a straight, flat road. Same cause, same check.
- A new vibration or noise. AAA notes that a hard impact can dislodge wheel weights, damage a tire or wheel, or bend or break suspension parts, and that new noises or vibrations should be inspected promptly.

chunks.title: Hit a Curb or Pothole? Tire and Alignment Signs
chunks.text:
Over the next few days: what the car tells you
- A tire that keeps losing air. It may be a bent rim, a slow leak at the bead or a puncture you didn't see.
Our car shaking checker walks through vibration symptoms by speed and when they happen.
Can it be repaired?
It depends on where the damage is. USTMA's repair guidance limits repairs to punctures in the tread area, and rules out repairs in the sidewall or shoulder. Impact damage usually lands right there.
Tap the area of your tire that was hit:
For the full answer on punctures and repairs, try Can My Tire Be Repaired?, and see our guide to plugs vs patches.

chunks.title: Hit a Curb or Pothole? Tire and Alignment Signs
chunks.text:
Alignment: what it is and when to check
Alignment sets the angles of the wheels relative to each other and the road. When a hard hit moves those angles, the car pulls and the tires wear unevenly, often on one edge. That wear is slow and silent, so it's easy to miss until a new set is half gone.
Have it checked if:
- the car pulls or the wheel is off-center after an impact,
- you see wear on one edge of a tire, or
- you're putting on new tires after a hit you remember.
We offer four-wheel alignment at our Sunrise shop.

chunks.title: Hit a Curb or Pothole? Tire and Alignment Signs
chunks.text:
How to make the next hit hurt less
You can't steer around every pothole, but AAA's advice helps:
- Keep tires at the placard pressure. AAA notes that underinflated or badly worn tires are more likely to be damaged by a pothole. Check monthly, cold.
- Keep enough tread. A worn tire has less rubber to absorb a hit.
- Watch the road ahead, especially in construction zones and after heavy rain when holes fill with water.
- Slow down before a hole you can't avoid, checking your mirror before any hard braking.
- Keep the suspension healthy. AAA says changes in handling, vibration or uneven tire wear can point to worn parts.

If the tire needs replacing, shop by size and match the size, load index and speed rating on your door placard. In Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we install at our Sunrise shop, or our mobile van can come to you if the spare isn't an option. Shipping is free to the 48 contiguous states and DC.

chunks.title: Hit a Curb or Pothole? Tire and Alignment Signs
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- AAA says the tires, wheels and suspension take the brunt of a pothole impact, and that one in 10 drivers in its survey needed a repair after hitting one.
- A bulge or bubble in the sidewall means damaged cords. Michelin says it can't be repaired, so put on the spare and have it inspected.
- If the car pulls left or right afterward, AAA's advice is to have the alignment checked.
- New noises or vibrations after an impact should be inspected promptly, AAA says, because weights, wheels and suspension parts can all be knocked loose or bent.
- Correct pressure and good tread are the best protection. AAA notes underinflated or badly worn tires are more likely to be damaged.

chunks.title: Hit a Curb or Pothole? Tire and Alignment Signs
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How do I know if a pothole damaged my tire?
Pull over where you can and look at the sidewall on both sides of the tire for a bulge, bubble or cut, and check the rim edge for a bend or crack. Watch the pressure over the next day. A tire that's losing air, or one with a bulge, needs attention before you drive on it again.
Can a tire with a sidewall bubble be repaired?
No. Michelin says a sidewall bulge generally means the cords inside were damaged by an impact, and a tire with a bulge must be replaced. USTMA's repair guidance also rules out repairs in the sidewall or shoulder.
Do I need an alignment after hitting a pothole?
Not after every bump, but AAA says a hard hit can knock the wheels out of alignment. If the car pulls to one side, or the steering wheel is off-center on a straight road, have the alignment checked.
Why does my car shake after hitting a curb?

chunks.title: Hit a Curb or Pothole? Tire and Alignment Signs
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
AAA notes that a hard impact can dislodge wheel weights, damage a tire or wheel, or bend suspension parts. Any of those can cause a new vibration. Have it inspected rather than waiting to see if it goes away.
