chunks.title: EV Tires Wear Faster: How to Budget and Stretch Them
chunks.text:
EV, Truck & Fleet
EV Tires Wear Faster: How to Budget and Stretch Them
Do EV tires wear faster? Michelin says about 20% on average. Why weight and torque do it, how to plan for replacement, and the habits that stretch a set.
By TireDrop Team, Extreme Tires, Sunrise FL·Published Oct 2, 2026·Updated Oct 2, 2026·4 min read
Yes, faster. Here's how much, and what to do about it
If your first set of EV tires didn't last as long as the tires on your old gas car, you're not imagining it. Michelin says EVs wear tires about 20% faster on average than comparable combustion vehicles.
That doesn't mean you're stuck with it. Wear is predictable once you measure it, and a few habits slow it down. This post is about planning for the next set and stretching the current one. For what makes an EV tire different in the first place, see our Learn guide on EV tires.

chunks.title: EV Tires Wear Faster: How to Budget and Stretch Them
chunks.text:
Why EVs are harder on tires
Michelin points to two causes:
- Weight. The battery pack makes an EV heavy for its size, and that weight presses on every tire on every mile.
- Instant torque. Electric motors deliver full torque from a standstill. Hard launches put extra twisting stress on the driven tires and scrub rubber off the tread.
South Florida adds a third factor you can't change: hot pavement for much of the year. Our guide to Florida heat and tires explains what heat does.

chunks.title: EV Tires Wear Faster: How to Budget and Stretch Them
chunks.text:
Budget with your own numbers, not an average
A 20% average says little about your car. Your own measurements say a lot. Here's a simple way to forecast your next set, with no guesswork about price:
- Measure tread depth in three grooves on each tire, and note the lowest reading and your odometer.
- Measure again at the next rotation. Note the miles driven between readings.
- Work out your wear rate: 32nds lost divided by miles driven.
- Project forward to 4/32, the point where AAA recommends replacing for wet roads.
An example, with made-up numbers: you measure 8/32 at 10,000 miles and 7/32 at 16,000 miles. That's 1/32 every 6,000 miles. From 7/32, you have about 3/32 to go before 4/32, or roughly 18,000 more miles. If you drive 1,000 miles a month, plan to replace in about a year and a half.

chunks.title: EV Tires Wear Faster: How to Budget and Stretch Them
chunks.text:
Budget with your own numbers, not an average
Redo the math at every rotation. If one axle is wearing faster, you'll see it early, while there's still time to fix the cause.
The habits that stretch a set
Accelerate smoothly
Michelin says smooth, progressive acceleration rather than hard launches reduces EV tire wear in measurable ways. It's the single habit that's most specific to EVs. If your car offers a gentler acceleration setting, it does the smoothing for you.

chunks.title: EV Tires Wear Faster: How to Budget and Stretch Them
chunks.text:
Check pressure monthly, against the placard
Michelin recommends checking pressure manually at least once a month, using the number on your door jamb sticker, not the maximum printed on the sidewall. Low pressure increases rolling resistance, which costs range, and it changes how the tread meets the road. Check cold, before driving.
Rotate on schedule
Rotation keeps wear even across all four tires, so they reach the end together. Follow your vehicle maker's interval. Tesla, for example, recommends rotating the Model Y every 6,250 miles (10,000 km), or whenever the tread depth difference reaches 2/32 in (1.5 mm) or more, whichever comes first.
Some EVs use staggered sizes front and rear, which limits rotation options. Our Tesla rotation, alignment and TPMS guide covers that case.

chunks.title: EV Tires Wear Faster: How to Budget and Stretch Them
chunks.text:
Keep the alignment in check
Hitting a curb or a deep pothole can knock alignment out, and misalignment wears the inside or outside edge of a tire fast. If you see uneven wear across a tread, have the alignment checked.
What wears an EV set early
Most early wear on an EV comes from a short list of causes:
- Launches. Instant torque is fun, and it costs tread. The driven axle shows it first.
- Skipped rotations. On a heavy car, an axle that wears faster pulls ahead quickly.
- Low pressure. A slow leak that goes unnoticed for weeks wears the shoulders and costs range.
- Alignment knocked out by a curb or pothole. Watch the inner edges, which are hard to see without turning the wheel.
- Heat. Florida pavement is hot for much of the year, and heat speeds up wear and aging. Our guide to Florida heat and tires covers what you can control.

chunks.title: EV Tires Wear Faster: How to Budget and Stretch Them
chunks.text:
What wears an EV set early
None of these are unusual. Catching them at each rotation, with the log below, is what keeps a 20% average from becoming something worse.
Rotate even when the tires look even. On a heavy car, a difference of a 32nd or two between axles is hard to see by eye and easy to measure, and catching it early is what lets all four tires reach the replacement point together.

chunks.title: EV Tires Wear Faster: How to Budget and Stretch Them
chunks.text:
Where not to economize
When the time comes, the replacement has to match the original specification:
- Size, load index and speed rating from your door placard.
- XL or HL markings. Michelin says that if your EV came on HL (high load) tires, every replacement must also be HL. An XL tire of the same size isn't a substitute.
Beyond that spec, EV-focused tires add features like low rolling resistance for range and sound-absorbing foam for a quieter cabin. Continental and Michelin both describe tires engineered for EV weight, torque and noise. Whether those are worth it depends on how much you value range and quiet.

At each rotation, record
Why

Catches slow leaks

Next steps
Measure your tread with Do I Need Tires Yet?, check your pattern with the rotation tool, and when it's time, shop by size or vehicle. Model Y owners can start with our Model Y tire guide. In Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we install, rotate and balance at our Sunrise shop or by mobile van.

chunks.title: EV Tires Wear Faster: How to Budget and Stretch Them
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Michelin says EVs wear tires about 20% faster on average than comparable gas vehicles.
- Two causes: battery weight loads every tire on every mile, and instant torque scrubs the driven tires when you accelerate.
- Plan with your own numbers: track tread depth against miles and you can forecast your replacement month.
- Rotation, monthly pressure checks and smooth acceleration are the habits Michelin points to for slowing wear.
- Replacements must match the original load rating, including any XL or HL marking. That's not a place to economize.

chunks.title: EV Tires Wear Faster: How to Budget and Stretch Them
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Do EV tires really wear out faster?
On average, yes. Michelin says EVs wear tires about 20% faster than comparable combustion vehicles, because battery weight puts more load on every tire and instant torque puts more stress on the driven tires under acceleration. How much faster your tires wear depends on your car, your tires and how you drive.
How long do Tesla tires last?
There's no single number. Tread life depends on the tire, the wheel package, alignment, pressure, rotation and driving style. The most reliable estimate is your own: measure tread depth at each rotation, note the mileage, and you can project when you'll reach the replacement point.
How can I make EV tires last longer?

chunks.title: EV Tires Wear Faster: How to Budget and Stretch Them
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Michelin points to a few habits: accelerate smoothly instead of launching hard, check pressure at least monthly against the door placard, and rotate regularly to keep wear even. Tesla, for example, recommends rotating every 6,250 miles or when tread depth differs by 2/32 in or more.
Can I put cheaper non-EV tires on my electric car?
Any replacement must match the size, load index and speed rating your vehicle maker specifies, including XL or HL markings. Michelin says if your EV came on HL tires, every replacement must also be HL. Beyond that, EV-focused tires add things like low rolling resistance and noise reduction, which affect range and comfort.

chunks.title: Flat Tire on I-95? What to Do and Who to Call
chunks.text:
Travel & Roadside
Flat Tire on I-95? What to Do and Who to Call
Flat tire on the highway in South Florida? How to get off I-95, when to call *347 for FDOT Road Rangers, and what Florida's Move Over law now covers.
The worst place for a flat
A flat in a parking lot is an inconvenience. A flat on I-95 at highway speed, with traffic inches away and no shoulder in sight, is something else. It helps to have the plan in your head before it happens, because you won't want to look it up then.
Here's that plan, built from what FDOT, the Florida Highway Patrol's parent agency FLHSMV, and AAA publish. Read it once now, then save the one number that matters: *347.

chunks.title: Flat Tire on I-95? What to Do and Who to Call
chunks.text:
The first 30 seconds: keep it straight
You'll usually feel it before you see it: a thump, a pull to one side, a flapping noise, or the TPMS light. A sudden blowout feels more violent. Either way the steps are the same:
- Hold the wheel firmly with both hands. The car will pull toward the flat side.
- Ease off the gas. Let the car slow down on its own. Don't stomp the brakes.
- Signal and move right when there's a gap. Aim for the right shoulder, an exit ramp or a wide pull-off on solid, level ground.
- Turn on your hazard lights as soon as you're slowing.

chunks.title: Flat Tire on I-95? What to Do and Who to Call
chunks.text:
The first 30 seconds: keep it straight
If the car can still roll, keep it rolling at low speed to a better spot rather than stopping in a lane. FDOT's guidance says that if your vehicle is blocking a travel lane, Florida law requires you to make every effort to move it out of the regular flow of traffic. Driving a short distance on a flat may ruin the tire or even the wheel, but a tire is replaceable.
If the TPMS light came on with no thump and the car feels normal, it may be a slow leak, not a blowout. Take the next exit and check. Our guide to the TPMS light explains solid vs flashing.

chunks.title: Flat Tire on I-95? What to Do and Who to Call
chunks.text:
Once you're stopped: who to call
Dial *347 (*FHP) on your cell phone. FLHSMV describes it as the number motorists use to report crashes and stranded or disabled motorists, and the call to the nearest FHP communications center is free. FDOT uses the same number for Road Rangers, its highway service patrol.
What FDOT says Road Rangers do:
- Change flat tires (with your spare)
- Jump-start vehicles and make minor repairs
- Supply emergency gasoline, diesel and water
- Give stranded motorists two free local calls
- Clear disabled vehicles from travel lanes
FDOT says motorists are not charged for the service. If the problem is more than the Road Ranger can handle, they'll move the car out of the travel lane and FHP will contact a tow company, at your expense.

chunks.title: Flat Tire on I-95? What to Do and Who to Call
chunks.text:
Once you're stopped: who to call
In Broward and Palm Beach, FDOT District Four's Road Ranger guidelines describe patrols on the entire I-95 corridor from the Miami-Dade County line to the Brevard County line, plus parts of I-595 and I-75. Miami-Dade's expressways and Florida's Turnpike have their own Road Ranger patrols. FDOT notes that availability varies around the state, so if you're outside a covered stretch, *347 still reaches FHP.
Have a roadside assistance plan through your insurer, your car's maker or a motor club? Call it too. Tell them your direction of travel and the nearest mile marker or exit.

chunks.title: Flat Tire on I-95? What to Do and Who to Call
chunks.text:
Stay in the car, or get out?
The sources lean different ways here, so it's worth knowing both:
- FDOT's Road Ranger guidance: once you're out of the flow of traffic, stay inside your vehicle and wait for help to arrive.
- AAA's tire-change steps: if you're changing the tire yourself, have passengers get out and wait away from the road.
On a narrow interstate shoulder with traffic passing at speed, we'd follow FDOT: seat belts on, hazards on, phone in hand, and let the Road Ranger do the roadside work. If you must get out, use the door away from traffic and move well back from the lanes.

chunks.title: Flat Tire on I-95? What to Do and Who to Call
chunks.text:
Florida's Move Over law now covers you
Florida has long required drivers to move over for emergency, service and utility vehicles. Since January 1, 2025, FLHSMV says the law also protects any vehicle stopped on the side of the road with hazard lights flashing, emergency flares or visible emergency signage. In its words, even a vehicle with a flat tire is protected.
Drivers approaching you must move over a lane, or slow to 20 mph below the posted speed limit if they can't move over (5 mph where the limit is 20 mph or less). That's one more reason to switch your hazards on the moment you know you're stopping.

chunks.title: Flat Tire on I-95? What to Do and Who to Call
chunks.text:
Spare, kit or nothing?
What happens next depends on what's in your trunk. AAA says roughly 30 percent of new cars come without a spare, up from 5 percent in 2006, with a sealant and inflator kit or run-flat tires instead. AAA's advice is to review your car's flat-tire procedure now, not on the shoulder.
What you have
What it does
The limit
Compact spare ("donut")
Gets you to a shop
Low speed and short distance; check its label
Full-size spare
Can be used like a regular tire if it matches
Check its pressure and age
Sealant and inflator kit
Seals small punctures in the tread
AAA says kits don't work on larger leaks or sidewall damage
Run-flat tires
Keep going after losing air
A limited distance at reduced speed; see your manual
Nothing
You're calling for a tow
Know your roadside number

chunks.title: Flat Tire on I-95? What to Do and Who to Call
chunks.text:
Spare, kit or nothing?
Our spare tire types guide covers each option, and our guide to run-flat tires explains what they can and can't do.
After the highway: getting the tire sorted
A donut or a sealed tire is a way to reach a tire shop, not to finish a road trip. Once you're off I-95:
- Find out if it can be repaired. A puncture in the tread area, up to about a quarter inch, is often repairable from the inside. Damage in the sidewall or shoulder is not. Our repairability checker walks you through it, and our post on nails in tires explains the limits.
- Tell the shop if you used sealant. It has to be cleaned out before a repair, and it can affect the TPMS sensor.
- Check the other tires. If the flat came from a curb or debris, look at the wheel too.
- Replace the spare's air. Donuts usually need more pressure than your regular tires.

chunks.title: Flat Tire on I-95? What to Do and Who to Call
chunks.text:
After the highway: getting the tire sorted
If the tire can't be saved, shop by size or vehicle. In Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we install at our Sunrise shop, or our mobile van can come to your home or office once you're off the highway. We don't do roadside rescue; that's what *347 is for. Shipping is free to the 48 contiguous states and DC.
Before your next long drive
The best flat-tire plan starts in the driveway: check pressure cold, look at the tread and sidewalls, and confirm what's in the trunk. Our road trip tire check covers it step by step.

chunks.title: Flat Tire on I-95? What to Do and Who to Call
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Hold the wheel, ease off the gas and get out of the travel lanes. Don't brake hard or stop in a lane if the car can still roll.
- Dial *347 (*FHP) for help. FDOT says Road Rangers don't charge, and they can change a flat with your spare.
- Since January 1, 2025, Florida's Move Over law also covers a car stopped with its hazard lights on, flat tire included.
- No spare? About 30 percent of new cars come without one, AAA says. Know what's in your trunk before the trip.
- A donut or a sealant kit gets you to a tire shop. It isn't a fix for the rest of the drive.

chunks.title: Flat Tire on I-95? What to Do and Who to Call
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What should I do if I get a flat tire on the highway?
Hold the steering wheel firmly, ease off the accelerator and let the car slow down. Signal and get to the right shoulder, an exit or a wide pull-off, away from traffic. Turn on your hazard lights. Then call for help: *347 on a cell phone reaches FHP and FDOT's Road Rangers, or call your roadside assistance plan.
Who are the Road Rangers and what do they cost?
Road Rangers are FDOT's highway service patrol. FDOT says motorists are not charged for the service. Its list of services includes changing flat tires, emergency fuel, jump starts and two free local calls. If the car needs more than they can do, FHP arranges a tow at your expense.
Does Florida's Move Over law protect me if I have a flat?

chunks.title: Flat Tire on I-95? What to Do and Who to Call
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Yes. Since January 1, 2025, it covers any vehicle stopped on the side of the road with its hazard lights flashing, flares out or emergency signage showing. FLHSMV specifically says a vehicle with a flat tire is protected. Other drivers must move over a lane or slow to 20 mph below the posted limit.
Should I stay in the car or get out?
FDOT's Road Ranger guidance is to get out of the flow of traffic, then stay inside the vehicle and wait for help. AAA's tire-change steps say passengers should get out and wait away from the road if you're changing the tire yourself. On a busy interstate shoulder, staying belted in and calling *347 is usually the better choice.

chunks.title: Car Sat in Floodwater? What to Check on Tires and Wheels
chunks.text:
Hurricanes & Flooding
Car Sat in Floodwater? What to Check on Tires and Wheels
Flooded car, what to do first: don't start it, don't drive it, then what to have checked on the tires, wheels and brakes. Plus NHTSA's flooded-EV rule.
When the water was around the car, not under it
Splashing through a flooded street is one thing. Coming out after a storm to find your car parked in water up to the hubcaps, or higher, is another. The water sat there for hours, maybe days, and some of it probably got into places it was never meant to go.
This post is about that second case: a car that sat in floodwater. (If you drove through tidal water on a king tide day, our post on salt water and your wheels covers the rinse-and-watch routine instead.) We'll start with what not to do, then what to have checked on the tires, wheels and brakes, which is the part of the car we know best.

chunks.title: Car Sat in Floodwater? What to Check on Tires and Wheels
chunks.text:
First: don't start it, don't drive it
Two pieces of guidance come before everything else:
- Don't start the engine. AAA advises against starting a car right after it has been through a flood. If water got into the engine, turning it on can cause more damage.
- Don't drive it until it's been checked. NHTSA's guidance is not to drive a flooded vehicle until a qualified technician has inspected it, because flood damage isn't always visible.
If the car has to move, have it towed.

chunks.title: Car Sat in Floodwater? What to Check on Tires and Wheels
chunks.text:
Hybrids and EVs
NHTSA adds a specific warning for vehicles with lithium-ion batteries. Don't park a flood-damaged hybrid or EV in a garage, or within 50 feet of a house or other structure, another vehicle or anything combustible. Tell the tow operator it's an electrified vehicle that sat in floodwater.
How high did the water get?
That question shapes everything a technician will check. Look for the high-water mark on the body, and then look inside.
The National Insurance Crime Bureau lists warning signs of flood damage, including musty odors, water stains, rust, silt or mud, and moisture inside the vehicle's parts. If you find those in the cabin or the trunk, the water got in, and the car needs more than a look at its tires.
A note on insurance: we're a tire and service shop, not an insurance advisor. Your insurer and your policy are the place for coverage questions.

chunks.title: Car Sat in Floodwater? What to Check on Tires and Wheels
chunks.text:
The tires: clean, then inspect
Floodwater isn't clean water. A technical bulletin from Mickey Thompson, a tire and wheel maker, notes that it carries oil, grease, salt and other contaminants that can damage tires. Its guidance for tires mounted on a flooded vehicle:
- Clean them with a mild soap and clean water, without a pressure washer.
- Inspect them for physical damage such as cuts, tears, holes or scrapes that could let contaminants into the tire.
- If there's damage, the bulletin says the tire should be taken out of service.
Two more things are worth checking once the water is gone:
- Pressure, cold, against the door placard. A tire that sat against debris, or on a curb hidden under the water, may have a slow leak you can't see.

chunks.title: Car Sat in Floodwater? What to Check on Tires and Wheels
chunks.text:
The tires: clean, then inspect
- The sidewalls. A car can drift or get pushed in moving water. A bubble on the sidewall means cord damage from an impact, and it can't be repaired. Our guide to sidewall bubbles explains what to look for.
Wheels, brakes and bearings
The tires aren't the only parts that sat in the water. The wheels, brakes, wheel bearings and suspension were in it too, and they're harder to check from the driveway. We'd have a technician look at them before the car goes back to regular driving, and more so if the water was salty storm surge. AAA notes that salt water is more corrosive to a car than fresh water.
Warning signs to mention to the technician, or to watch for once the car is cleared to drive:
- grinding, squealing or a soft brake pedal
- a new pull to one side
- a vibration through the wheel or seat
- a humming or growling noise that changes with speed

chunks.title: Car Sat in Floodwater? What to Check on Tires and Wheels
chunks.text:
Wheels, brakes and bearings
- a TPMS light that comes on and stays on
Extreme Tires does brake repair, suspension work and alignment at the Sunrise shop, and tire and TPMS service there or by mobile van in the local install area. For a car that sat in floodwater, call (954) 773-1896 before you bring it in, and ask what we can check and what belongs with the vehicle maker's service department or another specialist.

chunks.title: Car Sat in Floodwater? What to Check on Tires and Wheels
chunks.text:
If you're replacing tires afterward
If the inspection says one or more tires need replacing, match them to your door placard: USTMA's guidance is the same size, load index and speed rating the vehicle calls for, with a load index equal to or above the placard. You can shop by size and have them fitted at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van where the car is parked.
The order of operations
Step
What to do
Why
1
Don't start the engine
AAA: water in the engine can cause more damage
2
Don't drive it; tow if it must move
NHTSA: damage may not be visible
3
Hybrid or EV: not in a garage, 50 feet from structures, vehicles and combustibles
NHTSA lithium-ion battery guidance
4
Check the cabin for water, silt and odor
NICB flood-damage signs
5
Clean the tires gently; inspect for cuts and damage
Tire maker's flood bulletin
6
Have brakes, bearings and suspension checked
They sat in the same water

chunks.title: Car Sat in Floodwater? What to Check on Tires and Wheels
chunks.text:
The order of operations
Coverage questions go to your insurer
Not something this post covers
And the best flood advice is the oldest: if a street is under water, turn around. Our hurricane car prep checklist covers what to do before the next storm, and if you're shopping for a used car after the season, see the tire clues that flag a flooded car.
Key takeaways
- Don't start it. AAA advises against starting a car right after a flood, because water in the engine can cause more damage.
- Don't drive it until a technician has checked it. NHTSA says flood damage may not be visible.
- For a hybrid or EV, NHTSA says not to park it in a garage or within 50 feet of a home, another vehicle or anything combustible.
- Floodwater carries oil, grease, salt and other contaminants. A tire maker's bulletin says to clean flooded tires gently and inspect them for cuts, tears and scrapes.

chunks.title: Car Sat in Floodwater? What to Check on Tires and Wheels
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Brakes, wheel bearings and suspension sat in the same water. Have them looked at before regular driving.
Questions people ask
What should I do if my car was in a flood?
Don't start it and don't drive it. AAA advises against starting a flooded car because water in the engine can cause more damage, and NHTSA says not to drive a flooded vehicle until a technician has checked it. Have it towed if it needs to move. For coverage questions, talk to your insurer.
Can floodwater damage tires?
It can. A Mickey Thompson technical bulletin notes floodwater contains oil, grease, salt and other contaminants that can damage tires, and says tires on a flooded vehicle should be cleaned and inspected for cuts, tears, holes or scrapes. Debris hidden under the water can also cause punctures and impact damage.
Should I start a car that sat in floodwater?

chunks.title: Car Sat in Floodwater? What to Check on Tires and Wheels
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
No. AAA advises not to start a car right after it has been through a flood, because turning it on with water in the engine can cause more damage. Have a technician inspect it first.
What should I do with a flooded electric vehicle?
Follow NHTSA's guidance: don't drive it until it has been checked, and don't park a flood-damaged vehicle with a lithium-ion battery in a garage or within 50 feet of a house or other structure, another vehicle or combustibles.

chunks.title: Sun, Heat and Dry Rot: How Florida Ages Your Tires
chunks.text:
Rain, Heat & Weather
Sun, Heat and Dry Rot: How Florida Ages Your Tires
Tire dry rot in Florida: what sidewall cracking looks like, why sun, heat and ozone cause it, which cracks mean replace, and how to slow it down.
The cracks you notice while pumping gas
You're at the pump, glance down, and see it: a web of thin lines across the sidewall, or little cracks at the base of the tread blocks. The tread still looks deep. So is the tire wearing out or not?
In South Florida this question comes up a lot, because the conditions that age rubber are the ones we live in all year. Here's what the cracking is, why the climate speeds it up, and how to tell the harmless-looking kind from the kind that means new tires.

chunks.title: Sun, Heat and Dry Rot: How Florida Ages Your Tires
chunks.text:
What "dry rot" actually is
Goodyear defines tire dry rot, also called sidewall weathering, as visible cracking in a tire's tread or sidewall caused when the rubber compounds break down. The signs it lists:
- Cracking in the sidewall, often as a web of hairline cracks or lines running around the tire
- Cracking in the tread, usually at the base of the grooves
- A brittle surface that feels hard rather than supple
- A faded or gray color in place of the original black
Michelin calls the early, hairline version weather checking: a sign the rubber has started to dry out.

chunks.title: Sun, Heat and Dry Rot: How Florida Ages Your Tires
chunks.text:
Why Florida speeds it up
Tire rubber contains weathering agents meant to protect it, but they don't last forever. Several things wear the rubber down faster:
- UV from sunlight. Goodyear says too much UV exposure, especially in consistently warmer climates, is a leading cause of premature sidewall weathering.
- Heat. NHTSA lists exposure to sunlight and a warmer climate among the factors that contribute to tire aging, and says aging is a greater concern in the more southern parts of the Sun Belt states. That's us.
- Ozone. Michelin warns that ozone from electrical equipment and UV from sunlight are among the most damaging things a stored tire can face. It says a tire stored next to an electric motor or against a sunny wall can crack within weeks.

chunks.title: Sun, Heat and Dry Rot: How Florida Ages Your Tires
chunks.text:
Why Florida speeds it up
- Sitting still. NHTSA lists infrequent use as an aging factor too. A car that sits in a sunny lot for weeks, or all summer, gets the exposure without the flexing.
- Low pressure. Goodyear lists underinflation among the causes, because it overworks the sidewall.
None of this gives a Florida tire a set lifespan. Nobody publishes a "Florida number," and we won't invent one. It does mean that here, the calendar and the sidewall deserve as much attention as the tread.

chunks.title: Sun, Heat and Dry Rot: How Florida Ages Your Tires
chunks.text:
Which cracks matter
This is the part drivers most want to know, and the honest answer is that it takes a trained eye. NHTSA says plainly that you cannot detect tire aging simply by looking at your tires. Still, the makers give a useful split:
What you see
What Michelin and Goodyear say
What to do
Thin, shallow surface lines
A sign of age and drying rubber
Note it, check the DOT date, have it inspected
Cracks that open when the sidewall flexes
Degraded beyond use
Replace
Deep or numerous cracks
Degraded beyond use
Replace
Cracks with a bulge, cut or exposed cords
Structural damage
Replace; don't drive on it
Goodyear's view is that once deterioration becomes noticeable, the best course is to replace the tires. If you're unsure, that's exactly what an inspection is for. A bulge is a separate, more urgent problem; our guide to sidewall bubbles explains why.

chunks.title: Sun, Heat and Dry Rot: How Florida Ages Your Tires
chunks.text:
Check the age while you're down there
Cracking and age go together, so read the DOT date code on the sidewall: the last four digits are the week and year it was made. Try it here:
Then compare it with the guidance:
- Michelin: after five years in service, a thorough inspection by a trained professional at least once a year, and replacement ten years after manufacture regardless of tread.
- Bridgestone: an inspection is essential after five years, and tires made ten or more years ago should be replaced. Same for the spare.
- FLHSMV: Florida's tire safety page is stricter, saying never to operate a vehicle on tires more than six years old.
Our guide to how old is too old lays the guidance side by side, and our DOT date code guide shows where to find the code.

chunks.title: Sun, Heat and Dry Rot: How Florida Ages Your Tires
chunks.text:
How to slow it down
You can't stop rubber from aging, but you can avoid speeding it up:
- Park in the shade when you can. A garage, a covered space or the shady side of the lot all cut UV exposure.
- Keep the pressure at the door placard, checked cold, once a month. Our pressure guide shows how.
- Drive the car. If it will sit for weeks, see our post on a car that sat all summer.
- Clean with soap and water. Goodyear recommends water and a mild dish soap and warns that petroleum-based cleaning products may degrade the rubber's weathering agents and lead to early cracking.
- Store spare tires indoors, cool, dry and dark, away from motors, generators and sunny walls, as Michelin advises. Our post on unused tires aging covers storage.
- Look monthly. Goodyear suggests inspecting sidewalls and tread every month for cracks, discoloration and bulges.

chunks.title: Sun, Heat and Dry Rot: How Florida Ages Your Tires
chunks.text:
How to slow it down
For more on what Florida heat does to pressure and load, see our guide to Florida heat and tires.
If it's time
Not sure your tires are done? Do I Need Tires Yet? walks you through tread, age and damage. If they are, shop by size or vehicle and check the new tires' DOT dates when they're mounted. In Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we install at our Sunrise shop or at your home or office with our mobile van. Shipping is free to the 48 contiguous states and DC.

chunks.title: Sun, Heat and Dry Rot: How Florida Ages Your Tires
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Dry rot, or sidewall weathering, is cracking in the sidewall or tread as the rubber compounds break down. Goodyear names UV from sunlight as a leading cause in warm climates.
- NHTSA lists sunlight and a warmer climate among the causes of tire aging, and says aging is a greater concern in the southern Sun Belt.
- Thin surface cracks show age. Cracks that open when the rubber flexes, or that are deep or numerous, mean replace now, Michelin says.
- Shade, correct pressure, regular driving and plain soap and water slow it down. Goodyear warns against petroleum-based cleaners.
- Check the DOT date too. Michelin and Bridgestone want a yearly inspection from five years and replacement at ten; FLHSMV's own tire page says six.

chunks.title: Sun, Heat and Dry Rot: How Florida Ages Your Tires
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What is tire dry rot?
Dry rot, also called sidewall weathering, is visible cracking in a tire's sidewall or tread caused when the rubber compounds break down. It shows up as a web of small cracks, a brittle surface, or a faded, grayish color. Sunlight, heat, ozone, low pressure and long periods without driving all speed it up.
Can I drive on tires with dry rot?
It depends on how far it has gone, and that's a call for a trained tire inspector, not a glance in the driveway. Michelin says thin, shallow cracks indicate age, while cracks that open when the tire flexes, or that are deep or numerous, mean the tire should be replaced. NHTSA also notes you can't detect tire aging just by looking.
Do tires age faster in Florida?

chunks.title: Sun, Heat and Dry Rot: How Florida Ages Your Tires
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
NHTSA lists exposure to sunlight and a warmer climate among the things that contribute to tire aging, and says aging is a greater concern in the more southern parts of the Sun Belt states. That doesn't put a fixed expiration date on a Florida tire, but it makes age and sidewall checks more important here.
Does tire shine cause dry rot?
Goodyear advises against petroleum-based cleaning products, which it says may degrade the rubber's weathering agents and lead to premature cracking. It recommends cleaning tires with water and a mild dish soap. If you like a dressing, choose one that says it is water-based.

chunks.title: Ford F-150 Tires: P-Metric, LT and Load Range Basics
chunks.text:
Vehicle Guides
Ford F-150 Tires: P-Metric, LT and Load Range Basics
Best tires for an F-150, answered by load, not logos: P-metric vs LT on your truck, load range, pressure when you switch, and towing in Florida heat.
Start with load, not brand
The F-150 does more jobs than almost any other vehicle on the road. The same truck can be a family car on weekdays and a boat hauler on Saturday, or a contractor's rig that's loaded every day. That's why "best tires for F-150" has no single answer.
The question that sorts it out is how much weight your tires need to carry, and how often. Brand comes after that. This guide covers the F-150-specific parts: P-metric or LT, load range, and pressure. Our Learn guide on LT vs P-metric tires has the full background.

chunks.title: Ford F-150 Tires: P-Metric, LT and Load Range Basics
chunks.text:
Step 1: Read your placard
Ford fits a wide range of tire sizes across F-150 trims and wheel packages. Some trucks leave the factory on P-metric (passenger) tires, others on LT (light truck) tires.
The Tire and Loading Information placard on the driver's door pillar tells you:
- the original size, including a P or LT prefix
- the load index and speed rating
- the cold pressure for the original tires
- the truck's maximum load, and Ford lists maximum vehicle and axle weights on its labels too
Ford's own tire replacement guidance is to use tires of the same size, load index and speed rating the truck was originally equipped with. Check any tire against yours:

chunks.title: Ford F-150 Tires: P-Metric, LT and Load Range Basics
chunks.text:
Step 2: Understand what P-metric means on a truck
P-metric tires are designed for passenger vehicles. When a vehicle maker puts them on a truck or SUV, federal safety standard FMVSS No. 110 requires it to divide the tire's load rating by 1.10. In other words, a P-metric tire on your F-150 is counted as carrying less than its sidewall says.
That's not a problem for the use Ford designed the truck around. It does mean there's less spare capacity than the sidewall number suggests, which matters if you tow or haul more than the original owner did.

chunks.title: Ford F-150 Tires: P-Metric, LT and Load Range Basics
chunks.text:
Step 3: LT tires and load range
LT tires are built for heavier loads. Instead of XL or standard load, they carry a load range letter, such as C, D or E, which replaced the old ply ratings. A higher letter means a higher maximum pressure and a higher load limit.
What changes if you move from P-metric to LT:
Feature
P-metric
LT
Built for
Passenger loads, comfort
Heavier loads, tougher use
Load marking
Standard or XL
Load range C, D, E and up
Pressure for the same load
Lower
Higher
Ride
Usually softer
Usually firmer, heavier
The key point: size for size, an LT tire needs more air pressure to carry the same load as a P-metric tire. So the placard pressure, which Ford set for the original tires, doesn't automatically apply after a switch. The right pressure comes from the tire maker's load and inflation table, as Toyo's guidelines describe.

chunks.title: Ford F-150 Tires: P-Metric, LT and Load Range Basics
chunks.text:
Step 3: LT tires and load range
If your truck came on LT tires, stay with LT. Going from LT to P-metric reduces capacity and isn't a like-for-like swap.
Step 4: Match the tire to the work
How you use the truck
What to look at
Daily driving, light loads
Placard spec; highway or all-season tread; comfort
Regular towing (boat, camper)
Load capacity with margin; LT if your loads call for it
Work truck, loaded daily
LT load range that covers your real loads; durability
Dirt, sand, job sites
All-terrain tread; see our all-terrain vs highway guide
Whatever you pick, never go below the original load capacity. Our load index guide explains how to read it.

chunks.title: Ford F-150 Tires: P-Metric, LT and Load Range Basics
chunks.text:
Leveled, lifted or plus-sized trucks
Many F-150s don't stay stock. Bigger wheels, taller tires and leveling kits all change the tire question:
- Overall diameter affects the speedometer. A taller tire turns fewer times per mile, so the speedometer reads low. Our plus-size calculator shows the difference for any size change.
- Load capacity still has to match. A larger, more aggressive tire is not automatically a stronger one. Check its load index or load range against the original.
- Clearance is real. Wider and taller tires can rub at full steering lock or under suspension compression. Fitment depends on wheel offset as well as tire size; our offset and backspacing guide explains why.
- The placard won't cover the new size. Pressure for a non-original size comes from the tire maker's load and inflation table, not the door label.

chunks.title: Ford F-150 Tires: P-Metric, LT and Load Range Basics
chunks.text:
Florida heat under load
Heat and weight work together. A loaded truck on hot summer asphalt puts more stress on tires than the same truck empty in January. Two habits help:
- Check pressure cold, before you hook up, against the placard or the load table for your tires. Low pressure plus a heavy load builds heat.
- Inspect before long tows. Look for cuts, bulges and uneven wear, and check the trailer's tires too.
NHTSA's tire safety guidance also reminds drivers not to overload: the placard's maximum load is a limit, not a target.

chunks.title: Ford F-150 Tires: P-Metric, LT and Load Range Basics
chunks.text:
Don't forget the trailer
If you tow a boat or camper, the trailer's tires carry part of the load too, and they often sit for weeks between trips. Check their pressure against the trailer maker's label, read their DOT date codes, and look for cracks and bulges before each season. A trailer tire that fails on the Turnpike stops the whole rig, however good the truck's tires are.
Work trucks and fleets
If your F-150 earns its keep, tire downtime costs money. Our commercial tires page quotes multi-vehicle orders per tire, and our mobile van can come to a job site or yard in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach.

chunks.title: Ford F-150 Tires: P-Metric, LT and Load Range Basics
chunks.text:
Next steps
- Read your placard: P or LT, load index, speed rating, pressure.
- Decide how much load you really carry, and how often.
- Use Find My Tires or shop by size, and filter by type.
- If you're switching between P-metric and LT, ask us to set pressure from the tire maker's load table. Call (954) 773-1896.
Key takeaways
- Ford says to use replacement tires with the same size, load index and speed rating the truck was originally equipped with.
- F-150s leave the factory on P-metric or LT tires depending on the trim. The door placard tells you which.
- On a truck, FMVSS No. 110 makes the vehicle maker divide a P-metric tire's load rating by 1.10, which leaves less margin than the sidewall suggests.
- LT tires need more air to carry the same load, so the placard pressure for P-metric tires doesn't carry over to an LT swap.

chunks.title: Ford F-150 Tires: P-Metric, LT and Load Range Basics
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Never go below the original load capacity. Towing and hauling in Florida heat is when it counts most.
Questions people ask
Should I put LT tires on my F-150?
If your F-150 came on LT tires, stay with LT. If it came on P-metric tires, LT tires can work, but they're heavier and stiffer, and they need different pressures to carry the same load, which means using the tire maker's load and inflation tables. Whatever you choose, the new tires must carry at least the original load capacity.
What does load range E mean?
Load range is a letter on LT tires (C, D, E and up) that replaced the old ply rating. A higher letter means the tire can be inflated to a higher pressure and carry more load. Whether you need a higher load range depends on what you actually tow and haul; the minimum is the load capacity of the tires your truck came with.

chunks.title: Ford F-150 Tires: P-Metric, LT and Load Range Basics
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What tire pressure should I run on my F-150 when towing?
Start with the Tire and Loading Information placard on the driver's door pillar, which Ford bases on the original tires. Ford's placard also lists maximum vehicle and axle weights. If you've changed to a different tire type or load range, the original pressure may not apply; ask your installer to set pressure from the tire maker's load and inflation table.
What size tires does an F-150 use?
It varies a lot by model year, trim and wheel package, and Ford fits many sizes across the F-150 range. Match the size, load index and speed rating on your door placard, or enter your year and trim in our Find My Tires tool.

chunks.title: How to Get Tires Installed After Buying Them Online
chunks.text:
Buying & Price
How to Get Tires Installed After Buying Them Online
Bought tires online? How to find an installer anywhere in the US, what to ask before you order, where to ship them, and what to check at the appointment.
By TireDrop Team, Extreme Tires, Sunrise FL·Published Oct 2, 2026·Updated Oct 2, 2026·6 min read
The part of buying tires online nobody mentions first
Finding the right tire online is the easy part. You can compare specs, sizes and load ratings at your own pace. Then the order confirmation lands and the real question shows up: who's going to put these on?
The answer is simple once you plan for it, and annoying if you don't. Here's how to get tires bought online installed anywhere in the US, in the order that saves you the most trouble.

chunks.title: How to Get Tires Installed After Buying Them Online
chunks.text:
The part of buying tires online nobody mentions first
One note up front: TireDrop ships free to any address in the 48 contiguous states and DC, but our own installation covers South Florida only. If you live elsewhere, this guide is about choosing and working with an installer near you.
Step 1: Find an installer before you check out
Do this first. It takes a couple of phone calls and it decides where you ship.
Places that commonly mount and balance passenger tires include independent tire shops, general repair shops, some dealership service departments and mobile tire services. Policies vary from shop to shop, so don't assume. Shortlist two or three near you and call.

chunks.title: How to Get Tires Installed After Buying Them Online
chunks.text:
Step 2: Ask these questions on the phone
The same short list works anywhere:
- Do you install tires a customer brings in? Some shops do, some don't, and some only for certain tire types or sizes.
- What does it cost, and what's included? Mounting and balancing are the core. Ask whether valve stems, TPMS service and disposal of the old tires are included or extra.
- Can I ship the tires to you? If yes, ask how they want the box addressed and who calls whom when it arrives.
- Can you handle my wheels? Mention large wheels, low-profile tires, run-flats or anything unusual so they can confirm the equipment.
- How do you handle TPMS? If your car has pressure sensors, ask whether a reset or relearn is part of the job.
- Do you torque wheels to the vehicle maker's spec? A torque wrench at the end, not only an impact gun.

chunks.title: How to Get Tires Installed After Buying Them Online
chunks.text:
Step 2: Ask these questions on the phone
- Is there anything you won't install? Some shops have rules about tire age or condition. Better to hear it now.
Write the answers down. A clear "yes, and here's the price" is worth more than the closest address.
Step 3: Choose where to ship
TireDrop ships free to any address in the 48 contiguous states and DC, and that includes a tire shop. Our shipping page notes that plenty of customers ship to work or to the shop doing their fitting. Two options:
Ship to...
Good when
Watch for
Your home or work
You want to inspect the tires yourself first, or the shop won't accept deliveries
Four tires take real space and they're heavy; you'll need a way to get them to the shop
The installer
The shop has agreed, and you'd rather not handle the tires

chunks.title: How to Get Tires Installed After Buying Them Online
chunks.text:
Step 3: Choose where to ship
Ask the shop to check the tires against your order, read you the date codes, and hold off mounting until you're happy
Make sure someone is there to receive the delivery. We don't promise transit times on our pages, because they depend on which distributor warehouse has your size. Checkout shows the estimate for your order once your address is in, and tracking comes to you as soon as it exists. A set can arrive in more than one shipment if it comes from more than one warehouse, so book the appointment once you know the boxes are there.

chunks.title: How to Get Tires Installed After Buying Them Online
chunks.text:
Step 4: Check the tires before anything is mounted
This is the step people skip, and it's the one that matters most for an online order. Once a tire is mounted on a wheel, it can't be returned, even if it was never driven on. So check first:
- Size, load index and speed rating against the Tire and Loading Information placard on your door edge or door post. USTMA's guidance is that replacement tires match the size, load index and speed rating your vehicle maker recommends.
- Same model on every tire you ordered.
- The four-digit DOT date code on each tire. Our post on how old tires are when you buy online shows how to read it and what to do with it.
- Shipping damage along the beads and sidewalls.
If something's wrong with a TireDrop order, call (954) 773-1896 before the tires go on a wheel. Our shipping page covers how damaged or wrong tires are handled.

chunks.title: How to Get Tires Installed After Buying Them Online
chunks.text:
Step 5: At the appointment
A good installer will do most of this without being asked. It's still worth knowing what to look for:
- Valve stems. USTMA's service bulletin on tubeless valves says to always remove and replace used snap-in valves when replacing tires, and never reuse them. On wheels with TPMS sensors, USTMA recommends replacing the parts in the sensor's service kit.
- TPMS. Some vehicles need a relearn after tire work and some reset on their own. The procedure varies by make, model and year, which is why the Tire Industry Association publishes a relearn chart for technicians.
- Balancing. Each tire and wheel assembly should be balanced after mounting.

chunks.title: How to Get Tires Installed After Buying Them Online
chunks.text:
Step 5: At the appointment
- Wheel torque. The Tire Industry Association teaches a wheel installation routine called RIST: Remove foreign objects, Inspect components, Snug fasteners, and Torque to specs. Ask whether the shop finishes with a torque wrench set to your vehicle maker's spec, and whether it recommends a torque re-check after the first drive.
- Pressure. Set to the door placard, not the number on the tire's sidewall.
- Position. Replacing only two? The new pair goes on the rear axle. Here's why: new tires on the front or the back?

chunks.title: How to Get Tires Installed After Buying Them Online
chunks.text:
Step 6: After the install
Two small jobs protect you later:
Keep the full DOT numbers. Photograph each one. A recall lookup needs the whole number.
Make sure the tires are registered. Registration is how a tire maker reaches you if a tire is recalled. Federal rules in 49 CFR 574.8 require independent tire dealers to give buyers a registration form with the tire identification numbers recorded, or to register the tires for them. Ask how it's handled for your purchase, and register online with the tire maker if it isn't. You can search tire recalls on NHTSA's recall site at any time.

chunks.title: How to Get Tires Installed After Buying Them Online
chunks.text:
In South Florida? We can do the fitting
If the car is in Miami-Dade, Broward or Palm Beach County, you have two more options:
- Free ship-to-store at Extreme Tires in Sunrise, with the fitting done in the shop for a per-tire charge. See how ship-to-store works.
- A mobile van that fits the tires where the car is parked, inside the local install area. See mobile tire service.
Our post on getting online tires installed in Broward walks through both routes.

chunks.title: How to Get Tires Installed After Buying Them Online
chunks.text:
The whole plan on one card
When
What to do
Before ordering
Call two or three installers; confirm they fit customer-supplied tires, the price and what's included
At checkout
Ship to home or to the installer (free to the 48 contiguous states and DC)
On delivery
Check size, load and speed rating, model, date codes and damage before mounting
At the appointment
Ask about valve stems, TPMS, balancing, torque and pressure
After
Photograph DOT numbers and confirm registration
Still deciding where to buy? Our comparison of buying online versus at a local shop lays out the trade-offs. Ready now? Shop by size or vehicle and line up your installer before you check out.

chunks.title: How to Get Tires Installed After Buying Them Online
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Line up an installer before you order. Not every shop fits tires the customer brings in, and each sets its own fitting price.
- TireDrop ships free to any address in the 48 contiguous states and DC, including the shop doing your install.
- Check size, load index, speed rating, date codes and condition before anything is mounted. A mounted tire can't be returned.
- At the appointment, ask about valve stems, TPMS, balancing and wheel torque.
- TireDrop installs only in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties. Everywhere else, you choose the installer.

chunks.title: How to Get Tires Installed After Buying Them Online
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Will a tire shop install tires I bought online?
Many will, but not all, and each shop sets its own price for fitting tires a customer brings in. Call before you order and ask whether they install customer-supplied tires, what's included in the price and whether you can ship the tires to them.
Can I ship tires straight to the installer?
Yes. TireDrop ships free to any address in the 48 contiguous states and DC, and that includes a tire shop. Ask the shop first whether it accepts deliveries for customers, and agree on who calls whom when the tires arrive.
What should be included in a tire installation?
Ask the shop to spell it out. Mounting and balancing are the core of it. Valve stems, TPMS service, disposal of the old tires and any fees may be separate line items. USTMA's service guidance calls for replacing snap-in valve stems whenever tires are replaced.

chunks.title: How to Get Tires Installed After Buying Them Online
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Does TireDrop install tires outside South Florida?
No. TireDrop's installation, at the Extreme Tires shop in Sunrise or by mobile van, covers Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties only. Outside that area, orders ship free to the address you choose and you pick the installer.

chunks.title: A Glovebox Tire Kit for Florida Storms and Road Trips
chunks.text:
Travel & Roadside
A Glovebox Tire Kit for Florida Storms and Road Trips
A car emergency kit for Florida built around the tires: gauge, inflator, sealant kit limits, the spare, and the numbers to save before storms or a trip.
Why build the kit around the tires
Most car emergency kit lists are written for snow country: ice scrapers, blankets, cat litter for traction. In South Florida, the things that strand drivers look different. A flat from storm debris. A slow leak found on the way to the airport. An evacuation drive on a tire you meant to check last month.
So this kit starts with the general basics from Ready.gov and AAA, then adds the tire tools that actually get used here. Nothing on this list is a brand recommendation. Buy what fits your car and budget.

chunks.title: A Glovebox Tire Kit for Florida Storms and Road Trips
chunks.text:
The general basics
Ready.gov and AAA both publish car kit lists. The items that make sense year-round in Florida:
- Phone charger for the car
- First-aid kit
- Flashlight with fresh spare batteries
- Jumper cables or a portable jump pack
- Reflective triangles or flares to warn traffic
- Basic tools, plus duct tape
- Rain poncho and gloves. Tire trouble in an afternoon storm is common here.
- Drinking water, our own addition for the heat; swap it out every few months

chunks.title: A Glovebox Tire Kit for Florida Storms and Road Trips
chunks.text:
1. A tire pressure gauge
This is the one item NHTSA names directly: keep a tire pressure gauge in your vehicle. Its advice is to check all tires, including the spare, at least once a month when cold, meaning the car hasn't been driven for at least three hours. A simple dial or digital gauge is enough. Our guide to checking tire pressure compares the types, and our post on TPMS vs a gauge explains why the dash light isn't a substitute.

chunks.title: A Glovebox Tire Kit for Florida Storms and Road Trips
chunks.text:
2. A 12-volt inflator
A small compressor that plugs into the car's power outlet lets you top up a slow leak and get to a shop, rather than driving on a soft tire. Many cars without a spare already carry one as part of a sealant kit; check before you buy a second.
3. Know what you have instead of a spare
AAA found nearly one-third of new vehicles were sold without a spare tire, with a sealant and inflator kit or run-flat tires in its place. Open the trunk floor today and find out which you have:
- Compact spare: check its pressure, which is usually higher than your regular tires and printed on its label.
- Full-size spare: check its pressure and its DOT date; it can be as old as the car.
- Sealant kit: check the expiration date (more below).
- Run-flats: nothing to carry, but know your car's distance and speed limits.
Our spare tire types guide explains each one.

chunks.title: A Glovebox Tire Kit for Florida Storms and Road Trips
chunks.text:
4. Know your sealant kit's limits
Sealant kits are for small punctures in the tread. The limits vary by car, which is why your own manual is the source to trust:
Manual
Don't use the kit when
Speed after sealing
Tesla Model Y
Puncture larger than 1/4 inch (6 mm), severe tread damage, damaged sidewall
Drive within the limit shown on the kit, not at high speed or for long periods
Honda CR-V Hybrid (2025)
Puncture or cut larger than 3/16 inch (4 mm), damage to the sidewall or outside the contact area, more than one tire punctured
Do not exceed 50 mph
Tesla's manual also says not to remove a foreign object, such as a nail, that's embedded in the tire before sealing. Both treat the kit as a temporary repair to reach a tire shop.
Where is the puncture on your tire? See which zones can be repaired:

chunks.title: A Glovebox Tire Kit for Florida Storms and Road Trips
chunks.text:
5. Check the expiration date
AAA's research found inflator kits typically have a four- to eight-year shelf life. If your car is a few years old and you've never looked, the sealant may already be out of date. The date is printed on the canister or bottle.
6. The small things that save a lot of time
- The wheel lock key, if your car has locking lug nuts. Keep it where you can find it.
- The jack and lug wrench, if your car has a spare. Find them now.
- The owner's manual, or a saved copy on your phone, open to the flat-tire section.
- A piece of cardboard or a mat to kneel on.

chunks.title: A Glovebox Tire Kit for Florida Storms and Road Trips
chunks.text:
The numbers to save
- *347 reaches the Florida Highway Patrol and, on covered highways, FDOT's Road Rangers. Our post on what to do with a flat on I-95 explains what they do.
- Your roadside assistance number, from your insurer, your car's maker or a motor club.
Storm season additions
FDEM's 2026 hurricane guidance says a good rule of thumb is to keep fuel tanks at least halfway full throughout hurricane season, and EV batteries between 50 and 80 percent, depending on the manufacturer's advice. Before a storm, run through our hurricane car prep checklist, and after one, expect nails and debris on the roads; our post on storm cleanup nails covers what's repairable.

chunks.title: A Glovebox Tire Kit for Florida Storms and Road Trips
chunks.text:
Where to keep it, and when to check it
Keep the gauge in the glovebox or door pocket, where you'll actually reach for it. Everything else fits in a small bag in the trunk, next to the spare or the sealant kit so it's all in one place.
Then put two reminders in your phone: one in late May, before hurricane season starts on June 1, and one in November, before holiday travel. Each time, check the spare's pressure, the sealant's date, the flashlight batteries and the water.

chunks.title: A Glovebox Tire Kit for Florida Storms and Road Trips
chunks.text:
After you've used the kit
A sealed tire or a donut gets you to a shop. Tell the shop if you used sealant, and have the tire inspected from the inside. Can My Tire Be Repaired? walks through the limits. If it can't be saved, shop by size or vehicle. In Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we install at our Sunrise shop or with our mobile van. Shipping is free to the 48 contiguous states and DC.

chunks.title: A Glovebox Tire Kit for Florida Storms and Road Trips
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- NHTSA's advice is simple: keep a tire pressure gauge in your vehicle and check all tires, spare included, monthly.
- Sealant kits have hard limits. Tesla's manual stops at punctures over 1/4 inch; a Honda manual stops at 3/16 inch and says not to exceed 50 mph.
- Kits expire. AAA says inflator kits typically have a four- to eight-year shelf life, so check the date on yours.
- FDEM says keep the tank at least half full all hurricane season, and EV batteries between 50 and 80 percent.
- Save *347 and your roadside assistance number in your phone before you need them.

chunks.title: A Glovebox Tire Kit for Florida Storms and Road Trips
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What should be in a car emergency kit in Florida?
Start with Ready.gov and AAA's lists: phone charger, first-aid kit, flashlight with spare batteries, jumper cables or a jump pack, reflective triangles or flares, basic tools, gloves and a rain poncho. For the tires, add a pressure gauge, a 12-volt inflator, and whatever your car carries instead of a spare, plus the wheel lock key if you have locking lug nuts.
Should I keep a tire pressure gauge in my car?
Yes. NHTSA recommends keeping one in your vehicle. TPMS only warns when a tire is significantly low, and a gauge lets you check all four tires and the spare, cold, against the door placard pressure.
Do tire sealant kits work on every flat?

chunks.title: A Glovebox Tire Kit for Florida Storms and Road Trips
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
No. They're meant for small punctures in the tread. Tesla's Model Y manual says to call roadside assistance for punctures larger than 1/4 inch, severe tread damage or a damaged sidewall. A Honda CR-V Hybrid manual sets the limit at 3/16 inch and says not to use the kit if more than one tire is punctured. Read your own manual.
Does tire sealant expire?
Yes. AAA reported that inflator kits typically have a shelf life of four to eight years. Check the date printed on your sealant canister or bottle, and replace it if it has expired or been used.

chunks.title: Choosing Tires for a Honda Civic in South Florida
chunks.text:
Vehicle Guides
Choosing Tires for a Honda Civic in South Florida
Best tires for a Honda Civic, without rankings: Honda's replacement rules, Si and sport trims, bigger wheels, and wet grip on a commuter budget.
The commuter car with a sporty streak
The Civic does a lot of different jobs in South Florida. It's a first car, a student's car, a daily I-595 commuter, and in Si or sport trim, a weekend toy. That spread is why "best tires for a Civic" has no single answer.
We don't rank brands. This guide covers what Honda's manual asks for, how the sport trims change the choice, what bigger wheels really involve, and where a tight budget should go first.

chunks.title: Choosing Tires for a Honda Civic in South Florida
chunks.text:
Step 1: Start with Honda's rules
Honda's Civic owner's manual is short and specific. Replacement tires should be radials of the same size, load range, speed rating and maximum cold tire pressure rating as the originals, as shown on the tire's sidewall.
It also explains why. Honda says tires of a different size or construction can cause systems such as the ABS and Vehicle Stability Assist (VSA) to work incorrectly. If you replace wheels too, Honda asks that the wheel's specifications match the originals.
On replacing, Honda says it's best to replace all four tires at the same time. If that isn't possible, replace the front or rear tires in pairs.
Your size is on the Tire and Loading Information placard on the driver's door pillar. Our Find My Tires tool looks it up by year and trim, and the tire size decoder explains each part of the code.

chunks.title: Choosing Tires for a Honda Civic in South Florida
chunks.text:
Step 2: Know which Civic you have
Civic trims differ more than most cars in the same family, and the tire on your car tells you which kind of driver Honda had in mind.
- Base and mid trims usually run touring or all-season tires on smaller wheels, with taller sidewalls that absorb potholes and expansion joints.
- Sport trims and the Si use wider, lower-profile tires on bigger wheels, often with a higher speed rating. The steering feels sharper, and the tires usually cost more to replace.
- Some sport models come on summer tires. Honda's manual notes that summer tires are not designed for winter driving conditions. In South Florida that rarely matters, but it does if you drive north for the holidays.

chunks.title: Choosing Tires for a Honda Civic in South Florida
chunks.text:
Step 2: Know which Civic you have
Whatever the trim, the rule from Step 1 holds: match the size, load range and speed rating on the placard. Michelin explains that the load index is the most weight a tire can carry at its specified pressure, and the speed symbol is the top sustained speed it's rated for. Going below either is the one mistake to rule out.
Step 3: Thinking about bigger wheels?
Upsizing is a common Civic question, and the honest answer starts with Honda's own words: same size, or the ABS and VSA may not work as designed.

chunks.title: Choosing Tires for a Honda Civic in South Florida
chunks.text:
Step 3: Thinking about bigger wheels?
If you still want a change, plus sizing is the standard method. It pairs a larger wheel with a lower-profile tire, so the overall diameter stays close to the original. Michelin says a change from the specified size should be made only with guidance from a trained tire professional, because diameter affects the speedometer, clearance and the stability systems.
The trade-offs to accept going in:
- A firmer ride. Less sidewall means more of every bump reaches the cabin.
- More exposure to curb and pothole damage. A low-profile tire leaves less rubber between the rim and the road edge.
- Load index still has to match or beat the original. A low-profile tire in a new size must carry at least what the placard calls for.
See how a size change moves your speedometer:

chunks.title: Choosing Tires for a Honda Civic in South Florida
chunks.text:
Step 3: Thinking about bigger wheels?
Compares a current and a new tire size by overall diameter, sidewall height and revolutions per mile, and shows what the speedometer reads at 30, 45, 60 and 70 mph. The common 3% diameter figure is a guideline, not a fitment approval, so have fitment confirmed before you order.
Our guide to changing tire size covers clearance and load in more depth, and the full plus-size calculator compares any two sizes.

chunks.title: Choosing Tires for a Honda Civic in South Florida
chunks.text:
Step 4: Wet grip on a commuter budget
A Civic on the Turnpike in a July storm needs grip more than anything else. If money is tight, spend it in this order:
- The right load and speed rating. Non-negotiable, and it narrows the field quickly.
- Wet braking. The UTQG traction grade (AA, A, B or C) is a straight-line wet braking signal. Our UTQG guide explains the grades.
- Tread life. The UTQG treadwear grade compares a tire with a control tire on a government test course. NHTSA's consumer guide says real-world results can differ significantly, so compare grades within one brand, not as miles. A mileage warranty, where there is one, is the better guide.
- Noise and comfort. Worth paying for if the budget allows, especially on a long commute.

chunks.title: Choosing Tires for a Honda Civic in South Florida
chunks.text:
Step 4: Wet grip on a commuter budget
Tread depth matters as much as the tire you pick. AAA's testing found tires worn to 4/32 of an inch took an average of 87 feet longer to stop on wet pavement than new ones, and AAA recommends replacing at 4/32. Our post on why 4/32 matters in Florida rain explains the numbers.
Mistakes we'd steer you away from
- Choosing by price and size alone. Check the load index and speed rating against the placard before you compare prices.
- Mixing two different tires on one axle. Honda asks for pairs at minimum, and the same tire across an axle.
- Going big without checking the numbers. Diameter, load and clearance all have to work.
- Keeping summer tires on for a winter trip north. Honda's manual is clear they aren't designed for winter conditions.
- Running the last 2/32 through rainy season. Replace at 4/32 if you drive in afternoon downpours.

chunks.title: Choosing Tires for a Honda Civic in South Florida
chunks.text:
Civic vs Camry: different priorities
The Civic and Camry share a lot, but the questions differ. Camry owners mostly ask about comfort and noise on long highway miles; our Camry guide covers that. Civic owners ask more about sport trims, upsizing and stretching a budget, which is why this guide leads with them.
Keep a new set lasting
- Check pressure monthly, with the tires cold, against the door placard, not the sidewall maximum.
- Rotate on the schedule your Maintenance Minder or manual gives. Our rotation pattern tool shows the pattern for your drivetrain.
- Register your tires and check for recalls on NHTSA's site by vehicle and by tire.

- Honda's Civic manual calls for replacement radials with the same size, load range, speed rating and maximum cold pressure rating as the originals.
- Honda says a different tire size or construction can make the ABS and stability assist (VSA) work incorrectly, so bigger wheels are a fitment decision, not a style pick.

- On a budget, spend on wet grip and the right load and speed rating first. Compare treadwear grades within a brand, not as mileage.

chunks.title: Choosing Tires for a Honda Civic in South Florida
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What size tires does a Honda Civic use?
It depends on the model year and trim. The Civic has been sold with several wheel sizes, and sport trims use wider, lower-profile tires than base models. The Tire and Loading Information placard on the driver's door pillar lists your car's original size and pressure, or enter your year and trim in our Find My Tires tool.
Can I put bigger wheels and tires on my Civic?
Honda's manual asks for replacement tires of the same size, and warns that a different size can make the ABS and stability assist work incorrectly. If you still want to change size, keep the overall diameter close to the original, never go below the original load index or speed rating, and have the fitment confirmed by a tire professional first.
Do I need summer tires on a Civic Si?

chunks.title: Choosing Tires for a Honda Civic in South Florida
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
If your Si or other sport trim came on summer tires, Honda's replacement rule still applies: match the size, load range and speed rating. In South Florida many drivers choose a performance all-season tire instead for year-round rain. Honda's manual notes that summer tires aren't designed for winter driving, so plan ahead if you drive north in winter.
Do I have to replace all four tires on a Civic?
Honda's owner's manual says it's best to replace all four tires at the same time, and if that isn't possible, to replace the front or rear tires in pairs. If you only replace two, the new pair should be the same as the tires already on the car.

chunks.title: Honda CR-V Tires: AWD Matching and Rain Grip
chunks.text:
Vehicle Guides
Honda CR-V Tires: AWD Matching and Rain Grip
Best tires for a Honda CR-V, without rankings: what Honda's manual says about size, load and AWD, carrying a full family load, and wet grip in Florida.
The family crossover question
The CR-V spends a lot of its life full: kids, car seats, beach chairs, a week of groceries, a suitcase for every family member on the drive to Orlando. That's the angle most "best tires for CR-V" lists skip, and it's where this guide starts.
We don't rank brands. Instead, here's what Honda's own manual says, what a full load means for tire choice, and how to judge wet grip for South Florida.

chunks.title: Honda CR-V Tires: AWD Matching and Rain Grip
chunks.text:
Step 1: Honda's replacement rules
Honda's CR-V owner's manual is specific. Replacement tires should be radials of the same size, load range, speed rating and maximum cold tire pressure rating as the originals, as shown on the sidewall. It also says to use the size and type of tires the manual recommends.
The reason is spelled out too. Honda warns that tires of a different size or construction can cause the ABS, vehicle stability assist (VSA), hill start assist and the AWD system to malfunction. Modern crossovers read wheel speeds constantly, and mismatched tires confuse them.
If you're replacing wheels as well, Honda says the wheel specifications should match the originals, and to use only TPMS-specified wheels approved for the vehicle.
Find your size on the door placard, or let the decoder explain it:

chunks.title: Honda CR-V Tires: AWD Matching and Rain Grip
chunks.text:
Step 1: Honda's replacement rules
A size such as 225/45R17 94W breaks down into section width in millimeters (225), aspect ratio (45), radial construction (R), wheel diameter in inches (17), load index (94) and speed rating (W). The demo also works out sidewall height and overall diameter, including LT and flotation sizes like 33x12.50R20.
Step 2: All four, or matched pairs
Honda's manual says it's best to replace all four tires at the same time. If that isn't possible, replace the front or rear tires in pairs.
On an AWD CR-V, take the "all four" advice seriously. A new tire is taller than a worn one, and an AWD system notices differences between axles. Before you replace just two:
- Measure the remaining tires in three grooves each.
- Compare them with the new tire's tread depth.
- Check your manual for any limits.

chunks.title: Honda CR-V Tires: AWD Matching and Rain Grip
chunks.text:
Step 2: All four, or matched pairs
Our myth check on replacing all four tires compares what tire makers and other vehicle makers say, and our RAV4 guide covers the same question for the CR-V's closest rival.
Step 3: Loaded for a road trip
Every vehicle's door placard states the most it should carry. Under federal standard FMVSS No. 110, the Tire and Loading Information placard lists the vehicle's seating capacity and the maximum combined weight of occupants and cargo, along with the tire size and cold pressure.
What that means when you shop:
- Never go below the original load rating. The load index on the new tire must be at or above what Honda specifies.

chunks.title: Honda CR-V Tires: AWD Matching and Rain Grip
chunks.text:
Step 3: Loaded for a road trip
- XL is about load, not quality. Michelin explains that XL (extra load) tires are built to carry more weight at higher pressure than standard load tires of the same size. If your CR-V came on XL tires, replace them with XL. Our XL vs SL guide explains the difference.
- Pressure is part of capacity. A tire's load rating assumes correct inflation. Check pressure cold before a loaded trip, using the placard.
Our load index guide shows how to read the number on any tire.

chunks.title: Honda CR-V Tires: AWD Matching and Rain Grip
chunks.text:
Step 4: Rain grip for Broward roads
A family car spends a lot of time on wet school runs from May to October. Grip in the rain depends on two things you can check:
- The tire's wet-braking credentials. The UTQG traction grade (AA, A, B or C) is a straight-line wet braking signal; independent test results add hydroplaning and handling. See our UTQG guide.
- How much tread is left. AAA's tests found tires worn to 4/32 of an inch took an average of 87 feet longer to stop on wet pavement than new ones. AAA recommends replacing at 4/32.
Measure yours:

chunks.title: Honda CR-V Tires: AWD Matching and Rain Grip
chunks.text:
Step 5: Hybrid or gas, same rules
The CR-V Hybrid follows the same rules: match the size, load range, speed rating and pressure rating Honda specifies. Hybrid owners often care about rolling resistance because it affects fuel economy, so it's worth asking about once the spec is met. Correct pressure matters too; under-inflation costs mileage on any car.
Mistakes we'd steer you away from
- Picking a tire by size alone. Honda's manual asks for the same load range, speed rating and pressure rating too.
- Mixing tire constructions or sizes. Honda warns it can make the ABS, VSA and AWD systems malfunction.
- Packing for a road trip without checking pressure. A full car on under-inflated tires builds heat. Check cold, before you load up.
- Waiting for the wear bars before rainy season. Plan around 4/32, not 2/32. Our post on why 4/32 matters in Florida rain explains why.

chunks.title: Honda CR-V Tires: AWD Matching and Rain Grip
chunks.text:
Mistakes we'd steer you away from
- Swapping wheels without checking TPMS. Honda says to use only TPMS-specified wheels approved for the vehicle.
Before a loaded road trip
A few minutes in the driveway before the drive to Orlando or the Keys:
- Check pressure cold on all four tires, plus the spare if you have one, against the door placard.
- Look at the load. People plus luggage plus anything on a roof rack or hitch counts toward the placard's maximum.
- Measure the tread if it's been a while; long highway runs in summer rain are exactly where 4/32 matters.
- Scan the sidewalls for cuts or bulges from curbs and parking garages.

chunks.title: Honda CR-V Tires: AWD Matching and Rain Grip
chunks.text:
Keep it even
- Rotate on the schedule in your owner's manual or maintenance reminders. If none is given, USTMA's fallback is every 5,000 to 8,000 miles. Our rotation tool shows the pattern.
- Check pressure monthly, cold.
- Register your tires and check recalls on NHTSA's site.

chunks.title: Honda CR-V Tires: AWD Matching and Rain Grip
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What size tires does a Honda CR-V use?
It depends on the model year and trim, and Honda has used several wheel sizes on the CR-V. The Tire and Loading Information placard on the driver's door pillar and the owner's manual list the original size, load and pressure. You can also enter your year and trim in our Find My Tires tool.
Do I need to replace all four tires on an AWD CR-V?
Honda's owner's manual says it's best to replace all four tires at the same time, and if that isn't possible, to replace the front or rear tires in pairs. It also warns that tires of a different size or construction can cause the AWD system to malfunction. On AWD, measure the other tires before replacing only two.
Does the CR-V Hybrid need different tires?

chunks.title: Honda CR-V Tires: AWD Matching and Rain Grip
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
It needs tires that match the size, load range, speed rating and pressure rating Honda specifies for that model. Hybrid owners often look for low rolling resistance to protect fuel economy, but the placard specification comes first.
Should I get XL tires for my CR-V?
Only if the specification calls for it or you're replacing XL tires. The rule is to match or exceed the original load rating, never go below it. If your CR-V came on XL tires, replace them with XL. Keeping within the placard's maximum load matters more than the tire's marking.
