chunks.title: How Old Are Tires When You Buy Online? Read the DOT Date
chunks.text:
Buying & Price
How Old Are Tires When You Buy Online? Read the DOT Date
New tires can carry any build date. How to read the DOT date code when an online order arrives, what age guidance says, and what to check before mounting.
Four new tires, one small number
The box is on the porch. The tires smell new, the tread is perfect and the labels are still on. Then you spot four small digits near the rim and realize you have no idea when these tires were made.
That's a fair question to ask about any tire, and a common worry about buying online. Here's how to read the date, what the official guidance says about age, and what to do before a single tire is mounted.

chunks.title: How Old Are Tires When You Buy Online? Read the DOT Date
chunks.text:
The short answer: "new" means unused, not freshly built
A tire sold as new is a tire that hasn't been used. It isn't a promise about when it came off the line.
NHTSA has addressed this directly. In an interpretation letter about a tire that was several years old when it was sold as new, the agency said it has no regulation requiring a tire to be sold within a certain amount of time from its date of manufacture.
So the age isn't set by any rule. It's written on the tire. Every tire sold in the US carries a DOT tire identification number, and the last four digits tell you exactly how old it is. NHTSA's Tire Buyers' FAQ tells drivers to check that date when purchasing tires and to know their vehicle maker's recommended tire replacement timeframe.

chunks.title: How Old Are Tires When You Buy Online? Read the DOT Date
chunks.text:
The clock starts at the factory, not at your car
It's tempting to think a tire's life starts the day it's mounted. The tire makers don't see it that way.
- Michelin says its guidance (a thorough inspection every year from five years, and replacement ten years after manufacture) runs from the date of manufacture, whether the tire was in use or in storage.
- Bridgestone recommends replacing tires ten years after they were made, regardless of tread depth, with a professional inspection at least once a year from five years.
- NHTSA's TireWise guidance notes that some vehicle and tire makers recommend replacing tires that are 6 to 10 years old, regardless of treadwear.

chunks.title: How Old Are Tires When You Buy Online? Read the DOT Date
chunks.text:
The clock starts at the factory, not at your car
Storage matters too. Michelin's storage advice is a cool, dry, dark place away from heat sources and electric motors, because rubber does age on the shelf. You can't see a warehouse's conditions from your porch, which is one more reason the date code is worth reading.
How to read the date when the box arrives
Find the letters DOT on the sidewall near the rim. The number after it ends in four digits:
- the first two are the week of manufacture
- the last two are the year
NHTSA's example: 0308 means the third week of 2008. The full number may be stamped on only one side, so if you find DOT but no four-digit ending, check the other sidewall.
Type the four digits from each tire here to see its age:
A three-digit code means the tire was built before 2000. Our guide to reading the tire date code covers that case and the rest of the DOT number.

chunks.title: How Old Are Tires When You Buy Online? Read the DOT Date
chunks.text:
So what age is reasonable for a "new" tire?
Nobody publishes a single cut-off for tires at the point of purchase, and we won't invent one. What you can do is put the date next to the guidance that does exist:
Question
Where the answer comes from
When should this tire be replaced by age?
Your vehicle maker's owner's manual, then the tire maker (Bridgestone and Michelin: 10 years after manufacture)
When should it start getting yearly inspections?
Bridgestone and Michelin: from 5 years after manufacture
How much of that time is already used?
The four-digit DOT date code on each tire

chunks.title: How Old Are Tires When You Buy Online? Read the DOT Date
chunks.text:
So what age is reasonable for a "new" tire?
Think of it this way: every year between the build date and the day you mount the tire is a year off the time the tire makers expect it to stay in service. If your owner's manual sets a shorter timeframe than the tire maker, plan around the shorter one. Our guide to how old is too old for tires lays the guidance out side by side.
Online or local, tires travel the same road
A tire on a local shop's rack and a tire shipped to your door both started at a plant and moved through distribution before they reached you. The date code doesn't care which route it took. That's why the check is the same either way: read the four digits before the tires go on the car.
What changes with an online order is timing. At a counter, you can read the sidewall before you pay. Online, the first chance is when the box arrives, so make that moment count.

chunks.title: How Old Are Tires When You Buy Online? Read the DOT Date
chunks.text:
How TireDrop handles it
TireDrop doesn't keep its own stock. Orders ship from distributor warehouses, which move tires through rather than holding them on a showroom floor. We don't print an age promise on top of that, because the date that matters is the one molded into your tires, and you can read it yourself.
If a date code on your order is older than you expected, call (954) 773-1896 before anything is mounted. Under our terms, a tire that has been mounted on a wheel can't be returned, even if it was never driven on. The conversation has to happen while the tires are still unmounted. Our shipping page covers how damaged or wrong tires are handled.

chunks.title: How Old Are Tires When You Buy Online? Read the DOT Date
chunks.text:
The arrival checklist
Do this before the tires go to an installer, or before the installer mounts them:
- Count and match. Same brand and model on every tire you ordered.
- Check the size, load index and speed rating against your door placard, not just your old tires.
- Read all four date codes. Write them down by position.
- Look for shipping damage along the beads and sidewalls.
- Photograph each full DOT number. A recall lookup needs the whole number, not just the date.
- Raise anything odd before mounting. Once a tire is on a wheel, your options narrow.
If you're shipping straight to an installer, ask them to read the date codes to you, or to set the tires aside until you've seen them. Our guide on getting tires installed after buying online covers that handoff and the questions to ask the shop.

chunks.title: How Old Are Tires When You Buy Online? Read the DOT Date
chunks.text:
After the install
The date code keeps being useful long after the box is gone:
- Recalls. Tire recalls are tracked by the tire identification number, so keep your photos.
- The five-year mark. Note when your tires reach five years from their build date. That's when Bridgestone and Michelin want a professional looking at them every year.
- Mixed sets. If you later replace two tires, the set will carry two ages. Track both.
Want a quick read on tread and age together? Try Do I Need Tires Yet?. Ready to shop? Browse by size or vehicle, and read the dates when your order arrives.

chunks.title: How Old Are Tires When You Buy Online? Read the DOT Date
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- "New" means unused, not freshly built. NHTSA has said it has no regulation requiring a tire to be sold within a set time of its manufacture date.
- A tire's age starts at the four-digit DOT date code, whether it was on a car or sitting in a warehouse.
- NHTSA's Tire Buyers' FAQ says to check that date when you buy, and to know your vehicle maker's replacement timeframe.
- Check every tire's date when the box arrives and before anything is mounted. A mounted tire can't be sent back.
- Keep a photo of each full DOT number. It's what a recall lookup needs.

chunks.title: How Old Are Tires When You Buy Online? Read the DOT Date
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How old can new tires be when you buy them?
There's no single legal limit. NHTSA has said it has no regulation requiring a tire to be sold within a certain amount of time from its date of manufacture. Its Tire Buyers' FAQ suggests checking the date code when you buy and knowing your vehicle maker's recommended replacement timeframe, so you can judge whether a given date suits you.
Where do I find the date on a new tire?
Look for the letters DOT on the sidewall near the rim. The last four digits of the number that follows are the week and year the tire was made, so 0308 means the third week of 2008. NHTSA notes the full number may be on only one side, so check both sidewalls.
Do unused tires age in storage?

chunks.title: How Old Are Tires When You Buy Online? Read the DOT Date
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Yes. Michelin's guidance is that its five-year inspection and ten-year replacement timeline runs from the date of manufacture, whether the tire was in use or in storage. Storage conditions affect how a tire ages, but the clock starts at the DOT date.
What should I do if an online order arrives with an older date than I expected?
Raise it before anything is mounted, because a mounted tire generally can't be returned. Photograph the full DOT number on each tire and call the seller. For a TireDrop order, call (954) 773-1896 before the tires go on a wheel.

chunks.title: Hurricane Car Prep Checklist: The Tire Check First
chunks.text:
Hurricanes & Flooding
Hurricane Car Prep Checklist: The Tire Check First
A hurricane car prep checklist for South Florida that starts with tires: tread, pressure, the spare, a half tank, your zone and what to check afterward.
By TireDrop Team, Extreme Tires, Sunrise FL·Published Sep 30, 2026·Updated Sep 30, 2026·5 min read
Why tires go at the top of the list
Every South Florida hurricane checklist covers water, batteries and shutters. Fewer mention the four things that have to carry you out if an evacuation order comes.
Atlantic hurricane season runs June 1 to November 30, per NOAA. That leaves the rest of October and all of November. The best time to find a worn tire or a flat spare is on a quiet weekday afternoon in Sunrise, not on the shoulder of I-95 with half of Broward headed the same way.

chunks.title: Hurricane Car Prep Checklist: The Tire Check First
chunks.text:
Why tires go at the top of the list
So here's the order we'd do it in: a 15-minute tire check now, a short list for when a storm is forecast, and what to look at after it passes.
Now, while the sky is clear: the 15-minute check
1. Tread depth
Grab a penny, a quarter or a tread depth gauge and check three grooves on each tire: inside, center and outside.
- 2/32 of an inch is where NHTSA says to replace. That's the depth where the built-in wear bars sit flush with the tread, and where Lincoln's whole head shows in the penny test.
- 4/32 is where AAA recommends replacing. In its wet-road testing at 60 mph, tires worn to 4/32 took an average of 87 feet longer to stop than new ones.
An evacuation drive in tropical-storm rain is exactly the wet road AAA tested for. Slide the gauge to see where your reading falls:
Our tread depth chart has the full breakdown in 32nds and millimeters.

chunks.title: Hurricane Car Prep Checklist: The Tire Check First
chunks.text:
2. Pressure, cold
Set all four tires to the pressure on your door placard, not the number on the sidewall. NHTSA defines "cold" as parked for at least three hours, so do it first thing in the morning before the car moves. A loaded car with low tires on a long, hot drive is the combination you want to avoid.
If your TPMS light is already on, handle that first. Our TPMS light guide explains what solid and flashing mean.

chunks.title: Hurricane Car Prep Checklist: The Tire Check First
chunks.text:
3. Sidewalls
Look along both sidewalls for cuts, scrapes, bulges or cracks. Run a hand around the tread for nails or screws. If you find anything, have it inspected now, while shops are open on a normal schedule.
4. The spare, and what kind it is
NHTSA's advice is to check pressure monthly on every tire, spare included. Pull the trunk floor up and find out what you actually have:
- A full-size spare. Check its pressure and its date code like any other tire.
- A compact temporary spare. Its speed and distance limits are printed on the spare or its label, and in your owner's manual. Read them now.
- A sealant and inflator kit, or nothing. Some cars have no spare at all. Know that before you're relying on it.
Our guide to spare tire types covers each one.

chunks.title: Hurricane Car Prep Checklist: The Tire Check First
chunks.text:
Know your zone and keep the tank half full
Two Florida Division of Emergency Management resources are worth five minutes this week:
- Know Your Zone. Enter your address on FloridaDisaster.org and it shows whether you're in an evacuation zone. Save a screenshot; a storm is no time to find out.
- Halfway Full, Halfway There. FDEM asks residents to keep at least half a tank of gas all season, because storm prep and evacuation orders drive up demand at gas stations and chargers. For electric vehicles, its guidance is to keep the battery between 50% and 80%, depending on the vehicle and what its manual recommends.
Half a tank you already have is worth more than a full tank you're waiting in line for.

chunks.title: Hurricane Car Prep Checklist: The Tire Check First
chunks.text:
When a storm is in the forecast
Once there's a named storm with Broward in the cone, the to-do list gets long fast. Keep the tire part short:
- Recheck pressure cold on all four and the spare.
- Handle any tire you flagged earlier as soon as you can. If a tire is at or near 4/32, has a bulge, or keeps losing air, this is not the week to hope.
- Pack a small kit: a tire gauge, the owner's manual, a phone charger and a flashlight.
- Photograph your DOT codes and tread if you want a record for later.
Extreme Tires in Sunrise installs tires in the shop and by mobile van across its local install area, and repairs punctures after an internal inspection. Storms change everyone's schedule, including ours, so we won't promise availability around one. Call (954) 773-1896 to ask.

chunks.title: Hurricane Car Prep Checklist: The Tire Check First
chunks.text:
After the storm passes
The roads you drove last week may not be the same roads now. What to watch for:
- Floodwater. Don't drive into it. The National Weather Service says 12 inches of rushing water can carry away most cars and 2 feet can carry away SUVs and trucks, and the road underneath may be damaged. Turn around.
- Debris. Roofing nails, screws and broken glass end up in the street during cleanup. After driving through debris, walk around the car and look at the tread. If you find a nail or screw, have the tire inspected. Our post on storm cleanup nails covers which punctures can be repaired.

chunks.title: Hurricane Car Prep Checklist: The Tire Check First
chunks.text:
After the storm passes
- A car that sat in water. NHTSA's guidance is not to drive a flooded vehicle until a technician has checked it, because damage may not be visible. For hybrids and EVs, NHTSA also says not to park a flood-damaged vehicle with a lithium-ion battery in a garage or within 50 feet of a home, another vehicle or anything combustible. More in our post on a car that sat in floodwater.
- Warning lights. A TPMS light, a pull to one side or a new vibration after driving through storm damage are all reasons to have the tires and wheels looked at.

Deciding when to replace? Our guide to the best time to buy tires in South Florida lines tire timing up with the rainy and hurricane seasons.
Want a second opinion on your readings? Run them through Do I Need Tires Yet?, and if a tire needs replacing, shop by size with installation in Sunrise or by mobile van in the local install area.

chunks.title: Hurricane Car Prep Checklist: The Tire Check First
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Atlantic hurricane season runs June 1 to November 30. Do the tire check while the sky is clear, not when the cone is on the news.
- Measure tread in three grooves: NHTSA says replace at 2/32, and AAA recommends replacing at 4/32 for wet roads.
- Set pressure to the door placard, cold, and check the spare too.
- Florida's emergency managers ask you to keep at least half a tank of gas, or an EV at least half charged, all season.
- Never drive into floodwater. The National Weather Service says 12 inches of moving water can carry away most cars.

chunks.title: Hurricane Car Prep Checklist: The Tire Check First
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What should I check on my car before a hurricane?
Start with tires: tread depth, cold pressure against the door placard, sidewall damage and the spare. Then fuel or charge, since Florida's emergency managers recommend keeping at least half a tank or half a charge all season, and know your evacuation zone.
Should I check my spare tire before hurricane season?
Yes. NHTSA's guidance is to check pressure monthly on all tires, spare included. Also confirm what kind of spare you have. Many cars carry a compact temporary spare or a repair kit, and their limits are printed on the spare or in the owner's manual.
How much gas should I keep during hurricane season?
The Florida Division of Emergency Management's Halfway Full, Halfway There campaign asks residents to keep at least half a tank of gas, or an electric vehicle at least half charged, throughout hurricane season.

chunks.title: Hurricane Car Prep Checklist: The Tire Check First
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Can I drive through standing water after a storm?
Don't. The National Weather Service says 12 inches of rushing water can carry away most cars and 2 feet can carry away SUVs and trucks, and a road can be damaged under the water where you can't see it. Turn around.

chunks.title: How to Avoid Hydroplaning in Broward's Afternoon Storms
chunks.text:
Rain, Heat & Weather
How to Avoid Hydroplaning in Broward's Afternoon Storms
How to avoid hydroplaning when a Broward storm hits at rush hour: tread and pressure first, habits in the rain, and what to do if the car starts to float.
By TireDrop Team, Extreme Tires, Sunrise FL·Published Sep 30, 2026·Updated Sep 30, 2026·5 min read
The 4 p.m. storm, explained by the calendar
If you commute in Broward, you know the pattern: a clear morning, clouds building through the afternoon, and a downpour right as everyone gets on I-595.
That isn't bad luck. It's the season. The National Weather Service office in Miami defines South Florida's rainy season as May 15 to October 15, the stretch when 60 to 70 percent of the year's average rainfall arrives, with showers and thunderstorms developing almost every day.

chunks.title: How to Avoid Hydroplaning in Broward's Afternoon Storms
chunks.text:
The 4 p.m. storm, explained by the calendar
NWS Miami also notes that June is usually the wettest month, followed by September and August. The calendar end date doesn't switch the rain off. But it's a good reminder that for five months a year, driving on wet pavement is the normal commute here, not the exception.
Hydroplaning in one minute
Your tread's job in the rain is to move water out from under the tire so rubber can stay on the road. When water arrives faster than the grooves can clear it, pressure builds under the tire and lifts the tread off the pavement. The tire is now riding on water instead of road.
When that happens, steering, braking and acceleration stop working the way you expect until the tire touches down again. The factors that make it more likely all push in the same direction:
- More speed gives water less time to escape.
- Less tread gives water less room to escape.

chunks.title: How to Avoid Hydroplaning in Broward's Afternoon Storms
chunks.text:
Hydroplaning in one minute
- More water, like a puddle or a low spot, gives the tread more to move.
There's no single speed or water depth where it starts for every car, and you should be skeptical of anyone who gives you one. For the physics in more depth, see our Learn guide on hydroplaning.
Why wet roads deserve the respect
The Federal Highway Administration's road weather numbers are worth knowing. Based on 10-year averages from 2007 to 2016:
- 75 percent of weather-related crashes happened on wet pavement.
- 47 percent happened during rainfall.
Snow and ice get the headlines nationally. Rain and wet pavement are what actually dominate the weather-crash numbers, and South Florida gets a lot of both.

chunks.title: How to Avoid Hydroplaning in Broward's Afternoon Storms
chunks.text:
Before the storm: the tire side
You can't control the weather. You can control what's touching the road.
Tread depth. The usual replacement line and the wet-weather line aren't the same. The familiar penny-test line is 2/32 of an inch. AAA recommends replacing at 4/32 after testing new tires against tires worn to that depth on wet pavement at 60 mph: the worn tires took an average of 87 feet longer to stop, a 43 percent increase. Our tread depth chart shows both lines in 32nds and millimeters.
Quarter test. Put a quarter upside down in a groove. If you can see all of Washington's head, you're at about 4/32.
Pressure. Set tires to the pressure on your door placard, checked cold. Don't go by the number on the sidewall; that's a maximum, not a target. Our max PSI myth check explains the difference.

chunks.title: How to Avoid Hydroplaning in Broward's Afternoon Storms
chunks.text:
Before the storm: the tire side
If your readings are close to 4/32, run them through Do I Need Tires Yet? before the next storm rather than after it. Replacing only two? The new pair goes on the rear axle for wet grip; here's why the back, not the front.
In the storm: how to avoid hydroplaning
Here's the short list, drawn from AAA's wet-weather advice and Florida law:
- Slow down. Speed is the one factor you control on the spot.
- Turn off cruise control. AAA's reasoning: you may need to slow by easing off the accelerator, and you can't do that while cruise control is holding a speed.
- Leave more room. Increase your following distance so you don't need hard braking.
- Avoid sudden moves. No sharp steering or sudden braking on wet pavement.
- Steer around standing water when you can do it without changing lanes abruptly. Puddles hide depth, and they're where tread gets overwhelmed.

chunks.title: How to Avoid Hydroplaning in Broward's Afternoon Storms
chunks.text:
In the storm: how to avoid hydroplaning
- Headlights on. Florida Statute 316.217 requires lighted lamps during any rain, smoke or fog. It's also how the driver behind you sees you through the spray.
- Don't drive into flooded roads. If you can't see the pavement markings under the water, you can't see how deep it is. Turn around.
Before the drive, AAA also suggests checking your tires, wipers, lights and washer fluid, and building extra time into the trip when heavy rain is forecast.

chunks.title: How to Avoid Hydroplaning in Broward's Afternoon Storms
chunks.text:
If the car starts to float
If the steering suddenly feels disconnected from the road, AAA's guidance is:
- Ease off the accelerator. Don't stomp the brakes.
- Avoid hard braking. Braking hard while the tires are on water can make things worse.
- Steer gently in the direction you want to go. Small inputs, not a jerk of the wheel.
- Wait for the tires to grip again before making normal steering or braking inputs.
Then, once you're through it, slow down further for the rest of the storm.

chunks.title: How to Avoid Hydroplaning in Broward's Afternoon Storms
chunks.text:
After the storm
A few things are worth a look after a heavy-rain season:
- Tread. Recheck depth monthly. Wet-weather grip fades gradually, and it's easy to miss.
- Pulling or vibration. If you hit a hidden pothole in standing water, a new pull or shake is a reason to have the tires and alignment checked. Extreme Tires does alignments in the Sunrise shop.
- TPMS light. If it comes on, check pressures with a gauge and have any tire that keeps losing air inspected.

chunks.title: How to Avoid Hydroplaning in Broward's Afternoon Storms
chunks.text:

AAA: replace at 4/32. Placard is the vehicle maker's number.

Not sure how much tread is enough? Our post on why 4/32 matters more than 2/32 in Florida rain explains the numbers.

Key takeaways
- NWS Miami puts South Florida's rainy season at May 15 to October 15, with showers and thunderstorms nearly every day.
- Per FHWA's 10-year averages (2007 to 2016), 75% of weather-related crashes happen on wet pavement and 47% during rainfall.
- Worn tread moves less water. AAA recommends replacing tires at 4/32, not the 2/32 minimum.
- In the rain: slow down, turn off cruise control, leave more room and keep headlights on, which Florida law requires in rain.
- If the car starts to float, ease off the gas, avoid hard braking and steer gently where you want to go.

chunks.title: How to Avoid Hydroplaning in Broward's Afternoon Storms
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How do you avoid hydroplaning?
Keep tread depth and tire pressure where they belong, slow down on wet roads, avoid standing water when you can, turn off cruise control and leave extra following distance. AAA also advises avoiding sudden braking or steering in the rain.
What should you do if you hydroplane?
AAA's advice is to ease off the accelerator, avoid hard braking and steer gently in the direction you want the car to go, then wait for the tires to regain contact with the road before making normal steering or braking inputs.
Is there a speed where hydroplaning starts?
There's no single number that applies to every car. Tread depth, water depth, speed and the road surface all play a part, which is why the reliable advice is simply to slow down and keep tires in good shape.
Do I need my headlights on in the rain in Florida?

chunks.title: How to Avoid Hydroplaning in Broward's Afternoon Storms
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Yes. Florida Statute 316.217 requires lighted lamps during any rain, smoke or fog, in addition to the hours between sunset and sunrise.

chunks.title: Jeep Wrangler Tires for Street, Sand and Rain
chunks.text:
Vehicle Guides
Jeep Wrangler Tires for Street, Sand and Rain
Best tires for a Jeep Wrangler, without rankings: highway vs all-terrain for a mostly-pavement Jeep, bigger tires, five-tire rotation and Florida rain.
The Jeep that mostly lives on pavement
Plenty of Wranglers in Broward never see a trail. They see I-95, school pickup lines, beach parking lots and, from May to October, a lot of afternoon rain. Tire marketing for Jeeps is all mud and rocks, but the right tire starts with where your miles actually happen.
We don't rank brands. This guide covers how to pick a tread type, what the owner's manual says about size, how bigger tires change things, and why the spare belongs in the conversation.

chunks.title: Jeep Wrangler Tires for Street, Sand and Rain
chunks.text:
Step 1: Be honest about your driving
Tire makers group Jeep tires into three main families. Our all-terrain vs highway guide goes deeper, but in short:
- Highway (H/T). Built for pavement. Bridgestone describes a smoother, quieter ride and efficient everyday performance.
- All-terrain (A/T). Deeper tread, wider grooves and larger blocks than a highway tire, for traction on dirt, gravel, grass and sand, usually with more road noise.
- Mud-terrain (M/T). Large blocks and wide voids that clear mud. Tire makers note the trade-off: more noise, less on-road grip and shorter tread life.
A quick way to choose:
Your week
Tread type to look at first
Commuting, errands, highway trips
Highway
Mostly pavement, some dirt roads, boat ramps or sandy lots
All-terrain
Regular trail days in mud
Mud-terrain, with the on-road trade-offs

chunks.title: Jeep Wrangler Tires for Street, Sand and Rain
chunks.text:
Step 1: Be honest about your driving
Where beach driving is allowed at all, local rules come first, and many beaches don't allow it. If you air down for soft sand anywhere, follow the tire maker's guidance and put the placard pressure back before you're on pavement.
Step 2: What the manual says about size
The Wrangler owner's manual tells you not to use a tire size, load rating or speed rating other than the one specified for your vehicle, and points you to the Tire and Loading Information placard on the driver's door for the details. It also warns that replacing the original tires with a different size may result in false speedometer and odometer readings.
That's the starting point for any Wrangler shopping list:
- Read the size, load index and speed rating on your placard or current tires.
- Decide on the tread type from Step 1.

chunks.title: Jeep Wrangler Tires for Street, Sand and Rain
chunks.text:
Step 2: What the manual says about size
- Check whether the tire you like comes in a P-metric or LT version of your size. Many all-terrain and mud-terrain sizes are LT tires, which use load ranges and different pressures. Our LT vs P-metric guide explains what changes.
Step 3: Bigger tires, with eyes open
"What's the biggest tire I can fit?" is the most-asked Jeep tire question, and the answer depends on the model, the trim and any lift. Before you commit:
- Overall diameter moves the speedometer. A taller tire makes it read slower than your true speed. Michelin says a change from the specified size should be made only with guidance from a trained tire professional.
- Clearance matters at full steering lock and full suspension travel, not just parked.
- Load index can't drop. A bigger tire still has to carry at least what the placard calls for.

chunks.title: Jeep Wrangler Tires for Street, Sand and Rain
chunks.text:
Step 3: Bigger tires, with eyes open
- The spare has to fit too. A bigger set usually means a bigger spare and a check of the carrier.
See what a size change does to your speedometer:
Compares a current and a new tire size by overall diameter, sidewall height and revolutions per mile, and shows what the speedometer reads at 30, 45, 60 and 70 mph. The common 3% diameter figure is a guideline, not a fitment approval, so have fitment confirmed before you order.
The full plus-size calculator compares any two sizes. If you're adding a lift first, we fit lift kits at our Sunrise shop.

chunks.title: Jeep Wrangler Tires for Street, Sand and Rain
chunks.text:
Step 4: Rain is the real test
South Florida's rainy season runs from mid-May to mid-October, and a Jeep's tall, boxy shape doesn't change the physics of standing water. Two things you control:
- Tread depth, measured properly. Big A/T and M/T blocks can look deep while the grooves that clear water are shallow. AAA's testing found tires worn to 4/32 of an inch took an average of 87 feet longer to stop on wet pavement than new ones, and AAA recommends replacing at 4/32.
- Pressure, checked cold. Use the placard number, or the load-and-inflation guidance from the tire maker for an LT size.
Our post on why 4/32 matters in Florida rain explains the numbers.

chunks.title: Jeep Wrangler Tires for Street, Sand and Rain
chunks.text:
Step 5: Put the spare in the rotation
Many Wranglers carry a spare that matches the other four. Mopar's own tire guide says that if you have a full-size spare, like on a Jeep Wrangler, you can include it in the rotation, and to check your owner's manual or ask a technician for the pattern. Mopar describes the rearward cross as its suggested method for most vehicles.
Five evenly worn tires mean the spare is a real match on the day you need it, and the wear is spread across five tires instead of four. Our rotation pattern tool shows the four-tire patterns; for five, follow your manual. While you're at it, register the new tires and check for recalls by vehicle and by tire on NHTSA's site.

chunks.title: Jeep Wrangler Tires for Street, Sand and Rain
chunks.text:
Mistakes we'd steer you away from
- Buying a mud-terrain tire for a pavement Jeep. You pay for it in noise, rain grip and tread life.
- Going bigger without checking load and clearance. Diameter is only one of the numbers.
- Leaving the spare out of the plan. A new set and an old spare don't match.
- Trusting the look of the tread. Measure in a main groove, not on a block edge.

chunks.title: Jeep Wrangler Tires for Street, Sand and Rain
chunks.text:
The Wrangler checklist
Check
Where to find it
What to look for
Size, load and speed rating
Door placard, owner's manual
As specified, or a professionally confirmed alternative
Tread type
Your actual driving
Highway, all-terrain or mud-terrain
LT or P-metric
Tire sidewall
Load range and pressure that suit your use
Spare
Carrier and spare sidewall
Same size and type if it joins the rotation
Wet grip
Tread gauge, AAA
Replace at 4/32
When you're ready, shop by size or compare options with Find My Tires. Shipping is free to the 48 contiguous states and DC, and in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we install at our Sunrise shop or by mobile van.

chunks.title: Jeep Wrangler Tires for Street, Sand and Rain
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Choose the tread for where your miles really happen. Most South Florida Wranglers live on pavement and in summer rain, not on trails.
- The Wrangler owner's manual asks for the tire size, load rating and speed rating specified for the vehicle, and warns that a different size can throw off the speedometer and odometer.
- Many all-terrain and mud-terrain sizes are LT tires, with different load ranges and pressures. Check the placard before you switch.
- If your spare matches the other four, Mopar says it can join the rotation. Five even tires stay matched longer.
- Plan to replace at 4/32 for rain. Big tread blocks look deep long after wet grip has started to fade.

chunks.title: Jeep Wrangler Tires for Street, Sand and Rain
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Should I get all-terrain or highway tires for my Wrangler?
Pick by your driving, not the look. Highway tires are built for pavement and a quieter ride. All-terrain tires have deeper tread and bigger blocks for dirt, gravel and sand, usually with more road noise. If nearly all your miles are on pavement, a highway tire is aimed more squarely at that use.
Can I put 33-inch tires on a stock Wrangler?
It depends on the model, trim and any lift. The owner's manual asks for the size specified for your vehicle and warns that a different size can make the speedometer and odometer read wrong. A bigger tire also changes clearance and load. Have the fitment checked by a tire professional before you order.
Should I rotate my spare into the set?

chunks.title: Jeep Wrangler Tires for Street, Sand and Rain
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
If the spare is the same size and type as the other four, Mopar says you can include it in the rotation. Keeping all five evenly worn means the spare is a true match when you need it. Check your owner's manual for the pattern.
Are mud-terrain tires a bad idea for Florida rain?
They're a trade-off. Tire makers note that mud-terrain tires give up on-road grip, noise and tread life for traction in mud. For a Jeep that rarely leaves pavement, an all-terrain or highway tire usually fits South Florida weather better.

chunks.title: Driving Through Salt Water? King Tides and Your Wheels
chunks.text:
Hurricanes & Flooding
Driving Through Salt Water? King Tides and Your Wheels
Driving through salt water on a king tide day? What tidal flooding is, why salt is harder on a car than rain, and a simple rinse-and-check routine after.
The flood that shows up on a sunny day
You know the scene. Blue sky, no rain in the forecast, and a stretch of Las Olas or A1A under several inches of water anyway. Drivers slow down, look at each other, and roll through.
That's a king tide. The water isn't rain. It's the ocean, pushing up through storm drains and over low spots. And that means it's salt water, which is a different problem for a car than an afternoon downpour.

chunks.title: Driving Through Salt Water? King Tides and Your Wheels
chunks.text:
What a king tide actually is
King tide isn't a scientific term. NOAA calls it a popular, non-scientific name for an exceptionally high tide. The astronomy behind it: when a new or full moon lines up with the moon at perigee, its closest point to Earth, tides run higher than usual. NOAA's tides and currents FAQ says these "perigean spring tides" happen six to eight times a year.
The flooding they cause has an official name too. NOAA calls it high tide flooding, also known as sunny-day or nuisance flooding: ocean water that covers low-lying areas at high tide, spilling onto streets or bubbling up from storm drains. NOAA says it's happening more often every year as sea levels rise.
In Broward, it clusters in the fall. The City of Fort Lauderdale posts the season's predicted king tide dates on its King Tides page. Two things to know about those dates:

chunks.title: Driving Through Salt Water? King Tides and Your Wheels
chunks.text:
What a king tide actually is
- They're predictions from tide tables. Wind and rain can push the water higher than forecast, or keep it lower.
- High water usually peaks around high tide, so the same street can be passable a few hours later. If you can wait it out, wait it out.
Why salt water is harder on your car
Rain is fresh water. Tidal floodwater is salt water, and salt speeds up corrosion.
AAA's advice on flood-damaged cars draws the line clearly: a car damaged by fresh water has a better chance of being repaired than one damaged by salt water, because salt is highly corrosive to both the interior and the mechanical parts.
A drive through a few inches of tidal water isn't the same as a car sitting in a flood. But the parts that meet the splash are the parts that live closest to the road:
- wheels and lug hardware
- brake components
- suspension parts
- the whole underside of the car

chunks.title: Driving Through Salt Water? King Tides and Your Wheels
chunks.text:
Why salt water is harder on your car
NHTSA has made the same point about salt in another context. In a 2015 safety advisory about brake-line corrosion from winter road salt, it urged drivers to wash the underside of their vehicles to remove salt and to have brake lines inspected for corrosion. Salt is salt, whether it came from a snowplow or Port Everglades.
Before you drive through it
The best tide-day strategy is not to drive through it at all.
The National Weather Service's Turn Around Don't Drown guidance is blunt: 12 inches of rushing water can carry away most cars, and 2 feet can carry away SUVs and trucks. You also can't see what's under the surface. A road can be damaged beneath standing water with no sign from above.
Practical options on a king tide morning:
- Check the tide and local alerts before you leave if your route runs near the Intracoastal or the beach.

chunks.title: Driving Through Salt Water? King Tides and Your Wheels
chunks.text:
Before you drive through it
- Detour to higher streets, even if it costs you ten minutes.
- Wait for the tide to fall when the trip can move.
- If you truly can't tell how deep it is, turn around.
Already drove through it? The rinse routine
If you went through salt water, do this soon after:
- Rinse the underside. A car wash with an underbody spray or a garden hose aimed under the car both work. Get the wheel wells.
- Rinse the wheels and brakes. Spray through the wheel spokes, not just the face of the wheel.
- Rinse again if you drove through it more than once, or on several days during the tide cycle.
That's it. You're not trying to detail the car, just get the salt off before it sits.

chunks.title: Driving Through Salt Water? King Tides and Your Wheels
chunks.text:
A tide-day routine for people who live near the water
If you live or park east of US-1 or along the Intracoastal, a few habits help during the fall king tides:
When
Habit
Before the season
Save your city's king tide page and sign up for local alerts
Predicted tide days
Check the time of high tide before you leave; plan trips around it
Parking overnight
Park on higher ground when a high tide is predicted, if you can
After any salt-water drive
Rinse the underside, wheel wells and wheels with fresh water
Monthly
Look and listen for brake, steering or TPMS changes
None of this is complicated. It just works better as a routine than as a scramble on the morning the street floods.

chunks.title: Driving Through Salt Water? King Tides and Your Wheels
chunks.text:
Signs it's time to have it inspected
Watch the car for the next week or two. Have a technician take a look if you notice:
- New brake noise, like grinding or squealing that wasn't there before
- A pull to one side when braking or driving straight
- A new vibration through the steering wheel or seat
- A TPMS light that comes on and stays on (our TPMS light guide explains what it means)
- Water inside the car. That's no longer a splash. Treat it as a flooded vehicle and don't drive it until it's been checked. Our post on what to check after a car sits in floodwater covers that case.
Extreme Tires in Sunrise does brake repair and alignments in the shop, and tire rotations, balancing and TPMS service at the shop or by mobile van in the local install area. If something feels off after tide season, call (954) 773-1896 and ask, or book an appointment.

chunks.title: Driving Through Salt Water? King Tides and Your Wheels
chunks.text:
Signs it's time to have it inspected
And if the rest of your storm-season prep is still on the list, our hurricane car prep checklist starts with the tires.
Key takeaways
- A king tide is a popular name for an exceptionally high tide. NOAA's term for the street flooding it causes is high tide flooding.
- Tidal floodwater is salt water, and AAA notes salt is far more corrosive to a car than fresh water.
- Don't drive into water you can't see the bottom of. The National Weather Service says 12 inches of moving water can carry away most cars.
- If you did drive through it, rinse the underside and wheels with fresh water soon after.
- New brake noise, a pull, a vibration or a TPMS light afterward are reasons to have it inspected.

chunks.title: Driving Through Salt Water? King Tides and Your Wheels
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What is a king tide?
NOAA calls it a popular, non-scientific term for an exceptionally high tide. It happens when the new or full moon lines up with the moon at its closest point to Earth, which NOAA says occurs six to eight times a year.
Is it bad to drive through salt water?
Salt water is corrosive, and AAA notes a car damaged by fresh water has a better chance of repair than one damaged by salt water. Avoid it when you can. If you can't, rinse the underside and wheels with fresh water afterward and watch for brake or handling changes.
Should I wash my car after driving through a flooded street?
Yes. Rinse the underside, wheel wells and wheels with fresh water. NHTSA has urged drivers to wash the underside of their vehicles to remove corrosive salt and to have brake lines inspected for corrosion.
When are king tides in Fort Lauderdale?

chunks.title: Driving Through Salt Water? King Tides and Your Wheels
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
They cluster in the fall. The City of Fort Lauderdale posts predicted king tide dates on its King Tides page each season. Wind and rain can push water higher than the prediction, so check local alerts on the day.

chunks.title: Low Rolling Resistance Tires: Worth It for Hybrids?
chunks.text:
EV, Truck & Fleet
Low Rolling Resistance Tires: Worth It for Hybrids?
Low rolling resistance tires for hybrids: what NHTSA's testing found on fuel economy, why pressure matters as much, and how to keep wet grip first.
You bought a hybrid to save fuel. Do the tires matter?
Hybrid owners notice small changes in mpg, so the question comes up at every tire change: should the new set be "low rolling resistance" (LRR)? The short answer is that it helps a little, pressure helps about as much, and grip in the rain should come first. Here's the evidence for each part.

chunks.title: Low Rolling Resistance Tires: Worth It for Hybrids?
chunks.text:
What rolling resistance is
Rolling resistance is the energy a tire uses up just by rolling: the rubber flexes as it meets the road and recovers as it leaves, and some of that energy turns into heat. Every bit of it has to come from the engine or the battery.
Tire makers lower it with tread compounds, construction and tread design. Michelin, for example, says tires made for electric cars are designed with low rolling resistance in mind to help range.

chunks.title: Low Rolling Resistance Tires: Worth It for Hybrids?
chunks.text:
How much fuel it saves
NHTSA tested this directly while building its tire fuel efficiency program. In report DOT HS 811 154, tires of 15 different models with known rolling resistance were fitted to the same car. A 10% decrease in rolling resistance gave about a 1.1% increase in fuel economy.
So LRR tires save fuel, but in small steps. What that means for your car depends on:
- Which two tires you're comparing. The gap between the most and least efficient tire in a size can be large or small.
- How you drive. Speed, loads and the mix of highway and city miles all change the result.
- How long you keep the set. Small savings add up over tens of thousands of miles.

chunks.title: Low Rolling Resistance Tires: Worth It for Hybrids?
chunks.text:
Do the math for your own car
The 1.1% figure is easiest to judge in your own numbers. As a worked example, a hybrid averaging 50 mpg would gain a little over half an mpg from tires with 10% lower rolling resistance. A car averaging 30 mpg would gain about a third of an mpg. Over a set's life that adds up to real fuel, but it's not a reason to accept a tire that brakes worse in the rain.
Two questions make the comparison fairer:
- Compared with what? "Low rolling resistance" is a description, not a rating with a fixed threshold. Ask how the tire compares with the one you have now, not with an average.
- For how long? Wet grip changes as a tire wears. A tire that's efficient and grippy when new still needs replacing at 4/32.

chunks.title: Low Rolling Resistance Tires: Worth It for Hybrids?
chunks.text:
Hybrid-specific checks
Hybrids carry a battery pack, and some are heavier than the gas version of the same model. That makes two things worth a second look:
- Load index. Use the number on the door placard as the floor. If the original tires were XL (extra load), the replacements should be too. Our load index guide explains the chart.
- Noise. Hybrids run quietly at low speed, so tire noise is easier to hear. If quiet matters to you, weigh it alongside efficiency.

chunks.title: Low Rolling Resistance Tires: Worth It for Hybrids?
chunks.text:
The free version: pressure
Before you pay extra for efficiency, make sure you're not giving it away. Fueleconomy.gov says keeping tires at the correct pressure improves gas mileage by 0.6% on average, and up to 3% in some cases. Under-inflated tires can lower mileage by about 0.2% for every 1 psi drop in the average pressure of all four tires.
Two notes from the same page: use the pressure on the sticker in the door jamb or in your owner's manual, and don't use the maximum pressure printed on the sidewall. Our sidewall max PSI post explains why.
A tire that's low by a few psi can cancel out much of what a more efficient tire would save. Check cold, monthly. Our pressure guide shows how.

chunks.title: Low Rolling Resistance Tires: Worth It for Hybrids?
chunks.text:
The trade-off to watch: wet grip
Tire makers balance three things against each other: rolling resistance, grip and tread life. Push one hard and the others can move. That's why Consumer Reports' advice is to look first for a tire with good braking, handling and hydroplaning resistance, and then use rolling resistance as a tie-breaker.
In South Florida, that order matters. Our rainy season brings heavy afternoon storms for months, and hydroplaning is the risk that costs more than any fuel bill. When you compare tires:
- Match the size, load index and speed rating your vehicle maker specifies. That's first, always.
- Check wet braking. The UTQG traction grade (AA, A, B or C) is a starting point for straight-line wet braking. Try the explainer below.
- Look at independent test results for hydroplaning and handling where you can find them.

chunks.title: Low Rolling Resistance Tires: Worth It for Hybrids?
chunks.text:
The trade-off to watch: wet grip
- Then compare rolling resistance among the tires that pass the first three.
Our UTQG guide explains all three grades.
Tread depth matters more than the label
An efficient tire on worn tread is still a worn tire. AAA's testing found tires worn to 4/32 of an inch took an average of 87 feet longer to stop on wet pavement than new tires, and AAA recommends replacing at 4/32. Our post on why 4/32 matters in Florida rain has the details.

chunks.title: Low Rolling Resistance Tires: Worth It for Hybrids?
chunks.text:
Hybrid vs EV: what's different
Hybrids and EVs both care about efficiency, but EVs add weight and instant torque, which wear tires faster. If you drive a plug-in or full EV, read our post on EV tire wear and budgeting and our EV tires guide too. For a conventional hybrid, the steps above are the whole story.
Where not to economize
- Load index. Never below the original, whatever the efficiency rating.
- Wet grip. A fraction of an mpg isn't worth a weaker wet-braking tire in our climate.
- Matching. Replace in sets or pairs as your manual asks, so an axle doesn't run two different tires.

chunks.title: Low Rolling Resistance Tires: Worth It for Hybrids?
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Rolling resistance is the energy a tire uses just to roll. Lower it, and the engine and battery do a little less work.
- In NHTSA's testing, a 10% cut in rolling resistance gave about a 1.1% gain in fuel economy. Real, but modest.
- Pressure is the free version. Fueleconomy.gov says correct inflation improves mileage by 0.6% on average, and up to 3% in some cases.
- Consumer Reports' advice is to choose for braking, handling and hydroplaning first, then use rolling resistance as a tie-breaker.
- In South Florida rain, wet grip and tread depth come before the last fraction of an mpg.

chunks.title: Low Rolling Resistance Tires: Worth It for Hybrids?
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Do low rolling resistance tires really save fuel?
Yes, a little. In NHTSA's testing for its tire fuel efficiency program, a 10% decrease in rolling resistance gave about a 1.1% increase in fuel economy on the test car. How much you save depends on the tires you're comparing, your car and how you drive.
What are the best tires for a hybrid?
The ones that match your vehicle's size, load index and speed rating, with strong wet braking, and then low rolling resistance. If you want to keep your hybrid's efficiency, ask about rolling resistance, but don't trade away wet grip for it.
Do low rolling resistance tires have less grip in the rain?

chunks.title: Low Rolling Resistance Tires: Worth It for Hybrids?
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Not necessarily, but it's the trade-off to check. Tire makers balance rolling resistance, grip and tread life against each other. Consumer Reports suggests choosing a tire with good braking, handling and hydroplaning resistance first, and using rolling resistance as the tie-breaker.
Is tire pressure more important than the tire itself for mpg?
It's the part you control every month. Fueleconomy.gov says under-inflated tires can lower gas mileage by about 0.2% for every 1 psi drop in the average pressure of all four tires. Checking pressure cold against the door placard costs nothing.

chunks.title: Mobile Tire Install at a Condo or Office: What to Know
chunks.text:
Local Buying & Service
Mobile Tire Install at a Condo or Office: What to Know
Getting tires installed at your condo or office in Broward: the space the van needs, gate codes and garage rules, what the van can and can't do, and prep.
By TireDrop Team, Extreme Tires, Sunrise FL·Published Sep 30, 2026·Updated Oct 1, 2026·4 min read
Why condos and offices are their own case
A house with a driveway is the easy version of mobile tire installation. The van parks, the work gets done, and nobody else is involved.
A condo tower in Fort Lauderdale or an office park off Sawgrass is different. There's a gate, a garage with a height bar, a management office, assigned spaces, maybe a security desk. None of that rules out having your tires installed where you park. It just means a few questions are worth answering before the appointment, not during it.

chunks.title: Mobile Tire Install at a Condo or Office: What to Know
chunks.text:
Why condos and offices are their own case
This post covers those questions. For how booking and pricing work, the mobile service page is the place to start.
What the van actually needs
Less than most people expect. Per Extreme Tires' mobile service:
- One standard parking space next to your vehicle
- About ten feet of clearance on the side where the work happens
- A reasonably flat surface: a driveway, a flat stretch of street, an office lot or a jobsite staging area all work
What it doesn't need:
- Your garage. The work happens beside the car.
- A lift. The van carries a rated jack, stands and a cart for heavy assemblies.
- Your outlet. It runs on its own generator, with its own work lights.

chunks.title: Mobile Tire Install at a Condo or Office: What to Know
chunks.text:
At a condo or apartment complex
This is where a little planning pays off.
Tell us how to get in. When you book, include the complex name, any gate code and any call-up instructions. That's what lets the technician reach your car without a phone tag session at the gate.
Know your association's rules. Every building is different, and we won't guess at yours. Per Extreme Tires' mobile service, some complexes want the van checked in at the gate, and some ask that work happen in a visitor space rather than a covered garage. Check your association's rules or ask management before the appointment. If the rules point to a visitor space, the car can be moved there first.
Mind the height bar. If your assigned spot is inside a low-clearance garage, plan on meeting the van at a surface space.

chunks.title: Mobile Tire Install at a Condo or Office: What to Know
chunks.text:
At the office
An office lot is often easier than a condo, with a couple of things to confirm:
- Is the lot open to service vehicles? Some office parks and garages restrict them. Property management will know.
- Is there a security desk or gate? Add the details to your booking.
- Keys. The technician needs the car unlocked and, depending on the job, the keys. Plan how you'll hand them over if you're in a meeting.
- The wheel lock key. If your wheels have locking lug nuts, make sure the key is in the car.
Then you get on with your day. The mobile service page puts a four-tire installation at about 45 to 75 minutes, and your confirmation lists the estimate for the exact service you booked.

chunks.text:

chunks.title: Mobile Tire Install at a Condo or Office: What to Know
chunks.text:
Before the appointment
- Get the tires to the van. Order from TireDrop and choose free ship-to-store at checkout, and the van brings your set from the Sunrise shop. Or ship them to your address and the van fits them there. Our post on getting tires installed after buying online covers both routes.
- Check the size against your door placard. USTMA's guidance is that replacement tires match the size, load index and speed rating on the vehicle placard, with a load index equal to or above what the placard requires.
- Know whether your car has TPMS. Under the federal FMVSS No. 138 rule, vehicles of 10,000 lb gross vehicle weight rating or less built from September 1, 2007 on have one. Installation includes a TPMS reset where the vehicle has it.
- Clear the work side. Move anything stored beside the car, and leave room for the van next to it.

chunks.title: Mobile Tire Install at a Condo or Office: What to Know
chunks.text:
Before the appointment
- Send access details. Gate code, building name, where the car is parked.
What about the weather?
Afternoon showers are part of South Florida. Per Extreme Tires' mobile service, short showers rarely stop the work, because the van carries lighting and cover for the work area. If there's lightning or sustained heavy rain, you get a call, the job pauses and it's rescheduled.

chunks.title: Mobile Tire Install at a Condo or Office: What to Know
chunks.text:
After the van leaves
Your old tires leave with the van and are recycled, so nothing gets left in the parking garage. The wheels are torqued to your vehicle maker's spec and pressures are set to the door placard.
From there it's the usual routine: NHTSA's guidance is to check pressure with a gauge at least once a month, spare included, with the tires cold. If a TPMS light shows up afterward, our TPMS light guide explains what it's telling you.
Mobile installation covers Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties, and the ZIP code where the car is parked decides it. Outside those three counties, your tires still ship to you, or you can bring the car to the Sunrise shop. See mobile service or call (954) 773-1896 to ask.

chunks.title: Mobile Tire Install at a Condo or Office: What to Know
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- The van needs one standard parking space next to your car and about ten feet of clearance on the work side. No garage, lift or outlet needed.
- At a condo or apartment complex, give the complex name and any gate code or call-up instructions when you book.
- Some complexes want the van checked in at the gate or working in a visitor space rather than a covered garage. Check your association's rules first.
- Installation, balancing, puncture repair, rotation and TPMS service happen where you park. Alignment, brakes and suspension are shop work.
- Mobile installation covers Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties, decided by the ZIP code where the car is parked.

chunks.title: Mobile Tire Install at a Condo or Office: What to Know
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Can a mobile tire installer come to my condo?
Yes, inside the local install area. When you book, give the complex name and any gate code or call-up instructions. Some complexes want the van checked in at the gate or ask that work happen in a visitor space rather than a covered garage, so check your association's rules before the appointment.
How much space does a mobile tire van need?
One standard parking space next to your vehicle and about ten feet of clearance on the work side. A driveway, a flat stretch of street, an office lot or a jobsite area all work. The van doesn't need your garage, a lift or your electrical outlet.
Can I get new tires installed at my office?

chunks.title: Mobile Tire Install at a Condo or Office: What to Know
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Yes, if your office is in the install area and the lot has room next to your car. Check with building or property management about service vehicles, give the van any access instructions when you book, and have your keys and any wheel lock key ready.
What can't a mobile tire service do in a parking lot?
At Extreme Tires, brakes, alignment, suspension, lift kits and diagnostics need a lift or an alignment rack, so they happen at the Sunrise shop. If the technician spots something like that during a mobile appointment, you get an estimate and a shop booking.

chunks.title: Moving to Florida? Tire Tips for New Residents
chunks.text:
Travel & Roadside
Moving to Florida? Tire Tips for New Residents
Moving to Florida with your car: the FLHSMV deadlines and VIN check, plus the tire changes that matter here: winter tires off, rain and heat routines on.
Welcome to Florida. Your car needs a few things too.
Moving here comes with a long list: utilities, schools, a new address on everything. Your car has its own list, and it has deadlines. Then there's what South Florida's climate does to tires, which surprises a lot of people who drove for years up north without thinking about rain or heat.
Here's both: the paperwork FLHSMV requires, and the tire changes worth making in your first few months.

chunks.title: Moving to Florida? Tire Tips for New Residents
chunks.text:
Part 1: The paperwork and its deadlines
All of this comes from FLHSMV's page for new residents. Check it for the current details before you go, because requirements can change.
- Driver license: 30 days. You must get a valid Florida driver license no later than 30 days after establishing residency to drive on Florida roads.
- Insurance, title and registration: 10 days. You must get insurance from a Florida-licensed insurance agent and title and register your vehicles no later than 10 days after establishing residency. Ten days goes quickly during a move, so line up the insurance before the moving truck arrives.
- What counts as residency. FLHSMV's list includes starting a job or business here, enrolling your children in Florida public schools, registering to vote, filing for a homestead exemption, and living here more than six consecutive months.

chunks.title: Moving to Florida? Tire Tips for New Residents
chunks.text:
The VIN verification
Vehicles coming from another state need their vehicle identification number physically inspected and verified. FLHSMV says that can be done by:
- A law enforcement officer
- A military police officer
- A licensed Florida dealer
- A county tax collector employee or a Division of Motorist Services compliance examiner
The form is HSMV 82042, the Vehicle Identification Number and Odometer Verification.

chunks.title: Moving to Florida? Tire Tips for New Residents
chunks.text:
If you drove up north on winter tires
Snow tires and winter tires have no job in South Florida. Michelin's winter tire guide explains why they shouldn't stay on: the compound that makes them effective in cold weather wears faster on hot summer roads, which is why they should be swapped off before warm weather returns. Here, warm weather never really leaves.
If you moved with a set on the car, plan to replace them with all-season tires in your vehicle's placard size. Our guide to all-season vs all-weather tires explains the difference, and Find My Tires shows the sizes for your vehicle.

chunks.title: Moving to Florida? Tire Tips for New Residents
chunks.text:
Get ready for the rain
The National Weather Service in Miami defines the South Florida wet season as May 15 to October 15, the months when 60 to 70 percent of the average yearly rainfall falls. Much of it comes in short, heavy afternoon storms that leave standing water on highways and ramps.
That makes tread depth more important here than in many places. Tires are legally worn out at 2/32 inch, but as tread wears, its ability to clear water drops. Check yours:
Our guide to hydroplaning explains what happens in standing water, and our post on why 4/32 matters in Florida rain makes the case for replacing earlier.

chunks.title: Moving to Florida? Tire Tips for New Residents
chunks.text:
Watch the pressure, and the heat
Pressure moves with temperature. USTMA says it goes up or down by 1 to 2 psi for every 10°F. A car that arrives in July from a cooler state will read higher in the afternoon. That's normal; set the pressure cold, in the morning, to the number on the driver's door placard. Never let air out of warm tires to match the placard.
Heat and sun also age rubber. NHTSA lists exposure to sunlight and a warmer climate among the causes of tire aging, and says aging is a greater concern in the southern Sun Belt. Our guide to Florida heat and tires covers what to do about it.

chunks.title: Moving to Florida? Tire Tips for New Residents
chunks.text:
Know FLHSMV's tire guidance
Florida's own tire safety page is short and worth knowing:
FLHSMV says
How often
Check pressure with a gauge, tires cold
Monthly
Look for bulges, cuts and cracks
Weekly
Check the spare
Monthly
Rotate tires
Every 5,000 miles or as your manufacturer requires
Replace when tread is level with the wear bars
When it happens
Don't drive on tires more than six years old
Check the DOT date
The six-year line is stricter than many tire makers' guidance; Michelin and Bridgestone recommend replacement at ten years with yearly inspections from five. Our guide to how old is too old for tires compares them.

chunks.title: Moving to Florida? Tire Tips for New Residents
chunks.text:
Hurricane season is a car issue too
Hurricane season runs June 1 to November 30. If you ever need to evacuate, it will be by car, often on I-95, the Turnpike or I-75. Our hurricane car prep checklist starts with the tires.
Your first-month checklist
- Get insurance from a Florida-licensed agent, the VIN verification, and the title and registration, all in the first 10 days.
- Get your Florida driver license in the first 30 days.
- Swap any winter tires for all-season tires.
- Measure tread depth in three grooves on every tire.
- Set pressure cold to the door placard, spare included.
- Read the DOT date on each tire.
- Save *347 in your phone; it reaches the Florida Highway Patrol and FDOT's Road Rangers.

chunks.title: Moving to Florida? Tire Tips for New Residents
chunks.text:
Need tires for your new home?
Not sure your tires are up to Florida weather? Do I Need Tires Yet? walks you through it. When it's time, shop by size or vehicle. In Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we install at our Sunrise shop or at your new place with our mobile van. Shipping is free to the 48 contiguous states and DC.
Key takeaways
- FLHSMV gives new residents 30 days for a Florida driver license and 10 days to title and register a vehicle, with Florida insurance.
- Out-of-state vehicles need a VIN verification, done by an officer, a licensed Florida dealer or a tax collector employee, on form HSMV 82042.
- Bringing winter tires? Michelin says their compound wears faster on hot roads. Swap them for all-season tires.
- South Florida's wet season runs May 15 to October 15. Tread depth and pressure matter more here than most newcomers expect.

chunks.title: Moving to Florida? Tire Tips for New Residents
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- FLHSMV's tire page says check pressure monthly, look for damage weekly, and don't run tires over six years old.
Questions people ask
How long do I have to register my car after moving to Florida?
FLHSMV says new residents must get insurance from a Florida-licensed agent and title and register their vehicles no later than 10 days after establishing residency. You have 30 days to get a Florida driver license. FLHSMV lists what counts as establishing residency, including starting a job here or enrolling children in Florida public schools.
Does Florida require a VIN inspection for out-of-state cars?

chunks.title: Moving to Florida? Tire Tips for New Residents
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Yes. FLHSMV requires the vehicle identification number to be physically inspected and verified by a law enforcement officer, a military police officer, a licensed Florida dealer, or a county tax collector employee or Division of Motorist Services compliance examiner. The form is HSMV 82042.
Can I use winter tires in Florida?
You can, but it's a poor match. Michelin says the compound that makes winter tires effective in cold weather wears faster on hot summer roads, which is why they should be swapped off before warm weather returns. In South Florida, that's essentially all year.
What tires are best for driving in Florida?

chunks.title: Moving to Florida? Tire Tips for New Residents
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
There's no single best tire, but the priorities here are wet grip and heat. Look for a quality all-season tire in your vehicle's placard size and load rating, check the UTQG traction and temperature grades, and replace before tread gets low, since heavy rain is part of daily life for half the year.

chunks.title: Why New-Car Tires Sometimes Wear Out Early
chunks.text:
EV, Truck & Fleet
Why New-Car Tires Sometimes Wear Out Early
Why did my original tires wear out so fast? How carmakers choose factory tires, the habits and conditions that speed wear, and how to choose the next set.
"It's barely two years old"
It's one of the most common surprises at the tire counter. The car is new, the payments have barely started, and the original tires are already near the wear bars. Owners reasonably ask whether something is wrong with the tires, the car or the way they drive.
Usually it's a mix, and most of it is explainable. Here's our view of why first sets sometimes wear early, based on what tire makers and regulators publish, and what to do about it.

chunks.title: Why New-Car Tires Sometimes Wear Out Early
chunks.text:
A factory tire is chosen for the whole car
When a vehicle maker picks tires for a new model, it's balancing a long list: ride comfort, steering feel, wet and dry grip, cabin noise, fuel economy or range, and tread life. No tire maximizes all of them at once. If a carmaker leans toward a quiet ride, crisp handling or efficiency, tread life may not be the top priority.
Michelin is direct about one case: for electric vehicles, carmakers often prioritize range when optimizing original-equipment tires, and that comes with trade-offs such as less grip or greater tire wear.
That isn't a flaw. It's a choice made for the car as delivered. The good news is that at replacement time, you get to make your own choice.

chunks.title: Why New-Car Tires Sometimes Wear Out Early
chunks.text:
What actually wears a tire
Goodyear's tread life warranty terms list the things that affect how long tread lasts: tire type, tread compound, construction, the vehicle, maintenance, road and weather conditions, and driving habits. Some of those you chose when you bought the car. Several you control every day.
Weight and torque. Michelin says vehicle weight is a critical factor in how fast a tire wears. EVs add battery weight and instant torque, and Michelin puts their average wear at about 20% faster than comparable gas vehicles. Our post on EV tire wear covers how to budget for it.
Heat and pressure. NHTSA explains that underinflation, excessive speed and overloading cause heat build-up in a tire. South Florida's heat adds to it. A tire run a few psi low wears faster and unevenly.

chunks.title: Why New-Car Tires Sometimes Wear Out Early
chunks.text:
What actually wears a tire
Missed rotations. Front and rear tires do different jobs and wear at different rates. Without rotation, one pair wears out well before the other. Tesla's Model Y manual, for example, asks for rotation every 6,250 miles, or sooner if tread depths differ by 2/32 inch or more. Where a manual gives no interval, USTMA's recommendation is every 5,000 to 8,000 miles.
Alignment. AAA notes that hitting a pothole can knock the wheels out of alignment, and that uneven tire wear can point to worn or damaged parts. A misaligned car can scrub one edge of a tire for thousands of miles before anyone notices.
Driving style. Hard launches, fast cornering and heavy braking all take rubber off. That's especially true with instant torque.

chunks.title: Why New-Car Tires Sometimes Wear Out Early
chunks.text:
Read the wear, not just the depth
How the tires wore tells you more than how fast. Look across the tread of each tire:
What you see
Likely cause
What to do
Both edges worn more than the center
Running under-inflated
Check pressure monthly, cold, at the placard number
Center worn more than the edges
Running over-inflated
Use the placard, not the sidewall maximum
One edge worn, or feathered ribs
Alignment
Alignment check before the new set
Front pair much more worn than rear
No rotation
Rotate on the manual's schedule
Even wear, just fast
Tire choice, weight, torque or driving style
Choose the next set with tread life in mind
Our rotation pattern tool shows the right pattern for your drivetrain:

chunks.title: Why New-Car Tires Sometimes Wear Out Early
chunks.text:
Could it be a defect?
Fast, even wear is usually down to the tire's design and how the car is used. A defect is different, and it tends to show up as something you can see or feel rather than just shallow tread. Signs worth a closer look:
- A bulge, bubble or separation anywhere on the tire.
- A vibration that started suddenly and doesn't go away after balancing.
- One tire wearing very differently from its partner on the same axle, with pressure and alignment checked.
What to do:
- Check for recalls. NHTSA's recall lookup covers both vehicles and tires. Have the tire's DOT code handy.
- Have the tire inspected and keep the findings in writing.
- Read the tire's warranty terms. Tread life coverage and workmanship coverage are usually separate, and each has its own conditions.

chunks.title: Why New-Car Tires Sometimes Wear Out Early
chunks.text:
Choosing the second set
This is where you get to set the priorities.
- Match the specification. Same size, and a load index and speed rating at or above what the placard calls for. EVs and some heavier vehicles may need an XL or HL load rating.
- Decide what matters most. If the first set wore too fast for you, look for a tire whose maker puts more weight on tread life, and check its mileage warranty, if it has one.
- Use the UTQG treadwear grade carefully. NHTSA's consumer guide explains that the grade compares a tire's wear with a control tire on a test course, and that real-world results can differ significantly. Compare grades within one brand, not as miles.
- Don't give up wet grip. In South Florida rain, a long-wearing tire still needs strong wet braking.
Our guide to how long tires last explains warranties, grades and age limits in more depth.

chunks.title: Why New-Car Tires Sometimes Wear Out Early
chunks.text:
Make the next set last
- Check pressure monthly, cold, against the door placard.
- Rotate on schedule, and keep the records; tread life warranties such as Goodyear's ask for them.
- Get an alignment after a hard hit or when you see one-sided wear. We offer wheel alignment at our Sunrise shop.
- Measure tread every few months, and plan to replace at 4/32 for rainy-season grip.
Not sure if it's time? Do I Need Tires Yet? walks you through it. When it is, shop by size or vehicle. Shipping is free to the 48 contiguous states and DC, and in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we install at our Sunrise shop or by mobile van.

chunks.title: Why New-Car Tires Sometimes Wear Out Early
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- A factory tire is chosen to balance many goals for that vehicle: ride, handling, noise, efficiency and wear. Long tread life is one goal among several.
- Goodyear lists what affects tread life: tire type, tread compound, construction, the vehicle, maintenance, road and weather conditions, and driving habits.
- Weight and torque matter. Michelin says EVs wear tires about 20% faster on average, and that carmakers often prioritize range on original EV tires.
- Missed rotations, low pressure and alignment knocked out by a pothole all shorten a first set's life, and all three are fixable.
- When you replace, you choose the trade-offs. Match the size, load and speed rating, then weigh tread life against grip and comfort.

chunks.title: Why New-Car Tires Sometimes Wear Out Early
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Why did my original tires wear out so fast?
Usually a mix of reasons. The factory tire was chosen to balance ride, handling, noise, efficiency and wear for that vehicle, so it may not be the longest-wearing tire in the size. Then weight, torque, heat, pressure, alignment, rotation habits and driving style all add up. Look at how the tires wore, not just how fast, for clues.
Are original-equipment tires worse than replacement tires?
Not worse, just chosen for a different brief. Vehicle makers pick tires to suit the whole car, and a long tread life is only one of the goals. When you replace them, you can choose a tire that puts more weight on tread life, as long as it matches the size, load index and speed rating your vehicle needs.
Do EV and hybrid tires wear out faster?

chunks.title: Why New-Car Tires Sometimes Wear Out Early
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
EVs often do. Michelin says EVs wear tires about 20% faster than comparable gas cars on average, mostly from battery weight and instant torque. Michelin also says carmakers often prioritize range when optimizing original EV tires, which can come with trade-offs such as greater tire wear.
Will rotating my tires make them last longer?
Rotation evens out wear between positions, so the set wears together instead of two tires wearing out first. Follow the interval in your owner's manual. If there isn't one, USTMA recommends every 5,000 to 8,000 miles.
