chunks.title: My Car Has TPMS. Do I Still Need a Tire Gauge?
chunks.text:
Myth-Busting
My Car Has TPMS. Do I Still Need a Tire Gauge?
Do you need a tire gauge if you have TPMS? Yes: the light is built to catch a tire 25% low, and NHTSA found it does little for milder underinflation.
The myth: "The car will tell me"
It's a fair assumption. Every new car and light truck built since September 2007 has a tire pressure monitoring system, and a light on the dash that should come on when a tire is low. So why would you still keep a cheap gauge in the glovebox?
Because of what "low" means to the system. TPMS was designed to catch a tire that has lost a lot of air, not to keep your pressure right. Those are different jobs, and the second one still belongs to a gauge.

chunks.title: My Car Has TPMS. Do I Still Need a Tire Gauge?
chunks.text:
What the federal rule actually requires
TPMS comes from the TREAD Act. NHTSA's standard, FMVSS No. 138, phased it in so that all light vehicles built on or after September 1, 2007 have it. The core requirement:
- The warning must come on when a tire is 25 percent or more below the vehicle maker's recommended cold pressure (the number on your door placard).
- It must come on after no more than 20 minutes of driving at normal road speeds.
- A separate malfunction signal has to tell you when the system itself isn't working.

chunks.title: My Car Has TPMS. Do I Still Need a Tire Gauge?
chunks.text:
What the federal rule actually requires
Automakers can set their systems to warn sooner, but 25 percent is the line the law draws. The same standard requires owner's manuals to say that TPMS is not a substitute for proper tire maintenance, and that keeping the correct pressure is the driver's responsibility even when the warning hasn't come on. NHTSA's tire page puts it plainly too: these systems only warn when a tire is significantly underinflated. Here's what that looks like on a few common placard numbers:
Placard pressure (cold)
25% below
A tire this low can leave the light off
32 psi
24 psi
26 psi (19% low)
35 psi
about 26 psi
29 psi (17% low)
42 psi
about 31.5 psi
35 psi (17% low)
A tire 17 or 19 percent low is a tire that's working too hard, running hotter and wearing faster, and on many cars the dash will say nothing about it.

chunks.title: My Car Has TPMS. Do I Still Need a Tire Gauge?
chunks.text:
What the federal rule actually requires
A steady tire pressure light means at least one tire may be well under-inflated, and a light that flashes for about 60 to 90 seconds and then stays on signals a system malfunction, per FMVSS No. 138. Either way, check pressures with a gauge when tires are cold, inflate to the door placard, and have the system inspected if the light stays on.

chunks.title: My Car Has TPMS. Do I Still Need a Tire Gauge?
chunks.text:
What NHTSA found when it checked real cars
In 2010 and 2011, NHTSA surveyed vehicles at gas stations across the country, measuring the actual pressure in all four tires. Its report, DOT HS 811 681, is the best evidence on how well TPMS works. The findings cut both ways:
The good news. Among 2004–2007 model-year vehicles, 23.1 percent without TPMS had at least one severely underinflated tire (25 percent or more low). With TPMS, that fell to 11.8 percent, and to 5.7 percent for 2008–2011 models with TPMS. NHTSA estimated TPMS produced a 55.6 percent reduction in the likelihood of a vehicle having a severely underinflated tire.

chunks.title: My Car Has TPMS. Do I Still Need a Tire Gauge?
chunks.text:
What NHTSA found when it checked real cars
The part the myth misses. NHTSA found TPMS was also effective, over 35 percent, against moderate underinflation of 10 percent or more. But in its words, it does not appear to have an effect on mild underinflation. And across all 2004–2011 passenger vehicles, 12.4 percent still had at least one severely underinflated tire.
So TPMS does its job: it catches big losses. Keeping all four tires at the right pressure day to day is still on you.

chunks.title: My Car Has TPMS. Do I Still Need a Tire Gauge?
chunks.text:
Direct vs indirect: some systems can't read pressure at all
NHTSA's report describes two kinds of TPMS:
- Direct systems put a pressure sensor inside each wheel, usually on the valve stem, with a battery-powered transmitter. Some show each tire's pressure on the dash. NHTSA found cars with tire-specific pressure displays had the lowest rate of severe underinflation in the survey.
- Indirect systems don't measure pressure. They use the anti-lock brake wheel-speed sensors and look for a wheel turning faster than the others, a sign its tire is smaller and may be low. NHTSA notes early indirect systems had trouble spotting low tires when several were low at once.
Indirect systems were rare by the time of the survey, fewer than 3 percent of the vehicles observed, but if your car has one, there's no number anywhere on the dash. The gauge is the only way to know the pressure.

chunks.title: My Car Has TPMS. Do I Still Need a Tire Gauge?
chunks.text:
Even a pressure readout isn't the whole story
If your dash shows each tire's psi, that's useful. Two things to keep in mind:
- Temperature changes the number. USTMA says pressure rises or falls about 1 to 2 psi for every 10°F change. After a drive, or a car parked in the Florida sun, the reading will be higher than the cold pressure the placard refers to. Set pressure cold, meaning parked for at least three hours.
- The spare. NHTSA's advice is to check all tires, including the spare. A flat spare is worth knowing about before you need it.
Our pressure and temperature tool shows how much a reading moves with heat.

chunks.title: My Car Has TPMS. Do I Still Need a Tire Gauge?
chunks.text:
Why the small losses matter
A few psi doesn't sound like much, but it adds up:
- Fuel economy. fueleconomy.gov says underinflated tires can lower gas mileage by about 0.2 percent for every 1 psi drop in the average pressure of all tires, and that proper inflation improves mileage 0.6 percent on average, up to 3 percent in some cases.
- Wear and heat. NHTSA's report notes underinflated tires flex more, which brings longer stopping distances, sluggish handling and heat buildup.
- The slow leak you'd otherwise miss. A tire that's always a few psi lower than the others is often a nail or a valve. A gauge spots the pattern long before the light does.

chunks.title: My Car Has TPMS. Do I Still Need a Tire Gauge?
chunks.text:
The routine that works with TPMS
Think of the TPMS light as a smoke alarm and the gauge as checking the stove. You want both.
- Keep a gauge in the car. NHTSA recommends it. A simple dial or digital gauge works; our guide to checking tire pressure compares the types.
- Check monthly, cold, against the door placard, not the sidewall maximum. Our post on why not to inflate to the sidewall number explains the difference.
- Treat the light as urgent when it does come on. Our TPMS light guide explains solid vs flashing.

chunks.title: My Car Has TPMS. Do I Still Need a Tire Gauge?
chunks.text:
The routine that works with TPMS
If the light flashes at startup and then stays on, the system has a fault: often a sensor battery or a sensor damaged during a tire change. Our TPMS service diagnoses and replaces sensors. In Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we do it at our Sunrise shop or with our mobile van. If a tire keeps losing air or is worn out, shop by size or vehicle; shipping is free to the 48 contiguous states and DC.

chunks.title: My Car Has TPMS. Do I Still Need a Tire Gauge?
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- The federal rule sets TPMS to warn when a tire is 25 percent or more below the placard pressure. On a 35 psi car, that's about 26 psi.
- NHTSA's field study found TPMS cut severe underinflation by 55.6 percent, but it did not appear to affect milder underinflation.
- A tire can sit well below the placard pressure with the dash dark. Only a gauge tells you the actual number.
- Indirect systems compare wheel speeds and can't give you a pressure reading at all.
- NHTSA's advice still stands: keep a gauge in the car and check all tires, spare included, once a month when cold.

chunks.title: My Car Has TPMS. Do I Still Need a Tire Gauge?
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Do I need a tire pressure gauge if my car has TPMS?
Yes. TPMS is a warning system, not a gauge. The federal standard requires the light when a tire is 25 percent or more below the recommended cold pressure, so a tire can be noticeably low without triggering it. NHTSA still tells drivers to keep a gauge in the car and check pressure monthly.
At what pressure does the TPMS light come on?
FMVSS No. 138 requires the warning when a tire is 25 percent or more below the vehicle maker's recommended cold pressure, after no more than 20 minutes of driving. Automakers can set it to warn sooner. For a car with a 35 psi placard, the required point is roughly 26 psi.
How accurate is the TPMS pressure reading on my dashboard?

chunks.title: My Car Has TPMS. Do I Still Need a Tire Gauge?
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Some direct systems show each tire's pressure on the dash, and NHTSA's study found those cars had the lowest rate of severe underinflation. Even so, the reading reflects the tire's current temperature, and a warm tire reads higher. For setting pressure, use a gauge on cold tires and the door placard number.
Why is my TPMS light off but my tire looks low?
Because the light only has to come on at a large pressure loss. A tire 15 or 20 percent low can leave the dash dark. Check it with a gauge, set all four to the placard pressure cold, and look for a nail or a leaking valve if one tire keeps dropping.

chunks.title: Driving the Turnpike to Orlando: Tire Prep and Stops
chunks.text:
Travel & Roadside
Driving the Turnpike to Orlando: Tire Prep and Stops
Driving Florida's Turnpike from South Florida to Orlando: a tire check before you go, the service plazas by milepost, and what Turnpike Road Rangers do.
The drive half of South Florida knows
Theme parks, the airport, a college visit, family for the holidays: for a lot of Broward and Palm Beach drivers, the Turnpike north to Orlando is a regular trip. It's a long stretch of highway at speed, often with a full car, often in the heat, and sometimes through an afternoon storm.
None of that is a problem for tires in good shape. This post covers the check to do before you go, the stops along the way, and what to do if a tire goes on the Turnpike.

chunks.title: Driving the Turnpike to Orlando: Tire Prep and Stops
chunks.text:
Before you leave: the 15-minute tire check
Do this in the driveway a few days ahead, so there's time to fix anything you find.
- Pressure, cold. Check all four tires and the spare against the driver's door placard, not the sidewall maximum. USTMA defines cold as parked for at least three hours. If your owner's manual lists a pressure for a fully loaded car, use it.
- Tread depth. Measure in three grooves on every tire. AAA recommends replacing at 4/32 inch; its testing found tires at that depth took an average of 87 feet longer to stop on wet pavement than new ones.
- Sidewalls. Look for bulges, cuts and cracks.
- The spare, or what replaced it. AAA says about 30 percent of new cars come without a spare, carrying a sealant kit or run-flat tires instead. Know which you have.

chunks.title: Driving the Turnpike to Orlando: Tire Prep and Stops
chunks.text:
Before you leave: the 15-minute tire check
- The load. The door placard also lists the most weight your car should carry in people and cargo. A family plus luggage adds up quickly.
Our road trip tire check goes through each step in more detail.
The stops, by milepost
Florida's Turnpike counts mileposts from the south. Heading north from Broward, its service plaza page lists:
Plaza
Milepost
Pompano Beach
65
West Palm Beach
94
Port St. Lucie / Fort Pierce
144

Starting from Miami-Dade, there's also Snapper Creek at milepost 19, a smaller convenience store with fuel.
What the Turnpike says the plazas offer:
- Fuel around the clock. All plaza stores with fuel are open 24 hours a day, with regular gasoline grades, diesel and E85.
- EV charging, with fees that vary. Tesla owners use Tesla Superchargers at the plazas.

chunks.title: Driving the Turnpike to Orlando: Tire Prep and Stops
chunks.text:
The stops, by milepost
- Restaurants, restrooms, ATMs, WiFi and enclosed dog parks.
The Turnpike also describes Turkey Lake as only the second location in the US offering passenger-car drivers its WheelRight tire-check technology. If you pass through, it's an easy second look at your tires before the drive home.
Amenities change, so check the Turnpike's plaza page before you leave. This list reflects it as of October 2026.

chunks.title: Driving the Turnpike to Orlando: Tire Prep and Stops
chunks.text:
Using the stops for your tires
A stop is a good moment for a 30-second walk-around:
- Look at each tire. Anything that looks lower than the others, or anything stuck in the tread?
- Remember the heat. Tires get warm on the highway, and warm tires read higher. Don't let air out of a hot tire to match the placard; that leaves it low once it cools.
- Check the dash. If the TPMS light came on during the drive, check that tire with a gauge at the plaza and add air if it's low. Our TPMS light guide explains solid vs flashing.

chunks.title: Driving the Turnpike to Orlando: Tire Prep and Stops
chunks.text:
Rain on the way
Between May 15 and October 15, the National Weather Service in Miami's wet season, an afternoon drive north has a good chance of running into a storm somewhere along the route. Heavy rain on a fast highway is where tread depth shows up: a worn tire can't clear water as well, and the car can start to float on standing water.
If it pours, slow down, leave more room, keep your headlights on and avoid the outer edges of the lane where water collects. If the car starts to feel light in the steering, ease off the gas and keep the wheel straight. Our post on hydroplaning in Broward downpours covers it in more detail.

chunks.title: Driving the Turnpike to Orlando: Tire Prep and Stops
chunks.text:
If a tire goes on the Turnpike
- Hold the wheel firmly and ease off the gas. Don't brake hard.
- Signal and get to the right shoulder or the next plaza or exit if the car can roll there at low speed.
- Hazard lights on. Under Florida's Move Over law, as FLHSMV describes it, drivers must move over or slow down for a vehicle stopped with its hazards on, flat tire included.
- Dial *347.
Florida's Turnpike runs its own Road Rangers patrol on the mainline, mileposts 0 to 308, 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and calls the service free. The services it lists:
- Tire changes with your vehicle's spare
- Emergency gas, up to 2 gallons
- Jump starts
- Water refills
- Minor emergency repairs

chunks.title: Driving the Turnpike to Orlando: Tire Prep and Stops
chunks.text:
If a tire goes on the Turnpike
That first item is the catch: no spare means no tire change. If your car has a sealant kit or run-flats, know their limits before the trip. Our spare tire types guide explains them, and our post on a flat tire on I-95 covers the roadside steps in more detail.
The drive home
Before you head back south, repeat the cold pressure check in the hotel parking lot in the morning. If you used a spare or a sealant kit on the way up, get to a tire shop before the long drive home; a donut is for reaching a shop, not for the whole drive home.

chunks.title: Driving the Turnpike to Orlando: Tire Prep and Stops
chunks.text:
Tires not up to the trip?
Do I Need Tires Yet? gives you a quick answer. If it's time, shop by size or vehicle early enough to install before you go. In Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we install at our Sunrise shop or at home with our mobile van. Shipping is free to the 48 contiguous states and DC.
Key takeaways
- Six full service plazas sit between Pompano Beach and Orlando: mileposts 65, 94, 144, 184, 229 and 263.
- The Turnpike says every plaza store with fuel is open 24 hours, and the plazas offer EV charging, including Tesla Superchargers.
- Turnpike Road Rangers patrol the whole mainline, mileposts 0 to 308, around the clock. Dial *347; the service is free.
- They'll change a tire with your spare. Without a spare, it's a tow, so know what's in your trunk.
- Check pressure cold, against the door placard, before you load up, and again before the drive home.

chunks.title: Driving the Turnpike to Orlando: Tire Prep and Stops
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Where are the service plazas on Florida's Turnpike between South Florida and Orlando?
Heading north, Florida's Turnpike lists Pompano Beach (milepost 65), West Palm Beach (94), Port St. Lucie/Fort Pierce (144), Fort Drum (184), Canoe Creek (229) and Turkey Lake (263), near Orlando. Snapper Creek (milepost 19) in Miami-Dade is a smaller convenience store with fuel.
What do I do if I get a flat tire on the Turnpike?
Get out of the travel lanes, turn on your hazard lights and dial *347. Florida's Turnpike says its Road Rangers patrol the mainline 24 hours a day and provide free help, including tire changes with your vehicle's spare, emergency gas, jump starts and water.
Can I charge an EV on the Turnpike?

chunks.title: Driving the Turnpike to Orlando: Tire Prep and Stops
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Yes. Florida's Turnpike says its service plazas offer a range of EV charging options, and Tesla owners use Tesla Superchargers there. Charging fees vary. Check the Turnpike's service plaza page for the current list before you leave.
Should I change my tire pressure for a road trip?
Use the cold pressure on your driver's door placard. Some owner's manuals list a different pressure for a fully loaded car, so check yours if the car is packed. Check before you drive, never after, because warm tires read high.

chunks.title: Unused Tires Still Age: The Garage and Spare Myth
chunks.text:
Myth-Busting
Unused Tires Still Age: The Garage and Spare Myth
Do tires expire if not used? Why stored tires and never-used spares still age, what NHTSA and tire makers say, and how to store tires in a Florida garage.
The myth
"It's never been on the road, so it's basically new." People say it about the set of tires in the garage, the spare that's never been used, and the bargain "new old stock" tires that sat in a warehouse.
Tread depth is the only thing that stays new. The rubber keeps aging from the day the tire is made. Here's what NHTSA and tire makers say, and what it means for the tires sitting in a hot Florida garage.

chunks.title: Unused Tires Still Age: The Garage and Spare Myth
chunks.text:
What the evidence says
Tires age whether or not they roll. NHTSA's TireWise guidance says tire aging comes from service, storage and environmental conditions. Storage is on that list. A tire on a shelf isn't wearing its tread, but it is getting older.
Age limits are measured from manufacture. NHTSA notes that some vehicle and tire makers recommend replacing tires that are 6 to 10 years old, regardless of treadwear. Bridgestone and Michelin recommend a professional inspection at least once a year from five years old, and replacement 10 years after the tire was made, even if the tread looks new. Your vehicle maker may set a shorter limit in the owner's manual. Our guide on how old is too old compares the recommendations.
Heat speeds it up. NHTSA's research found tire aging is a greater concern in the southern Sun Belt. A closed garage in a Broward summer is a warm place to keep rubber.

chunks.title: Unused Tires Still Age: The Garage and Spare Myth
chunks.text:
What the evidence says
So the myth is backwards. A stored tire doesn't stay new; it just stays unworn.
Where unused tires hide
The spare. It's often the oldest tire on the car, because it rarely touches the road and may be as old as the car itself. Bridgestone's guidance is to check the spare and replace it if it's more than 10 years old, even if it appears new. Our spare tire types guide explains what kind you may have.
The set in the garage. Old wheels and tires kept "just in case," or a second set for a car you sold. Their age started at their date code, not when they came off the car.
New old stock. A tire can sit in a warehouse before it's sold. NHTSA's Tire Buyers' FAQ suggests checking the date code when you buy and knowing your vehicle maker's recommended replacement timeframe. Our post on how old tires are when you buy online covers what to ask.

chunks.title: Unused Tires Still Age: The Garage and Spare Myth
chunks.text:
Where unused tires hide
The car that sat. Snowbirds know this one. Our post for cars that sat all summer covers the tires still on the car.
Find the real age
Every tire carries a DOT code on its sidewall. The last four digits are the week and year it was made. Try reading one:
Our DOT date code guide shows where to find it, including on tires that only print the full code on one side.

chunks.title: Unused Tires Still Age: The Garage and Spare Myth
chunks.text:
How to store tires in a Florida garage
You can't stop aging, but storage makes a difference. Michelin's advice for stored tires:
- Indoors, in a clean, cool, dry and dark place, out of direct sunlight.
- Away from heat sources such as hot pipes, and away from ozone sources such as electric motors and generators. That includes the garage freezer, the pool pump area and the generator you keep for hurricane season.
- Clean and dry before storage, so nothing corrodes on the wheels.
- Mounted on wheels? Stack them horizontally. Unmounted tires can stand upright, side by side.
In South Florida, the coolest dark place you have is often inside the house, not the garage. A covered spot off the concrete, away from the water heater and the generator, beats a sunny corner.

chunks.title: Unused Tires Still Age: The Garage and Spare Myth
chunks.text:
Should you buy tires ahead and store them?
Sometimes it makes sense: a second set of wheels, or a spare set for a vehicle you'll keep for years. But buying far ahead just to have tires on the shelf uses up part of their life before they ever roll. Three questions to ask first:
- How long until they'll go on? The longer the wait, the more of their age limit they'll have used.
- Do you have the right place to store them? Cool, dry, dark and away from ozone, per Michelin. Many South Florida garages don't qualify in summer.
- Will the size still be right? If you change cars, a stored set may not fit the next one.

chunks.title: Unused Tires Still Age: The Garage and Spare Myth
chunks.text:
Don't forget the spare's pressure
An unused spare loses air like any tire. NHTSA says to check pressure monthly on every tire, and that includes the spare. A spare that's in date but flat won't help on the shoulder of I-95.
Before you mount stored tires
- Read the DOT date on every tire, not just one.
- Look closely at the sidewalls and tread for cracks, bulges or flat spots.
- Have them inspected if they're five years old or more, as Bridgestone and Michelin recommend.
- Check that they match the size, load index and speed rating on your door placard.

chunks.title: Unused Tires Still Age: The Garage and Spare Myth
chunks.text:
The verdict
Claim
Verdict
"Unused tires don't age"
Myth. NHTSA lists storage as a cause of aging.
"The spare is new because it's never been used"
Myth. Bridgestone says replace it after 10 years even if it looks new.
"Storage conditions matter"
True. Michelin recommends cool, dry, dark and away from ozone.
"Tread depth tells you a tire's age"
Myth. Only the DOT date does.
If the spare or the stored set is past its limit, shop by size and ask about the DOT date on what you buy. Shipping is free to the 48 contiguous states and DC, and in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach we install at our Sunrise shop or by mobile van. Not sure about the set on the car? Do I Need Tires Yet? walks you through it.

chunks.title: Unused Tires Still Age: The Garage and Spare Myth
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Myth: a tire that's never been driven on stays new. NHTSA says tires age from service, storage and environmental conditions, so a stored tire still gets older.
- A tire's age starts at its DOT date code, not the day it went on a car or came out of the wrapper.
- Bridgestone says to replace the spare if it's more than 10 years old, even if it looks new. The spare is often the oldest tire on the car.
- Michelin's storage advice: indoors, clean, cool, dry and dark, away from sunlight, heat and ozone sources such as electric motors.
- NHTSA's research found tire aging is a greater concern in the hot Sun Belt, which includes South Florida garages.

chunks.title: Unused Tires Still Age: The Garage and Spare Myth
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Do tires expire if they're not used?
There's no printed expiration date, but tires age whether or not they're driven on. NHTSA says aging comes from service, storage and environmental conditions. NHTSA also notes that some vehicle and tire makers recommend replacing tires 6 to 10 years old regardless of treadwear, so the clock starts at the DOT date code.
How long can tires be stored before use?
There's no single number that fits every tire and storage space. Storage conditions matter a lot: Michelin recommends a clean, cool, dry, dark indoor space away from sunlight, heat and ozone sources. Check the DOT date before mounting stored tires, and have them inspected if they've been stored for years.
Is my never-used spare tire still good?

chunks.title: Unused Tires Still Age: The Garage and Spare Myth
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Check its age. Bridgestone recommends replacing a spare that's more than 10 years old, even if it appears new, and Bridgestone and Michelin both recommend a professional inspection at least once a year from five years old. Check the spare's pressure monthly too.
Should I worry about buying 'new old stock' tires?
Ask for the DOT date before you buy. NHTSA's Tire Buyers' FAQ suggests checking the date code at purchase and knowing your vehicle maker's recommended replacement timeframe. A tire that sat in a warehouse for years has already used some of its life.

chunks.title: Buying a Used Car After Storm Season: Tire Clues
chunks.text:
Hurricanes & Flooding
Buying a Used Car After Storm Season: Tire Clues
Buying a used car after hurricane season? How to check for flood damage, what the tires and spare well can tell you, and the free VIN checks to run first.
Storm season ends. The flood cars don't disappear.
Hurricane season officially ends November 30. Cars that sat in floodwater during the season don't all go to the crusher. Some are repaired properly and sold with an honest title. Others are dried out, cleaned up and offered for sale with no mention of the water.
Michigan's consumer protection office puts it plainly: flood-damaged vehicles can be shipped across the country in a matter of days and show up online or on lots far from the storm, without any obvious signs of damage. That works in both directions. A car flooded elsewhere can end up for sale in Broward.

chunks.title: Buying a Used Car After Storm Season: Tire Clues
chunks.text:
Storm season ends. The flood cars don't disappear.
This guide covers three layers of checking: the paperwork, the car, and the tires, which carry more clues than most buyers think.
Layer 1: Run the VIN before you drive across town
Two checks are worth running on any used car bought after a storm season:
- NMVTIS. The National Motor Vehicle Title Information System is a federal database overseen by the U.S. Department of Justice. A report covers the current title, brand history (labels states assign, such as "junk," "salvage" or "flood"), odometer readings, total-loss history and salvage history. Reports come from approved providers for a small fee.

chunks.title: Buying a Used Car After Storm Season: Tire Clues
chunks.text:
Layer 1: Run the VIN before you drive across town
- NICB VINCheck. The National Insurance Crime Bureau's free tool checks a VIN against insurer-reported salvage, flood and theft records. NICB is clear about its limits: it only covers participating insurers and isn't a complete vehicle history.
Also run the VIN through NHTSA's recall lookup . It won't show flood damage, but it will show open safety recalls.
A clean report is a good start, not proof. A car that was never reported won't carry a brand.

chunks.title: Buying a Used Car After Storm Season: Tire Clues
chunks.text:
Layer 2: Look, touch and smell
Michigan's guidance lists the signs to look for:
- Musty or "over-perfumed" smells, or signs of mold or mildew
- Water stains, mud or residue in the trunk, under the carpet and floor mats, and around the gas and brake pedals
- Grime in hard-to-reach places that are difficult to clean
AAA adds that salt water is harder on a car than fresh water, because salt is highly corrosive to both the interior and mechanical parts. In coastal South Florida, that matters.
Then get an independent inspection from a technician with no connection to the seller. NHTSA's own guidance on flooded vehicles is not to drive one until a technician has checked it, because damage may not be visible.

chunks.title: Buying a Used Car After Storm Season: Tire Clues
chunks.text:
Layer 3: What the tires and wheels can tell you
Tires are easy to inspect, and they say a lot about how a car has been treated.
The spare tire well
Lift the trunk floor. The spare well is a low point where water collects and a place most quick cleanups miss. Mud, silt, a waterline or rust here is worth asking about. Check the spare itself and the jack and tools stored with it.
The DOT date codes
Every tire carries a DOT code ending in a four-digit date: the week and year it was made. Read all four, and the spare:
- Four brand-new tires on an older car isn't a red flag by itself. But combined with new carpet or a fresh interior, ask why everything was replaced at once.
- Old tires are a budget item. Bridgestone and Michelin recommend replacement 10 years after a tire was made, and an annual inspection from five years. See how old is too old.

chunks.title: Buying a Used Car After Storm Season: Tire Clues
chunks.text:
Matching and wear
- A matched set with even wear suggests regular rotation and alignment.
- Four different brands or tread patterns can mean the car has had tires replaced one at a time. On an all-wheel-drive car, ask the seller about it; many AWD manuals call for matched tires.
- Wear on one edge points to alignment or suspension issues. Our noise and vibration checker helps on the test drive.

chunks.title: Buying a Used Car After Storm Season: Tire Clues
chunks.text:
Wheels and lug nuts
Look for heavy corrosion on the wheels, lug nuts and the brake parts visible through the spokes. Some rust is normal on an older car in a coastal state. Heavy corrosion on a car that looks spotless everywhere else is a question to ask.
Questions to ask the seller
A good seller won't mind these, and the answers are worth comparing with what you see:
- Where has the car been registered and driven? Ask for the title and any service records.
- Has it ever had water inside, or an insurance claim? Ask directly, then compare the answer with the NMVTIS and VINCheck results.
- When were the tires, carpet or seats last replaced, and why? Recent replacements are normal. Several at once deserve an explanation.
- Can my mechanic inspect it before I buy? If the answer is no, that tells you something too.

chunks.title: Buying a Used Car After Storm Season: Tire Clues
chunks.text:
Questions to ask the seller
- Is there a spare, jack and lug wrench? Missing equipment is common and easy to fix, but worth knowing before you agree a price.
Measure the tread before you negotiate
Tires are part of the price of a used car. Measure each tire in three grooves. AAA recommends replacing at 4/32 of an inch for wet roads; NHTSA's line is 2/32. Our post on why 4/32 matters in Florida rain explains the difference.

chunks.title: Buying a Used Car After Storm Season: Tire Clues
chunks.text:
The checklist
- Run NMVTIS and NICB VINCheck; check recalls on NHTSA
- Smell the cabin; look under mats and in the trunk
- Lift the trunk floor and inspect the spare well
- Read all five DOT date codes
- Check that the tires match and wear evenly
- Measure tread in three grooves per tire
- Get an independent inspection before you buy
Already own a car that sat in water? Our post on what to check after a car sits in floodwater covers that case. If the tires are due, run them through Do I Need Tires Yet? and shop by size or vehicle.

chunks.title: Buying a Used Car After Storm Season: Tire Clues
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Flooded cars can be moved across the country and sold far from the storm without obvious signs, Michigan's consumer protection office warns.
- Run the VIN first: NMVTIS reports state title brands such as 'flood' and 'salvage,' and NICB's free VINCheck looks for insurer-reported flood and salvage records.
- Look for mud, water stains or residue in the trunk and under carpets. The spare tire well is an easy place to start.
- The tires tell their own story: DOT date codes, matching sets and even wear all help you judge the car and budget for it.
- Get an independent inspection. NHTSA says flood damage may not be visible.

chunks.title: Buying a Used Car After Storm Season: Tire Clues
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How can I tell if a used car was in a flood?
Start with the VIN: an NMVTIS vehicle history report shows state title brands like flood or salvage, and NICB's free VINCheck searches insurer-reported flood and salvage records. Then look and smell: musty or over-perfumed interiors, water stains, and mud or residue in the trunk, under carpets and around the pedals. Finally, have an independent technician inspect it, because flood damage may not be visible.
Will a flood-damaged car always have a flood title?
Not always. A title brand depends on the car being reported, and Michigan's consumer protection office warns that flood cars can be shipped to other states and offered for sale without any mention of the damage. That's why the inspection matters as much as the paperwork.
What can the tires tell me about a used car?

chunks.title: Buying a Used Car After Storm Season: Tire Clues
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Several things. The DOT date code shows how old each tire is. A matched set with even wear suggests regular care, while four different brands or uneven wear across the tread can point to alignment, suspension or pressure issues. Mud or silt in the spare tire well or on the spare can be a flood clue.
Should I replace the tires on a car that was in a flood?
Have them inspected. Floodwater carries oil, salt and other contaminants, and debris under the water can cause punctures. If the car was submerged, treat the whole vehicle as flood-damaged and have a technician check it before driving, as NHTSA advises.

chunks.title: Why 4/32 Matters More Than 2/32 in Florida Rain
chunks.text:
Rain, Heat & Weather
Why 4/32 Matters More Than 2/32 in Florida Rain
When to replace tires by tread depth: 2/32 is the wear-bar line, but AAA's wet-braking tests point to 4/32. What that means in South Florida rain.
Two numbers, two different jobs
Most drivers know one tread number: 2/32 of an inch, the point where the penny shows all of Lincoln's head. It's a real line. It's just not the line that matters most on a wet Broward highway in August.
Here's the short version. 2/32 marks the end of a tire's life. 4/32 marks the point where wet braking has already slipped a long way. In a place where it rains hard most summer afternoons, the second number is the one to plan around.

chunks.title: Why 4/32 Matters More Than 2/32 in Florida Rain
chunks.text:
What 2/32 actually means
NHTSA's guidance is to replace a tire when the tread reaches 2/32 of an inch. Every tire has wear bars, small raised bridges molded into the bottom of the grooves. When the tread wears down to them and they sit flush with the surface, the tire is at 2/32 and done.
That's the line you shouldn't cross. But it describes a tire that has very little groove left to carry water away. It isn't a sign that the tire still grips well right up until that point.

chunks.title: Why 4/32 Matters More Than 2/32 in Florida Rain
chunks.text:
What AAA's wet-braking tests found at 4/32
In 2018, AAA worked with the Automobile Club of Southern California's Automotive Research Center to test new all-season tires against the same tires worn to 4/32 of an inch, on wet pavement at highway speed.
The results, as AAA reported them:
Measure
Worn to 4/32 vs new
Wet stopping distance, passenger car
87 feet longer on average
Wet stopping distance, light truck
86 feet longer on average
Increase in stopping distance
43% on average
Handling ability, passenger car
33% lower on average
AAA's conclusion was to replace tires at 4/32, when stopping distances have already begun to get noticeably worse, rather than waiting for 2/32. Note what that means: the tires in the test still had twice the tread of the legal-wear line, and they still needed the length of several cars more to stop.

chunks.title: Why 4/32 Matters More Than 2/32 in Florida Rain
chunks.text:
What AAA's wet-braking tests found at 4/32
At least one vehicle maker draws the line in the same place. Tesla's Model Y owner's manual recommends replacing a tire when any tread depth reading is 4/32 in (3 mm) or less.
Why this matters more in South Florida
Tread is a set of channels. On a wet road, the grooves give water somewhere to go so the rubber can stay in contact with the pavement. Shallower grooves move less water.
South Florida gives those grooves a lot of work:
- The rainy season runs May 15 to October 15, according to NWS Miami. Afternoon downpours are a normal part of the commute for five months.
- Heavy rain arrives fast. A dry road can carry standing water within minutes, before it drains.
- Hydroplaning can start at modest speeds. Bridgestone says it can happen at speeds as low as 35 mph, depending on the tires and the water.

chunks.title: Why 4/32 Matters More Than 2/32 in Florida Rain
chunks.text:
Why this matters more in South Florida
Our post on afternoon downpours on Broward roads covers how to drive through it. This one is about the tires you bring into it.
Measure, don't guess
You can't see 4/32 from the driver's seat. Measure it:
- Use a gauge if you can. They're inexpensive and read in 32nds.
- Measure three grooves per tire, inner, center and outer. Uneven wear often hides on the inside edge.
- Write down the lowest number on each tire. That's the one that counts.
- Check all four. Front and rear tires often wear at different rates.
No gauge? The quarter test gives a rough read: put a quarter upside down in a groove. If you can see all of Washington's head, you're at about 4/32 or less. Our tread depth chart shows both lines in 32nds and millimeters, and our guide to how to check tread depth covers the gauge, penny and quarter methods.

chunks.text:

If you're at 5/32 in October, you probably have the winter. If you're at 5/32 in April, the rainy season will arrive before the tires are done. That's the whole case for planning around 4/32.

chunks.title: Why 4/32 Matters More Than 2/32 in Florida Rain
chunks.text:
When one part of the tire wears first
Tires rarely wear evenly by themselves. The lowest groove on a tire sets its replacement date, so uneven wear brings that date forward. Three patterns are worth knowing:
- Both outer edges worn: often a sign of running under-inflated. Check pressure monthly, cold, against the door placard.
- Center worn: can point to over-inflation, such as filling to the sidewall maximum instead of the placard number. Our post on the sidewall max psi myth explains why that number isn't the target.
- One edge worn: usually alignment. A curb strike or a deep pothole can be enough to start it.
Rotating on schedule spreads normal wear across all four tires, and our rotation pattern tool shows the pattern for your drivetrain. If a new set starts wearing unevenly, fix the cause early. Otherwise one tire reaches 4/32 long before the rest.

chunks.title: Why 4/32 Matters More Than 2/32 in Florida Rain
chunks.text:
Tread isn't the only limit
A tire can be finished before the tread is. Age, sidewall cracking, bulges and repairs outside the tread area all count. Our guide on how old is too old explains the age guidance from tire makers, and our repair checker covers punctures.
Next steps
- Measure all four tires this week, in three grooves each.
- Run the numbers through Do I Need Tires Yet?.
- If you're at or near 4/32, shop by size or vehicle.
- In Miami-Dade, Broward or Palm Beach, have them installed at our Sunrise shop or by our mobile van. Free shipping covers the 48 contiguous states and DC if you're installing elsewhere.

chunks.title: Why 4/32 Matters More Than 2/32 in Florida Rain
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- 2/32 of an inch is where NHTSA says to replace a tire. It's where the built-in wear bars sit flush with the tread.
- AAA's wet-braking tests found tires worn to 4/32 took an average of 87 feet longer to stop than new tires, 43% farther.
- AAA recommends replacing at 4/32, before stopping distances in the wet get that much worse.
- South Florida's rainy season runs May 15 to October 15, per NWS Miami, so wet roads are a normal part of the year here.
- Measure in three grooves on every tire and replace on the lowest reading, not the average.

chunks.title: Why 4/32 Matters More Than 2/32 in Florida Rain
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
At what tread depth should I replace my tires?
NHTSA's line is 2/32 of an inch, where the wear bars molded into the tread become flush with the surface. AAA recommends replacing earlier, at 4/32, after its wet-braking tests showed worn tires needed much more distance to stop on wet pavement. If you drive in frequent heavy rain, 4/32 is the more useful planning number.
How much longer does it take to stop on worn tires in the rain?
In AAA's 2018 testing, tires worn to 4/32 of an inch took an average of 87 feet longer to stop from highway speed on wet pavement than new tires, an increase of 43%. That was a test at 4/32, so tires worn closer to 2/32 have even less tread left to clear water.
Is 4/32 a legal limit in Florida?

chunks.title: Why 4/32 Matters More Than 2/32 in Florida Rain
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
No. 4/32 is AAA's recommendation based on its wet-braking tests, not a legal minimum. The 2/32 line is the one NHTSA uses and the one the wear bars mark. Plan your replacement around 4/32 so you aren't caught out at the start of the rainy season.
How do I measure tread depth at home?
Use a tread depth gauge in the inner, center and outer grooves of each tire, and write down the lowest number. The penny and quarter tests give a rough read. Our tread gauge demo shows what each depth looks like, and our tread depth chart converts 32nds to millimeters.

chunks.text:
Free tool
Can your tire be repaired?
Where the damage is decides it as much as what caused it. Pick the spot on the tire and the kind of damage to see what USTMA and Tire Industry Association repair practice says. Only a small puncture in the tread area may be repairable, and only after a technician inspects the inside of the tire.
The tool
Maps where on a tire a puncture may be repairable after an internal inspection and where damage means the tire should be replaced under industry repair practice. A technician must inspect the inside of the tire before any repair.

- 2Choose what it looks like: a nail or screw, a larger puncture, a cut, a bulge, cracking or a curb scrape.
- 3Read the result. Replace means it isn't repairable under industry practice. Have it inspected means a technician needs to look first.

Questions
The things people ask next
Can a tire with a nail in it be repaired?
Sometimes. Under USTMA and TIA practice, a puncture 1/4 inch (6 mm) or smaller in the tread area may be repaired with a plug and patch together, fitted from the inside, once the tire is off the wheel and the inside has been inspected.
Can a puncture in the sidewall be patched?
No. USTMA says punctures or cuts in the sidewall or shoulder can't be repaired, because that part of the tire flexes the most and lacks the tread area's reinforcement. Replace the tire.
Is a plug from a roadside kit a proper repair?
No. USTMA calls a plug alone an unacceptable repair, and a tire with an earlier improper repair isn't repaired again. A plug pushed in from the outside can turn a repairable tire into one that has to be replaced.
Can a bulge or bubble be repaired?

chunks.title: Can My Tire Be Repaired? Puncture Repair Check
chunks.text:

No. A bulge means the tire's inner structure is damaged. Michelin says a tire with a bulge or bubble can't be repaired and must be replaced.

The things people ask next
Why does my steering wheel shake at highway speed?
A wheel out of balance is a common cause of a shake you feel in the steering wheel at highway speed. A tire that's out of round, a separated belt or a bent wheel can feel similar. A technician can check the balance and look over the tires and wheels.
Why does the car shake when I brake?
A vibration you feel through the brake pedal or steering wheel when braking can point to warped or worn brake rotors. Have the brakes inspected.
What does a hum that gets louder with speed mean?
Uneven or cupped tread and a worn wheel bearing can both make a hum or roar that rises with speed. They're hard to tell apart by ear, so have it inspected.

chunks.title: How Old Is Too Old for Tires? What Makers Recommend
chunks.text:
Tire Age, Storage & Records
How Old Is Too Old for Tires? What Makers Recommend
How old is too old for tires? NHTSA, Bridgestone and Michelin guidance side by side: yearly inspections from 5 years, replacement at 10, spare included.
Why there isn't one number
Search "how old is too old for tires" and you'll see 5, 6 and 10 years quoted with equal confidence. They aren't competing rules. They're different pieces of guidance from different organizations, and each one means something specific.
NHTSA's own TireWise guidance points back to the manufacturers: some vehicle and tire makers recommend replacing tires that are 6 to 10 years old, regardless of treadwear. So the useful question isn't "what's the law?" It's "what do the people who made my car and my tires say?"
Here's that guidance side by side, then how to find your tires' age and what to do with it.

chunks.title: How Old Is Too Old for Tires? What Makers Recommend
chunks.text:
What the manufacturers say
Who
What they recommend
Applies to
NHTSA (TireWise)
Notes that some vehicle and tire makers recommend replacing tires 6 to 10 years old, regardless of treadwear
Summary of industry guidance
Bridgestone
Inspection by a tire professional at least once a year from 5 years; replace 10 years after manufacture, regardless of tread depth
Bridgestone and Firestone tires, spare included
Michelin
After 5 years, a thorough inspection at least once a year by a trained professional; replace 10 years after the date of manufacture, even if the tires appear to be in good condition and haven't reached the wear bars
Michelin tires
Your vehicle maker
Some set their own timeframe, which can be shorter than 10 years
Check the owner's manual

chunks.title: How Old Is Too Old for Tires? What Makers Recommend
chunks.text:
What the manufacturers say
Two patterns stand out. The five-year mark is about inspection, not replacement: it's when the tire makers want a professional to start looking every year. And the 10-year mark is the outside limit the tire makers set, whatever the tread says.
When your vehicle maker and your tire maker disagree, the shorter timeframe is the one to plan around.
Find your tires' age
A tire's age starts at its DOT date code, the last four digits of the DOT number on the sidewall: two for the week, two for the year. Type them in to see where each tire sits against the guidance above:
The last four digits of a tire's DOT code are the week and year it was made, so 2319 means week 23 of 2019. Bridgestone recommends a professional inspection at least yearly from 5 years and replacing tires 10 years after manufacture, regardless of tread.

chunks.title: How Old Is Too Old for Tires? What Makers Recommend
chunks.text:
Find your tires' age
Can't find four digits? The full DOT number may be stamped on only one side, often the inboard one. Our guide to reading the tire date code shows where to look. Check every tire, because a set that's been rotated, patched or partly replaced can have more than one age on it.
Do tires expire if they're never used?
There's no expiration date stamped on a tire, but the aging doesn't wait for the first mile. NHTSA's TireWise guidance describes tire aging as the rubber and other components changing over time due to service, storage and environmental conditions. A tire that spent years in a warehouse, a garage or a trunk is still aging.
That matters in three places:
- The spare. It rarely touches the road, so it's often the oldest tire on the car. Bridgestone's guidance is to check the spare and replace it if it's more than 10 years old, even if it appears new.

chunks.title: How Old Is Too Old for Tires? What Makers Recommend
chunks.text:
Do tires expire if they're never used?
- A car that sits. Low miles don't mean young tires. A second car or a seasonal car can reach five years with most of its tread left.
- "New" tires. Unused doesn't mean freshly made. NHTSA's Tire Buyers' FAQ suggests checking the date code when you buy and knowing your vehicle maker's replacement timeframe. Look before the tires are mounted.

chunks.title: How Old Is Too Old for Tires? What Makers Recommend
chunks.text:
Age isn't the only clock
A young tire can still need replacing. Age runs alongside two other limits:
- Tread. NHTSA says to replace at 2/32 of an inch, where the wear bars sit flush with the tread. Our tread depth chart covers where AAA's 4/32 recommendation fits in.
- Damage. NHTSA's advice is to look for bulges, cuts and cracks when you check your tires. A bulge on a two-year-old tire is a reason to replace it, whatever the date says.
Whichever limit a tire reaches first is the one that counts.

chunks.title: How Old Is Too Old for Tires? What Makers Recommend
chunks.text:
What an age inspection looks for
Aging doesn't always show from the outside, which is why the tire makers ask for a professional to look once a tire reaches five years. A technician will typically check:
- cracking in the sidewall and in the grooves between tread blocks
- bulges, cuts and other damage on both sidewalls
- irregular wear across the tread
- anything you've noticed on the road, such as a new vibration
- the date codes, spare included
If the inspection finds a problem, the recommendation will be to consider replacing that tire. If it doesn't, the answer is to keep checking monthly and inspect again next year.

chunks.title: How Old Is Too Old for Tires? What Makers Recommend
chunks.text:
The Florida factor
Where a car lives affects how quickly its tires age. NHTSA's TireWise guidance lists exposure to sunlight and a warmer climate among the things that contribute to aging, and NHTSA's research found tire aging is a greater concern in the more southern parts of the Sun Belt states.
For South Florida drivers that's a reason to take the five-year inspection seriously rather than waiting on the 10-year mark. Our guide to Florida heat and tires covers what heat does day to day.

chunks.title: How Old Is Too Old for Tires? What Makers Recommend
chunks.text:
An age plan you can follow
Tire age
What to do
Under 5 years
Monthly pressure and visual check; tread and damage decide replacement
5 years and up
Professional inspection at least once a year (Bridgestone, Michelin), spare included
Past your vehicle maker's timeframe
Consider replacing, per your owner's manual
10 years and up
Bridgestone and Michelin recommend replacing, regardless of tread
Want a quick read on tread, age and damage together? Try Do I Need Tires Yet?. If it's time, shop by size and check the DOT dates on arrival.

chunks.title: How Old Is Too Old for Tires? What Makers Recommend
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- There's no single age that fits every tire. NHTSA notes that some vehicle and tire makers recommend replacing tires 6 to 10 years old, regardless of treadwear.
- Bridgestone and Michelin recommend a professional inspection at least once a year from five years old.
- Both recommend replacing tires 10 years after they were made, even if the tread looks new. That includes the spare.
- A tire's age starts at its DOT date, not the day it went on your car.
- Your vehicle maker may set a shorter timeframe, so check the owner's manual.

chunks.title: How Old Is Too Old for Tires? What Makers Recommend
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How old is too old for tires?
It depends on the tire and the vehicle. NHTSA notes that some vehicle and tire makers recommend replacing tires that are 6 to 10 years old regardless of treadwear. Bridgestone and Michelin recommend replacing tires 10 years after manufacture, with a professional inspection at least once a year from five years on. Your owner's manual may give a shorter timeframe.
Do tires expire if they're never used?
There's no printed expiration date, but tires age from the day they're made. NHTSA's TireWise guidance says aging comes from service, storage and environmental conditions, so a tire that sat on a shelf or in a trunk is still getting older. Read the DOT date code to know its age.
Should I replace a spare tire that's 10 years old?

chunks.title: How Old Is Too Old for Tires? What Makers Recommend
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Bridgestone's guidance is to check your spare and replace it if it's more than 10 years old, even if it appears new. The spare is often the oldest tire on the car because it rarely touches the road.
How old can new tires be when I buy them?
There's no single rule. NHTSA's Tire Buyers' FAQ suggests checking the date code when you buy and knowing your vehicle maker's recommended replacement timeframe. If a set is older than you'd like, ask before it's mounted.

chunks.title: Tire Recalls: Check Your DOT Number and Register Tires
chunks.text:
Tire Age, Storage & Records
Tire Recalls: Check Your DOT Number and Register Tires
How to check a tire recall with the full DOT number (TIN), where to find it on the sidewall, and how tire registration gets recall notices to you.
Recalls happen to tires too
Most drivers know to check their car for recalls. Fewer know that tires get recalled on their own, separately from the vehicle. A recall check by VIN covers the car; the tires you bought last year have their own lookups.
Two habits close that gap: knowing your tires' identification numbers, and registering them with the maker. Here's how to do both.

chunks.title: Tire Recalls: Check Your DOT Number and Register Tires
chunks.text:
Where the TIN is on a tire
Every tire sold in the US carries a tire identification number, or TIN. It starts with the letters DOT and sits on the sidewall near the rim.
The catch: the full number may not be on the side you can see. NHTSA advises checking both sides of the tire, because the full TIN may not be on both. On many cars that means a flashlight and a look at the inboard sidewall, the one facing under the car.
What you're looking for:
- The letters DOT, followed by a string of letters and numbers.
- A group of four digits at the end. Those are the week and year the tire was made.
- If the code stops short of four digits, you're probably on the partial side. Check the other sidewall.

chunks.title: Tire Recalls: Check Your DOT Number and Register Tires
chunks.text:
Where the TIN is on a tire
NHTSA's 2015 rule standardized a 13-symbol TIN with a three-symbol plant code for new tires, so you'll see both older, shorter numbers and newer, longer ones on the road. Either way, a recall lookup needs the whole thing, not just the date. The date tells you a tire's age. The full TIN tells a recall database which tires you have, down to the plant that built them, so one wrong character can turn a match into a miss. A clear photo beats copying it by hand on a dark garage floor.
Type the last four digits into the reader below to see when a tire was made. Then copy down the full number.
Our guide to reading the tire date code breaks down each part of the number.

chunks.title: Tire Recalls: Check Your DOT Number and Register Tires
chunks.text:
How to check a tire recall, step by step
- Find DOT on each tire, spare included. Check both sidewalls.
- Copy the full TIN for each tire, or take a clear photo of it.
- Enter it in the USTMA Tire Recall Lookup. The U.S. Tire Manufacturers Association's free lookup takes the full TIN and covers recalls on tires made by its members from 2000 on. If a tire matches, it gives you the maker's contact for the remedy.
- Search NHTSA's recall site at nhtsa.gov/recalls. For tires, it returns recalls, investigations and complaints by tire brand and tire line. Use it for brands outside USTMA's membership, or when you're not sure who made the tire.
- If a tire is recalled, contact the tire maker and follow its instructions for the remedy. Our post on what to do with a tire recall notice covers the free remedy and its deadline.

chunks.title: Tire Recalls: Check Your DOT Number and Register Tires
chunks.text:
How to check a tire recall, step by step
- Repeat for every tire. A set that has been partly replaced can mix makers and dates.
A TIN that won't read clearly is a reason to have an installer look, not to skip the check.
Registering your tires
A recall only helps if the maker can find you. That's what tire registration is for: it links your name and address to your tires' TINs, so the maker can mail you a recall notice.

chunks.title: Tire Recalls: Check Your DOT Number and Register Tires
chunks.text:
What the federal rules say
The rules live in 49 CFR Part 574, Tire Identification and Recordkeeping. In plain terms:
- Tire makers must supply registration forms to the dealers who sell their tires.
- Independent dealers, when they sell you tires, must either give you a registration form with the full TIN already filled in, or register the tires with the maker themselves, on paper or electronically.
- If a dealer registers you electronically, the rule says your invoice has to state that.
NHTSA's letter to new tire buyers puts the practical version simply: ask your retailer whether they registered you on site, or ask for a registration form.

chunks.title: Tire Recalls: Check Your DOT Number and Register Tires
chunks.text:
How to register
- Mail the form the dealer gave you, with the TIN filled in.
- Or register online. Many major tire makers take registrations on their own websites; you'll need your contact details and each tire's TIN.
- Sign up for alerts. NHTSA also offers tire recall email alerts, per its new-tire-purchase letter.
Register every tire, because each one has its own TIN, and the date digits can differ even within one set.

chunks.title: Tire Recalls: Check Your DOT Number and Register Tires
chunks.text:
Buying online? Plan the TIN handoff
When tires ship to you or to an installer, the person who sells them and the person who mounts them can be different. Two easy fixes:
- Photograph the full DOT number on each tire when the set arrives, before it's mounted. It's also when to check the date; our post on how old tires are when you buy online covers what to look for.
- Ask at installation whether registration is handled for you. If not, register each tire with the maker yourself.
Our post on getting online tires installed in Broward walks through that handoff.

chunks.title: Tire Recalls: Check Your DOT Number and Register Tires
chunks.text:
A once-a-year routine
- Read each tire's DOT date and note its age; our guide How Old Is Too Old for Tires? explains the five- and 10-year markers.
- Run each full TIN through the USTMA lookup.
- Check NHTSA's recall site for your tire brand and line.
- Run tread, age and damage through Do I Need Tires Yet?.
If it's time for new tires, shop tires by size, with your size read off the door-jamb sticker by the Tire Size Finder. Free shipping covers the 48 contiguous states and DC. Extreme Tires installs at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach; see how installation works, or call (954) 773-1896 with a code you can't read.

chunks.title: Tire Recalls: Check Your DOT Number and Register Tires
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- A tire recall check needs the full tire identification number (TIN), which starts with DOT on the sidewall.
- The full TIN may be on only one side of the tire, often the inboard side, so check both.
- USTMA's free lookup takes the full TIN for tires its members made from 2000 on. NHTSA's recall site covers tires by brand and line.
- Registering your tires is how the maker reaches you if they're recalled. Federal rules make dealers part of that process.
- Keep a photo of each tire's full DOT number, or ask for it on your invoice.

chunks.title: Tire Recalls: Check Your DOT Number and Register Tires
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How do I check if my tires are recalled?
Copy the full DOT number from each tire's sidewall and enter it in the U.S. Tire Manufacturers Association's free Tire Recall Lookup, which covers tires its members made from 2000 on. You can also search tire recalls by brand and tire line on NHTSA's recalls site.
Where is the tire identification number?
On the sidewall near the rim, after the letters DOT. NHTSA advises checking both sides, because the full number may be on only one of them. The last four digits are the week and year the tire was made.
Do I have to register my tires?

chunks.title: Tire Recalls: Check Your DOT Number and Register Tires
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
It isn't required of you, but it's how the tire maker can contact you about a recall. Federal rules (49 CFR Part 574) require tire makers to supply registration forms to dealers, and independent dealers must either give you a form with the full TIN filled in when you buy or send your registration to the maker themselves.
Did my installer register my tires?
Ask. NHTSA suggests asking your retailer whether they registered you on site, or asking for a registration form. If a dealer registers you electronically, the federal rule says the invoice must say so. Most major tire makers also take registrations on their own websites.

chunks.title: Parts of a Tire: Tread, Belts, Plies, Bead and Sidewall
chunks.text:
Tire Basics
Parts of a Tire: Tread, Belts, Plies, Bead and Sidewall
The parts of a tire, from tread and belts to body plies, bead and inner liner, and how each part explains a bulge, a repair limit or a slow leak.
A tire is layers, not a lump of rubber
From the outside a tire looks like one piece of black rubber. Inside it's a stack of layers, each with one job. Knowing them explains a lot: why a bubble can't be patched, why repairs stop at the shoulder, and where a slow leak can hide.
Here they are from the road inward, using the definitions in the federal tire standard (FMVSS No. 139) and the tire makers' own descriptions.
Part
Federal or maker definition
What it does
Tread
That portion of a tire that comes into contact with the road (FMVSS 139)
Grip, wear resistance, water clearance
Belts
Crown plies provide the rigid base for the tread (BFGoodrich)
Keep the tread flat and stiff

chunks.title: Parts of a Tire: Tread, Belts, Plies, Bead and Sidewall
chunks.text:
A tire is layers, not a lump of rubber
Body (carcass) plies
A layer of rubber-coated parallel cords (FMVSS 139)
Carry the load under pressure
Sidewall
That portion of a tire between the tread and bead (FMVSS 139)
Protects the plies; carries the markings
Bead
Made of steel wires, shaped to fit the rim (FMVSS 139)
Clamps the tire to the wheel
Inner liner
The layer(s) forming the inside surface of a tubeless tire that contains the inflating medium (FMVSS 139)
Holds the air in

chunks.title: Parts of a Tire: Tread, Belts, Plies, Bead and Sidewall
chunks.text:
Tread: the only part that touches the road
The tread is the patterned rubber on top. BFGoodrich says it provides traction and cornering grip and is designed to resist wear, abrasion and heat.
Continental names its pieces:
- Ribs, the raised sections running around the tire, made up of tread blocks.
- Tread blocks, the raised rubber segments that touch the road.
- Grooves, the deep channels between tread blocks, running around and across the tire. They move water out from under it.
- Sipes, small, thin slots molded into the tread blocks.
The federal standard adds treadwear indicators, the projections within the principal grooves that show how worn the tread is. When the tread is flush with them, you're at 2/32 inch. Our tread depth guide covers what that means.
Where the tread meets the sidewall is the shoulder. It matters for repairs, as you'll see below.

chunks.title: Parts of a Tire: Tread, Belts, Plies, Bead and Sidewall
chunks.text:
Belts: the stiff layer under the tread
Under the tread sit the belts, or crown plies. BFGoodrich says they provide the rigid base for the tread. USTMA describes the usual layout as typically, two belts with steel cords laid at opposing angles, which is where the term "steel-belted radial" comes from.
The belts are also why the tread area is the only place a tire can be repaired. USTMA limits repairs to punctures in the tread area, no larger than 1/4 inch (6 mm), and rules out the sidewall and shoulder, which flex the most and lack the tread area's reinforcement. Tap a zone below to see how the guidance treats each part of the tire:

chunks.title: Parts of a Tire: Tread, Belts, Plies, Bead and Sidewall
chunks.text:
Body plies: what actually carries the car
BFGoodrich describes the carcass ply as thin textile fiber cords bonded into the rubber, and says these cables are largely responsible for determining the strength of the tire. The federal standard defines the carcass as the tire structure, except tread and sidewall rubber which, when inflated, bears the load. USTMA adds that most tires have one or two body plies, each typically comprised of polyester, rayon, or nylon cords within a rubber layer.

chunks.title: Parts of a Tire: Tread, Belts, Plies, Bead and Sidewall
chunks.text:
Radial: how the plies are laid
The R in a size like 225/65R17 means radial. FMVSS 139 defines a radial ply tire as one in which the ply cords that extend to the beads are laid at substantially 90 degrees to the centerline of the tread. In other words, the cords run straight across from bead to bead, with the belts on top holding the tread flat. Our guide to reading tire size covers the rest of the size.

chunks.title: Parts of a Tire: Tread, Belts, Plies, Bead and Sidewall
chunks.text:
When the plies are damaged
This is what a sidewall bubble is. Michelin explains that a bulge or bubble generally indicates damaged cords caused by a severe impact, such as a pothole or curb. With the cords broken, air pressure pushes the rubber outward. No patch can rebuild cords, which is why our guide to a bubble in the tire sidewall ends in a replacement.
Michelin also warns that internal damage, such as broken cords or belt separation, is often invisible from the outside, which is why a hard impact is worth an inspection with the tire off the wheel.

chunks.title: Parts of a Tire: Tread, Belts, Plies, Bead and Sidewall
chunks.text:
Sidewall: protection and the label
The sidewall is everything between tread and bead. BFGoodrich says it protects the side of the tire from impacts with curbs and the road and is where the tire's details are printed.
It's also where the law puts the information. FMVSS 139 requires each tire to be marked with its size, maximum permissible inflation pressure and maximum load, and with the generic name of each cord material and the actual number of plies in the sidewall and in the tread area. Look closely and you'll find a short line listing the plies and cord materials under the tread and in the sidewall. That line is the tire's construction, in its own words. Our guide to tire sidewall markings covers the rest of the small print.

chunks.title: Parts of a Tire: Tread, Belts, Plies, Bead and Sidewall
chunks.text:
Bead: where the tire meets the wheel
The bead is the inner edge that sits on the wheel. FMVSS 139 defines it as the part made of steel wires, wrapped or reinforced by ply cords, shaped to fit the rim. BFGoodrich says the beads clamp firmly against the tire's rim to ensure an airtight fit.
This is a common place for slow leaks. Michelin notes pressure loss can come from a leaking valve, valve cap or even the wheel, and a damaged or corroded wheel lip where the bead seats is one way that happens. Our guide to pothole and curb damage covers what to look for on the wheel.

chunks.title: Parts of a Tire: Tread, Belts, Plies, Bead and Sidewall
chunks.text:
Inner liner: the air seal
Modern passenger tires are tubeless. The inner liner does the tube's job. BFGoodrich says today's tires use butyl rubber, which is virtually impenetrable to water and air.
The liner is why a proper repair has a patch on the inside. A plug fills the hole; only a patch seals the liner again. Our guide to tire plug vs patch explains the repair the industry accepts.

chunks.title: Parts of a Tire: Tread, Belts, Plies, Bead and Sidewall
chunks.text:
Putting it to use
You don't need to know any of this to buy tires, but it helps you read what you're buying and what a technician tells you. When you're ready, shop by size; every tire listed carries the same federally required construction line on its sidewall. Tires ship free to the 48 contiguous states and DC, and Extreme Tires installs them at its Sunrise shop or by mobile van across Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach.

chunks.title: Parts of a Tire: Tread, Belts, Plies, Bead and Sidewall
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- A tire is layers: tread on top, belts under it, body plies that carry the load, beads that hold it to the wheel and an inner liner that holds the air.
- The federal tire standard defines a radial tire as one whose ply cords run at substantially 90 degrees to the centerline of the tread.
- The carcass plies are largely responsible for the tire's strength, per BFGoodrich. A sidewall bulge means those cords are damaged, which is why it can't be repaired.
- Repairs are limited to the tread area, where the belts reinforce the tire, per USTMA.
- Federal rules require the ply count and cord materials to be marked on the sidewall.

chunks.title: Parts of a Tire: Tread, Belts, Plies, Bead and Sidewall
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What are the main parts of a tire?
The tread (the part that touches the road), the belts under the tread, the body or carcass plies that carry the load, the sidewall between tread and bead, the beads that seat the tire on the wheel, and the inner liner that holds the air in a tubeless tire.
What does radial mean on a tire?
It describes how the body plies are laid. The federal tire standard defines a radial ply tire as one whose ply cords that extend to the beads are laid at substantially 90 degrees to the centerline of the tread. The R in a size like 225/65R17 stands for radial.
What are tire belts made of?

chunks.title: Parts of a Tire: Tread, Belts, Plies, Bead and Sidewall
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
USTMA describes the typical passenger tire as having two belts with steel cords laid at opposing angles under the tread. Federal rules require the tire to list the generic names of its cord materials, and the number of plies in the tread area and sidewall, on the sidewall.
Why can't the sidewall of a tire be repaired?
USTMA says punctures or cuts in the sidewall or shoulder can't be repaired. That part of the tire flexes the most and doesn't have the belts that reinforce the tread area, so a patch there can't restore what was damaged.
