chunks.title: Types of Tires Explained: Which Kind Fits Your Car
chunks.text:
Tire Basics
Types of Tires Explained: Which Kind Fits Your Car
Types of tires explained by how you drive: all-season, summer, winter, all-weather, touring, performance, all-terrain, run-flat and tread pattern types.
Three questions sort every tire
Tire listings throw a lot of labels at you: all-season, grand touring, A/T, UHP, run-flat, directional. They make more sense once you see they answer three different questions:
- What climate is it built for? Summer, winter, all-season or all-weather.
- What kind of driving is it built for? Touring, performance or all-terrain, plus light truck construction for heavy loads.
- How does it handle a puncture? A regular tire or a run-flat.
A single tire answers all three. A "touring all-season" is one climate type and one driving type. Here's what each label means, in the tire makers' own terms.

chunks.title: Types of Tires Explained: Which Kind Fits Your Car
chunks.text:
By climate: summer, winter, all-season, all-weather
Michelin draws the line at 45°F:
Type
Michelin's description
Built for
Summer
Excellent cornering and braking above 45°F, on warm, dry or wet roads
Warm climates and performance cars
Winter
Stay flexible below 45°F, for snow, slush, ice and freezing rain
Real winters
All-season
Work year-round in moderate climates; good in rain and light snow, not heavy snow or ice
Most cars, most places
All-weather
Carry the 3PMSF snowflake for certified cold-weather performance in one set
Year-round use where winters bring some snow
Continental describes summer tires as having a dedicated rubber compound that delivers excellent grip and handling on both dry and wet roads in warmer conditions, and all-season tires as a hybrid of summer and winter characteristics.

chunks.title: Types of Tires Explained: Which Kind Fits Your Car
chunks.text:
By climate: summer, winter, all-season, all-weather
Two sidewall marks tell climate types apart. Michelin explains that M+S means the tire is designed for mud and snow based on the manufacturer's criteria, while the three-peak mountain snowflake (3PMSF) means it met standardized testing requirements for verified winter performance. Our guide to all-season vs all-weather tires goes deeper on that difference.
In South Florida, the realistic choice is between all-season, all-weather and summer tires. Snow isn't the deciding factor; wet grip, heat and tread life are.

chunks.title: Types of Tires Explained: Which Kind Fits Your Car
chunks.text:
By the kind of driving: touring, performance, all-terrain
Continental's definitions:
- Touring tires are built for long-distance driving, offering comfort, low noise, and durability.
- Performance (sport) tires have tread patterns aimed at strong traction in wet and dry conditions. Michelin notes their stiffer sidewalls and softer compound, which wears faster.
- All-terrain tires are a good match for off-road use on larger SUVs and trucks, with aggressive tread patterns.
Touring and performance tires are the main split for cars and crossovers; see touring vs performance tires. For pickups and SUVs, the split is highway vs all-terrain vs mud-terrain, covered in all-terrain vs highway tires.

chunks.title: Types of Tires Explained: Which Kind Fits Your Car
chunks.text:
Light truck (LT) and passenger tires
Construction is its own type. The federal tire standard defines an LT tire as one designated by its manufacturer as primarily intended for use on lightweight trucks or multipurpose passenger vehicles, and requires its load range letter on the sidewall. Many all-terrain sizes are LT tires, which changes load capacity and inflation pressures. Our LT vs P-metric guide covers when a truck needs LT.

chunks.title: Types of Tires Explained: Which Kind Fits Your Car
chunks.text:
By puncture handling: regular or run-flat
Most tires lose their ability to carry the car once they lose air. A run-flat tire is built to keep going for a limited distance after a puncture. Continental describes it as remaining operational until the driver can reach home or the nearest garage. Run-flats carry their own speed and distance limits from each maker, and they need a working TPMS because they don't look flat. See run-flat tires for those limits.

chunks.title: Types of Tires Explained: Which Kind Fits Your Car
chunks.text:
By tread pattern: symmetrical, asymmetric, directional
Inside any category, the tread itself comes in three layouts. Continental describes them:
Pattern
What it looks like
What Continental says it's good at
Mounting
Symmetrical
Both halves of the tire feature the same pattern
Smooth driving, directional stability, low rolling resistance
Any way round
Asymmetric
Two separate tread designs, one on the inner half and one on the outer
Handling, curve stability, wet grip
Marked side faces out
Directional
Lateral grooves that meet in the middle, like an arrowhead
Resisting aquaplaning, high-speed road holding
Must roll the way the sidewall arrow points
The mounting rule matters at rotation time: directional tires can't simply be swapped side to side on the same wheels. Our rotation pattern tool shows which patterns work for your setup.

chunks.title: Types of Tires Explained: Which Kind Fits Your Car
chunks.text:
Two more labels you'll run into
- Temporary spare. Michelin lists T at the start of a size as the mark of a temporary spare. It's a get-you-to-a-shop tire with its own speed limit and pressure printed on it; see spare tire types.
- EV tires. Many electric cars come on tires tuned for weight, quietness and low rolling resistance, sometimes with higher load ratings. They're still one of the climate and driving types above; our guide to EV tires explains what's different.

chunks.title: Types of Tires Explained: Which Kind Fits Your Car
chunks.text:
A quick way to narrow it down
If you drive...
Start with
A commuter car or crossover, mostly highway
Touring all-season
A sport sedan or a car that came on V, W or Y-rated tires
Performance all-season or summer
A pickup or SUV, all pavement
Highway (H/T) all-season
A pickup or SUV that leaves the pavement
All-terrain, often LT
A car that came on run-flats with no spare
Run-flats, or a plan for a flat
That's a starting point, not the answer. The answer starts with your door placard.

chunks.title: Types of Tires Explained: Which Kind Fits Your Car
chunks.text:
Whatever the type, match the placard
A tire type is a choice. The size, load index and speed rating are not. Replacement tires should match the size on your door placard and meet or exceed its load index and speed rating. If you're not sure what your car takes, find my tires looks it up by vehicle, and you can then shop by size within the type you want.
Tires ship free to the 48 contiguous states and DC. Extreme Tires installs at its Sunrise shop or by mobile van across Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach. Curious what's inside all these types? Our guide to the parts of a tire takes one apart.

chunks.title: Types of Tires Explained: Which Kind Fits Your Car
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Tire types sort along three lines: the season and climate they're built for, the job they do (touring, performance, all-terrain), and how they handle a puncture (run-flat or not).
- Michelin says summer tires give their best cornering and braking above 45°F, winter tires stay flexible below it, and all-season tires suit moderate climates.
- M+S is the maker's own claim for mud and snow; the three-peak mountain snowflake means the tire met a standardized winter test, per Michelin.
- Tread patterns come in three layouts: symmetrical, asymmetric and directional. Directional tires carry an arrow and must roll the way it points.
- Whatever the type, the size, load index and speed rating still have to match your door placard.

chunks.title: Types of Tires Explained: Which Kind Fits Your Car
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What are the main types of tires?
For cars and SUVs: all-season, summer, winter and all-weather tires by climate; touring, performance and all-terrain tires by the kind of driving; and run-flat tires by how they handle a puncture. Light truck (LT) tires and temporary spares are separate construction types marked on the sidewall.
What type of tire is best for Florida?
There's no single best type. With no snow and summer heat, the realistic choices are all-season, all-weather or summer tires, chosen for wet grip and tread life. Michelin notes summer tires perform best above 45°F, a line South Florida rarely crosses.
What is a directional tire?

chunks.title: Types of Tires Explained: Which Kind Fits Your Car
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
A tire whose tread is designed to roll forward in one direction only. Continental describes lateral grooves that meet in the middle like an arrowhead, and an arrow on the sidewall shows the direction. It has to be mounted and rotated so it keeps rolling that way.
What is the difference between M+S and the snowflake symbol?
Michelin explains that M+S means the tire is designed for mud and snow based on the manufacturer's own criteria. The three-peak mountain snowflake (3PMSF) means it met standardized testing requirements for verified winter performance.

chunks.title: Touring vs Performance Tires: Comfort, Grip, Tread Life
chunks.text:
Tire Basics
Touring vs Performance Tires: Comfort, Grip, Tread Life
Touring vs performance tires: what each is built for, how speed ratings and UTQG grades hint at the category, and the trade-offs in comfort, grip and wear.
Two tires, two jobs
Every tire is a compromise. Make the rubber softer and it grips harder but wears faster. Stiffen the sidewall and the steering sharpens but the ride firms up. Touring and performance tires are two ends of that trade.
Continental's definitions are a good starting point:
- Touring tires are built for long-distance driving, offering comfort, low noise and durability.
- Performance (sport) tires have tread patterns designed for strong traction in wet and dry conditions.
Both are road tires for cars, crossovers and SUVs. Neither is "better". The right one depends on the car and how you drive it.

chunks.title: Touring vs Performance Tires: Comfort, Grip, Tread Life
chunks.text:
What changes inside the tire
Tire makers describe the same set of trade-offs:
Feature
Touring
Performance
Rubber compound
Harder-wearing, built for mileage
Softer, built for grip
Sidewall
More flex, for ride comfort
Stiffer, to resist flex in corners
Ride and noise
Smoother and quieter
Firmer, with more road noise
Tread life
Longer
Shorter
Speed ratings
Varies; read the sidewall
H and V for performance touring; W, Y and Z for ultra-high performance (BFGoodrich)
Michelin explains the performance side: stiffer sidewalls that resist flex in corners, and a softer compound that makes the tire feel sharp but wears faster, particularly with aggressive driving. The cost, in Michelin's words, is a firmer ride, more road noise, and faster tread wear compared to touring or all-season tires. BFGoodrich lists the same price: faster tread wear, typically more road noise and a firmer ride.

chunks.title: Touring vs Performance Tires: Comfort, Grip, Tread Life
chunks.text:
Reading the category off the sidewall
Marketing names like "grand touring" or "max performance" aren't regulated, and every brand draws the lines a little differently. Two markings on the sidewall tell you more.
The speed rating
BFGoodrich groups tires by their speed symbol:
- H and V ratings are typically considered "performance touring."
- W, Y and Z ratings, with an aspect ratio of less than 55, are ultra-high performance sport tires, typically for wheels 16 inches and larger, made to sharpen handling.
A speed rating is a lab test result, not a suggested driving speed. Michelin defines it as the maximum speed at which a tire can carry its maximum load under specified conditions. Our speed rating guide has the full chart.

chunks.title: Touring vs Performance Tires: Comfort, Grip, Tread Life
chunks.text:
The UTQG treadwear grade
Most passenger tires carry a three-part UTQG grade, such as 500 AA A, under a federal rule (49 CFR 575.104). The first number is treadwear, measured against a control tire graded 100.
Michelin gives a sense of the spread: high performance summer tires commonly fall in the 200 to 300 range; touring tires can reach 700 or higher. That gap is the compound trade-off in a single number.
One caution. Each tire maker assigns its own grades from its own testing, so a 500 from one brand isn't directly comparable with a 500 from another. Compare treadwear within a brand. Enter a grade below to see what each part means:
Our UTQG ratings guide covers the traction and temperature grades too.

chunks.title: Touring vs Performance Tires: Comfort, Grip, Tread Life
chunks.text:
Touring tires: who they suit
Touring tires fit most daily drivers: commuters, family crossovers, ride-share cars and anyone who'd rather hear the radio than the road. Many are sold as all-season tires, with long tread life and a quiet, compliant ride as the selling points.
What you give up is some steering sharpness and ultimate grip, which most drivers on I-95 at rush hour never use.

chunks.title: Touring vs Performance Tires: Comfort, Grip, Tread Life
chunks.text:
Performance tires: who they suit
Performance tires make sense when the car was built around them. Michelin's point is direct: a vehicle that came equipped with a V, W, or Y speed-rated tire was engineered around performance-grade rubber. If your door placard or original tires show one of those ratings, the car was set up with performance tires in mind.
They come in two broad flavors:
- Performance all-season, which trades a little grip for a longer season and more tread life.
- Summer (max or ultra-high performance), which gives the most grip. Michelin notes UHP summer tires use a compound built for temperatures above 45°F.
That 45°F line rarely matters in South Florida, where summer tires are a realistic year-round choice for drivers who want them. The trade is tread life and noise, not climate.

chunks.title: Touring vs Performance Tires: Comfort, Grip, Tread Life
chunks.text:
Switching from one to the other
You can move between categories, within limits:
- Start at the door placard. The replacement must meet or exceed the vehicle maker's speed rating, Michelin says, and the load index has to be equal or higher too. Check any candidate with the load and speed rating check.
- Going from performance to touring usually means a quieter ride and more miles, as long as the speed rating still meets the placard. Michelin's advice for sport and luxury cars is to match or exceed the original speed rating and performance category to keep the driving experience.
- Going from touring to performance sharpens the steering and shortens tread life. Expect more noise.
- Keep all four the same. Pirelli's advice is that it's always best to avoid mixing tires with different characteristics, including speed rating.

chunks.title: Touring vs Performance Tires: Comfort, Grip, Tread Life
chunks.text:
Shopping with this in mind
Pick the speed rating first, from the placard. Then decide where you want to sit between quiet and long-lasting and sharp and grippy. The compare tool lines up speed ratings and UTQG grades side by side, and you can shop by size once you know what fits.
Tires ship free to the 48 contiguous states and DC. Extreme Tires installs at its Sunrise shop or with a mobile van across Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach.

Key takeaways
- Touring tires aim for comfort, low noise and long tread life. Performance tires aim for grip, steering response and high-speed capability.
- Michelin says high performance summer tires commonly fall in the 200 to 300 treadwear range, while touring tires can reach 700 or higher.
- BFGoodrich describes H- and V-rated tires as typically 'performance touring', and W, Y and Z ratings with aspect ratios under 55 as ultra-high performance.

chunks.title: Touring vs Performance Tires: Comfort, Grip, Tread Life
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Treadwear grades are assigned by each manufacturer, so compare them within one brand rather than across brands.
- Whatever the category, the replacement has to meet or exceed the load index and speed rating on your door placard.
Questions people ask
What is the difference between touring and performance tires?
Touring tires are built for comfort, low noise and long tread life over many miles. Performance tires use softer compounds and stiffer construction for grip and sharper handling, and Michelin and BFGoodrich both note the trade-off: a firmer ride, more road noise and faster tread wear.
Do performance tires wear out faster?

chunks.title: Touring vs Performance Tires: Comfort, Grip, Tread Life
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Generally, yes. Michelin says the softer compound that makes a performance tire feel sharp also wears faster, particularly with aggressive driving, and that high performance summer tires commonly fall in the 200 to 300 treadwear range compared with up to 700 or more for touring tires.
Can I put touring tires on a car that came with performance tires?
Only if they meet or exceed the load index and speed rating on your door placard. Michelin's advice is to match or exceed the original speed rating and performance category if you want to keep the car's driving character. A touring tire with a lower speed rating than the placard isn't a like-for-like replacement.
What is a grand touring tire?

chunks.title: Touring vs Performance Tires: Comfort, Grip, Tread Life
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
It's a marketing category, not a regulated one. Tire makers use it for touring tires with a little more handling focus. BFGoodrich calls H- and V-rated tires typically 'performance touring'. Read the speed rating and UTQG grades on the sidewall to see where a specific tire sits.

chunks.title: All-Season vs All-Weather Tires: M+S vs the Snowflake
chunks.text:
Buying Guides
All-Season vs All-Weather Tires: M+S vs the Snowflake
All-season vs all-weather tires: what M+S and the three-peak mountain snowflake (3PMSF) mean, how the snow test works, and how to pick for where you drive.
The short answer
Both all-season and all-weather tires are built to stay on the car twelve months a year. The difference is one symbol on the sidewall.
- All-season tires usually carry M+S only. Michelin describes them as built for everyday driving, with balanced dry and wet performance and acceptable snow traction where winters are light.
- All-weather tires carry the three-peak mountain snowflake (often shortened to 3PMSF), usually alongside M+S. That symbol means the tire met a measured snow traction standard.

chunks.title: All-Season vs All-Weather Tires: M+S vs the Snowflake
chunks.text:
The short answer
So the real question isn't "all-season or all-weather?" It's "do I need tested snow traction where this car actually goes?" In Sunrise or Kendall, the honest answer is usually no. In Asheville in January, it's a different conversation.
What M+S actually means
M+S stands for mud and snow. It's one of the oldest markings on a tire, and it's widely misunderstood.
Continental's explanation is blunt: manufacturers use M+S to show a tire is meant for winter conditions, but the performance of M+S tires is "neither defined nor measured." Michelin makes the same point: the M+S marking is based on tread geometry, not a certified performance test.
In practice, M+S tells you the tread pattern has the kind of grooves and edges associated with mud and snow use. It doesn't tell you how the tire performed on snow, because no snow test is required to put it on the sidewall.

chunks.title: All-Season vs All-Weather Tires: M+S vs the Snowflake
chunks.text:
What M+S actually means
That's why almost every all-season tire carries M+S. It's a description of the tread, not a grade.
What the three-peak mountain snowflake means
The 3PMSF symbol is different because it's earned in a test.
The U.S. Tire Manufacturers Association (USTMA) and the Rubber Association of Canada agreed on a performance-based definition for passenger and light truck tires for use in severe snow conditions. USTMA's bulletin on it, TISB 37, sets the bar like this:
- the tire is tested on packed snow under an ASTM test method,
- it's compared against a standard reference test tire rated 100,
- and it has to reach a traction index of at least 110 against that reference (112 when the 16-inch reference tire is used).

chunks.title: All-Season vs All-Weather Tires: M+S vs the Snowflake
chunks.text:
What the three-peak mountain snowflake means
A tire that meets the standard can carry the three-peak mountain snowflake pictograph. Continental notes that the same symbol is used under UNECE rules in Europe and other markets, as well as in the U.S. and Canada.
What the snow test doesn't cover
Here's the catch that matters for buyers. Michelin describes the qualifying test as a traction test on medium-packed snow, and notes that the symbol doesn't cover performance on pure ice.
So the snowflake tells you a tire cleared a real bar in one specific condition. It tells you nothing about:
- grip on ice,
- grip on wet roads,
- tread life,
- road noise or ride comfort,
- how the tire behaves in heat.

chunks.title: All-Season vs All-Weather Tires: M+S vs the Snowflake
chunks.text:
What the snow test doesn't cover
For those, you still need the tire maker's own spec page, its treadwear warranty, and the UTQG grades molded on the sidewall. Our guide to UTQG ratings explains what those three grades can and can't tell you.

Michelin describes winter tires as purpose-built for cold, ice, snow and slush, and all-weather tires as a way to get tested snow capability without switching sets each season.

chunks.title: All-Season vs All-Weather Tires: M+S vs the Snowflake
chunks.text:
If the car lives in South Florida
Snow traction almost never comes into it here. What does come into it is rain: afternoon downpours on I-95, standing water on the Sawgrass, and hot pavement the rest of the time.
Put your attention on:
- The size, load index and speed rating on your door placard. These come first, whatever the tire type. If you're not sure what yours are, our guide on how to read tire size walks through each piece.
- Wet performance claims on the maker's spec page. Read what the maker itself says about the tire.
- Tread life. Compare the treadwear warranty and the UTQG treadwear grade within the same brand.
- Heat and age. Florida heat ages rubber. Our Florida heat guide covers what that means for the tires you choose.
An all-weather tire isn't wrong for Florida. It just carries a capability you'll rarely use here, so weigh it against the things you will.

chunks.title: All-Season vs All-Weather Tires: M+S vs the Snowflake
chunks.text:
If you drive north in winter, or the car lives somewhere with snow
TireDrop ships free to the 48 contiguous states and DC, so plenty of our buyers do see snow. If yours does, the snowflake becomes a real filter:
- Occasional snow, no second set of tires: all-weather tires with the 3PMSF symbol are what makers aim at this driver.
- Regular snow, ice and deep cold: makers point you to dedicated winter tires, swapped out in spring.
- Mixed fleet or a winter road trip: check whether any state or mountain pass on your route has chain or traction-device rules before you go.

chunks.title: All-Season vs All-Weather Tires: M+S vs the Snowflake
chunks.text:
Don't mix types across the car
Michelin recommends the same tire model on all four positions where you can, and matching pairs on each axle at a minimum. Mixing an all-weather pair with an all-season pair gives the front and rear axles different grip in the very conditions where you want them to match.
Reading the sidewall in the store, or in the photo
When you're comparing tires online, look for these in the product photos or the spec table:
- M+S (sometimes M/S or M&S) molded near the size.
- The three-peak mountain snowflake, a small mountain outline with a snowflake inside it.
- The full size, load index and speed symbol, for example 225/65R17 102H.
If the snowflake isn't listed in the specs and you can't see it in a photo, don't assume it's there. Ask before you buy.

Next steps
Start with the size your vehicle maker specifies. The Tire Size Finder reads it off the door-jamb sticker, or you can type it in. Then shop tires by size and compare the markings above on each product page.

chunks.title: All-Season vs All-Weather Tires: M+S vs the Snowflake
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- M+S (mud and snow) is based on tread design. It isn't a snow performance test.
- The three-peak mountain snowflake (3PMSF) means the tire met a measured snow traction standard on packed snow.
- All-season tires usually carry M+S only. All-weather tires carry the 3PMSF symbol and are built to stay on the car year-round.
- The snow test measures traction on packed snow. It says nothing about ice, rain grip, tread life or noise.
- Whatever the type, the size, load index and speed rating still have to match your door placard.

chunks.title: All-Season vs All-Weather Tires: M+S vs the Snowflake
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What is the difference between all-season and all-weather tires?
Both are meant to stay on the car all year. All-season tires usually carry only the M+S marking, which is based on tread design. All-weather tires also carry the three-peak mountain snowflake symbol, which means they met a measured traction standard on packed snow.
What does the three-peak mountain snowflake symbol mean?
USTMA's definition for tires for severe snow conditions requires a traction index of at least 110 against a reference tire rated 100, measured in the ASTM test on packed snow. Tires that meet it can carry the three-peak mountain snowflake pictograph.
Does M+S mean a tire is good in snow?
Not on its own. Continental and Michelin both describe M+S as a marking tied to tread geometry rather than a measured snow test. For tested snow traction, look for the three-peak mountain snowflake.

chunks.title: All-Season vs All-Weather Tires: M+S vs the Snowflake
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Do I need all-weather tires in Florida?
For driving around South Florida, snow traction rarely comes into it. If you regularly drive north in winter or are buying for a car that lives somewhere with snow, the 3PMSF symbol is worth looking for. Either way, compare wet traction, tread life and noise on the tire maker's spec page.

chunks.title: All-Terrain vs Highway Tires: A/T, H/T and M/T Explained
chunks.text:
Buying Guides
All-Terrain vs Highway Tires: A/T, H/T and M/T Explained
All-terrain vs highway tires for trucks and SUVs: what A/T, H/T and M/T mean, and the trade-offs in noise, tread life and grip on and off the pavement.
Three letters, three jobs
Truck and SUV tires mostly fall into three families, and the abbreviations on product pages tell you which one you're looking at.
- H/T, highway terrain. Built for paved roads.
- A/T, all-terrain. Built to split the difference between pavement and dirt, gravel or grass.
- M/T, mud-terrain. Built for mud, rock and soft ground first, pavement second.
Each step from H/T to M/T trades some on-road manners for more off-road bite. The right pick depends on where your miles really happen, and for most trucks in Broward and Miami-Dade, that's on the pavement.

chunks.title: All-Terrain vs Highway Tires: A/T, H/T and M/T Explained
chunks.text:
Highway (H/T) tires
Bridgestone describes highway truck tires as optimized for paved roads, delivering a smoother, quieter ride and efficient everyday performance. They're the tires many pickups and SUVs leave the factory on.
Read Bridgestone's comparison the other way round and you get the highway tread: compared with an all-terrain tire, it has
- shallower tread,
- narrower grooves,
- smaller tread blocks,
all aimed at a smooth, quiet ride on asphalt.
Who they suit: commuters, highway miles, towing on paved roads, and drivers who never leave the pavement except for a gravel driveway or a grass lot at a ball game.

chunks.title: All-Terrain vs Highway Tires: A/T, H/T and M/T Explained
chunks.text:
All-terrain (A/T) tires
Bridgestone's comparison is specific: all-terrain truck tires have deeper tread depth, wider tread grooves and larger tread block elements than a highway truck tire, which promotes traction off the pavement.
Firestone describes its all-terrain tires as built for vehicles that switch between irregular terrain and regular road, aiming for durability on dirt, gravel and grass while staying comfortable on pavement. BFGoodrich's off-road guide puts all-terrain tires in the middle, with better highway comfort and quieter running than a mud-terrain tire while still handling moderate trails.
Who they suit: trucks that see real dirt, sand or gravel on a regular basis. Think beach access roads, construction sites, ranch roads, boat ramps and hunting land, with plenty of highway between them.

chunks.title: All-Terrain vs Highway Tires: A/T, H/T and M/T Explained
chunks.text:
The trade-offs
- Noise. Bigger blocks and wider grooves usually make more road noise than a highway tread. Makers have worked to bring that down, so read the maker's own claims for the specific tire.
- Ride. Compare what the maker says about comfort for the specific tire, especially if it's an LT size (more on that below).
- Tread life. Compare treadwear warranties tire by tire. Don't assume one family always lasts longer.

chunks.title: All-Terrain vs Highway Tires: A/T, H/T and M/T Explained
chunks.text:
Mud-terrain (M/T) tires
BFGoodrich and Continental describe mud-terrain tires the same way: large tread blocks and wide voids that clear out mud, sand and soft soil and grip uneven surfaces such as rocks and ruts.
They're also open about the cost. BFGoodrich notes that the big, widely spaced blocks come at the expense of road noise, on-road grip and tread life.
Who they suit: trucks that spend real time in deep mud, rock or soft sand. If the trail days are a few weekends a year and the rest is I-595, an M/T is a lot of tire to live with every day.

chunks.title: All-Terrain vs Highway Tires: A/T, H/T and M/T Explained
chunks.text:
What about rain and snow?
Florida drivers care more about a summer downpour than a snowbank.
Rain. None of these labels is a wet-grip rating. Look at what the tire maker says about wet traction for the specific tire, and keep an eye on tread depth as the tires wear. Our guide to tread depth explains why depth matters most in the wet.
Snow. Many A/T and M/T tires carry M+S, which is based on tread design rather than a snow test. Some all-terrain tires also carry the three-peak mountain snowflake, which means they met USTMA's measured packed-snow traction standard. If your truck heads north in winter, check for the symbol on the spec page. Our guide to all-season vs all-weather tires explains both markings.

chunks.title: All-Terrain vs Highway Tires: A/T, H/T and M/T Explained
chunks.text:
Check the size type before you switch
Here's where people get caught out. Many all-terrain and mud-terrain tires are sold in LT (light truck) sizes or flotation sizes like 33x12.50R20, while the truck may have come with P-metric highway tires.
An LT tire isn't a drop-in swap for a P-metric tire:
- it carries a load range (C, D, E and so on) instead of standard or extra load,
- it needs different inflation pressures to carry the same load,
- and it can change ride and weight.
Our guide to LT vs P-metric tires covers load range and when a truck needs LT. Before you buy, compare the new tire's load index against your current one with the load and speed rating check.
And if you're also changing the tire's overall height, say going from a 265/70R17 to a taller size, check clearance and speedometer change first with the plus size calculator.

chunks.title: All-Terrain vs Highway Tires: A/T, H/T and M/T Explained
chunks.text:
A quick way to decide
- Where do 90% of your miles happen? Pavement points to H/T. A regular mix points to A/T.
- What does the off-road part look like? Gravel and sand suit A/T. Deep mud and rock are M/T territory.
- How much noise will you live with? Each step toward M/T usually adds some.
- What does the placard say? Size, load index and speed rating still come first. The Tire Size Finder reads them off the door-jamb sticker.
Ready to compare? Shop tires by size. See how installation works, or call (954) 773-1896 with questions about a specific truck.

chunks.title: All-Terrain vs Highway Tires: A/T, H/T and M/T Explained
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- H/T (highway terrain) tires are built for pavement: Bridgestone describes a smoother, quieter ride and efficient everyday performance.
- A/T (all-terrain) tires have deeper tread, wider grooves and larger tread blocks than highway tires, for traction on dirt, gravel and grass.
- M/T (mud-terrain) tires use large blocks and wide voids to clear mud, at a cost in road noise, on-road grip and tread life.
- Pick by where the miles actually happen, not by how the truck looks.
- Many A/T and M/T sizes are LT tires, which changes the load range and pressures. Check your placard before you switch.

chunks.title: All-Terrain vs Highway Tires: A/T, H/T and M/T Explained
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What is the difference between all-terrain and highway tires?
Highway (H/T) tires are designed for paved roads, with a tread aimed at a smooth, quiet ride. All-terrain (A/T) tires have deeper tread, wider grooves and larger tread blocks for grip off the pavement, which usually brings more road noise.
Are all-terrain tires good for daily driving?
Tire makers describe all-terrain tires as a balance between on-road comfort and off-road traction, and many drivers use them every day. If nearly all your miles are on pavement, a highway tire is aimed more squarely at that use. Compare the maker's noise and tread life claims for the specific tires.
What does M/T mean on a tire?

chunks.title: All-Terrain vs Highway Tires: A/T, H/T and M/T Explained
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
M/T means mud-terrain. These tires have large tread blocks and wide gaps between them to clear mud, sand and soft soil. Tire makers note the trade-off: more road noise, less on-road grip and shorter tread life than an all-terrain tire.
Can I put all-terrain tires on my SUV?
Often, as long as the size, load index and speed rating match what your vehicle maker specifies. Some all-terrain tires come only in LT sizes, which use different load ranges and pressures, so check your door placard and owner's manual first.

chunks.title: EV Tires: What's Different and What to Match
chunks.text:
Buying Guides
EV Tires: What's Different and What to Match
Why EVs use specific tires: weight and HL load ratings, noise foam, rolling resistance and range, torque and wear, and carmaker marks like Tesla's T0.
By TireDrop Team, Extreme Tires, Sunrise FL·Published Oct 2, 2026·Updated Oct 2, 2026·5 min read
Same tire size, different job
An electric car rolls on the same kind of tire sizes as a gas car. What it asks of those tires is different.
The battery makes an EV heavy for its size. The motor delivers its pull instantly. The cabin is quiet enough that you hear the road. And every bit of energy the tires waste comes straight out of the battery. Michelin's EV guidance lists those same pressures: weight, torque, noise and range.
That's why EV tires exist as a category. Here's what each difference means when you're buying.

chunks.title: EV Tires: What's Different and What to Match
chunks.text:
Weight: load index, XL and HL
Battery packs add weight without making the car any bigger. Michelin explains that EVs are heavier because of their batteries and so need tires with higher load indexes.
You'll see three load classes on passenger tires:
- SL (standard load), the default.
- XL (extra load), which carries more at a higher pressure. Our XL vs SL guide explains how it works.
- HL (high load), the newest. Michelin describes HL as a standard developed for the heaviest EVs and large hybrid SUVs, carrying more load than an XL tire of the same size at the same pressure.
Pirelli says the HL marking is printed in front of the size, as in HL 265/35R21, and that an HL tire carries about 6% to 9% more than an XL tire of the same size.

chunks.title: EV Tires: What's Different and What to Match
chunks.text:
Weight: load index, XL and HL
The rule is simple. Michelin says that if your EV came from the factory on HL tires, every replacement must also be HL. The same goes for load index: match or exceed what the door placard says. The load and speed checker compares two tires side by side.
Noise: why many EV tires have foam inside
With no engine noise to cover it, the sound of tread on pavement is what you hear. Michelin notes that because EVs make less noise, tire and road noise is more noticeable, and that tires tuned for EVs pair quieter tread designs with noise-reduction technology such as Michelin Acoustic.
The common fix is a layer of sound-absorbing foam bonded inside the tire. Makers sell it under their own names: Continental's ContiSilent, Pirelli's Noise Cancelling System (PNCS) and Michelin Acoustic. Tesla says it uses acoustic foam and tuned tread patterns in Tesla-designed tires.

chunks.title: EV Tires: What's Different and What to Match
chunks.text:
Noise: why many EV tires have foam inside
One practical point: foam changes how a puncture is repaired. Continental says a ContiSilent tire must be inspected by a trained specialist and repaired with an approved method, with part of the foam removed around the puncture. Tell the shop before a repair. Our guide to Tesla-marked and acoustic tires goes deeper.
Range: rolling resistance
A rolling tire flexes, and that flexing turns some energy into heat. Michelin calls it hysteresis and says it can't be avoided, only minimized. Tires engineered for lower rolling resistance help extend an EV's range.
What you control is pressure. Michelin says every psi below your vehicle's recommended pressure increases rolling resistance and reduces range, and that tires lose about 1 psi a month. Check pressure cold, monthly, against the door placard.

chunks.title: EV Tires: What's Different and What to Match
chunks.text:
Torque and wear
An electric motor delivers full pulling power from a standstill. Michelin says EV tire wear comes largely from battery weight and instant torque, and puts the average at about 20% faster wear than a comparable gas car.
Michelin's ways to slow it down:
- Keep pressure correct.
- Rotate regularly so all four wear evenly. The rotation pattern tool shows the pattern for your setup; your owner's manual's schedule comes first.
- Accelerate smoothly. Hard launches spike torque and scrub rubber off the driven tires.
- Choose tires with compounds built for EV use.

chunks.title: EV Tires: What's Different and What to Match
chunks.text:
Carmaker marks: T0, T1 and others
Some sidewalls carry a short code showing the tire was developed for a specific carmaker. Pirelli lists examples: T0 for Tesla, N0 for Porsche, MO for Mercedes and AO for Audi.
For Tesla, the owner's manuals say a Tesla-approved tire carries a T mark such as T0, T1 or T2. Tesla's tires page says T0 is the first version of a Tesla-designed tire, and later versions with new tuning are marked T1, T2 and so on.
A tire without the mark can still fit, as long as it matches the size, load index (including XL or HL) and speed rating. What changes is the tuning: noise, ride, handling and range can differ. Our Tesla tire basics and Tesla tire sizes guides cover each model, and the Model Y tire guide is on the blog.

chunks.title: EV Tires: What's Different and What to Match
chunks.text:
Do you have to buy an "EV tire"?
No. What you have to match is the specification on the door placard: size, load index (including any XL or HL marking) and speed rating. A tire that meets all three can go on an EV.
What an EV-specific tire adds is tuning for the four pressures above: compounds built for weight and torque, low rolling resistance for range, and often foam for a quieter cabin. A standard all-season in the right size and ratings can do the job, but it may be louder, wear differently or cost you some range. Decide which of those trade-offs matter to you, then compare tires on them.

chunks.title: EV Tires: What's Different and What to Match
chunks.text:
No spare in the trunk
Many EVs carry no spare. Teslas generally don't come with one; Tesla sells an optional repair kit. Our guide to spare tire types explains the options and their limits.
Before you order
- Read the size, load index, speed rating and any XL or HL marking from the door placard or your current tires. The Tire Size Finder reads the door-jamb sticker for you.
- Decide whether you want a carmaker-marked tire, foam inside, or both.
- Check whether your car is staggered, with different front and rear sizes.
Planning for faster wear? Our post on budgeting for EV tire wear shows how to forecast your next set from your own tread readings.

chunks.title: EV Tires: What's Different and What to Match
chunks.text:
Before you order
Then shop tires by size. Extreme Tires installs at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties. Anywhere else in the 48 contiguous states and DC, we ship to your address for a local installer. See how installation works, or call (954) 773-1896 to talk through tires for your EV.
Key takeaways
- EVs are heavy for their size because of the battery, so their tires need enough load capacity. Some heavy EVs specify HL (high load) tires.
- If your EV came on HL tires, Michelin says every replacement must also be HL. An XL tire in the same size isn't a substitute.
- EVs are quiet, so tire noise stands out. Many EV tires add sound-absorbing foam inside, such as ContiSilent, Pirelli's PNCS or Michelin Acoustic.

chunks.title: EV Tires: What's Different and What to Match
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Rolling resistance draws energy straight from the battery. Michelin says pressure below the recommended number increases it and cuts range.
- Michelin says battery weight and instant torque mean EVs wear tires about 20% faster on average than comparable gas cars.
- Carmaker marks on the sidewall, like Tesla's T0 and T1, show a tire was developed for that maker's cars.

chunks.title: EV Tires: What's Different and What to Match
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Do electric cars need special tires?
They need tires that match the vehicle maker's size, load index and speed rating, including any XL or HL marking. EV-specific tires add things that suit EVs, like low rolling resistance for range, foam for quieter cabins and compounds built for extra weight and torque. Any tire that matches the placard specification can fit; EV tuning changes how it rides, sounds and wears.
What does HL mean on a tire?
High load. Michelin describes HL as a newer standard for the heaviest EVs and large hybrids that carries more load than an XL tire of the same size at the same pressure. Pirelli says the HL marking is printed in front of the size, like HL 265/35R21. If your EV came on HL tires, replace them with HL tires.
Why do EV tires wear out faster?

chunks.title: EV Tires: What's Different and What to Match
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Michelin points to two causes: the battery's weight, which loads every tire on every mile, and instant torque, which scrubs rubber from the driven tires under hard acceleration. Michelin puts the average at about 20% faster wear than a comparable gas car. Correct pressure, regular rotation and smooth acceleration all help.
What does T0 or T1 on a Tesla tire mean?
It's Tesla's approval mark. Tesla's owner's manuals say a Tesla-approved tire carries a T mark such as T0, T1 or T2 on the sidewall, and Tesla's tires page says T0 marks the first version of a Tesla-designed tire, with later versions marked T1, T2 and so on.

chunks.title: LT vs P-Metric Tires: Load Range C, D and E Explained
chunks.text:
Buying Guides
LT vs P-Metric Tires: Load Range C, D and E Explained
LT vs P-metric tires: what load range C, D and E and ply rating mean, why LT tires need different pressures, and when a truck or SUV needs LT tires.
Two tires, one size, different jobs
Search for tires for a pickup and you'll often see the same size twice: P265/70R17 and LT265/70R17. Same numbers, different letters in front. That letter matters more than most people expect.
NHTSA's tire safety material lists what the leading letters mean: P for passenger car and LT for light truck. Michelin adds that a P means the tire's loads follow U.S. Tire and Rim Association standards for passenger tires.
- P-metric tires go on cars, minivans, crossovers, many SUVs and plenty of half-ton pickups.
- LT tires are built for heavier service: towing, hauling, heavy-duty pickups, vans and many off-road builds.

chunks.title: LT vs P-Metric Tires: Load Range C, D and E Explained
chunks.text:
Two tires, one size, different jobs
The two are different service types. Treat any change from one to the other as a fitment question, not a style choice.
Load range and ply rating
LT tires carry a load range letter, usually shown on the sidewall and in the spec table as "Load Range E" or just "LRE".
Bridgestone's definition: load range replaces the former ply rating term and identifies a tire's load and inflation limits. So when you hear "10-ply tires," that's the old language for what's now marked as load range E. The number is a rating, not a count of the layers inside the tire.
The letters you'll see most on light trucks:
Load range
Old "ply rating" language
Load and pressure limits
C
6-ply rating
The lowest of these three
D
8-ply rating
Higher than C
E
10-ply rating
Higher than D

chunks.title: LT vs P-Metric Tires: Load Range C, D and E Explained
chunks.text:
Load range and ply rating
A higher letter means the tire is built to carry more weight, at a higher maximum inflation pressure. The exact maximum load and pressure for any tire are molded on its sidewall near the bead, so read them there rather than from a chart.
Two load numbers on one tire
LT tires usually show a load index like 121/118. Cooper explains that the first number is the load capacity for a tire in a single application and the second is for dual application, such as pairs on a dually's rear axle. On a regular pickup, compare the first number.
Check it against your current tire here:

chunks.title: LT vs P-Metric Tires: Load Range C, D and E Explained
chunks.text:
Why P-metric tires get "de-rated" on trucks
There's a rule that surprises a lot of truck owners. Under the federal tire selection standard, FMVSS No. 110, when a vehicle maker puts passenger tires on a multipurpose passenger vehicle, truck, bus or trailer, each tire's load rating is divided by 1.10 before it's checked against the axle's weight rating.
In other words, a P-metric tire on a pickup or SUV is counted as carrying less than its full passenger-car rating. Toyo's technical bulletin on light trucks explains why: P-metric tires are designed mainly for passenger cars and may see more severe service on light trucks.
You don't need to do this math yourself. The vehicle maker already did it when it chose the tire size and pressure on your door placard. It's the reason you shouldn't drop to a lower load index, or move from LT to P-metric, on your own.

chunks.title: LT vs P-Metric Tires: Load Range C, D and E Explained
chunks.text:
Why pressures change when you switch
Toyo's bulletin makes a second point that catches people out: size for size, an LT tire needs more air pressure to carry the same load as a P-metric tire. It warns that failing to adjust pressure to meet the vehicle's load requirement leads to tire fatigue and eventual failure from excessive heat build-up.
So if you move a half-ton truck from P-metric to LT tires, the placard pressure may no longer be the right number for the new tires. The fix is to look up the pressure that gives at least the original load capacity in the tire maker's load and inflation table, which is exactly what Toyo's guidelines for using those tables cover.
That's a job for the installer with the tables in hand, not a guess at the air pump.

chunks.title: LT vs P-Metric Tires: Load Range C, D and E Explained
chunks.text:
When does a truck need LT tires?
Use this order:
- The placard says LT. If your vehicle maker fitted LT tires, the replacements should be LT with at least the same load range and load index. Toyo's rule for any light truck: a replacement must offer equal or higher load carrying capacity than the original equipment tire.
- You tow or haul near the vehicle's limits. Heavy trailers, slide-in campers, work trucks loaded with tools and material. Check your owner's manual for any tire guidance it gives for towing.
- You're switching tread type. Many all-terrain and mud-terrain tires come mainly in LT sizes. Our guide to all-terrain vs highway tires covers that choice.

chunks.title: LT vs P-Metric Tires: Load Range C, D and E Explained
chunks.text:
When does a truck need LT tires?
And when a truck probably doesn't need LT tires: a half-ton pickup or SUV that came on P-metric tires and is used as a daily driver, with occasional light towing within the owner's manual limits. Moving to LT there isn't wrong, but it changes pressures, and you may notice the ride.
P-metric, LT, XL: how they relate
P-metric tires come in two load versions, standard load and extra load (XL). LT tires use load range letters instead. Our guide to XL vs SL tires covers the passenger side of that.
Marking
Tire type
How load is shown
P265/70R17 113T
P-metric, standard load
Load index
P265/70R17 115T XL
P-metric, extra load
Load index plus XL
LT265/70R17 121/118S E
Light truck, load range E
Single/dual load index plus load range
Those example markings show the format, not a recommendation for any vehicle.

chunks.title: LT vs P-Metric Tires: Load Range C, D and E Explained
chunks.text:
Before you order
- Read the placard. It lists the size, including whether it starts with P or LT, and the cold pressure. Our guide on how to read tire size walks through every piece.
- Match or beat the load. Compare load index and speed rating with the load and speed rating check.
- Plan the pressure. If you're changing type, have the installer set pressures from the tire maker's load and inflation tables.
Driving an F-150? Our F-150 tire guide applies all of this to Ford's half-ton.
The Tire Size Finder reads the size off your door-jamb sticker. Then shop tires by size. Extreme Tires installs at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties; elsewhere in the 48 states and DC, the order ships to your address. See how installation works, or call (954) 773-1896.

chunks.title: LT vs P-Metric Tires: Load Range C, D and E Explained
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- P means a passenger tire and LT means a light truck tire. They're different service types, not interchangeable labels.
- Load range is a letter (C, D, E and up) that replaced the old ply rating. A higher letter means a higher load and inflation limit.
- When a vehicle maker fits P-metric tires to a truck or SUV, FMVSS No. 110 makes it divide their load rating by 1.10.
- Size for size, an LT tire needs more air pressure to carry the same load as a P-metric tire, so pressures change when you switch.
- A replacement should carry at least the load the original tires did. If the placard calls for LT, stay with LT.

chunks.title: LT vs P-Metric Tires: Load Range C, D and E Explained
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What is the difference between LT and P-metric tires?
P-metric tires are passenger tires sized to U.S. Tire and Rim Association standards for cars, minivans, SUVs and light pickups. LT tires are light truck tires built for heavier loads and carry a load range letter such as C, D or E. Size for size, an LT tire needs more air pressure to carry the same load as a P-metric tire.
What does load range E mean?
Load range is the letter that replaced the old ply rating. It identifies a tire's load and inflation limits. Load range E is commonly described as a 10-ply rating; it doesn't mean the tire has ten physical plies. The tire's maximum load and pressure are molded on its sidewall.
Can I put LT tires on a half-ton truck that came with P-metric tires?

chunks.title: LT vs P-Metric Tires: Load Range C, D and E Explained
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
It's often possible, but it isn't a simple swap. The LT tire must carry at least the load the original tires were rated for at the pressure you set, and the pressure usually has to change. Toyo's technical bulletin on replacing light truck tires says to use the tire maker's load and inflation tables. Have the installer check it for your truck.
Can I replace LT tires with P-metric tires?
Not if your vehicle maker specifies LT tires. Replacement tires should match or exceed the load capacity of the original equipment, and a P-metric tire in the same size carries less. Check the door placard and owner's manual.

chunks.title: Run-Flat Tires: How They Work, Limits and Repairs
chunks.text:
Buying Guides
Run-Flat Tires: How They Work, Limits and Repairs
Run-flat tire basics: self-supporting vs support ring designs, why they need TPMS, how far and fast you can drive flat, and whether they can be repaired.
What a run-flat tire does
A regular tire carries the car on air. Lose the air and the sidewalls fold, the wheel drops toward the road, and you're stopping on the shoulder.
A run-flat is built to keep carrying the car for a limited distance, at a limited speed, after it loses pressure. Bridgestone puts the purpose simply: you can keep driving after a puncture long enough to reach a shop or a level, out-of-the-way spot to sort it out, instead of changing a tire on the side of I-95.
That's the whole promise. A run-flat isn't puncture-proof, and it isn't meant to be driven flat indefinitely.

chunks.title: Run-Flat Tires: How They Work, Limits and Repairs
chunks.text:
Two ways to build one
Bridgestone describes two main designs.
Self-supporting. The common type on passenger cars. The sidewalls are reinforced, usually with extra rubber inserts, so they can hold the car up with little or no air inside. Pirelli's self-supporting run-flats work the same way, with reinforcements built into the sidewall structure.
Support ring. A ring of firm rubber or another structure sits inside the tire, under the tread, and carries the weight when pressure drops.
On the sidewall, makers mark run-flats with their own abbreviations, such as RFT, ZP, SSR or ROF, or simply "Run Flat". If you're not sure what's on your car, check the sidewall and the tire's spec table.

chunks.title: Run-Flat Tires: How They Work, Limits and Repairs
chunks.text:
How far and how fast
There's no single federal number for run-flat distance. Each tire maker rates its own products, and the limits depend on load, speed, temperature and how the car is driven.
Two examples, as the makers publish them:
Product line
Published limit after pressure loss
Bridgestone run-flat tires, including DriveGuard Plus
Up to 50 miles at up to 50 mph
Michelin run-flat tires
Up to 50 miles at a maximum of 50 mph, depending on road and driving conditions
Those are the makers' figures for their own tires, not a rule for every run-flat. Your owner's manual and the spec page for your exact tire are the final word.
A few practical points:
- Distance is "up to", not "at least". A heavily loaded car on a hot day may not get the full figure.
- Slow down when the warning comes on. The rated speed is a ceiling for driving flat.

chunks.title: Run-Flat Tires: How They Work, Limits and Repairs
chunks.text:
How far and how fast
- Head for a shop, not your destination. The point is to get off the road and have the tire inspected.
Why run-flats need TPMS
Here's the catch with a tire that holds the car up without air: you may not be able to tell it's flat. The car can sit level and drive almost normally.
That's why Bridgestone says a car on run-flat tires needs a tire pressure monitoring system, and why Michelin says its zero-pressure benefits depend on proper wheels and an operational low-pressure warning system.

chunks.title: Run-Flat Tires: How They Work, Limits and Repairs
chunks.text:
Why run-flats need TPMS
Most cars already have one. The federal standard, FMVSS No. 138, has required TPMS on passenger cars, SUVs, trucks and buses of 10,000 lb or less built from September 1, 2007. What matters for a run-flat is that it works. If your TPMS light flashes at startup and then stays on, the system has a fault, and you could be driving a flat run-flat without knowing. Our guide to the TPMS light explains what each pattern means.

chunks.title: Run-Flat Tires: How They Work, Limits and Repairs
chunks.text:
Can a run-flat be repaired?
Sometimes, and it's the tire maker's call, not the shop's.
USTMA's puncture repair procedures say run-flat punctures may be repaired under certain restrictions and specifically prescribed procedures, and that the tire manufacturer must be consulted for its repair policy. Bridgestone says the repairability of its run-flats depends on:
- the damage itself,
- how much pressure was lost,
- and how the car was driven while low or flat: speed, load and maneuvering.
The general USTMA rules apply on top of that: the tire comes off the wheel for a full inspection from the inside, the repair is limited to the tread area, and it's a combination of a stem or plug to fill the injury and a patch to seal the inner liner. Our guide to patch vs plug repairs covers those rules.

chunks.title: Run-Flat Tires: How They Work, Limits and Repairs
chunks.text:
Can a run-flat be repaired?
The honest expectation: Bridgestone warns that driving on an underinflated tire risks hidden damage, which is why the makers tie repair to how the tire was driven. Be ready for the answer to be a replacement. Try the repairability check to see where your puncture falls, then have the tire inspected.
Replacing run-flats
With run-flats again
This is the like-for-like route: same size, load index and speed rating as the placard, and run-flat construction. The Tire Size Finder reads your size off the door-jamb sticker.
Keep in mind that some cars on run-flats are also staggered, with different front and rear sizes. Our guide to staggered tires explains buying two of each.

chunks.title: Run-Flat Tires: How They Work, Limits and Repairs
chunks.text:
With regular tires
On many cars, it's possible. Before you do it, check:
- What the car carries for a flat. Michelin notes that one advantage of run-flats is not needing a spare tire or the tools to change a wheel. So a car sold on run-flats may have no spare tire and no jack. With regular tires, you'll want a spare, a repair kit or roadside help lined up.
- The owner's manual. Some vehicle makers say whether non-run-flat tires are approved for the car.
- The load and speed ratings. The replacement still has to match or exceed the placard. Our guide to XL vs SL tires covers load markings.
- Ride and handling. The car may ride and handle differently on regular tires. Ask your installer what to expect on your model.
Don't mix run-flats and regular tires on the same axle. Michelin recommends four matching tires, and matching pairs on each axle at a minimum.

chunks.title: Run-Flat Tires: How They Work, Limits and Repairs
chunks.text:
Before you order
- Confirm the size and whether your car came on run-flats: the placard, owner's manual and current sidewall tell you.
- Confirm TPMS is working: no flashing light at startup.
- Decide your plan for a flat if you switch to regular tires.
Then shop tires by size. Extreme Tires installs at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties; elsewhere in the 48 states and DC, your order ships to your address for a fitter you trust. See how installation works, or call (954) 773-1896 to talk through run-flats on your car.

chunks.title: Run-Flat Tires: How They Work, Limits and Repairs
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Most run-flats are self-supporting: reinforced sidewalls hold the car up for a limited distance after a loss of pressure.
- Distance and speed limits are set per product. Bridgestone and Michelin both quote up to 50 miles at up to 50 mph for their run-flat lines, depending on conditions.
- Because a run-flat can look and feel normal when it's flat, the car needs a working tire pressure monitoring system (TPMS).
- Repair is up to the tire maker's policy. USTMA says the maker must be consulted, and many punctured run-flats end up replaced.
- Switching from run-flats to regular tires is possible on many cars, but check what the car carries for a flat first: many have no spare.

chunks.title: Run-Flat Tires: How They Work, Limits and Repairs
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How far can you drive on a run-flat tire?
It depends on the tire. Bridgestone rates its run-flat tires for up to 50 miles at up to 50 mph after a loss of pressure, and Michelin quotes up to 50 miles at a maximum of 50 mph depending on road and driving conditions. Check the limits for your exact tire in the owner's manual or on the maker's spec page.
Can run-flat tires be repaired?
Sometimes. USTMA says punctures in a run-flat may be repaired only under certain restrictions and that the tire manufacturer must be consulted for its repair policy. Bridgestone says repairability depends on the damage, how much pressure was lost and how the vehicle was driven while flat.
Do run-flat tires need TPMS?

chunks.title: Run-Flat Tires: How They Work, Limits and Repairs
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Yes. Bridgestone and Michelin both tie their run-flat tires to a working tire pressure monitoring system, because a run-flat can keep the car level with no air in it and you may not notice the loss.
Can I replace run-flat tires with regular tires?
On many cars it's possible, but cars that come on run-flats may have no spare tire or jack. Before switching, check the owner's manual and plan what you'll carry for a flat, such as a spare or a repair kit.

chunks.title: XL vs SL Tires: Extra Load, Standard Load and Pressure
chunks.text:
Buying Guides
XL vs SL Tires: Extra Load, Standard Load and Pressure
XL vs SL tires: what extra load and standard load mean, why XL capacity depends on pressure, and why it matters on EVs, SUVs and crossovers.
Two versions of the same size
Look up a common crossover size like 235/55R19 and you'll often find it listed twice: once with a plain load index, and once with a higher load index followed by XL.
- SL, standard load. The default. Most tires don't print "SL" at all; no load marking means standard load.
- XL, extra load. Toyo and Continental both describe extra load, or reinforced, tires the same way: they're built to carry more load at a higher inflation pressure than a standard load tire of the same size. You may also see "Extra Load" or "Reinforced" on the sidewall for the same idea.
That second half of the sentence, at a higher inflation pressure, is the part most people miss.

chunks.title: XL vs SL Tires: Extra Load, Standard Load and Pressure
chunks.text:
Where the extra capacity comes from
An XL tire isn't simply a tougher version of the same tire. Its construction is reinforced so that it can run at higher pressure, and the higher pressure is what lets it carry more weight.
Toyo's guidelines for using load and inflation tables give these reference points for P-metric passenger tires:
Load type
Reference pressure for maximum load
Standard load (SL)
35 psi
Extra load (XL)
41 psi
The consequence: an XL tire's extra capacity is tied to that higher pressure. Toyo describes XL tires as carrying additional load at a higher inflation pressure, and Continental notes that reinforced tires are designed to run at higher pressure than standard load tires. Run an XL tire at a standard load pressure and you aren't using the capacity it's rated for.

chunks.title: XL vs SL Tires: Extra Load, Standard Load and Pressure
chunks.text:
Where the extra capacity comes from
So a car specified with XL tires at its placard pressure is relying on that construction. Swap in standard load tires of the same size and the load capacity can fall short of what the vehicle maker designed for.
The sidewall number is a ceiling, not a target
Every tire has its maximum load molded near the bead, along with the pressure that load applies to, in a line such as "Max. load 1,201 lbs at" a stated psi. Toyo's replacement bulletin points to this marking as the way to compare tires.
That maximum pressure is not the pressure to run. Your target is the cold pressure on the vehicle's door placard, unless an installer has worked out a different one from the tire maker's tables because the tire type or size changed.

chunks.title: XL vs SL Tires: Extra Load, Standard Load and Pressure
chunks.text:
Load index: the number that has to match
The load index is the number right after the size, like the 104 in 235/55R19 104V XL. Michelin's load rating guide covers how each index maps to a weight per tire.
USTMA's rule for replacements is to use a load index equal to or above what your vehicle placard requires, and Toyo's bulletin says a replacement should carry at least the same maximum load as the original. When the original was XL, that usually means the replacement has to be XL too, because the standard load version of the size has a lower load index.
Compare your current tire and a candidate here, including any XL marking:

chunks.title: XL vs SL Tires: Extra Load, Standard Load and Pressure
chunks.text:
Why it matters on EVs, SUVs and crossovers
XL tires show up most on vehicles that are heavy for their tire size.
EVs. Battery packs add weight without making the car any bigger. Michelin's EV guidance explains that some EVs need tires rated for more load than XL can give at normal pressures, which is why the HL class below exists. Our Tesla tire basics guide covers this for Tesla models specifically.
SUVs and crossovers. Heavier vehicles on passenger-car tire sizes are where XL versions of a size tend to appear. Your door placard, not the vehicle's type, tells you whether yours calls for one.

chunks.title: XL vs SL Tires: Extra Load, Standard Load and Pressure
chunks.text:
HL: the next step up
There's now a load class above XL. Michelin explains that HL (high load) tires are engineered to stay the same relative size as a passenger tire but carry a heavier load: on average, more than an XL tire of the same size at the same pressure. Michelin notes the HL standard was adopted in Europe in 2021 and in the U.S. in 2023.
If your placard or current tires show HL, the replacement needs to be HL. An XL tire in the same size isn't a like-for-like substitute.

chunks.title: XL vs SL Tires: Extra Load, Standard Load and Pressure
chunks.text:
Switching between SL and XL
From XL to SL. If your vehicle maker specifies XL, don't. The load index drops below the original.
From SL to XL. Usually possible, but it isn't automatic. The XL tire's extra capacity comes with its higher pressure, so you're not gaining capacity unless the pressure changes, and a higher pressure changes how the car rides. Toyo's replacement bulletin warns about the opposite risk: fitting tires that carry less than the originals, or failing to adjust pressure so the new tires carry the original load. The answer for any change is the same: the installer looks up the right pressure in the tire maker's load and inflation table.
Different size at the same time. If you're also plus-sizing, run the numbers first with the plus size calculator, then match the load.

Before you order
- Read the size, load index and any XL or HL marking from your door placard or current tires. The Tire Size Finder can read the door-jamb sticker for you, and our guide on how to read tire size explains each piece.
- Compare the candidate tire with the load and speed rating check.
- Set pressure to the placard, cold, once the tires are on (our Honda CR-V guide shows how load matters on a family crossover), unless your installer has calculated a different figure for a changed tire type or size.
Then shop tires by size. Extreme Tires installs at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties; elsewhere in the 48 states and DC, your order ships to your address. See how installation works, or call (954) 773-1896.

chunks.title: XL vs SL Tires: Extra Load, Standard Load and Pressure
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- XL (extra load) tires are built to carry more weight than a standard load (SL) tire of the same size, at a higher inflation pressure.
- In the load tables for P-metric tires, 35 psi is the reference pressure for standard load and 41 psi for extra load.
- XL capacity depends on pressure. The extra load an XL tire is rated for comes with the higher inflation pressure.
- If your car came on XL tires, replace them with XL (or whatever load marking the placard shows). Never go below the original load index.
- Some heavy EVs specify HL (high load) tires, which Michelin says carry more than XL tires of the same size at the same pressure.

chunks.title: XL vs SL Tires: Extra Load, Standard Load and Pressure
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What does XL mean on a tire?
XL stands for extra load. Toyo and Continental describe XL, or reinforced, tires as able to carry additional load at a higher inflation pressure than standard load tires of the same size. A tire with no load marking is standard load (SL).
Should I inflate XL tires to a higher pressure?
Inflate to the cold pressure on your vehicle's door placard when the tires are the size and load type the vehicle maker specified. If you're changing from SL to XL, or to a different size, have the installer check the tire maker's load and inflation table so the new tires carry at least the original load.
Can I replace XL tires with standard load tires?

chunks.title: XL vs SL Tires: Extra Load, Standard Load and Pressure
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Not if your vehicle maker specifies XL. Replacement tires should match or exceed the original load index, and the XL marking is part of how that capacity is reached. Check the door placard and owner's manual.
Are XL tires better?
Not in general. They're built for more load, which matters on a heavy vehicle that calls for them. On a car specified with standard load tires, an XL tire isn't automatically an upgrade, and pressure still has to be set correctly.

chunks.title: Nail in Tire or Flat Tire? What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Damage, Flats & Repair
Nail in Tire or Flat Tire? What to Do Next
Found a nail in your tire, or a tire going flat? What to do in the first hour, why not to pull the nail out, and when a puncture can be repaired.
By TireDrop Team, Extreme Tires, Sunrise FL·Published Oct 2, 2026·Updated Oct 2, 2026·6 min read
The first five minutes
You see the shiny head of a nail in the tread, or the tire pressure light comes on and one corner looks low. Either way, the next few decisions matter more than the nail does.
Here's the order to take them in:
- Leave the nail where it is. Michelin's tire damage guide is direct about it: do not pull it out yourself.
- Check the pressure with a gauge. Compare it with the pressure on your door placard, not the number molded on the tire.
- Look at where the nail is. Tread, or near the edge and sidewall? That decides whether a repair is even possible.

chunks.title: Nail in Tire or Flat Tire? What to Do Next
chunks.text:
The first five minutes
- Decide how the car gets to a technician. Spare, mobile service or roadside help, rather than driving on a tire that's losing air.
The rest of this guide explains each step.
Why the nail stays in
A nail or screw that went straight in can sit in its own hole and slow the leak. Pull it out in a parking lot and you may turn a slow leak into a flat on the spot.
There's a second reason. The repair can't be done from the outside anyway. USTMA says the tire must be removed from the rim or wheel and inspected for all possible damage, and that an outside-in or on-the-wheel repair should never be done. The technician removes the object with the tire off the wheel, sees the angle it went in at and checks the inner liner. Leaving it in place helps them see what happened.

chunks.title: Nail in Tire or Flat Tire? What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Holding air, or going flat?
Your gauge reading puts you on one of two paths.
The tire is close to placard pressure. The nail may be sealing for now. That doesn't make it a repair, and it can let go. Have it inspected before driving further on it. If you need the car today, the spare or a mobile visit is the lower-risk way to get there.
The tire is low or flat. Don't keep driving on it. Michelin's repair criteria are blunt on this: a tire qualifies for repair only if it has not been driven on when flat, because even a short distance driven while completely flat can cause internal damage to the sidewall and carcass. Michelin lists any tire that was driven flat among those that need replacement, not repair.
That's the real cost of "just getting home" on a flat: a repairable nail turns into a new tire.

chunks.title: Nail in Tire or Flat Tire? What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Where the nail is decides whether it can be repaired
The repairable zone is narrow. Under USTMA guidance and Michelin's criteria:
- Tread area only. USTMA considers a repair only when the damage is limited to the tread area.
- 1/4 inch (6 mm) or smaller. A bigger hole means a replacement.
- Not the sidewall or shoulder. Michelin says a nail in the sidewall is never repairable. USTMA rules out repairs where the injury extends into the shoulder or belt edge, or runs at an angle into the shoulder.
- Not over an old repair. USTMA says repairs can't overlap.
Tap where your nail is on the map below to see how the guidance treats that spot.
The same check lives on its own page: can my tire be repaired?

chunks.title: Nail in Tire or Flat Tire? What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Changing to the spare
If you have a spare and you're somewhere you can work, AAA's steps for changing a tire start well before the jack comes out:
- Get off the road. AAA suggests a parking lot or side street, on solid, level ground that's well lit.
- Secure the car. Park, switch off, set the parking brake and turn on the hazard lights. AAA also suggests wedges at the wheel on the opposite corner from the flat.
- Loosen the lug nuts before you lift. The car's weight holds the wheel still while you break them loose.
- Use the jack point in your owner's manual. AAA says the manual shows where it goes.
- Tighten in a star pattern. Opposite nut next, not the one beside it.

chunks.title: Nail in Tire or Flat Tire? What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Changing to the spare
Then mind the spare's limits. A compact "donut" spare is a temporary tire with its speed limit printed on it; AAA's advice is not to drive over 50 mph on one until your regular tire is back on. Our guide to spare tire types covers the full-size, compact and kit options.
On an interstate shoulder, with traffic close, a tire change is a job for roadside assistance or a mobile van, not for you.

chunks.title: Nail in Tire or Flat Tire? What to Do Next
chunks.text:
No spare in the trunk?
Plenty of newer cars carry a sealant and inflator kit or run-flat tires instead of a spare. AAA has documented how often new vehicles come without one. Look under the trunk floor now, before you need it, so you know which you have.
If you use a sealant kit, tell the technician before they dismount the tire. A kit gets you moving; it isn't the repair the industry guidance describes, so the tire still needs an internal inspection and then a proper repair or a replacement. Run-flat tires have their own repair rules from each tire maker.

chunks.title: Nail in Tire or Flat Tire? What to Do Next
chunks.text:
A slow leak with no nail in sight
Sometimes the tire keeps dropping a few psi a week and there's nothing in the tread. Michelin notes that pressure loss could also be a leaking valve, valve cap or even the wheel. From the driver's seat, those look exactly like a puncture you can't see.
NHTSA's advice to check pressure monthly with a gauge, cold, is how you catch this early. If one tire keeps reading low, have it inspected. Our guide to the TPMS light explains when the dashboard warning comes on and why it isn't an early warning.

chunks.title: Nail in Tire or Flat Tire? What to Do Next
chunks.text:
What a proper repair looks like
If the puncture qualifies, the accepted repair is a plug and patch combination fitted from the inside. Michelin requires the combined plug-and-inside-patch type for all repairs, and USTMA calls a plug alone an unacceptable repair. The full breakdown is in tire plug vs patch.
Extreme Tires' tire repair follows that method:
- dismount the tire and inspect it inside
- repair with a combination patch-plug
- rebalance after the repair
- set pressure to your door placard
It's done at the Sunrise shop or from the mobile van, which covers Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach. If the nail is in the shoulder or sidewall, or the tire was driven flat, the van can fit a replacement where you're parked instead. See mobile service or call (954) 773-1896.

chunks.title: Nail in Tire or Flat Tire? What to Do Next
chunks.text:
If it needs a new tire
When a repair is ruled out, match the replacement to your door placard: size, load index and speed rating. All-wheel-drive cars can be stricter about tread depth differences between tires, and your owner's manual has the rule for yours. Shop by size to see what fits. Tires ship free to the 48 contiguous states and DC, and installation is available in South Florida.
