Driving through storm debris? Our blog post on nails in tires after a storm cleanup covers the weeks after a hurricane, when roofing nails are everywhere.

chunks.title: Nail in Tire or Flat Tire? What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Michelin's advice for a nail in the tire is simple: don't pull it out yourself.
- A puncture may be repairable only if it's in the tread area and no larger than 1/4 inch (6 mm), per USTMA and Michelin.
- A nail or screw in the sidewall or shoulder can't be repaired. Neither can a tire that was driven while flat, per Michelin.
- The tire has to come off the wheel so the inside can be inspected before any repair.
- Driving on a flat, even a short distance, can damage the sidewall inside, so put the spare on or call for help rather than driving on it.

chunks.title: Nail in Tire or Flat Tire? What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Can I drive with a nail in my tire?
Have it inspected before driving further on it. A nail can be holding air in for now and let go later, and Michelin notes that even a short distance driven completely flat can damage the tire inside. If you have a spare, fit it. If you can't, a mobile tire service can come to you.
Should I pull the nail out of my tire?
No. Michelin's tire damage guide says not to pull it out yourself. A technician removes it with the tire off the wheel, finds the path it took through the tread and checks the inside before deciding on a repair.
Can a tire with a screw in it be repaired?
Sometimes. Under USTMA and Michelin repair criteria, the puncture has to be in the tread area, 1/4 inch (6 mm) or smaller, and the tire can't have been driven flat. The repair itself is a plug and patch combination fitted from the inside after the tire is dismounted.

chunks.title: Nail in Tire or Flat Tire? What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Why does my tire keep losing air with no nail in it?
A slow leak doesn't always come from a puncture. Michelin lists a leaking valve, valve cap or even the wheel as other causes of pressure loss. A technician can check the tire, valve and bead seat to find the source.

chunks.title: Tire Plug vs Patch: What a Proper Repair Looks Like
chunks.text:
Damage, Flats & Repair
Tire Plug vs Patch: What a Proper Repair Looks Like
Tire plug vs patch: why industry guidance accepts neither on its own, the 1/4-inch tread-area limit, and why the tire must come off the wheel.
The short answer
"Plug or patch?" sounds like a choice between two repairs. Under industry guidance it isn't. Neither one on its own is an accepted repair. A proper repair uses both at once, from the inside of the tire, after the tire has been taken off the wheel and inspected.
Here's what each piece does, the limits on where a tire can be repaired, and what to ask for when you have a nail in the tread.

chunks.title: Tire Plug vs Patch: What a Proper Repair Looks Like
chunks.text:
What a plug does, and what it doesn't
A plug is a cord of sticky rubber pushed into the puncture from the outside. AAA describes the process: the hole is reamed to clean it, then the plug is threaded through and pushed deep into it.
A plug fills the hole. What it doesn't do is seal the inner liner, the airtight layer on the inside of the tire. The Tire Industry Association puts it plainly: a plug by itself does not permanently seal the innerliner. USTMA's procedures call a plug alone an unacceptable repair.

chunks.title: Tire Plug vs Patch: What a Proper Repair Looks Like
chunks.text:
What a patch does, and what it doesn't
A patch is applied to the inside of the tire, over the inner liner. It seals the air in.
What it doesn't do is fill the channel the nail or screw made through the tread and belts. TIA's explanation: a patch by itself does not fill the void left by the penetrating object, which allows water to enter the body of the tire.
The repair the industry accepts: both, from the inside
USTMA's guidance for passenger and light truck tires is that a rubber stem, or plug, must fill the puncture injury and a patch must seal the inner liner. Only this plug and patch combination is considered permanent.

chunks.title: Tire Plug vs Patch: What a Proper Repair Looks Like
chunks.text:
Where a tire can be repaired, and where it can't
USTMA and TIA draw the repairable zone tightly:
- Tread area only. USTMA recommends considering a repair only when the damage is limited to the tread area.
- 1/4 inch (6 mm) or smaller. The puncture can't be larger than 1/4 inch in diameter.
- Not the sidewall or shoulder. USTMA says punctures or cuts there can't be repaired, because that part of the tire flexes the most and lacks the tread area's reinforcement.
- Not at the edge, or at an angle into it. TIA adds that a repair can't be made where the injury extends into the shoulder or belt edge area, or runs at an angle into the shoulder.
- No overlapping repairs. A new repair can't overlap an old one.
Where the damage is
Size
Under USTMA/TIA guidance
Tread area

May be repairable, after the inside is inspected
Tread area
Larger than 1/4 in

Some tire makers set their own limits on top of these, for run-flat tires and other types. USTMA notes this, so a technician will follow the tire maker's rules where they're stricter.

chunks.title: Tire Plug vs Patch: What a Proper Repair Looks Like
chunks.text:
Why the tire has to come off the wheel
USTMA is firm on this: the tire must be removed from the rim or wheel and inspected for all possible damage, including damage to the inner liner. Its procedures say never perform an outside-in repair or an on-the-wheel repair.
The reason is simple: damage to the inner liner can't be seen from the tread side. The only way to find it is to look inside.

chunks.title: Tire Plug vs Patch: What a Proper Repair Looks Like
chunks.text:
About roadside plug kits and sealant
Plug kits and cans of sealant are sold for roadside use, and some cars ship with a sealant kit instead of a spare. Whatever they do on the shoulder, they aren't the repair the industry guidance describes.
One rule is worth knowing before you use a plug kit. USTMA's procedures say never repair a tire that has an existing, improper repair; the tire must be scrapped. A plug on its own is an improper repair under that same guidance. If you've plugged a tire yourself, tell the technician, and expect them to judge the tire with that in mind.

chunks.title: Tire Plug vs Patch: What a Proper Repair Looks Like
chunks.text:
How Extreme Tires repairs a puncture
Extreme Tires' tire repair follows the approach above:
- dismount the tire and inspect it inside
- repair with a combination patch-plug
- rebalance after the repair
- set pressure to your door placard
It's available at the Sunrise shop or from the mobile van in the local install area. If the damage turns out to be outside the repairable zone, the answer is a replacement, and the van can fit that where you park too. See mobile service or call (954) 773-1896 and ask.

Found a bulge on the side of the tire rather than a hole in the tread? That's cord damage, and our guide to a bubble in the tire sidewall explains why it can't be repaired at all.

chunks.title: Tire Plug vs Patch: What a Proper Repair Looks Like
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Industry guidance accepts neither a plug alone nor a patch alone. A proper repair fills the hole with a rubber stem and seals the inner liner with a patch.
- USTMA limits repairs to the tread area, for punctures no larger than 1/4 inch (6 mm).
- Punctures or cuts in the sidewall or shoulder can't be repaired.
- The tire must come off the wheel so the inside can be inspected. USTMA says never repair from the outside or on the wheel.
- Repairs can't overlap, and a tire with an existing improper repair must be scrapped rather than repaired again.

chunks.title: Tire Plug vs Patch: What a Proper Repair Looks Like
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Is a tire plug or a patch better?
Neither is enough on its own. The Tire Industry Association explains that a plug by itself doesn't permanently seal the inner liner, and a patch by itself doesn't fill the hole the object left, so water can get into the tire's body. USTMA's guidance calls for both: a rubber stem to fill the injury and a patch to seal the liner.
How close to the sidewall can a tire be patched?
Under USTMA guidance, repairs are limited to the tread area. Punctures or cuts in the sidewall or shoulder can't be repaired. The Tire Industry Association adds that a repair can't be made where the damage extends into the shoulder or belt edge area, or runs at an angle into the shoulder.
Is a tire plug a permanent fix?

chunks.title: Tire Plug vs Patch: What a Proper Repair Looks Like
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Not under industry guidance. USTMA calls a plug alone an unacceptable repair and considers only the plug and patch combination permanent. USTMA also says a tire with an existing improper repair must be scrapped rather than repaired again.
Can a tire be patched more than once?
Sometimes, if each puncture qualifies on its own. USTMA's guidance says repairs can't overlap. A technician checks the spacing and the condition of the inside of the tire before deciding.

chunks.title: Bent Rim After a Pothole or Curb? Wheel and Tire Checks
chunks.text:
Damage, Flats & Repair
Bent Rim After a Pothole or Curb? Wheel and Tire Checks
Bent rim symptoms after a pothole or curb: where wheels crack and leak, why tire damage can hide inside, and what to have checked before it costs a tire.
Two parts took the hit
A pothole or a curb doesn't just hit the tire. AAA puts it plainly: when a car strikes a pothole, the tires, wheels and suspension get the brunt of the impact. In AAA's 2021 survey, 1 in 10 drivers had pothole damage bad enough to need a repair.
Most advice after a pothole focuses on the tire, and our blog post on hitting a curb or pothole walks through the tire and alignment signs. This guide covers the two things that are easiest to miss: the wheel itself, and tire damage you can't see from outside.

chunks.title: Bent Rim After a Pothole or Curb? Wheel and Tire Checks
chunks.text:
Damage that hides inside the tire
Michelin's tire damage guide is clear that looks can deceive:
- Internal damage (broken cords, belt separation or carcass damage from an impact) is often invisible from the outside.
- A tire that looks normal after hitting a pothole may have structural damage that will eventually fail.
- That's why Michelin recommends having tires professionally inspected after any significant impact, which means removing the tire from the wheel to examine the inside.
So a clean-looking sidewall the morning after isn't the end of it. If the hit was hard enough to make you wince, or the TPMS light came on, have it inspected. And keep looking: if a bulge or bubble shows up on the sidewall later, that's cord damage, and Michelin says the tire can't be repaired. Our guide to a bubble in the tire sidewall covers what to do next.

chunks.title: Bent Rim After a Pothole or Curb? Wheel and Tire Checks
chunks.text:
Where to look on the wheel
Trade magazine Tire Review gives a simple method: with your eyes at wheel level, look closely at the inboard and outboard edges of the wheel, right where the metal meets the rubber. That's the lip, or flange, where the tire seals against the wheel. It's also where a pothole edge or curb usually lands.
What you're looking for:
What you see on the wheel
What it can mean
Next step
Scuffs on the painted or polished face

Check the inboard side too. On many cars you can only see it with the wheel turned, or from underneath. A crack there doesn't show from the curb side at all.

chunks.title: Bent Rim After a Pothole or Curb? Wheel and Tire Checks
chunks.text:
Bent rim symptoms
A bent wheel often tells you it's there before you see it:
- A new vibration at certain speeds. Tire Review notes that a wheel can be slightly bent or out of round and still balance within specification, then vibrate once it's on the road. Rebalancing alone may not cure it.
- A tire that keeps losing air on one corner. Tire Review describes a wheel whose lip was rolled over, creating a constant air leak in addition to vibration.
- A pull or uneven wear. Michelin notes that a significant pothole or curb impact can misalign the wheels and damage the tire simultaneously. Misaligned wheels scrub the tire sideways, so the wear shows up on one edge.
Answer a few questions about what you feel and hear, and the checker lists the likely causes and the service that checks each:

chunks.title: Bent Rim After a Pothole or Curb? Wheel and Tire Checks
chunks.text:
Bent rim symptoms
Answer when a noise or vibration happens, where you feel it and what you hear to see up to four possible causes, such as balance, a tire or wheel problem, alignment wear, brake rotors or a wheel bearing, with the service that checks each. The list comes from a simple rules table, not a diagnosis, so have it inspected.
The same tool is on its own page: car shaking checker.

chunks.title: Bent Rim After a Pothole or Curb? Wheel and Tire Checks
chunks.text:
Can a bent wheel be fixed?
Sometimes, but it's a specialist's call, not a tire shop shortcut. Tire Review is blunt about alloy wheels: cold hammering an alloy wheel will most likely crack it before it becomes straight. It also says a reputable wheel repair shop will scrap rather than attempt to fix a wheel it considers unsound.
The practical rule:
- Cracked: replace the wheel.
- Bent: have a wheel specialist assess it. Some can be straightened, some can't.
- Cosmetic curb rash only: it's a cosmetic decision, not a mechanical one.
If you're replacing a wheel, it has to match more than the bolt pattern. Our guides to bolt pattern and wheel offset and backspacing explain what to match, and you can browse wheels when you know what fits.

chunks.title: Bent Rim After a Pothole or Curb? Wheel and Tire Checks
chunks.text:
Can the tire be repaired?
Impact damage usually lands on the sidewall or shoulder, which is exactly where industry guidance says no. USTMA limits repairs to punctures in the tread area, 1/4 inch (6 mm) or smaller, and rules out the sidewall and shoulder. A tire that was cut or bulged by a curb is a replacement, not a patch. Our damage map shows the zones.
Florida's version of the pothole
South Florida doesn't have freeze-thaw winters, but it has afternoon storms. AAA's warning applies every rainy season: puddles may disguise a deep pothole. A flooded right lane on a side street can hide an edge that bends a wheel lip.
AAA's advice for a hole you can't avoid is to slow down as much as you can beforehand and avoid braking abruptly over it. Correct tire pressure, set to your door placard and checked monthly, gives the tire and wheel their full cushion.

chunks.title: Bent Rim After a Pothole or Curb? Wheel and Tire Checks
chunks.text:
What to have checked, and where
- The tire. Off the wheel and inspected inside, per Michelin, if the hit was significant.
- The wheel. Lip, face and inboard side, measured if there's a vibration.
- The alignment. If the car pulls or the steering wheel sits off-center afterward.
Extreme Tires does four-wheel alignment at the Sunrise shop, and its mobile vans mount, balance and inspect tires and wheels at your home or office across Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach. See mobile service or call (954) 773-1896. If a tire needs replacing, shop by size and match the size, load index and speed rating on your door placard. Tires ship free to the 48 contiguous states and DC.

chunks.title: Bent Rim After a Pothole or Curb? Wheel and Tire Checks
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- AAA says the tires, wheels and suspension take the brunt of a pothole impact.
- Michelin warns that internal tire damage from an impact is often invisible, and recommends a professional inspection after any significant impact, with the tire off the wheel.
- A bent wheel can still balance within spec and then vibrate on the road, and a bent lip can leak air constantly, per Tire Review.
- Look where the metal meets the rubber, inboard and outboard, for bends, cracks and deep gouges.
- A flooded street hides holes. AAA notes that puddles may disguise a deep pothole.

chunks.title: Bent Rim After a Pothole or Curb? Wheel and Tire Checks
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What are the symptoms of a bent rim?
The usual ones are a vibration that appears at certain speeds, a tire on that corner that keeps losing air, and a visible flat spot or kink in the wheel lip. Trade press notes a slightly bent wheel can still balance within spec and vibrate on the road, so have it measured rather than just rebalanced.
Can a bent alloy wheel be repaired?
Sometimes, by a wheel specialist, but not always. Tire Review warns that cold hammering an alloy wheel will most likely crack it before it becomes straight, and that a reputable wheel repair shop will scrap a wheel it considers unsound rather than fix it. Cracked wheels are a replacement.
Is curb rash on a wheel a problem?

chunks.title: Bent Rim After a Pothole or Curb? Wheel and Tire Checks
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Light scuffing on the face of the rim is usually cosmetic. Damage at the lip where the tire seats, a bend, or a crack is different, because it can cause air loss or vibration. If you can't tell which you have, have the wheel inspected.
Should I get my tires checked after hitting a pothole?
After a hard hit, yes. Michelin says a tire that looks normal after a pothole may have structural damage that will eventually fail, and it recommends a professional inspection after any significant impact, which means taking the tire off the wheel to look inside.

chunks.title: Spare Tire Types: Full-Size, Donut, Repair Kit and More
chunks.text:
Damage, Flats & Repair
Spare Tire Types: Full-Size, Donut, Repair Kit and More
Full-size spare, compact donut, run-flat tires or a repair kit: how each handles a flat, the limits printed on temporaries, and checking spare pressure.
Find out before you need it
The worst time to learn what your car carries for a flat is on the shoulder, in the rain, with traffic going by. Lift the trunk floor or check the owner's manual this week, and you'll know which of these four you're working with.
Type
What it is
The main limit
Full-size spare
A fifth regular tire, on a regular wheel
Needs space; check its pressure and age like any tire
Compact temporary spare
A small, light "donut" built for short trips
Speed and distance limits printed on it
Run-flat tires
Tires that carry the car for a while with no air
Maker's distance and speed limits after pressure loss
Sealant and inflator kit

chunks.title: Spare Tire Types: Full-Size, Donut, Repair Kit and More
chunks.text:
Find out before you need it
Sealant plus a 12-volt compressor
Small tread punctures only
Full-size spare
A full-size spare is a fifth tire and wheel the same size as the four on the car. Goodyear splits these into two kinds:
- Matching. Same tire and wheel as the other four. Goodyear notes it also keeps the car looking the way it should.
- Non-matching. Full size, but a different tire or a plain steel wheel. It works as a spare; treat it as a way to get to a shop.
The trade-off is space and weight, which is why fewer cars carry one. The upside, as Goodyear puts it, is that you may not have to drive straight to a repair shop after a flat.
Two things to check on a full-size spare: pressure, against the door placard, and age. A spare that's never touched the road still ages. Our guide to the DOT date code shows how to read when it was made.

chunks.title: Spare Tire Types: Full-Size, Donut, Repair Kit and More
chunks.text:
Compact temporary spare (the "donut")
This is the most common spare: a narrow tire on a small wheel, built to get you off the road and to a shop.
Goodyear describes compact temporary spares as lightweight with a shallow tread depth, with much smaller dimensions than a regular tire. Michelin adds that they have less load capacity than your regular tires and aren't built for normal driving.

chunks.title: Spare Tire Types: Full-Size, Donut, Repair Kit and More
chunks.text:
The limits are printed on it
Temporary spares carry their limits on the sidewall or on a label nearby. NHTSA's interpretations of the federal tire standard describe temporary-use spares marked with wording like "Temporary use only", an inflation pressure, and a 50 mph maximum speed.
What the makers say:
- Speed. Michelin says not to exceed 50 mph on a compact spare, and to avoid aggressive acceleration, hard braking and sharp cornering.
- Distance. AAA's general advice is to drive no more than 50 miles on a donut-type spare before replacing it with a regular tire.
- Your car's numbers win. Michelin's advice is to check the spare's own sidewall for its restrictions, because they vary. The owner's manual has them too.
In practice, a donut is a ride to a tire shop, not a plan for the rest of the week.

chunks.title: Spare Tire Types: Full-Size, Donut, Repair Kit and More
chunks.text:
Run-flat tires
Some cars carry no spare because the tires themselves are the plan. A run-flat keeps carrying the car for a limited distance after it loses pressure.
The limits are set per product. Bridgestone and Michelin both quote up to 50 miles at up to 50 mph for their run-flat lines, and Goodyear says driving deflated on its run-flat tires is restricted to a maximum of 50 mph for up to 50 miles. Load, heat and how you drive affect how far you actually get.
Because a run-flat can look normal when it's flat, it depends on a working TPMS warning. Our run-flat tire guide covers how they work and when they can be repaired.

chunks.title: Spare Tire Types: Full-Size, Donut, Repair Kit and More
chunks.text:
Sealant and inflator kit
Many newer cars come with a kit instead of a spare: a bottle of sealant and a small 12-volt compressor. AAA's 2017 research found nearly one-third of new vehicles were sold without a spare tire.
AAA's view of the kits is clear about the limits:
- They can temporarily repair small punctures.
- They can't fix sidewall damage or blowouts, or larger leaks.
- The sealant has a shelf life; AAA puts it at four to eight years, so check the date on yours.
Use only the sealant your vehicle maker specifies. Tesla's manual, for example, warns that other sealants can damage the tire pressure sensors. A sealant fix is temporary; the tire still needs a shop inspection afterward. Our patch vs plug guide explains what a permanent repair involves, and the repairability check shows where your puncture falls.

chunks.title: Spare Tire Types: Full-Size, Donut, Repair Kit and More
chunks.text:
Sealant and inflator kit
EVs often fall in this group. Teslas generally don't come with a spare; see our guide to a Tesla flat with no spare, and our EV tire guide for how EV tires differ.
Checking the spare's pressure
NHTSA's advice is to check pressure monthly on every tire, spare included, with the tires cold. The spare is the one everybody forgets, and a flat spare is no spare.
- Find the right number. A full-size spare usually matches the door placard. A compact spare usually needs much more air: Goodyear says generally 60 psi. The spare's sidewall or label, or your owner's manual, has the figure for yours.
- Check it cold with a gauge, the same way you check the other four.
- Look it over. Cracks or bulges are reasons to have it inspected. A bubble in any tire is a stop sign; our sidewall bubble guide explains why.

chunks.title: Spare Tire Types: Full-Size, Donut, Repair Kit and More
chunks.text:
Checking the spare's pressure
- Check the jack and tools are where the manual says they should be.
After you've used the spare
Get the original tire inspected promptly. If it can be repaired, the shop does it from the inside with the tire off the wheel. If it can't, you'll need a replacement that matches the size, load index and speed rating on your door placard. The Tire Size Finder reads that sticker for you, and you can shop tires by size.
Extreme Tires installs at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties, so a mobile van can come to you if you're on a donut. Anywhere else in the 48 contiguous states and DC, we ship to your address for a local installer. See how installation works, or call (954) 773-1896.

chunks.title: Spare Tire Types: Full-Size, Donut, Repair Kit and More
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Cars handle a flat one of four ways: a full-size spare, a compact temporary spare (the donut), run-flat tires, or a sealant and inflator kit.
- A compact temporary spare is for getting to a shop. Its speed limit is printed on its sidewall or label; Michelin says not to exceed 50 mph on one.
- Compact spares usually need much more air than your regular tires. Goodyear says generally 60 psi; the spare's own label has the number.
- Run-flats carry their own limits: Bridgestone, Michelin and Goodyear each quote up to 50 miles at up to 50 mph for their run-flat lines.
- Repair kits can temporarily seal small tread punctures only. AAA says they can't fix sidewall damage or blowouts.
- NHTSA says to check pressure monthly on every tire, spare included.

chunks.title: Spare Tire Types: Full-Size, Donut, Repair Kit and More
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How fast can you drive on a donut spare?
Follow the limit printed on the spare's sidewall or label and in your owner's manual. Michelin says not to exceed 50 mph on a compact spare and to avoid aggressive acceleration, hard braking and sharp cornering. NHTSA's interpretations describe temporary-use spares labeled with a 50 mph maximum.
How far can you drive on a compact spare?
Only as far as you need to reach a tire shop. Distance guidance varies; AAA's general advice for a donut-type spare is no more than 50 miles. Your owner's manual and the spare's label are the final word for your car.
What PSI should a spare tire be?
Use the number printed on the spare or its label, or in your owner's manual. A full-size spare usually matches the door placard. Goodyear says compact temporary spares generally need about 60 psi, much more than a regular tire.

chunks.title: Spare Tire Types: Full-Size, Donut, Repair Kit and More
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What if my car has no spare tire?
Many newer cars come with a sealant and inflator kit or run-flat tires instead. Kits can temporarily seal small tread punctures, but AAA says they can't fix sidewall damage or blowouts. Know what your car carries before you need it, and have a roadside or mobile tire option lined up.

chunks.title: Bubble in Tire Sidewall: What It Means and What to Do
chunks.text:
Damage, Flats & Repair
Bubble in Tire Sidewall: What It Means and What to Do
A bubble in the tire sidewall means damaged cords inside, and it can't be repaired. How to tell it from a normal indentation, and what to do next.
What you're looking at
You're loading groceries and notice it: a rounded bump on the side of one tire, like a small egg pressing out from inside the rubber. It wasn't there last week.
That's a sidewall bubble, also called a bulge. It looks minor. It isn't. Here's what it means, how to tell it apart from a harmless dip, and what to do next.

chunks.title: Bubble in Tire Sidewall: What It Means and What to Do
chunks.text:
What a sidewall bubble means
A tire's sidewall gets its strength from layers of cords, called plies, running inside the rubber. Michelin explains that a bulge or bubble on the sidewall generally indicates damaged cords caused by a severe impact. Once cords are broken or the plies separate, the air pressure inside pushes out against the rubber, and the rubber alone forms the bump you can see.
In other words, the bubble is the visible part of damage you can't see. The structure that holds the air in is compromised at that spot. Michelin warns that this exposes you to a rapid loss of pressure if the bubble bursts.

chunks.title: Bubble in Tire Sidewall: What It Means and What to Do
chunks.text:
Bubble or indentation? How to tell
Not every irregular spot on a sidewall is a bubble. Michelin describes sidewall indentations, shallow dips where the cords overlap inside the tire, as normal on radial tires. They don't affect performance.
What you see
Direction
What it usually is
Rounded bump that stands out from the sidewall
Outward
Bulge or bubble: damaged cords; replace
Narrow, shallow dip or crease
Inward
Indentation: normal on radial tires
Cut, gouge or scrape with a bump near it
Mixed
Damage; have it inspected
Running your fingers lightly over the spot helps: a bubble stands proud of the surface. If you can't tell which you have, treat it as a bubble until a technician says otherwise.

chunks.title: Bubble in Tire Sidewall: What It Means and What to Do
chunks.text:
What causes them
Michelin names the usual cause: a severe impact, such as driving into a pothole or hitting a curb. The cords can be damaged without any cut you can see on the outside.
That's why a bubble can seem to come from nowhere. The impact might have been a pothole on a flooded street where you couldn't see the edge, or a curb in a tight parking garage. After a hard hit, it's worth walking around the car and looking at both sidewalls.

chunks.title: Bubble in Tire Sidewall: What It Means and What to Do
chunks.text:
Can a tire bubble be repaired?
No. There's no patch for broken cords.
- USTMA's repair guidance says punctures or cuts in the sidewall or shoulder of a tire can't be repaired, because that part of the tire flexes the most and lacks the reinforcement of the tread area.
- Michelin says a tire with a bulge or bubble can't be repaired and must be replaced.
Be wary of anyone who offers to fix one. The only fix is a replacement tire.

chunks.title: Bubble in Tire Sidewall: What It Means and What to Do
chunks.text:
What to do next
- Put the spare on. Michelin's advice is to replace the tire with the spare immediately and have it inspected. Know what kind of spare you have first: a compact spare has speed and distance limits printed on its label and in the owner's manual. Our guide to spare tire types explains each one.
- No spare, or can't change it where you are? Call for help rather than driving on the bubble. In South Florida, Extreme Tires' mobile vans install tires at your home, office or other parking spot across the local install area. See mobile service or call (954) 773-1896.
- Don't wait for a convenient day. The damage behind a bubble doesn't heal, and a bubble can lose air suddenly.

chunks.title: Bubble in Tire Sidewall: What It Means and What to Do
chunks.text:
What to do next
- Check the wheel too. An impact hard enough to break cords can also bend a wheel or knock the alignment out. A new pull or vibration after you replace the tire is a reason to have both checked. Extreme Tires does alignments at the Sunrise shop.
Replacing one tire: match what's on the car
You'll often be replacing a single tire, and it needs to fit with the other three. USTMA's guidance is that replacement tires should be the same size, load index and speed rating recommended by the vehicle maker, as shown on the door placard, with a load index equal to or above what the placard requires. USTMA recommends replacing all four at once for best performance, and if you replace only one or two, keeping to those same specifications.

chunks.title: Bubble in Tire Sidewall: What It Means and What to Do
chunks.text:
Replacing one tire: match what's on the car
All-wheel-drive vehicles can be stricter: some makers limit how much the tread depth can differ between tires. Your owner's manual has the rule for your car.
To find a match, shop by size or bring the old tire's size, and have the other three measured when the new one goes on.
Quick reference
You find
What it means
Next step
Outward bubble on the sidewall
Damaged cords
Spare on; replace the tire
Inward dip, tire holds air normally
Indentation, normal on radials
Keep checking monthly
Bubble after a pothole or curb
Impact damage
Replace the tire; have the wheel and alignment checked
Not sure which it is
Could be either
Have it inspected before driving further

chunks.title: Bubble in Tire Sidewall: What It Means and What to Do
chunks.text:
Quick reference
NHTSA's advice is to look for bulges, cuts and cracks whenever you check your tire pressure. A bubble caught on your driveway is a lot easier to handle than one found on I-595. And if you have a nail in the tread rather than a bubble on the side, that's a different story: see plug vs patch.
Key takeaways
- Per Michelin, a sidewall bulge or bubble generally means cords inside the tire were damaged, usually by a severe impact such as a pothole or curb.
- It can't be repaired. USTMA says punctures or cuts in the sidewall or shoulder can't be repaired, and Michelin says the same for a bulge.
- A shallow dip in the sidewall is different. Michelin calls indentations normal on radial tires.
- Michelin's advice is to put on the spare and have the tire inspected.
- A replacement should match the size, load index and speed rating on your door placard.

chunks.title: Bubble in Tire Sidewall: What It Means and What to Do
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Can a bubble in a tire sidewall be repaired?
No. A bubble means the cords that give the sidewall its strength are damaged, and a patch can't restore them. USTMA's repair guidance rules out repairs in the sidewall or shoulder, and Michelin says a tire with a bulge must be replaced.
What causes a bubble on a tire?
Michelin says a sidewall bulge generally indicates damaged cords caused by a severe impact, such as driving into a pothole or hitting a curb. Air pressure then pushes through the damaged plies and forms the bubble.
Is a dent or dip in my tire sidewall a problem?
Usually not. Michelin describes sidewall indentations as normal on radial tires, where cords overlap inside the tire. What matters is direction: a dip inward is typically an indentation, while a bump outward is a bulge. If you're not sure which you have, have it inspected.

chunks.title: Bubble in Tire Sidewall: What It Means and What to Do
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Can I drive on a tire with a bubble?
Michelin's advice is to replace it with the spare right away and have the tire inspected. If you can't change it where you are, a mobile tire service can come to you. A bubble can lose air suddenly, so don't plan on the tire lasting until a convenient day.

chunks.title: Bolt Pattern: How to Read and Measure It (5x114.3)
chunks.text:
Wheels & Fitment
Bolt Pattern: How to Read and Measure It (5x114.3)
How to read a bolt pattern like 5x114.3, what lug count and PCD mean, how to measure 4, 5, 6 and 8-lug wheels, and the center bore and lug seat checks.
The two numbers in a bolt pattern
Every wheel spec starts with a bolt pattern, written like 5x114.3 or 6x5.5. It's two numbers:
- Lug count. How many studs or bolts hold the wheel on: 4, 5, 6 or 8 on most cars, SUVs and trucks.
- Bolt circle diameter. The diameter of an imaginary circle that runs through the center of every lug hole. You'll also see it called the PCD, for pitch circle diameter.
Wheel Pros defines it the same way in its wheel specs, with examples like 4x100 mm, 5x4.5 in, 6x5.5 in and 8x170 mm. So the bolt pattern isn't the distance between two neighboring lugs. It's the size of the circle all of them sit on.

chunks.title: Bolt Pattern: How to Read and Measure It (5x114.3)
chunks.text:
Millimeters or inches: same pattern, two names
Bolt patterns are written in millimeters or inches, and many common ones have both names. There are 25.4 millimeters in an inch, so:
Written in mm
Written in inches
The math
5x114.3
5x4.5
4.5 × 25.4 = 114.3
5x127
5x5
5 × 25.4 = 127
6x139.7
6x5.5
5.5 × 25.4 = 139.7
5x139.7
5x5.5
5.5 × 25.4 = 139.7
The table shows how the numbers convert, not which vehicles use them. Your vehicle's published spec is what counts.
Notice that the lug count still has to match. A 5x139.7 wheel and a 6x139.7 wheel share a bolt circle, but one has five holes and the other six.

chunks.title: Bolt Pattern: How to Read and Measure It (5x114.3)
chunks.text:
How to measure a bolt pattern
The best source is always the vehicle's own spec: the owner's manual, the vehicle maker's published specs or a fitment database. Measuring is a backup, and it's easier on a wheel that's off the car.
4, 6 and 8-lug wheels
With an even number of lugs, every stud has one directly across from it. Konig describes this for 4-lug wheels: measure from the center of one stud straight across the hub to the center of the opposite stud. That distance is the bolt circle diameter.

chunks.title: Bolt Pattern: How to Read and Measure It (5x114.3)
chunks.text:
5-lug wheels
With five lugs, no stud sits directly across from another, so a center-to-center measurement across the hub comes out wrong. Konig's method uses two neighboring studs instead: measure from the center of one stud to the center of the stud next to it, then divide by 0.5878. The result is the bolt circle diameter.
On a 5x114.3 wheel, for example, neighboring studs sit about 67.2 mm apart (114.3 × 0.5878). That's fiddly to measure with a tape, and it's where most mistakes happen.

chunks.title: Bolt Pattern: How to Read and Measure It (5x114.3)
chunks.text:
Don't round a close call
Some 5-lug patterns are very close in size. Wheel catalogs list patterns like 5x114.3 and 5x115 as separate fitments. That's 0.7 mm apart: far too small to see by eye, and still not the same pattern. If your measurement lands between two patterns, don't round it. Look up the spec, or have a shop check it with a bolt pattern gauge.
A matching pattern is only step one
A wheel that bolts on isn't necessarily a wheel that fits. Once the pattern matches, these come next.

chunks.title: Bolt Pattern: How to Read and Measure It (5x114.3)
chunks.text:
Center bore
The center bore is the hole in the middle of the wheel that fits over the vehicle's hub. Konig explains that for a wheel to seat properly, the bore should match the hub.
- Bore exactly matches the hub: the wheel is centered by the hub, called hub-centric.
- Bore larger than the hub: common with aftermarket wheels. Wheel Pros explains that hub-centric rings fill the gap, adapting the wheel's bore to the hub so the wheel is centered while it's tightened.
- Bore smaller than the hub: the wheel won't go on. A ring can only make a larger bore smaller, never the other way round.

chunks.title: Bolt Pattern: How to Read and Measure It (5x114.3)
chunks.text:
Lug seat type and thread size
Wheel Pros and Konig both stress the seat, the spot where the lug nut or bolt meets the wheel. Common seats are:
- conical, or tapered,
- spherical, or ball,
- flat, with a washer-like face.
The seat on the nut or bolt has to match the seat on the wheel. Aftermarket wheels can use a different seat from the factory wheels, so check before reusing the factory lugs.
The thread size has to match the vehicle's studs too. Lug sizes are written as diameter and pitch, such as M12x1.5. Konig notes that stud size and thread pitch vary from vehicle to vehicle, and that the lugs need enough thread engagement on the studs.
Finally, lugs are tightened with a torque wrench to the vehicle maker's torque spec. Konig's tightening guide says the owner's manual figure takes precedence over any general chart.

chunks.title: Bolt Pattern: How to Read and Measure It (5x114.3)
chunks.text:
Offset, width and brake clearance
The bolt pattern says nothing about where the wheel sits in the wheel well. A wheel can match your pattern and still rub the fender or hit a strut or brake caliper. That's what offset and backspacing describe; our guide to wheel offset and backspacing explains them.
Adapters and spacers
Adapters that convert one bolt pattern to another, and spacers that push a wheel outward, both exist. They change how the wheel is held on and where it sits, so treat either one as a fitment question for a technician rather than a fix for the wrong pattern.

chunks.title: Bolt Pattern: How to Read and Measure It (5x114.3)
chunks.text:
Before you buy wheels
- Get the exact pattern from the vehicle's published spec. Measure only to confirm, with a gauge for 5-lug wheels.
- Check center bore, and whether you'll need hub-centric rings.
- Match the lug seat and thread to the new wheels.
- Check offset, width and brake clearance for your vehicle.
- Size the tires to keep the overall diameter close to stock. The plus size calculator compares sizes, and our guide on how to read tire size explains each number.
The wheel catalog filters by bolt pattern, and our wheel fitment guidance walks through the same checks. TireDrop confirms fitment before an order ships. If you're running different sizes front and rear, see our guide to staggered tires.

chunks.title: Bolt Pattern: How to Read and Measure It (5x114.3)
chunks.text:
Before you buy wheels
Extreme Tires mounts and installs wheel and tire packages at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties; elsewhere in the 48 states and DC, the order ships to your address. See how installation works, or call (954) 773-1896 with your vehicle and the wheel you're looking at.
Key takeaways
- A bolt pattern has two numbers: the lug count, then the diameter of the circle through the lug centers (the PCD).
- 5x114.3 and 5x4.5 are the same pattern, one in millimeters and one in inches.
- On 4, 6 and 8-lug wheels, measure center to center across opposite studs. On 5-lug wheels, the measurement is different.
- Several 5-lug patterns are only a millimeter or two apart, so use a bolt pattern gauge or the vehicle's published spec rather than a tape measure alone.

chunks.title: Bolt Pattern: How to Read and Measure It (5x114.3)
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- A matching bolt pattern is only the start: center bore, lug seat type, thread size, offset and brake clearance all have to work too.
Questions people ask
What does 5x114.3 mean?
Five lug studs or bolts, arranged on a circle 114.3 mm in diameter measured through the center of each lug. The same pattern is often written 5x4.5, because 114.3 mm is 4.5 inches.
How do you measure a 5-lug bolt pattern?
Because no stud sits directly opposite another, Konig's method measures from the center of one stud to the center of the stud next to it, then divides that distance by 0.5878 to get the bolt circle diameter. Some 5-lug patterns are very close in size, so confirm the result against the vehicle's published spec.
Can I use a wheel with a slightly different bolt pattern?

chunks.title: Bolt Pattern: How to Read and Measure It (5x114.3)
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Don't force it. Patterns like 5x114.3 and 5x115 are close enough to look like a match but they aren't the same. A wheel should match the vehicle's bolt pattern exactly; have fitment confirmed before buying.
What is PCD on a wheel?
PCD stands for pitch circle diameter, the diameter of the imaginary circle that runs through the center of every lug hole. It's the second number in a bolt pattern, like the 114.3 in 5x114.3.

chunks.title: Changing Tire Size: Diameter, Load and Speedometer
chunks.text:
Wheels & Fitment
Changing Tire Size: Diameter, Load and Speedometer
Can you use a different tire size? What to keep the same: overall diameter, load index and speed rating, plus the speedometer effect and clearance checks.
The short answer
You can change tire size on many cars, but the tire makers' starting point is not to. USTMA says replacement tires should be the same size, load index and speed rating as recommended by the vehicle or tire manufacturer. Michelin adds that a change from the specified size should only be made with guidance from a trained tire professional.
That's not because a different size never works. It's because the size on your door placard was chosen to fit everything else on the car: the speedometer, the ABS and stability systems, the wheel wells and the load the car carries. Change the tire and you need to keep all of those working.

chunks.title: Changing Tire Size: Diameter, Load and Speedometer
chunks.text:
The short answer
The simplest change is between sizes the vehicle maker already approved. Michelin's guidance is to use the same size designation or approved options recommended by the vehicle or tire manufacturer, and some owner's manuals list more than one size. Anything beyond that list is where the checks below come in.
Here's what has to stay the same, and what to check.
1. Keep the overall diameter close
Overall diameter is how tall the tire stands, rim plus two sidewalls. It's the number that matters most when you change size, because the car's systems are calibrated to it.
Michelin says altering overall diameter affects speedometer accuracy, the clearance between the tire and the wheel well, and potentially how the ABS and stability control systems behave.

chunks.title: Changing Tire Size: Diameter, Load and Speedometer
chunks.text:
1. Keep the overall diameter close
You can work it out from the size. Our guide on how to read tire size walks through the math. Using 225/65R17 as the original, about 28.5 inches tall:
Size
Overall diameter
Change
225/65R17 (original)
28.5 in
235/65R17 (wider, same profile)
29.0 in
+1.8%
235/55R18 (plus 1)
28.2 in
−1.2%
235/50R19 (plus 2)
28.2 in
−0.9%
225/45R19 (looks similar)
27.0 in
−5.4%
The last row shows why sizes aren't interchangeable just because the width matches.
How close is close enough? Fitment guides commonly work to about 3% of the original diameter. Treat that as a guideline, not an approval. The car's maker and a fitment check have the final say.

chunks.title: Changing Tire Size: Diameter, Load and Speedometer
chunks.text:
2. Plus sizing: bigger wheel, same height
Most size changes are plus sizing: a larger wheel with a lower-profile tire.
Michelin explains it with a simple example: going from a 14-inch to a 15-inch wheel is plus 1. The tire's aspect ratio drops as the wheel grows, so the overall diameter stays about where it was. Michelin also describes the other route: keeping the same wheel and going wider, such as P195/75R14 to P215/65R14.
The right width and aspect ratio depend on the exact sizes, so compare the overall diameter of the old and new size before you buy. The plus-size calculator does the math for any two sizes.
Plus sizing usually means new wheels too. The width, offset and bolt pattern of those wheels have to suit the car; our guide to wheel offset and backspacing explains what changes.

chunks.title: Changing Tire Size: Diameter, Load and Speedometer
chunks.text:
3. Load index and speed rating: never lower
A different size doesn't lower what the tire has to carry.
- Load index. USTMA and Michelin both say not to choose a tire with less load-carrying capacity than the original. Match or exceed the load index on the door placard. If the new size carries an XL marking, our XL vs SL guide explains what it means for pressure.
- Speed rating. Match or exceed the speed rating the vehicle maker specifies.
The load and speed checker compares a new tire's ratings against your current ones.

chunks.title: Changing Tire Size: Diameter, Load and Speedometer
chunks.text:
4. The speedometer effect
Your speedometer counts wheel turns and assumes the original tire size. The result:
- A taller tire covers more ground per turn, so the speedometer reads slower than your actual speed.
- A shorter tire covers less ground per turn, so it reads faster.
Using the table above, a 1.8% taller tire means that when the speedometer shows 60 mph, you're doing about 61. The 5.4% shorter size would have you at about 57 with the needle on 60. The odometer is off by the same proportion.
The calculator below shows what your speedometer would read at 30, 45, 60 and 70 mph for any two sizes. It's also on its own page as the plus-size calculator.

chunks.title: Changing Tire Size: Diameter, Load and Speedometer
chunks.text:
4. The speedometer effect
Compares a current and a new tire size by overall diameter, sidewall height and revolutions per mile, and shows what the speedometer reads at 30, 45, 60 and 70 mph. The common 3% diameter figure is a guideline, not a fitment approval, so have fitment confirmed before you order.
5. Clearance and everything around the tire
A size that's right on paper still has to physically fit. Check:
- Clearance to the fender, wheel well and suspension. Michelin names wheel-well clearance as one of the things a diameter change affects.
- The wheel. The tire has to suit the width of the wheel it goes on, and a new wheel's offset changes where the tire sits.
- Front and rear. On a staggered car, the front and rear sizes differ, so a size change involves both axles. Our staggered tires guide explains the setup.
This is the part a fitment check exists for.

chunks.title: Changing Tire Size: Diameter, Load and Speedometer
chunks.text:
Before you order a new size
- Find your current size, load index and speed rating on the door placard. The Tire Size Finder reads the sticker for you.
- Compare the new size's overall diameter in the plus-size calculator.
- Confirm the new tire meets or exceeds the load index and speed rating.
- Have the fitment confirmed for your car and wheels before you order.
Then shop tires by size or browse wheels. Extreme Tires installs at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties. Anywhere else in the 48 contiguous states and DC, we ship to your address for a local installer. See how installation works, or call (954) 773-1896 to check a size change before you buy.

chunks.title: Changing Tire Size: Diameter, Load and Speedometer
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Tire makers say to replace tires with the size the vehicle maker recommends, or an approved option. Changing size is a fitment decision, best made with a tire professional.
- Keep the overall diameter close to the original. Plus sizing pairs a larger wheel with a lower-profile tire so the overall height stays about the same.
- Never go below the load index or speed rating on the door placard. USTMA and Michelin both say not to choose less load-carrying capacity than the original.
- A taller tire makes the speedometer read slower than you're actually going; a shorter one makes it read faster.
- Clearance to the body and suspension, wheel width and offset all have to work too. The common 3% diameter figure is a guideline, not an approval.

chunks.title: Changing Tire Size: Diameter, Load and Speedometer
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Can I put a different size tire on my car?
Sometimes. Tire makers say to use the size the vehicle maker recommends or an approved option. Michelin says a change from the specified size should only be made with guidance from a trained tire professional, because overall diameter affects the speedometer, clearance and how the ABS and stability systems behave.
How much bigger can my tires be?
There's no one number for every car. Fitment guides commonly work to about 3% of the original overall diameter, but that's a guideline, not an approval. Load index, speed rating, clearance and wheel width all have to work too, so have the fitment confirmed before you order.
Do bigger tires change the speedometer?

chunks.title: Changing Tire Size: Diameter, Load and Speedometer
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Yes. A taller tire covers more ground per turn than the original, so the speedometer reads slower than your actual speed. A shorter tire does the opposite. The plus-size calculator shows what the speedometer would read at common speeds.
Can I use a lower load index if the new size is bigger?
No. USTMA says replacement tires should not have less load-carrying capacity than originally specified. The load index has to meet or exceed the door placard, whatever the size.

chunks.title: Staggered Tires: Fitment, Rotation and Buying 2+2
chunks.text:
Wheels & Fitment
Staggered Tires: Fitment, Rotation and Buying 2+2
Staggered tires explained: why some cars run wider rear tires, how rotation works when sizes differ, what it means for wear and warranty, and buying 2+2.
Square vs staggered
Most cars are square: the same tire size on all four wheels. A staggered car runs different sizes front and rear, usually with wider tires at the back, and often wider or different-diameter wheels there too.
Michelin describes staggered fitments as common on rear-wheel-drive performance cars and some sports models, where the rear axle handles more power. Some EVs are staggered too, as our Tesla guides cover for certain Tesla models.
Here's how a staggered door placard might read:
Axle
Size on the placard
Front
245/40R19
Rear
275/35R19

chunks.title: Staggered Tires: Fitment, Rotation and Buying 2+2
chunks.text:
Square vs staggered
That's an example of the format, not a recommendation for any car. Your door-jamb sticker lists the exact pair for yours.
How to tell if your car is staggered
- Read the door-jamb placard. A staggered car lists two sizes, one for the front axle and one for the rear.
- Compare the sidewalls. Look at one front tire and one rear tire. If the sizes differ, you're staggered.
- Check the owner's manual. Some cars came staggered on certain trims or wheel packages and square on others.
The Tire Size Finder reads both sizes straight off the door-jamb sticker. When it sees two sizes, it keeps both, so you shop front and rear separately.

chunks.title: Staggered Tires: Fitment, Rotation and Buying 2+2
chunks.text:
Rotation: what you can and can't do
This is the biggest practical difference from a square car. Michelin's and Goodyear's rotation guides describe the same limits.
No axle-to-axle rotation. The front and rear tires are different sizes, so they can't swap axles.
Side-to-side, if non-directional. If the tires don't have a rotation arrow, they can usually swap from left to right on the same axle.
No rotation, if directional. Directional tires have to keep rolling the way the arrow points. Swap them side to side and they'd roll backwards, unless they're dismounted and remounted on the wheels. Goodyear notes that directional tires on a staggered car can't be moved from one side to the other, so each tire's position is effectively fixed.

chunks.title: Staggered Tires: Fitment, Rotation and Buying 2+2
chunks.text:
Rotation: what you can and can't do
Michelin's advice applies to every car, staggered or not: check the vehicle and tire maker's recommendations before rotating. Pick your setup here to see the pattern:
What it means for wear
On a square car, rotation spreads wear across all four tires. On a staggered car, the front and rear pairs stay on their own axles for life.
Wheel Pros spells out the result: because of the front and rear size difference, the tires can't be rotated, which can lead to premature wear. In practice that means:
- Check tread depth per axle. Don't assume the fronts and rears wear together. Our guide to tread depth shows how to measure it.
- Expect to replace pairs at different times. The rears and fronts can reach the end of their tread at different mileages.
- Keep alignment in check. Uneven wear that rotation would normally even out stays where it starts.

chunks.title: Staggered Tires: Fitment, Rotation and Buying 2+2
chunks.text:
Warranty terms can differ
Treadwear warranties are written with rotation in mind. Some tire makers set different terms when sizes differ front and rear. Pirelli's U.S. limited warranty, for example, says that on vehicles with different replacement tire sizes front and rear, treadwear coverage for the rear tires is 50% of the stated mileage.
Other makers write their own terms. Read the warranty booklet for the specific tire before you rely on a mileage figure.

chunks.title: Staggered Tires: Fitment, Rotation and Buying 2+2
chunks.text:
Buying staggered tires: 2+2
You're buying two sizes, so you're really buying two pairs.
Match the sizes to the placard. Front size on the front, rear size on the rear. Load index and speed rating should meet or beat what the placard lists for each axle.
Keep the same tire model on both axles. Michelin recommends four matching tires where possible, the same brand, model, load index and speed rating, and at minimum matching pairs on each axle. On a staggered car, that means the same model in two sizes. Mixing models front and rear gives the two axles different grip.
Replace in pairs per axle. Tires on the same axle should always match. If only the rears are worn, a rear pair in the same model is the usual route.

chunks.title: Staggered Tires: Fitment, Rotation and Buying 2+2
chunks.text:
Buying staggered tires: 2+2
All-wheel drive needs extra care. Michelin notes that AWD and 4WD systems are sensitive to differences in tire circumference between positions. On a staggered AWD car, the vehicle maker sets the front and rear sizes so the rolling diameters work together. Check your owner's manual for its rules on tread depth differences and matching before replacing only one pair. Our Tesla rotation and alignment guide shows how one maker handles this.

chunks.title: Staggered Tires: Fitment, Rotation and Buying 2+2
chunks.text:
Going square instead
Some owners ask about running one size all around so they can rotate. On many staggered cars the wheels themselves differ front and rear, and on AWD cars the sizes are set by design. Treat it as a question for the owner's manual and a fitment check, not a shortcut. If you're changing wheels to do it, our guides to wheel offset and backspacing and bolt patterns cover what has to line up.

chunks.title: Staggered Tires: Fitment, Rotation and Buying 2+2
chunks.text:
How TireDrop handles staggered orders
- The Tire Size Finder keeps your front and rear sizes from the door-jamb sticker.
- When a tire in your cart matches the front or rear size you gave, the cart reminds you that you'll need 2 front + 2 rear.
- TireDrop confirms fitment before an order ships.
Then shop tires by size. Extreme Tires installs staggered sets at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties; elsewhere in the 48 states and DC, your order ships to your address for a fitter you trust. See how installation works, or call (954) 773-1896 and tell us both sizes.

chunks.title: Staggered Tires: Fitment, Rotation and Buying 2+2
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- A staggered setup uses different tire sizes front and rear, usually wider at the back. A square setup uses one size on all four.
- Staggered tires can't swap axles. Non-directional ones can swap sides on the same axle; directional ones stay put unless remounted.
- Without front-to-rear rotation, the two axles can wear at different rates, so check tread depth on each axle separately.
- Some treadwear warranties cover staggered rear tires for less mileage. Pirelli's, for example, covers them at 50% of the stated mileage.
- Buy staggered tires as 2 front + 2 rear, matched in brand and model across the car, at the sizes on your door placard.

chunks.title: Staggered Tires: Fitment, Rotation and Buying 2+2
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What does staggered fitment mean?
It means the front and rear tires are different sizes, and often the wheels too. The rear is usually wider. Michelin notes staggered fitments are common on rear-wheel-drive performance cars and some sports models.
Can you rotate staggered tires?
Not front to back, because the sizes differ. If the tires are non-directional, they can usually be swapped side to side on the same axle. If they're directional, Goodyear notes they can't be moved from one side to the other either, so they typically can't be rotated at all without remounting. Your owner's manual comes first.
Do I have to replace all four staggered tires at once?

chunks.title: Staggered Tires: Fitment, Rotation and Buying 2+2
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Not necessarily. Because the axles can wear at different rates, many owners replace front and rear pairs at different times. Replace at least the pair on an axle together, and on an all-wheel-drive car check the owner's manual for its rules on matching tires.
Can I put the same size tire on all four corners of a staggered car?
Only if the vehicle maker lists that as an approved option for your car. On many staggered cars the wheels themselves differ front and rear, and on all-wheel-drive cars the front and rear rolling diameters are set by design. Check the owner's manual and have fitment confirmed.

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Backspacing Explained: ET, Poke and Rub
chunks.text:
Wheels & Fitment
Wheel Offset and Backspacing Explained: ET, Poke and Rub
Wheel offset and backspacing explained: what ET45 means, positive vs negative offset, how width and offset move a wheel in or out, and how to avoid rub.
Where the wheel sits, in one number
Two wheels can share a diameter, width and bolt pattern and still sit in completely different places on the car. One tucks neatly under the fender. The other sticks out past it, or rubs the suspension. The difference is offset.
Wheel Pros, KMC, Konig and Method Race Wheels define it the same way:
Offset is the distance from the wheel's centerline to its mounting surface, the flat face that bolts against the hub. It's measured in millimeters.

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Backspacing Explained: ET, Poke and Rub
chunks.text:
Where the wheel sits, in one number
Picture a line around the middle of the wheel barrel, halfway between the inner and outer lips. That's the centerline. Offset tells you how far the mounting face sits from that line, and in which direction.
Positive, zero and negative offset
Offset
Where the mounting surface sits
What it does to the wheel
Positive (ET35, ET45)
Toward the outer face of the wheel
Tucks the wheel in, toward the brakes and suspension
Zero (ET0)
Right on the centerline
Wheel is centered on the mounting surface
Negative (ET-12)
Toward the back of the wheel
Pushes the wheel out, away from the suspension
Konig notes that most front-wheel-drive cars have positive offset wheels, and Method Race Wheels says positive offset is common on modern AWD and 4WD vehicles. Method describes negative offset as the choice for off-road builds and vehicles that need a wider track.

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Backspacing Explained: ET, Poke and Rub
chunks.text:
Reading ET on the wheel
KMC Wheels points out that offset can usually be found on the back of the wheel, after the letters ET. ET comes from the German Einpresstiefe. So:
- ET45 means +45 mm offset,
- ET0 means zero offset,
- ET-12 means −12 mm offset.
Offset can't be measured directly with a ruler, as Wheel Pros notes, because the centerline isn't a physical edge. That's why it's stamped on the wheel and listed in every wheel spec.

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Backspacing Explained: ET, Poke and Rub
chunks.text:
Backspacing: the inch version
Backspacing is the older way to describe the same thing. KMC Wheels defines it as the distance, in inches, from the mounting surface to the back edge of the wheel.
- Higher backspacing sits the wheel further in, closer to the suspension.
- Lower backspacing sits it further out, sometimes past the fender.
Konig puts the link simply: offset and backspacing are two ways to measure the same thing, and a more positive offset creates more backspacing.

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Backspacing Explained: ET, Poke and Rub
chunks.text:
Measuring backspacing yourself
KMC's method, on a wheel that's off the car:
- Lay the wheel face down on a flat surface.
- Lay a straight board or yardstick across the back of the wheel, lip to lip.
- Measure from the underside of the straightedge down to the mounting surface, in inches.
That number is the backspacing. Because offset is measured from the centerline, backspacing works out to half the wheel's overall width plus the offset. The overall width here is measured across the outer lips, which is a little more than the nominal width in the wheel's size.

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Backspacing Explained: ET, Poke and Rub
chunks.text:
How changes move the wheel
This is the part that decides whether a new wheel rubs. Two rules cover most of it, and both are just geometry.
Rule 1: change the offset, keep the width. The whole wheel moves by the difference, inside and out.
Rule 2: change the width, keep the offset. The extra width is split evenly: half goes inward, half goes outward.
Worked examples against an 18x8 ET45 wheel:
New wheel
Outer face moves
Inner edge moves
Why
18x8 ET35
10 mm (0.39 in) out
10 mm out
Rule 1: offset down 10 mm
18x9 ET45
12.7 mm (0.5 in) out
12.7 mm (0.5 in) in
Rule 2: 1 in (25.4 mm) wider, split in half
18x9 ET35
22.7 mm out
2.7 mm in
Both: 12.7 + 10 out; 12.7 − 10 in
The examples show the math, not a recommendation for any vehicle. To try your own numbers, use the wheel offset check. The tire's own width and sidewall bulge sit on top of these numbers.

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Backspacing Explained: ET, Poke and Rub
chunks.text:
Poke, rub and clearance
Poke is when the wheel or tire sticks out past the fender. It usually comes from offset that's too low for the car, a wider wheel, or both.
Rub is the tire or wheel touching something it shouldn't. It can happen in two directions:
- Outward: the tire hits the fender lip or the fender liner, often over bumps or at full steering lock.
- Inward: the wheel or tire hits the strut, spring or control arm. Our wheel fitment guidance sums it up: too little offset and the tire rubs the fender; too much and it hits the strut or control arm.
Brake clearance is a third check that offset alone doesn't answer. Large factory calipers need room behind the spokes, and the spoke shape matters as much as the offset.
A few things make clearance tighter:
- a wider tire than the original, even on the same wheel,

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Backspacing Explained: ET, Poke and Rub
chunks.text:
Poke, rub and clearance
- a taller tire, which also changes your speedometer reading. Check that first with the plus size calculator,
- suspension changes such as lowering springs or a lift.
How to choose an offset
- Start with the factory wheel. Its offset is usually stamped on the back, and the vehicle maker's specs list it. Staying close to it at the same width keeps the wheel where the vehicle maker designed it to sit.
- Changing width? Use the two rules above to see where the extra goes.
- Check the other numbers. Bolt pattern, center bore and lug seat all have to match too. Our guide to bolt patterns covers them.
- Size the tire. Keep the overall diameter close to stock. Our guide on how to read tire size explains the sidewall math.
- Have fitment confirmed. Clearance depends on your exact vehicle, suspension and tire.

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Backspacing Explained: ET, Poke and Rub
chunks.text:
How to choose an offset
Running different widths front and rear? Our guide to staggered tires explains what that means for rotation and buying.
Shopping for wheels
Wheels in the wheel catalog list diameter, width, bolt pattern and offset in their specs, and TireDrop confirms fitment before an order ships. Extreme Tires mounts and installs wheel and tire packages at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties; elsewhere in the 48 states and DC, the order ships to your address for a fitter you trust. See how installation works, or call (954) 773-1896.

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Backspacing Explained: ET, Poke and Rub
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Offset is the distance in millimeters from the wheel's centerline to its mounting surface. It's stamped on the wheel, usually after ET.
- Positive offset tucks the wheel in toward the suspension. Negative offset pushes it out toward the fender.
- Backspacing is the same idea measured in inches, from the mounting surface to the back lip of the wheel.
- Lower the offset by 10 mm at the same width and the whole wheel moves 10 mm further out.
- A wider wheel at the same offset grows by half the extra width on each side, inside and out.

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Backspacing Explained: ET, Poke and Rub
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What does ET mean on a wheel?
ET is the offset in millimeters. KMC Wheels notes that the offset can usually be found on the back of the wheel after the letters ET, so ET45 means a 45 mm offset. ET comes from the German Einpresstiefe.
What is the difference between offset and backspacing?
Both describe where the wheel sits. Offset is measured in millimeters from the wheel's centerline to the mounting surface. Backspacing is measured in inches from the mounting surface to the back lip of the wheel. More positive offset means more backspacing.
Does lower offset make a wheel stick out more?
Yes. At the same width, lowering the offset moves the whole wheel outward by the same amount. Going from ET45 to ET35 moves the wheel 10 mm, about 0.39 inch, further out.
How do I know what offset my car needs?

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Backspacing Explained: ET, Poke and Rub
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Start from the factory wheel's offset, usually stamped on the back of the wheel, and the vehicle maker's published specs. A wheel seller or installer can confirm what range clears your suspension, brakes and fenders.

chunks.title: Florida Heat and Tires: Pressure, Aging and Blowouts
chunks.text:
Florida Driving & Weather
Florida Heat and Tires: Pressure, Aging and Blowouts
How Florida heat works on your tires: why low pressure and heavy loads build heat, what NHTSA found about tire aging in the Sun Belt, and a summer routine.
By TireDrop Team, Extreme Tires, Sunrise FL·Published Sep 30, 2026·Updated Oct 2, 2026·5 min read
Heat is part of every drive here
In most of the country, summer is a season for tires. In South Florida it's most of the year. The car sits in a sunny lot in Sunrise, then runs the Sawgrass at highway speed, then sits again, day after day.
Heat alone rarely ruins a tire. What does the damage is heat on top of the things that already make a tire run hot: low pressure, a heavy load and sustained speed. This guide covers where that heat comes from, what NHTSA's research says about tires aging in the Sun Belt, and a routine that fits a Florida summer.

chunks.title: Florida Heat and Tires: Pressure, Aging and Blowouts
chunks.text:
Where damaging heat actually comes from
A tire makes its own heat. Every time it rolls, the sidewall and tread flex where they meet the road, and flexing warms the rubber. The outside air sets the starting point; the way the tire is used decides how hot it gets from there.
NHTSA's consumer brochure Tire Safety: Everything Rides On It names the three conditions to watch: excessive speed, underinflation or excessive loading, either separately or in combination, can cause heat build-up and possible tire failure.
Of the three, pressure is the one that goes wrong quietly. NHTSA's summer driving guidance is direct about it: underinflation is the leading cause of tire failure. A low tire flexes more with every turn of the wheel, and a hot day doesn't give it any margin.

chunks.title: Florida Heat and Tires: Pressure, Aging and Blowouts
chunks.text:
Pressure: heat raises the reading, not the need
Warm air in a tire pushes harder than cool air. USTMA's tire care guidance says inflation pressure goes up in warm weather and down in cold weather by one to two pounds for every 10 degrees of temperature change.
That's why a gauge reading taken after a drive, or in the afternoon sun, can look healthy on a tire that's actually low. Two rules from NHTSA keep it straight:
- Check cold. NHTSA defines cold as parked for at least three hours, so first thing in the morning is the easy time.
- Use the door placard, not the sidewall. The number molded on the tire is the maximum it can hold, not the pressure your vehicle calls for.

chunks.title: Florida Heat and Tires: Pressure, Aging and Blowouts
chunks.text:
Pressure: heat raises the reading, not the need
And one rule for hot days: don't let air out of warm tires. NHTSA's guidance is that pressure rises as tires heat up, so bleeding them down to the placard number leaves them low once they cool. Recheck when they're cold instead.
The numbers behind all of this, including what a cool front does to a tire set on a hot afternoon, are in our guide to tire pressure and temperature.

chunks.title: Florida Heat and Tires: Pressure, Aging and Blowouts
chunks.text:
Load: the number on your door
Summer is road-trip, beach-gear and moving-day season, and every extra pound is carried by four contact patches.
Your Tire and Loading Information placard, on the driver's door edge or door post, lists the vehicle's capacity in plain words. Under the federal placard rule, it reads: "The combined weight of occupants and cargo should never exceed" a stated number of pounds. That line includes people, luggage and anything on a roof rack or hitch.
A loaded car on underinflated tires at highway speed is all three of NHTSA's heat conditions at once. If the trip is long and the car is full, set the pressure cold before you leave. Our post on finding your car's real weight limit walks through the placard math.

chunks.title: Florida Heat and Tires: Pressure, Aging and Blowouts
chunks.text:
Aging: what NHTSA found about the Sun Belt
Heat doesn't only matter on the day you drive. It also affects how fast the rubber ages.
NHTSA's tire aging research describes the process as the combined effect of heat and oxygen on the rubber compound over time. Its TireWise guidance lists exposure to sunlight and a warmer climate, along with infrequent use, poor storage and poor maintenance, among the things that contribute to tire aging. And its research found that tire aging is a greater concern in the more southern parts of the Sun Belt states.

chunks.title: Florida Heat and Tires: Pressure, Aging and Blowouts
chunks.text:
Aging: what NHTSA found about the Sun Belt
South Florida is about as far south in the Sun Belt as the mainland goes. That doesn't give a tire a Florida expiration date. It means age deserves attention alongside tread depth. NHTSA notes that some vehicle and tire makers recommend replacing tires that are 6 to 10 years old regardless of treadwear, and Bridgestone and Michelin both recommend a professional inspection at least once a year from five years on. Our guide to how old is too old for tires lays out the manufacturer guidance side by side.

chunks.title: Florida Heat and Tires: Pressure, Aging and Blowouts
chunks.text:
The temperature grade on your sidewall
Most passenger tires sold in the US carry three UTQG grades on the sidewall (deep-tread winter tires, temporary spares and a few other types are exempt). The last one, temperature, is graded A, B or C. NHTSA's consumer guide describes it as the tire's ability to dissipate the heat generated by driving, with A the highest.
Two things to know before leaning on it:
- The grade comes from a laboratory test at set speeds, not from Florida roads.
- NHTSA notes that the grade applies to a tire that is properly inflated and not overloaded. Low pressure or a heavy load takes away the conditions the grade assumes.
Type a UTQG code from your sidewall to see what each part means:
For the full breakdown of treadwear, traction and temperature, see our UTQG ratings guide.

chunks.title: Florida Heat and Tires: Pressure, Aging and Blowouts
chunks.text:
Where you park matters too
Sunlight is on NHTSA's list of aging factors, and a Florida car can spend more hours parked in the sun than driving. You can't always choose, but when you can:
- Take the covered or shaded space at home and at work.
- If the car will sit for weeks, park it out of direct sun and set the pressure to the placard before you leave. (Snowbirds, our post on a car that sat all summer covers the return trip.)
- Look at the sidewalls of a car that lives outdoors. Cracking in the sidewall or between the tread blocks is a reason to have the tires inspected.
