chunks.title: Florida Heat and Tires: Pressure, Aging and Blowouts
chunks.text:
A South Florida summer routine
Extreme Tires in Sunrise measures tread depth at every corner during a tire rotation and sets pressures to the placard, at the shop or by mobile van in the local install area. For a quick self-check first, run your readings through Do I Need Tires Yet?.
Key takeaways
- NHTSA lists excessive speed, underinflation and excessive loading as the conditions that can cause heat build-up and possible tire failure.
- NHTSA calls underinflation the leading cause of tire failure, so the monthly cold pressure check matters more in a hot climate, not less.
- Hot weather raises the gauge reading. Don't let air out of warm tires; set pressure to the door placard when the tires are cold.
- NHTSA's research found tire aging is a greater concern in the southern parts of the Sun Belt, and sunlight and a warmer climate add to it.

chunks.title: Florida Heat and Tires: Pressure, Aging and Blowouts
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- From five years old, Bridgestone and Michelin recommend a professional inspection at least once a year.
Questions people ask
Does hot weather cause tire blowouts?
Heat is one part of it. NHTSA says excessive speed, underinflation or excessive loading, alone or together, can cause heat build-up and possible tire failure, and it calls underinflation the leading cause of tire failure. Hot weather adds to the heat a tire already makes, so pressure and load matter more in summer.
Should I let air out of my tires when it's hot?
No. NHTSA's guidance is that pressure rises as tires warm, so a high reading on a hot tire is normal. Letting air out can leave the tire underinflated once it cools. Check and set pressure when the tires are cold, parked for at least three hours.
Do tires age faster in Florida?

chunks.title: Florida Heat and Tires: Pressure, Aging and Blowouts
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
NHTSA's tire aging research found aging is a greater concern in the more southern parts of the Sun Belt states, and its TireWise guidance lists exposure to sunlight and a warmer climate among the things that contribute to aging. Florida fits that description.
What does the temperature grade on a tire mean?
It's part of the federal UTQG grading: A, B or C for a tire's ability to dissipate heat in a lab test, with A the highest. NHTSA notes the grade applies to a tire that is properly inflated and not overloaded.

chunks.title: Hydroplaning: Why It Happens and What to Do
chunks.text:
Florida Driving & Weather
Hydroplaning: Why It Happens and What to Do
What hydroplaning is, how tread depth, speed and standing water set it up, what to do if the car starts to float, and how to get ready for Florida storms.
What hydroplaning is
On a dry road, the tread presses rubber straight onto the pavement. On a wet road, the tread has a second job first: it has to push water out of the way so the rubber can reach the road at all.
Hydroplaning is what happens when it can't keep up. Bridgestone describes it as the tires losing their grip on the road surface and traveling on a film of water sitting on top of it. Water builds up in front of the tire faster than the grooves can clear it, pressure rises underneath, and the tread lifts off the pavement.

chunks.title: Hydroplaning: Why It Happens and What to Do
chunks.text:
What hydroplaning is
From the driver's seat, it feels like the steering has gone light or disconnected. That's because it has. Bridgestone notes that hydroplaning dramatically reduces your ability to steer and brake until the tires touch down again.
The four things that set it up
Bridgestone lists the causes as a combination of road conditions, vehicle speed, tread depth and vehicle weight. Three of them are worth understanding in detail.

chunks.title: Hydroplaning: Why It Happens and What to Do
chunks.text:
Speed
Tires need time to move water out from under the tread. The faster you go, the less time each part of the tread has to do it. Bridgestone says hydroplaning can happen at speeds as low as 35 mph, depending on the tires' tread depth and design and how much water is on the road.
That's not a line where it starts for every car, and you should be skeptical of anyone who gives you one. It's a reminder that you don't need to be on the highway for it to happen.

chunks.title: Hydroplaning: Why It Happens and What to Do
chunks.text:
Water depth
More water means more for the tread to move. Bridgestone says the risk worsens as standing water gets deeper than about 1/10 of an inch. That's not much: a puddle in a low spot, the outside lane where water collects, or ruts worn into the pavement can all hold that much in a heavy shower.
Tread depth
Tread grooves are the channels water escapes through. As tread wears, those channels get shallower and hold less.
Two lines matter here:
- 2/32 of an inch is where NHTSA says to replace tires, the point where the built-in wear bars sit flush with the tread. Bridgestone says even the best tires offer little resistance to hydroplaning at 2/32 or less.
- 4/32 of an inch is where AAA recommends replacing. In AAA's tests on wet pavement at 60 mph, tires worn to 4/32 took an average of 87 feet longer to stop than new tires.

chunks.title: Hydroplaning: Why It Happens and What to Do
chunks.text:
Tread depth
Our tread depth chart shows both lines in 32nds and millimeters, and the gauge below shows what each reading means.
A note on the UTQG traction grade printed on the sidewall: it comes from straight-line wet braking tests and doesn't measure hydroplaning. Our UTQG guide explains what it does and doesn't tell you.
What to do if the car starts to float
The instinct is to brake hard or yank the wheel. Both work against you while the tires are on water. AAA's guidance is:
- Ease off the accelerator. Let the car slow on its own.
- Avoid hard braking. Braking hard while the tires have no grip can make things worse.
- Steer gently in the direction you want to go. Small inputs, not a jerk of the wheel.
- Wait for the tires to grip again before making normal steering or braking inputs.

chunks.title: Hydroplaning: Why It Happens and What to Do
chunks.text:
What to do if the car starts to float
Once you're through it, slow down further for the rest of the drive. The conditions that caused it are still there.
How to lower the odds
Most of the work happens before the rain starts.
Keep tread above 4/32. Check three grooves on every tire and go by the shallowest reading. The quarter test is a quick check: put a quarter upside down in a groove, and if you can see all of Washington's head, you're at about 4/32. If you're close, run your readings through Do I Need Tires Yet?.
Set pressure to the door placard, cold. The number on the door-jamb sticker is the vehicle maker's recommendation. The number on the sidewall is a maximum, not a target.
In the rain, the habits that help come from Bridgestone's and AAA's wet-weather advice:

chunks.title: Hydroplaning: Why It Happens and What to Do
chunks.text:
How to lower the odds
- Slow down. Bridgestone suggests 5 to 10 mph below your usual speed on wet roads, and more where you see standing water.
- Turn off cruise control. You want to be able to ease off the gas yourself.
- Steer around puddles and standing water when you can do it without a sudden lane change.
- Leave more following distance so you're not forced into hard braking.
- Never drive into a flooded road. You can't see how deep it is.

chunks.title: Hydroplaning: Why It Happens and What to Do
chunks.text:
The South Florida factor
Hydroplaning isn't a once-a-year problem here. The National Weather Service office in Miami puts South Florida's rainy season at May 15 to October 15, with showers and thunderstorms developing almost every day. For five months a year, wet pavement is part of the normal commute.
The national numbers back up the respect. Per the Federal Highway Administration's 10-year averages (2007 to 2016), 75 percent of weather-related crashes happened on wet pavement and 47 percent during rainfall.
Florida law adds one requirement: Statute 316.217 says headlights must be on during any rain, smoke or fog. It also helps the driver behind you see you through the spray.
Our post on hydroplaning in Broward's afternoon storms turns all of this into a storm-day checklist. Heat matters to tires here too; our guide to Florida heat and tires covers that side.

chunks.title: Hydroplaning: Why It Happens and What to Do
chunks.text:
When it's time for new tires
If your tread is at or near 4/32, replace before the next rainy season rather than during it. The Tire Size Finder reads your size off the door-jamb sticker, and you can shop tires by size from there.
Extreme Tires installs at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties. Anywhere else in the 48 contiguous states and DC, your order ships to your address for a local installer. See how installation works, or call (954) 773-1896 with questions.

chunks.title: Hydroplaning: Why It Happens and What to Do
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Hydroplaning is when a tire rides up on a film of water and loses its grip on the road, so steering and braking stop working the way you expect.
- Speed, tread depth, water depth and vehicle weight all play a part. Bridgestone says it can happen at speeds as low as 35 mph, depending on the tires and the water.
- Worn tread moves less water. NHTSA's replacement line is 2/32 of an inch; AAA recommends replacing at 4/32 after its wet-braking tests.
- If the car starts to float, AAA says to ease off the gas, avoid hard braking and steer gently where you want to go.
- South Florida's rainy season runs May 15 to October 15, per NWS Miami, so wet roads are part of the normal commute here.

chunks.title: Hydroplaning: Why It Happens and What to Do
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What causes hydroplaning?
Water arriving faster than the tread can clear it. Pressure builds under the tire and lifts the tread off the pavement. Bridgestone lists road conditions, vehicle speed, tread depth and vehicle weight as the factors, and says the risk rises as standing water gets deeper than about a tenth of an inch.
At what speed can you hydroplane?
There's no single number for every car. Bridgestone says hydroplaning can happen at speeds as low as 35 mph, depending on the tires' tread depth and design and how much water is on the road. Slowing down in the rain is the one factor you control on the spot.
What should you do if your car hydroplanes?
AAA's advice is to ease off the accelerator, avoid hard braking and steer gently in the direction you want the car to go, then wait for the tires to grip again before making normal steering or braking inputs.

chunks.title: Hydroplaning: Why It Happens and What to Do
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Does tread depth affect hydroplaning?
Yes. Tread grooves are what carry water out from under the tire. Bridgestone says even the best tires offer little resistance to hydroplaning once tread is worn to 2/32 of an inch, and AAA recommends replacing tires at 4/32 because worn tires took much longer to stop on wet pavement in its tests.

chunks.title: How to Check Tire Pressure: Cold, With a Gauge
chunks.text:
Pressure & TPMS
How to Check Tire Pressure: Cold, With a Gauge
How to check tire pressure the right way: when the tires are cold, which gauge to use, where your PSI is printed (not the sidewall) and how to add air.
Five minutes, once a month
Checking tire pressure takes one gauge, one sticker and five minutes. Doing it at the wrong time, or against the wrong number, makes the reading useless.
NHTSA's guidance is simple: check the pressure in all four tires and the spare at least once a month, when the tires are cold. Here's what that means, what to use, and the steps.

chunks.title: How to Check Tire Pressure: Cold, With a Gauge
chunks.text:
When to check: cold means parked for three hours
NHTSA defines a cold tire as one that hasn't been driven for at least three hours. The pressure your vehicle maker recommends is a cold pressure, so that's the only reading you can compare against it.
Driving warms the tires, and warm air pushes harder. A tire checked right after a run down I-595 reads higher than the same tire did that morning, even though it holds the same air.
The easy routine:
- First thing in the morning, before the car moves.
- Or after it's been parked in the shade for a few hours.
- Not right after a drive, unless you have no choice. More on that below.

chunks.title: How to Check Tire Pressure: Cold, With a Gauge
chunks.text:
What to check with: pick a gauge
Don't rely on the gauge built into a gas station air hose. Tire makers' guides recommend using your own gauge: check with it, add air with the station's hose, then check again with your gauge.
Three common types:
Gauge type
How you read it
Worth knowing
Dial
A needle on a round face
No batteries needed
Digital
A number on a screen
Easy to read in low light; needs a battery
Stick (pencil)
A bar slides out of the tube
The most compact; can be harder to read
Any of them works if it seals on the valve and you read it carefully. Keep it in the glove box so it's there when you need it.

chunks.title: How to Check Tire Pressure: Cold, With a Gauge
chunks.text:
What to check with: pick a gauge
And your TPMS light? It isn't a gauge. Under the federal standard, FMVSS No. 138, the warning has to come on once a tire is 25 percent or more below the placard pressure. A tire can be well under the right number with the light still off. Our TPMS light guide covers what the light does and doesn't tell you.
Where to find your number: the door placard
Your target pressure is printed on the Tire and Loading Information label. NHTSA says it's on the driver's side door edge or door post (the B-pillar) and in the owner's manual. On a vehicle without a B-pillar, look at the rear edge of the driver's door.
A few things to read on that label:
- Front and rear. Some vehicles list different pressures for each axle.
- The spare. A compact spare often has its own pressure.

chunks.title: How to Check Tire Pressure: Cold, With a Gauge
chunks.text:
Where to find your number: the door placard
- The tire size. The label assumes the size your vehicle maker fitted. If you're running a different size or load type, ask your installer what pressure to use.
The same sticker lists your original tire size, which is how our Tire Size Finder reads it.
Not the number on the tire
The tire's sidewall has a pressure on it too, usually after "Max. Press." USTMA explains that this is the maximum the tire is built to hold, whatever vehicle it's on. It isn't your target. Our post on why not to inflate to the sidewall max goes into why the two numbers differ.

chunks.title: How to Check Tire Pressure: Cold, With a Gauge
chunks.text:
How to check tire pressure, step by step
- Read the placard and note the cold pressure for the front, the rear and the spare.
- Start with cold tires, parked for at least three hours.
- Unscrew the valve cap and put it somewhere you won't lose it.
- Press the gauge straight onto the valve stem, firmly, until the hiss stops. A hiss that keeps going means it isn't sealed.
- Read the number. If it looks off, take the reading again.
- Compare it to the placard for that position.
- If it's low, add air in short bursts and recheck with your gauge after each one.
- If it's high on a cold tire, let a little out by pressing the pin in the center of the valve, then recheck.
- Put the cap back on before you move to the next tire.
- Repeat on every tire, spare included.
Write the readings down. A tire that's lower than the others month after month is telling you something.

chunks.title: How to Check Tire Pressure: Cold, With a Gauge
chunks.text:
Checking at the gas station after a drive
Sometimes the air machine is the only chance you get, and the tires are warm. Two rules:
- Don't let air out of a warm tire to match the placard. NHTSA's summer guidance is not to bleed warm tires. The pressure drops as they cool, and a tire set to the placard while warm sits below it once it's cold.
- If a warm tire reads below the placard, it's low. Add air to bring it up, then recheck the next morning, cold, and adjust.

chunks.title: How to Check Tire Pressure: Cold, With a Gauge
chunks.text:
Florida heat and the reading
South Florida makes cold checks harder: the car is warm by mid-morning, and the air in an A/C garage and on a sunny driveway can be very different temperatures. Pressure moves with the air temperature, about 1 to 2 psi for every 10°F by the tire industry's rule of thumb. Our pressure and temperature guide explains the math, and the calculator below estimates how much a reading should move:
The takeaway: a hot afternoon can make a low tire read normal. Check early, and check monthly. Our guide to Florida heat and tires covers why pressure matters even more in the heat.

chunks.title: How to Check Tire Pressure: Cold, With a Gauge
chunks.text:
When the gauge says more than "add air"
A tire that loses a few psi between monthly checks, along with the other three, is normal. These aren't:
- One tire that keeps reading lower than the rest
- a tire that needs air every week
- a TPMS light that comes back right after you've set all four
Those point to a leak: a nail, a valve stem or a bead that isn't sealing. While the gauge is out, check the tread too; our guide on how to check tread depth takes two more minutes. Then run your readings through Do I Need Tires Yet?.
Driving for a living? Our post on tires for Uber and Lyft drivers shows what low pressure costs in fuel over a high-mileage year.

chunks.title: How to Check Tire Pressure: Cold, With a Gauge
chunks.text:
When the gauge says more than "add air"
If a tire won't hold air, Extreme Tires repairs punctures after taking the tire off the wheel to inspect it, at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach. If it's time for new ones, shop tires by size; free shipping covers the 48 contiguous states and DC, and installation in South Florida is either ship-to-store in Sunrise or the mobile van. See how installation works, or call (954) 773-1896.

chunks.title: How to Check Tire Pressure: Cold, With a Gauge
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Check all four tires and the spare at least once a month, with the tires cold: parked for at least three hours.
- Your target pressure is on the Tire and Loading Information label on the driver's door edge or door post, and in the owner's manual.
- The pressure molded on the sidewall is the tire's maximum, not your target.
- Use your own gauge. Dial, digital and stick gauges all work; read it, add air, then read it again.
- Don't let air out of warm tires. Recheck them cold and set them to the placard.

chunks.title: How to Check Tire Pressure: Cold, With a Gauge
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
When is the best time to check tire pressure?
When the tires are cold. NHTSA defines cold as not driven for at least three hours, so first thing in the morning, before the car moves, is the easiest time. NHTSA's guidance is to check at least once a month, spare included.
Where do I find the right tire pressure for my car?
On the Tire and Loading Information label, usually on the driver's side door edge or the door post (the B-pillar), and in the owner's manual. NHTSA notes that if a vehicle has no B-pillar, the label may be on the rear edge of the driver's door.
Should I use the PSI number on the tire?
No. The number on the sidewall is the maximum pressure the tire is built to hold, whatever vehicle it's on. USTMA says to use the vehicle maker's recommended cold pressure from the placard or owner's manual instead.
Can I check tire pressure after driving?

chunks.title: How to Check Tire Pressure: Cold, With a Gauge
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
You can, but the reading will be higher than the cold number because driving warms the tires. Don't let air out to match the placard. If a warm tire reads below the placard number, it's low: add air, then recheck once the tires are cold.

chunks.title: Tire Pressure and Temperature: How Much PSI Changes
chunks.text:
Pressure & TPMS
Tire Pressure and Temperature: How Much PSI Changes
How much tire pressure changes with temperature: the 1 to 2 psi per 10°F rule of thumb, the physics behind it, and how to set it right in any weather.
Same air, different reading
You set your tires to the door placard on Sunday afternoon. Monday morning, after the first cool front of the season, the gauge reads two psi low and the TPMS light is on. Nothing leaked. The air just got colder.
Temperature changes tire pressure every day, in both directions. Here's how much, why, and how to set your pressure so the number means something.

chunks.title: Tire Pressure and Temperature: How Much PSI Changes
chunks.text:
The rule of thumb: about 1 to 2 psi per 10°F
Three tire-industry sources put a number on it:
Source
How much pressure changes
USTMA (Tire Care Essentials)
One to two pounds for every 10 degrees of temperature change
Goodyear
1 to 2 pounds for every 10°F: up in warm weather, down in cold
Bridgestone Americas
About 1 psi for every 10°F change in ambient temperature
The direction is the same in all three. Warmer means higher, cooler means lower. NHTSA's winter guidance says it in one line: as the outside temperature drops, so does tire inflation pressure.
Treat the figure as a rule of thumb, not a measurement. The exact change depends on the tire, how much air is in it and how quickly the temperature moved.

chunks.title: Tire Pressure and Temperature: How Much PSI Changes
chunks.text:
Why it happens: the physics
A tire is a sealed container. Heat the air inside and its molecules move faster and push harder on the walls. Cool it and they push less. The amount of air hasn't changed, only its temperature.
The math is Gay-Lussac's law, which says the absolute pressure of a sealed gas rises and falls with its absolute temperature. For tires it needs two conversions, because a tire gauge reads pressure above the atmosphere and Fahrenheit doesn't start at absolute zero:
new psi ≈ (old psi + 14.7) × (new °F + 459.67) ÷ (old °F + 459.67) − 14.7
This assumes the tire's volume stays the same, which is close enough for an estimate. Here's what it gives for a tire set to 35 psi, used only as an example. Your vehicle's number is on the door placard.
Set at 35 psi at
Then the air is
Estimated reading
Change
75°F (A/C garage)
95°F (driveway in the sun)
about 36.9 psi
+1.9

chunks.title: Tire Pressure and Temperature: How Much PSI Changes

Why it happens: the physics
70°F (morning)
90°F (afternoon)
about 36.9 psi

70°F (next morning)
about 33.2 psi

80°F (before a front)
55°F (after a front)
about 32.7 psi
−2.3
That works out to a little under 1 psi per 10°F at this pressure, which sits at the low end of the industry range. Real tires can move more, which is why the sources give a range.

chunks.title: Tire Pressure and Temperature: How Much PSI Changes
chunks.text:
Driving heat is a separate effect
The table covers the air around the car. Driving adds heat of its own: the tire flexes as it rolls, the rubber warms up, and so does the air inside. A tire that's been on I-95 for half an hour reads higher than the same tire parked overnight, even on the same day.
That's why NHTSA defines cold as parked for at least three hours, and why its summer guidance says don't let air out of warm tires. Pressure rises as tires heat up; bleed them down to the placard while they're warm and they'll sit below it once they cool.

chunks.title: Tire Pressure and Temperature: How Much PSI Changes
chunks.text:
Florida situations where this shows up
The A/C garage to sunny driveway. A car filled in a cool garage and parked in the sun will read higher an hour later. It hasn't gained air. Set pressure before it goes out.
The gas station after a drive. The air machine is convenient, but your tires are warm. If a warm tire reads right at the placard number, it's likely a little low when cold. Add what's needed, then recheck in the morning.
The first cool front. Tires set on a warm day lose a couple of psi overnight. A tire that was already a bit low can cross the TPMS warning line. Our TPMS light guide explains what the light's behavior means.
Summer heat. Hot weather raises the reading, which can hide a tire that's low. Our guide to Florida heat and tires covers why pressure matters more, not less, in the heat.

chunks.title: Tire Pressure and Temperature: How Much PSI Changes
chunks.text:
How to set pressure so the number means something
- Check cold. First thing in the morning, before the car moves, is easiest.
- Use the door placard, not the sidewall. The number on the tire is a maximum, not the target. Here's why.
- Use a gauge. TPMS is designed to warn at a large loss, not a small one.
- Set all four and the spare. NHTSA's guidance is to check monthly, spare included.
- Recheck after a big temperature swing. A new season or a front is a good reminder.
Our guide to checking tire pressure walks through each step with a gauge.

chunks.title: Tire Pressure and Temperature: How Much PSI Changes
chunks.text:
When temperature isn't the explanation
Temperature moves all four tires by roughly the same amount at the same time. Tires also lose some air naturally: Bridgestone says about 1 psi a month on average, which is one more reason for the monthly check. Nitrogen fill slows that seepage a little but doesn't replace the check; see our nitrogen myth check.
What temperature doesn't explain:
- One tire that reads lower than the others, again and again
- a tire that needs air every week
- a TPMS light that comes back soon after you've set all four
Those point to a leak: a nail, a valve stem or a bead that isn't sealing. Have it inspected. Extreme Tires repairs punctures after dismounting and inspecting the tire, and its TPMS service covers sensor scans and relearns, at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in the local install area.

chunks.title: Tire Pressure and Temperature: How Much PSI Changes
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- USTMA and Goodyear put the change at one to two psi for every 10°F; Bridgestone says about 1 psi.
- Warmer air raises the reading and cooler air lowers it. The air in the tire is the same; only its temperature changed.
- Set pressure to the door placard with the tires cold, meaning parked for at least three hours.
- Don't let air out of warm tires. NHTSA's guidance is to recheck them cold.
- Temperature explains a small, even change on all four tires. One tire that keeps dropping points to a leak.

chunks.title: Tire Pressure and Temperature: How Much PSI Changes
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How much does tire pressure change with temperature?
USTMA's tire care guidance and Goodyear both say about one to two psi for every 10°F change in temperature, up when it's warmer and down when it's cooler. Bridgestone gives about 1 psi per 10°F. The gas-law math for a typical passenger tire lands at a little under 1 psi per 10°F.
Does heat increase tire pressure?
Yes. Warm air in a sealed tire pushes harder than cool air, so pressure rises on a hot day and rises again as the tires warm up from driving. That's normal, and it's why NHTSA asks you to check pressure when the tires are cold.
Should I let air out of hot tires?
No. NHTSA's guidance is that pressure rises as tires warm, and letting air out of a warm tire can leave it underinflated once it cools. Wait until the tires are cold, then set them to the door placard pressure.

chunks.title: Tire Pressure and Temperature: How Much PSI Changes
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Why is my tire pressure low on cold mornings?
NHTSA puts it simply: as the outside temperature drops, so does tire inflation pressure. A tire set on a hot afternoon can read a couple of psi lower after a cool night. If it's below the placard number when cold, add air.

chunks.title: TPMS Light On? Solid vs Flashing, and What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Pressure & TPMS
TPMS Light On? Solid vs Flashing, and What to Do Next
TPMS light on? Solid usually means a tire is low. Flashing, then solid, means the system has a fault. What the federal rule says and what to do next.
By TireDrop Team, Extreme Tires, Sunrise FL·Published Sep 30, 2026·Updated Oct 2, 2026·5 min read
What the TPMS light is actually telling you
The yellow horseshoe with an exclamation point is your tire pressure monitoring system, or TPMS. It became standard equipment because of a federal rule: passenger cars, SUVs, trucks and buses with a gross vehicle weight rating of 10,000 lb or less built from September 1, 2007 onward must have one.

chunks.title: TPMS Light On? Solid vs Flashing, and What to Do Next
chunks.text:
What the TPMS light is actually telling you
The rule, FMVSS No. 138, also sets when the light has to come on. The low-pressure warning must light up when a tire is 25 percent or more below the vehicle maker's recommended cold pressure (or a minimum level the standard sets, whichever is higher), within 20 minutes of reaching that point.
That 25 percent figure is the key to everything below. The light isn't a gentle reminder. By the time it's on, a tire is already well down.
There are two ways the light behaves, and they mean different things. Pick what your dash is doing:

chunks.title: TPMS Light On? Solid vs Flashing, and What to Do Next
chunks.text:
What the TPMS light is actually telling you
A steady tire pressure light means at least one tire may be well under-inflated, and a light that flashes for about 60 to 90 seconds and then stays on signals a system malfunction, per FMVSS No. 138. Either way, check pressures with a gauge when tires are cold, inflate to the door placard, and have the system inspected if the light stays on.

chunks.title: TPMS Light On? Solid vs Flashing, and What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Solid light: at least one tire is low
A light that comes on and stays on, with no flashing at startup, is the low-pressure warning.
What to do:
- Don't ignore it until the weekend. At the first practical stop, check all four tires with a gauge.
- Compare against the placard, not the sidewall. Your vehicle's recommended pressure is on the Tire and Loading Information label, usually on the driver's door edge or door post, and in the owner's manual. The number molded on the tire is a maximum, not a target.
- Know whether the tires are cold. NHTSA defines cold as parked for at least three hours. NHTSA notes that pressure normally rises as tires warm, so a reading right after a drive on I-595 can be higher than the cold number.

chunks.title: TPMS Light On? Solid vs Flashing, and What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Solid light: at least one tire is low
- Add air to the placard pressure. If the tires are warm, don't let air out to hit the placard number; NHTSA's advice is to recheck when they're cold before adjusting down.
- Watch that tire. If the light comes back within days, or one tire keeps reading low, you likely have a leak. Have it inspected.
A slow leak isn't always a visible nail, so let a technician find the source. Extreme Tires repairs tires with a combination patch-plug from the inside after dismounting and inspecting them, at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in the local install area.

chunks.title: TPMS Light On? Solid vs Flashing, and What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Flashing, then solid: the system has a fault
This is the one people misread. Under FMVSS No. 138, when the system detects a malfunction, the light must:
- flash for at least 60 seconds but no longer than 90 seconds after you turn the ignition on, then
- stay on continuously as long as the malfunction exists,
- and repeat that sequence at every startup until the problem is fixed.
So a flashing-then-solid light doesn't mean "very low tire." It means the system can't do its job. Your pressures could be right, or they could be low and the system can't tell you.
Until it's fixed, you're driving without the warning. Check your pressures with a gauge in the meantime, and have the system diagnosed. A technician with a TPMS scan tool can read which sensor isn't reporting.

chunks.title: TPMS Light On? Solid vs Flashing, and What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Flashing, then solid: the system has a fault
Extreme Tires' TPMS service covers a sensor scan and battery health check, sensor replacement where needed, and relearn and programming to the vehicle, in the shop or from the mobile van.
Came on during a cool morning?
South Florida doesn't get much cold, but a front does bring the occasional cool morning.
NHTSA's explanation is simple: as the outside temperature drops, so does tire inflation pressure. A tire that was already running a little low can cross the 25 percent line overnight and trip the light at 7 a.m. Then the day warms up, the pressure rises and the light may go out on its own.

chunks.title: TPMS Light On? Solid vs Flashing, and What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Came on during a cool morning?
The light going out doesn't mean the problem went away. The tire was low enough to trigger a warning, so set all four to the placard pressure, cold, before the afternoon heat hides it again. Our guide to tire pressure and temperature shows how much a front can move the reading.
Shows how a tire's pressure rises and falls with air temperature, using both the common rule of thumb and the gas-law calculation. Set pressures cold, to the value on the vehicle's door placard.

chunks.title: TPMS Light On? Solid vs Flashing, and What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Came on after new tires or a rotation?
A light that shows up right after tire work can point to the sensors rather than the air. Depending on the vehicle, sensors may need to be reset or relearned after they move positions or are replaced. Your owner's manual lists the procedure for your car.
A tire installation at Extreme Tires includes a TPMS reset where the vehicle has it. If the light appears after the fact, call (954) 773-1896 and ask.

chunks.title: TPMS Light On? Solid vs Flashing, and What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Light off doesn't mean pressure is right
Here's the part most drivers miss. The TPMS warning is designed to come on at a significant pressure loss, not a small one. A tire can be 15 or 20 percent low with the dash completely dark.
The regulation itself says it: TPMS is not a substitute for proper tire maintenance, and keeping correct pressure is the driver's job even when the light hasn't come on. NHTSA's guidance is to check pressure with a gauge at least once a month, spare included, with the tires cold.
On run-flat tires a working TPMS matters even more, because the car can sit level with a tire at zero pressure. Our run-flat tire guide explains why.

chunks.title: TPMS Light On? Solid vs Flashing, and What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Under the federal standard, the low-pressure warning comes on when a tire is 25% or more below the placard pressure.
- A light that flashes for 60 to 90 seconds at startup and then stays on signals a TPMS malfunction, not just a low tire.
- Check pressure with a gauge against the door placard, with the tires cold.
- Cooler air lowers tire pressure, so a cool morning can trip a tire that was already running low.
- TPMS is not a substitute for a monthly gauge check, spare included.

chunks.title: TPMS Light On? Solid vs Flashing, and What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Why is my tire pressure light on when the tires look full?
The federal standard sets the warning at 25% or more below the placard pressure, a loss you may not spot just by looking. Check all four with a gauge, cold, against the pressure on the door placard.
What does a flashing tire pressure light mean?
Under FMVSS No. 138, a light that flashes for 60 to 90 seconds when you start the car and then stays on means the system has detected a malfunction. It repeats at every start until the fault is fixed. Have the system checked by a technician with a TPMS tool.
Can I reset the TPMS light myself?
On many cars the light goes out on its own once all tires are set to the placard pressure. Some vehicles have a reset or relearn procedure. Your owner's manual says which applies to your car. If the light keeps returning, have the tires and sensors checked.

chunks.title: TPMS Light On? Solid vs Flashing, and What to Do Next
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How long can I drive with the TPMS light on?
There's no set distance. A solid light means at least one tire may be significantly underinflated. Check pressures at the first practical stop and have any tire that keeps losing air inspected before driving further on it.

chunks.title: TPMS Sensors: Batteries, Relearns and New Tires
chunks.text:
Pressure & TPMS
TPMS Sensors: Batteries, Relearns and New Tires
How TPMS sensors work, direct vs indirect systems, sensor battery life, relearns after a rotation, and what happens to the sensors when you get new tires.
What a TPMS sensor is, and why you have one
Passenger cars, SUVs, pickups and vans built for the US from September 1, 2007 onward have a tire pressure monitoring system. The federal rule, FMVSS No. 138, covers passenger cars, multipurpose vehicles, trucks and buses with a gross vehicle weight rating of 10,000 lb or less, except those with dual rear wheels.

chunks.title: TPMS Sensors: Batteries, Relearns and New Tires
chunks.text:
What a TPMS sensor is, and why you have one
The rule sets what the system must do: light a warning no more than 20 minutes after a tire drops to 25 percent or more below the vehicle maker's recommended cold pressure, and light a malfunction warning when the system itself stops working. Our guide to the TPMS light covers what the dash is telling you. This one is about the hardware behind it.

chunks.title: TPMS Sensors: Batteries, Relearns and New Tires
chunks.text:
Direct vs indirect TPMS
There are two ways a car can watch your tires.
Feature
Direct TPMS
Indirect TPMS
How it measures
A pressure sensor in each wheel
The ABS wheel-speed sensors
What it knows
The actual pressure in each tire
That one tire is turning at a different speed
Batteries to wear out
Yes, one per sensor
No separate sensors
After a rotation or new tires
May need a relearn so it knows which sensor is where
May need a reset, per the owner's manual
Pirelli describes direct TPMS as a pressure sensor attached to the back of each tire's valve, and indirect TPMS as using existing sensors, such as ABS and wheel speed sensors, with software inferring the pressure. Continental explains the indirect logic: a flat tire rotates faster than the others, and the system detects and flags it.

chunks.title: TPMS Sensors: Batteries, Relearns and New Tires
chunks.text:
Direct vs indirect TPMS
Your owner's manual says which system your car uses. If your dash shows a separate pressure reading for each tire, that points to a direct system.
Sensor batteries: the part that wears out
A direct TPMS sensor is a small radio transmitter with its own battery, sealed inside the wheel. That battery is the usual reason a sensor fails.
Pirelli puts it plainly: TPMS sensors most often need to be replaced because their batteries have reached the end of their 5- to 10-year lifespan. It adds that most sensor models have built-in, non-replaceable batteries, so the only solution is to replace the whole sensor.
There's a knock-on effect. Continental notes that you don't always need to replace all four when one fails, but the other sensors are likely close to failing too, due to old batteries. Sensors from the same car usually have the same birthday.

chunks.title: TPMS Sensors: Batteries, Relearns and New Tires
chunks.text:
Sensor batteries: the part that wears out
What a dying sensor looks like from the driver's seat: the TPMS light flashes at startup and then stays on, the malfunction pattern the federal rule requires. Pick that pattern on the explainer below to see what it means:
A steady tire pressure light means at least one tire may be well under-inflated, and a light that flashes for about 60 to 90 seconds and then stays on signals a system malfunction, per FMVSS No. 138. Either way, check pressures with a gauge when tires are cold, inflate to the door placard, and have the system inspected if the light stays on.

chunks.title: TPMS Sensors: Batteries, Relearns and New Tires
chunks.text:
Relearns: telling the car where each sensor is
Each direct sensor broadcasts its own ID. The car needs to know which ID belongs to which corner, and which IDs are on the car at all. Tire Review defines a TPMS relearn as the process of programming new sensor IDs or repositioning existing IDs in the vehicle control module.
When a relearn or reset can come up:
- After a rotation, when sensors change corners.
- After a new sensor is fitted.
- After a wheel swap, such as a second set of wheels.
How it's done varies by car. Continental notes the sensors recalibrate on their own in many cases, but sometimes you need to manually reset them, or replace them if the light stays on. Pirelli's advice is that TPMS resets should be done by a tire professional. Your owner's manual lists your car's procedure. Tesla owners can see how that maker handles it in our Tesla rotation, alignment and TPMS guide.

chunks.title: TPMS Sensors: Batteries, Relearns and New Tires
chunks.text:
What happens to the sensors when you get new tires
New tires don't automatically mean new sensors. A working sensor is moved over to the new tire on the same wheel. What does change:
- The seals and valve parts. Per Tire Review, USTMA, TIA and many vehicle OEMs all say that every time a tire is taken off the wheel, the sensor's wear items should be replaced. The reason given: rubber seals break down over time and are prone to leaking if the sensor is moved or twisted during dismounting and mounting. These parts come as a TPMS service kit.
- A check that the system still works. FMVSS No. 138 requires the owner's manual to tell you to check the TPMS malfunction telltale after replacing one or more tires or wheels, so the replacement tires and wheels allow the TPMS to continue to function properly. The rule notes that replacement tires or wheels can prevent the system from working.

chunks.title: TPMS Sensors: Batteries, Relearns and New Tires
chunks.text:
What happens to the sensors when you get new tires
- A conversation about age. If your sensors are in the 5- to 10-year range Pirelli describes, it can make sense to replace them while the tires are off anyway, rather than dismounting a new tire later.
TPMS is a backup, not a gauge
The warning comes on at 25 percent low. A tire can be well under the placard pressure with the light still off. NHTSA's advice stands no matter which system you have: check all four tires, and the spare, with a gauge at least once a month, cold. Our guide to checking tire pressure walks through it.

chunks.title: TPMS Sensors: Batteries, Relearns and New Tires
chunks.text:
TPMS at Extreme Tires
Every tire installation from Extreme Tires includes valve stem replacement and a TPMS reset where the car has one. Its TPMS service covers:
- sensor scan and battery health check
- sensor replacement where needed
- relearn and programming to your vehicle
- pressure set to placard spec
It's done at the Sunrise shop or from the mobile van at your home or office across Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach. Buying tires here? Tires ship free to the 48 contiguous states and DC, and you can book installation or a mobile visit when you order. Mention a TPMS light when you book; the van carries a TPMS programmer.

chunks.title: TPMS Sensors: Batteries, Relearns and New Tires
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Direct TPMS uses a pressure sensor in each wheel. Indirect TPMS uses the ABS wheel-speed sensors to infer a low tire.
- Pirelli says sensors most often need replacing because their batteries reach the end of a 5- to 10-year lifespan, and most batteries can't be replaced on their own.
- Per Tire Review, USTMA, TIA and many vehicle makers say the sensor's seals and valve parts should be replaced every time a tire is taken off the wheel.
- After a rotation or new sensors, the car may need a relearn so it knows which sensor is where. Your owner's manual gives the procedure.
- The federal TPMS rule tells owners to check the malfunction light after replacing tires or wheels, because some replacements stop the system working.

chunks.title: TPMS Sensors: Batteries, Relearns and New Tires
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How long do TPMS sensor batteries last?
Pirelli puts the typical sensor battery lifespan at 5 to 10 years, and notes most sensors have built-in batteries that can't be replaced, so the whole sensor is replaced. Continental adds that when one sensor fails from an old battery, the others are likely close to failing too.
What is a TPMS relearn?
It's the process of programming new sensor IDs into the vehicle, or teaching it where existing sensors now sit after a rotation. Some cars do it on their own while driving; others need a tool or a set procedure. Your owner's manual says which applies to yours.
Do I need new TPMS sensors with new tires?

chunks.title: TPMS Sensors: Batteries, Relearns and New Tires
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Not automatically. A working sensor moves to the new tire. What should be replaced each time the tire comes off the wheel are the sensor's seals and valve parts, per USTMA and TIA guidance as reported by Tire Review. Older sensors near the end of their battery life are worth discussing at the same visit.
How do I know if my car has direct or indirect TPMS?
Your owner's manual describes the system. A technician with a TPMS tool can also check for sensors at each wheel. Direct systems often show individual tire pressures on the dash; indirect systems infer low pressure from wheel speed instead.

chunks.title: Tire Date Code: How to Read the DOT Number on a Tire
chunks.text:
Reading Your Tire
Tire Date Code: How to Read the DOT Number on a Tire
Find the tire date code on your sidewall, read the four digits for the week and year it was built, and use the full DOT number to run a tire recall check.
Where the tire date code lives
Every tire sold in the US carries a tire identification number, or TIN. It starts with the letters DOT and sits on the sidewall near the rim. The date is hiding at the very end of it.
The catch: the full number isn't always on the side you can see. NHTSA tells drivers to look on both sides of the tire, because the TIN may not be on both. On a car parked in a tight Brickell garage, that usually means a flashlight and a look at the inboard sidewall, the one facing under the car.
What you're looking for:
- The letters DOT, often in a slightly raised oval or box.
- A string of letters and numbers after it.

chunks.title: Tire Date Code: How to Read the DOT Number on a Tire
chunks.text:
Where the tire date code lives
- A group of four digits at the end, sometimes set apart in its own oval.
If you find DOT followed by a short code that stops without four digits, you're probably on the partial side. Check the other sidewall.
Reading the four digits
Those last four digits are the build date. Per NHTSA and Goodyear, the first two are the week of the year and the last two are the year.
Code on the tire

Read it as

Week 01 is the first full week of the year, so a code starting with 01 means early January, not New Year's Day exactly. You don't need to be more precise than the month to use the date well.
Type yours into the reader below. It highlights the date digits and places the tire on a timeline.

chunks.title: Tire Date Code: How to Read the DOT Number on a Tire
chunks.text:
Three-digit codes: tires built before 2000
Before 2000, the date was only three digits. Goodyear explains the format: the first two digits are still the week, but the last digit is only the year within the decade. A code ending in 317 could mean week 31 of 1997, 1987 or 1977. The decade isn't shown.
In practice, the decade barely matters. A three-digit date code means the tire is more than 25 years old. If you find one on a car, a classic, a trailer or a spare that came with a used vehicle, don't just check the tread. Have it inspected, and plan on a conversation about replacing it.

chunks.title: Tire Date Code: How to Read the DOT Number on a Tire
chunks.text:
The rest of the DOT number
The characters between "DOT" and the date aren't random. General Tire breaks a DOT serial number into these parts:
- Plant code. Which factory built the tire.
- Tire size code. A manufacturer's code for the size.
- Tire type code. An optional group the manufacturer uses for its own tracking.
- Date code. The four digits covered above.
The format got more uniform in 2015. NHTSA's final rule that year:
- expanded the plant code from two symbols to three for new tires, because two-symbol codes had run out;
- standardized a new tire's TIN at 13 symbols;
- gave most manufacturers until 2025 before the new format became mandatory.
So on the road today you'll see both lengths. A shorter TIN with a two-symbol plant code is most likely the older format, not a mistake. Either way, the last four digits are still the date.

chunks.title: Tire Date Code: How to Read the DOT Number on a Tire
chunks.text:
Using the full DOT number for a recall check
This is where the whole number earns its keep. The date alone tells you age. The full TIN tells a recall database which tires you have.
Two free lookups:
- USTMA Tire Recall Lookup. Enter the full TIN. It covers recalls on tires made by U.S. Tire Manufacturers Association members from 2000 onward. If a tire matches, it gives you the manufacturer's contact for the remedy.
- NHTSA recalls. Search by tire brand and tire line. Use this for brands outside the USTMA membership, or if you're not sure who made the tire.
Better still, get ahead of recalls. Federal rules set up a tire registration program so manufacturers can reach the people who bought their tires. When you buy new tires, register them with the manufacturer using the TIN. Our guide to tire recalls and registration walks through it.

chunks.title: Tire Date Code: How to Read the DOT Number on a Tire
chunks.text:
What the date tells you, and what it doesn't
A date code is a birth certificate, not a health report.
- It tells you age. NHTSA's tire buyers' FAQ says to check this date when you buy, and to know your vehicle manufacturer's recommended replacement timeframe for tires.
- It doesn't tell you condition. Two tires built the same week can age very differently. One sat in a climate-controlled warehouse; the other baked on a car parked outside all summer.
- It doesn't set a legal deadline. Age guidance comes from vehicle and tire manufacturers, and it varies. We lay it out side by side in How Old Is Too Old for Tires?.
If the tread looks deep but the date is old, don't let the tread talk you out of a closer look. Cracking in the sidewall or between tread blocks is a reason to have it inspected.

chunks.title: Tire Date Code: How to Read the DOT Number on a Tire
chunks.text:
A 60-second routine
- Find DOT on each tire, spare included. Check both sidewalls.
- Write down the last four digits for each position.
- Save one full TIN per tire, or snap a photo of it.
- Run the full TIN through the USTMA lookup.
- Enter the dates in the Do I Need Tires Yet? check, alongside your tread depth.
Buying tires online? Check the dates when the set arrives, before anything gets mounted. Our post on how old tires are when you buy online covers what to look for, and our post on getting online tires installed in Broward covers that handoff.
Questions about a code you can't read? Call Extreme Tires in Sunrise at (954) 773-1896 and ask.

chunks.title: Tire Date Code: How to Read the DOT Number on a Tire
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- The last four digits of the DOT number are the build week and year: 3219 means week 32 of 2019.
- The full DOT number may be stamped on only one sidewall, so check the inboard side too.
- A three-digit code means the tire was built before 2000.
- The full number, not just the date, is what a recall lookup needs.
- The date tells you age, not condition. A technician can confirm what the rubber looks like.

chunks.title: Tire Date Code: How to Read the DOT Number on a Tire
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How do you read the date on a tire?
Find the letters DOT on the sidewall and read the last four digits of the number that follows. The first two are the week of manufacture and the last two are the year, so 2910 means the 29th week of 2010.
Where is the DOT code on a tire?
Near the rim on the sidewall. NHTSA advises looking on both sides, because the full tire identification number may not be on both. On many cars that means checking the side that faces under the car.
What if my tire date code only has three digits?
Three digits means the tire was made before 2000. The first two digits are the week and the last digit is the year within the decade, so the decade itself is not shown. Either way, that tire is well over two decades old.
Can I check a tire recall with the DOT number?

chunks.title: Tire Date Code: How to Read the DOT Number on a Tire
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Yes. The U.S. Tire Manufacturers Association runs a free lookup that takes the full tire identification number for tires its members made from 2000 on. NHTSA's recall site lets you search by tire brand and line.
Need tires, or a second look at yours?

chunks.title: How to Read Tire Size: What 225/65R17 Actually Means
chunks.text:
Reading Your Tire
How to Read Tire Size: What 225/65R17 Actually Means
How to read tire size, one piece at a time: width, aspect ratio, R, rim size, load index and speed symbol, plus LT and flotation sizes like 31x10.50R15.
By TireDrop Team, Extreme Tires, Sunrise FL·Published Sep 30, 2026·Updated Oct 2, 2026·4 min read
Start at the door, not the tire
Before you decode anything, find the right size to decode. There are two places a tire size lives, and they don't always agree.
- On the tire. This tells you what's on the car right now. If you bought the car used in Hialeah or Hollywood, someone may have changed it.
- On the placard. NHTSA describes the Tire and Loading Information label, usually on the driver's side door edge or door post, and the owner's manual. This tells you what the vehicle maker specified.

chunks.title: How to Read Tire Size: What 225/65R17 Actually Means
chunks.text:
Start at the door, not the tire
USTMA's standard practice is that replacement tires match the placard: the same size, load-carrying capacity and speed rating the vehicle maker lists. So when the tire and the placard disagree, the placard wins until someone qualified tells you otherwise.
225/65R17 102H, piece by piece
Here's a typical SUV size, broken down using Michelin's definitions.
Piece
In the example
What it means
What it changes on the road
Width
225
Section width in millimeters, at the widest point
Contact patch width and whether it fits the wheel well
Aspect ratio
65
Sidewall height as a percent of the width
Ride comfort, sidewall flex, overall diameter
Construction
R
Radial, the standard build on modern passenger tires
Nothing to choose: nearly everything is R
Rim diameter
17
Wheel diameter in inches; must match the wheel exactly
Which wheels the tire can mount on
Load index
102

chunks.title: How to Read Tire Size: What 225/65R17 Actually Means
chunks.text:
225/65R17 102H, piece by piece
A code for the maximum load one tire can carry when properly inflated
Whether the tire can carry your vehicle
Speed symbol
H
The maximum sustained speed the tire is rated for; H is 130 mph
A test rating, not a suggested driving speed
Type your own size into the decoder. It highlights each piece and explains it in one line.
The letter in front: P, LT, T, ST or nothing
Some sizes start with a letter. NHTSA's tire safety material lists what they mean:
- P: passenger car
- LT: light truck
- T: temporary (your compact spare)
- ST: special trailer
And if there's no letter at all? Michelin explains that a leading P means the tire's loads follow U.S. Tire and Rim Association standards, while no letter means the tire conforms to the European ETRTO standards. You'll see both on cars in the same Doral parking lot.

chunks.title: How to Read Tire Size: What 225/65R17 Actually Means
chunks.text:
The letter in front: P, LT, T, ST or nothing
Don't swap between P, LT and ST types on your own. They're different service types for different vehicles, so treat a change of type as a fitment question for a technician. Our guide to LT vs P-metric tires explains what changes.
Doing the math: how tall is the sidewall?
The aspect ratio is a percentage, which trips people up. Here's how to turn it into inches.
Sidewall height = width × aspect ratio
225 mm × 0.65 = 146.25 mm, or about 5.76 in
Overall diameter = rim + two sidewalls
17 in + (2 × 5.76 in) = about 28.5 in
Now compare a size that looks similar on paper, 225/45R19:
- Sidewall: 225 × 0.45 = 101.25 mm, about 3.99 in
- Overall diameter: 19 + (2 × 3.99) = about 27.0 in

chunks.title: How to Read Tire Size: What 225/65R17 Actually Means
chunks.text:
Doing the math: how tall is the sidewall?
Same width, but the second tire is about an inch and a half shorter overall with a much thinner sidewall. That's why sizes aren't interchangeable just because the first number matches. Overall diameter affects speedometer readings and clearance. Our guide on using a different tire size covers that trade-off.
The tire size tool does this math for you and can compare two sizes side by side.

chunks.title: How to Read Tire Size: What 225/65R17 Actually Means
chunks.text:
Load index and speed symbol
The two characters after the size are easy to skip and important not to.
Load index. A number that maps to how much weight one tire can carry at proper inflation. Michelin's chart lists load index 94, for example, as 670 kg, or about 1,477 lb, per tire. USTMA says to always use a load index equal to or above what your vehicle placard requires. Never go lower. You'll sometimes see XL after it, which marks an extra-load version of the size; our XL vs SL guide explains how it ties to pressure. The load index guide has the full chart.
Speed symbol. A letter for the maximum sustained speed the tire is rated to carry its load at. From Michelin's chart:
Symbol
Rated speed
H
130 mph
V
149 mph
W
168 mph
Y
186 mph

chunks.title: How to Read Tire Size: What 225/65R17 Actually Means
chunks.text:
Load index and speed symbol
A speed rating is a lab rating under set conditions, not a target for the Sawgrass Expressway. It matters when you buy: USTMA's guidance is to match the speed rating the vehicle maker recommends.
Flotation sizes: 31x10.50R15 and friends
Trucks and off-road builds sometimes use flotation sizes, which look nothing like metric ones. Bridgestone describes high flotation sizing for light trucks as overall diameter in inches, then section width in inches, then construction type, then rim diameter in inches. Read left to right:
- 31: overall diameter, 31 inches tall
- 10.50: section width, 10.5 inches
- R: radial
- 15: rim diameter, 15 inches
So with a flotation size, you get the overall diameter up front without doing any math. You'll often see these with LT after the numbers, as in Bridgestone's example 33x12.50R15LT, marking them as light truck tires.

chunks.title: How to Read Tire Size: What 225/65R17 Actually Means
chunks.text:
Three mistakes we'd rather you skip
- Buying by the first number. 225 tells you width only. Aspect ratio and rim size decide whether the tire will actually fit.
- Copying the old tires. If the previous owner put on a different size, you'll repeat the mistake. Check the placard.
- Ignoring the letters. A lower load index or speed symbol than the placard calls for isn't a like-for-like replacement.
Driving a sedan? Our Toyota Camry tire guide walks through size, noise and fuel economy for a commuter car.
Know your size? Find tires by vehicle or shop by size. Not sure what's on the placard versus the car? Call Extreme Tires at (954) 773-1896 and ask.

chunks.title: How to Read Tire Size: What 225/65R17 Actually Means
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Start from the size on your door placard, not the size on the tires the last owner put on.
- In 225/65R17, 225 is the width in millimeters, 65 is the sidewall height as a percent of that width, R is radial and 17 is the wheel diameter in inches.
- The load index and speed symbol after the size matter as much as the size itself.
- Flotation sizes like 31x10.50R15 are all in inches: overall diameter, width, then rim.
- Two sizes that look close can differ in overall diameter by more than an inch.

chunks.title: How to Read Tire Size: What 225/65R17 Actually Means
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What does 225/65R17 mean on a tire?
225 is the section width in millimeters. 65 is the aspect ratio, meaning the sidewall is 65% as tall as the tire is wide. R means radial construction. 17 is the wheel diameter in inches that the tire fits.
What does the R mean on a tire?
R stands for radial construction, the internal build used on modern passenger tires. It is not the rim size and it is not a speed rating.
Where do I find my tire size?
Your vehicle's recommended tire size is on the Tire and Loading Information placard, usually on the driver's door edge or door post, and in the owner's manual. The size molded on your current tires tells you what is on the car now, which may not match.
What does LT mean on a tire size?

chunks.title: How to Read Tire Size: What 225/65R17 Actually Means
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
LT marks a light truck tire. Other letters you may see are P for passenger car, T for a temporary spare and ST for a special trailer tire. No letter usually means a metric size built to European ETRTO standards.

chunks.title: Tire Load Index Chart: What the Number Means
chunks.text:
Reading Your Tire
Tire Load Index Chart: What the Number Means
What the tire load index means, a load index chart in lb and kg, how P-metric and LT tires differ, and why a replacement should never go below the placard.
The number after the size
Look at a tire size like 225/45R17 94V. The size ends at the 17. The 94 is the load index, and the V is the speed rating.
The load index is a code for the maximum load one tire can carry when it's properly inflated. It's not a weight in pounds or kilograms. You look it up in a standard chart, published by tire makers including Michelin and Goodyear, to get the weight.
It's printed in two places you can check:
- On the sidewall, right after the size.
- On your door placard or in the owner's manual, as part of the tire size your vehicle maker specified.

chunks.title: Tire Load Index Chart: What the Number Means
chunks.text:
The number after the size
The placard is the one that matters for buying. It's the load your vehicle maker designed around.
Load index chart: a short excerpt
Here's a slice of the standard chart covering common car, crossover, SUV and pickup fitments. Weights are per tire.

Two things to notice. The steps aren't even: one point of load index is 15 kg between 91 and 92, but 35 kg between 114 and 115. And small-looking gaps add up. A 91 and a 94 differ by 55 kg per tire, which is 220 kg across four.
Enter any load index, or your current tire and a candidate, to see the weight per tire and for all four, and whether the new tire measures up:

chunks.title: Tire Load Index Chart: What the Number Means
chunks.text:
Load index chart: a short excerpt
The same check lives on its own page as the load and speed rating check.
Never go below the placard
This is the one rule. USTMA says to use a load index equal to or above what your vehicle placard requires, and never lower.
Why it matters:
- The vehicle maker already did the math. It chose a tire size, load index and pressure that carry the vehicle at its rated load. A lower index means each tire is rated to carry less than that.
- The tire's maximum load is molded on the sidewall too, alongside the pressure it applies to. It's a ceiling for that tire, not a pressure to run.
- Overloading builds heat. NHTSA lists excessive loading among the conditions that can cause heat build-up and possible tire failure, which matters in South Florida heat.

chunks.title: Tire Load Index Chart: What the Number Means
chunks.text:
Never go below the placard
A higher load index meets the rule. It isn't automatically better, though: a higher index can come with a different construction or a higher pressure, as the next sections explain.
P-metric vs LT: why the same number reads differently
P-metric and Euro-metric passenger tires
Most cars, crossovers and many SUVs use passenger tires. Their load index works as in the chart above, at the pressures in the tire maker's load and inflation tables.
There's one twist for trucks. Under the federal tire selection standard, FMVSS No. 110, when a vehicle maker fits passenger tires to a truck, multipurpose passenger vehicle, bus or trailer, each tire's load rating is divided by 1.10 before it's checked against the axle rating. Your placard already accounts for that. It's one more reason not to swap tire types on your own.

chunks.title: Tire Load Index Chart: What the Number Means
chunks.text:
LT tires: two numbers and a load range
Light truck tires often show a load index like 121/118. Cooper Tire explains that the first number is the capacity for a tire used singly, and the second is for a tire used in a dual pair, such as the rear of a dually. On a regular pickup or van, compare the first number.
LT tires also carry a load range letter, like C, D or E, tied to how much pressure the tire is built for. Our LT vs P-metric guide covers load ranges and why pressures change when you switch types.

chunks.title: Tire Load Index Chart: What the Number Means
chunks.text:
XL and HL: same size, higher load index
Many passenger sizes come in two versions: standard load (SL) and extra load (XL), with a higher load index. Toyo's guidelines for load and inflation tables use 35 psi as the reference pressure for standard load and 41 psi for extra load. The extra capacity comes with the extra pressure.
So if your vehicle calls for an XL tire, the standard load version of the same size has a lower load index, and doesn't meet the placard. Some heavy EVs go a step further and specify HL (high load) tires, which Michelin says carry more than an XL tire of the same size at the same pressure. Our XL vs SL guide explains both.

chunks.title: Tire Load Index Chart: What the Number Means
chunks.text:
How to check the load index before you buy
- Read your placard or the Tire Size Finder to get the size, load index and any XL, HL or LT marking your vehicle maker specified.
- Read the candidate tire's listing for its load index and load marking.
- Compare them with the load and speed rating check. Equal or higher passes; lower doesn't.
- Match the type. XL for XL, HL for HL, LT for LT, unless an installer has confirmed a change with the tire maker's tables.
- Set pressure to the placard, cold, once the tires are on. Our guide on how to check tire pressure shows how.
New to sidewall codes? Our guide on how to read tire size explains every piece of the size line.

chunks.title: Tire Load Index Chart: What the Number Means
chunks.text:
How to check the load index before you buy
When you're ready, shop tires by size. Free shipping covers the 48 contiguous states and DC; Extreme Tires installs at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach. See how installation works, or call (954) 773-1896 to check a load index before you order.
Key takeaways
- The load index is the number after the tire size, like the 94 in 225/45R17 94V. It stands for the most weight one tire can carry at its proper pressure.
- It's a code, not a weight: load index 94 means 670 kg, or about 1,477 lb, per tire.
- Replacement tires should match or exceed the load index on your door placard. Never go lower.
- LT tires often show two numbers, like 121/118: the first for single tires, the second for duals.
- XL and HL tires reach a higher load index through construction and pressure, so match the marking your vehicle calls for.

chunks.title: Tire Load Index Chart: What the Number Means
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What does the load index on a tire mean?
It's a number that stands for the maximum load one tire can carry when properly inflated. Michelin's and Goodyear's load index charts translate it into kilograms and pounds; for example, 94 means 670 kg, or about 1,477 lb, per tire.
Can I use a tire with a lower load index?
No. USTMA says to use a load index equal to or above what your vehicle placard requires. A lower load index means each tire is rated to carry less weight than your vehicle maker specified.
Is a higher load index better?
Not automatically. A higher index meets the requirement, but it can come with a different construction or pressure, such as an XL tire. If you're moving to a different load type or size, have the installer check the tire maker's load and inflation table for the right pressure.
What do two load index numbers like 121/118 mean?

chunks.title: Tire Load Index Chart: What the Number Means
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
That's typical of LT (light truck) tires. Cooper Tire explains that the first number is the load capacity for a tire used singly, and the second is for a tire used in a dual pair, such as on a dually's rear axle. On a regular pickup, compare the first number.

chunks.title: Tire Sidewall Markings: M+S, Snowflake, Max Press and More
chunks.text:
Reading Your Tire
Tire Sidewall Markings: M+S, Snowflake, Max Press and More
The tire sidewall markings beyond the size: M+S, the snowflake, MAX PRESS and MAX LOAD, XL, ply lines, TUBELESS, run-flat marks, arrows and OUTSIDE.
The sidewall is a label the law writes
The big numbers on a tire, like 225/45R17 94V, get most of the attention. Around them is a ring of smaller print, and most of it is there because a federal rule requires it.
FMVSS No. 139, the federal standard for passenger and light truck radial tires, splits the markings in two:
Marked on each sidewall
Marked on at least one sidewall
The DOT symbol, certifying the tire meets federal standards
Generic name of each cord material
The tire size designation
Actual number of plies in the sidewall and in the tread area
Maximum permissible inflation pressure
TUBELESS or TUBE TYPE

chunks.title: Tire Sidewall Markings: M+S, Snowflake, Max Press and More
chunks.text:
The sidewall is a label the law writes
Maximum load rating, plus the load range letter on LT tires
RADIAL, if it's a radial tire
The rule also requires the maker's name or brand, and the tire identification number (TIN). For tires made from September 1, 2009, the full TIN goes on the intended outboard sidewall.
This guide covers the markings that other guides don't. For the main line, start with how to read tire size, or type a size into the decoder:

chunks.title: Tire Sidewall Markings: M+S, Snowflake, Max Press and More
chunks.text:
MAX PRESS and MAX LOAD
Near the bead you'll find something like MAX PRESS 51 PSI and MAX LOAD 1477 LBS.
- MAX PRESS is the maximum cold inflation pressure to which a tire may be inflated, in the federal standard's words. It's a ceiling, not a target. The pressure to run is on your door placard and in the owner's manual. Our blog post on why not to inflate to the max PSI explains why.
- MAX LOAD is the tire's maximum load rating, the most weight it's rated to carry. It corresponds to the load index in the size line. Our load index guide turns the number into pounds.
The federal rule also requires passenger tires at certain standard pressures to show the psi in parentheses after the kilopascal figure, and the pounds in parentheses after the kilograms, so both units appear.

chunks.title: Tire Sidewall Markings: M+S, Snowflake, Max Press and More
chunks.text:
The ply and cord line
Somewhere on the sidewall is a short line that lists what the tire is made of: how many plies sit under the tread and in the sidewall, and the cord material of each, such as polyester or steel. It's required by FMVSS 139, and it's the tire's construction in a single line. Our guide to the parts of a tire explains what each layer does.
TUBELESS and RADIAL
Both are required words. TUBELESS means the tire seals against the wheel and needs no inner tube. Michelin defines it simply: the tire does not require an inner tube. RADIAL confirms the construction the R in the size already tells you.

chunks.title: Tire Sidewall Markings: M+S, Snowflake, Max Press and More
chunks.text:
Load markings: XL, HL and Reinforced
Michelin lists XL / HL / Reinforced as tires designed to carry higher loads than standard tires of the same size. The federal standard defines an extra load tire as one designed to operate at higher loads and higher inflation pressure than the standard tire.
Michelin's advice for replacements: tires with reinforced or special load markings should always be replaced with an equivalent specification. If your placard calls for XL, the replacement needs to be XL too. Our guide to XL vs SL tires covers what that means for pressure.
On light truck tires, the load range letter (C, D, E and so on) does the same job. The federal rule requires it on each sidewall.

chunks.title: Tire Sidewall Markings: M+S, Snowflake, Max Press and More
chunks.text:
Size prefixes: P, LT, T and C
A letter can come before the size. Michelin lists them:
- P: passenger car
- LT: light truck
- T: temporary spare
- C: commercial van tire
Plenty of sizes have no prefix at all. The prefix matters when you replace a tire, because LT and passenger tires use different load tables and pressures.
M+S and the snowflake
Two winter-related marks look similar on a listing but mean different things. Michelin explains:
- M+S (mud and snow): designed for mud and snow conditions based on the manufacturer's criteria. No standardized snow test is behind it.
- 3PMSF, the three-peak mountain snowflake: the tire has met standardized testing requirements for verified winter performance.
In South Florida neither is likely to be the deciding factor, but they tell you how a tire was designed. The federal rule also sets out where the snowflake goes when a maker uses it.

chunks.title: Tire Sidewall Markings: M+S, Snowflake, Max Press and More
chunks.text:
Direction and side: arrows and OUTSIDE
Two markings tell the installer how to mount the tire:
- A rotation arrow marks a directional tire. Continental describes it as designed to roll forward in one direction only, with the arrow indicator printed on the sidewall. It must turn the way the arrow points.
- OUTSIDE (and sometimes INSIDE) marks an asymmetric tire, which Continental says has two separate tread designs, one on the inner half and another on the outer half. The OUTSIDE face goes out.
Both affect rotation. A directional tire stays on its side of the car unless it's remounted on the wheel. The rotation pattern tool shows which patterns your setup allows.

chunks.title: Tire Sidewall Markings: M+S, Snowflake, Max Press and More
chunks.text:
Run-flat marks
Run-flat tires carry their maker's own abbreviation, such as RFT, ZP, SSR or ROF, or simply "Run Flat". If a car came on run-flats and has no spare, the replacement plan matters. See our run-flat tires guide.
Checking a tire against your car
Read the size, load index, speed rating and any XL marking off your door placard, then compare with the sidewall. The Tire Size Finder helps read the placard, and the load and speed rating check compares two tires. When you're ready, shop by size. Tires ship free to the 48 contiguous states and DC, and Extreme Tires installs them at its Sunrise shop or by mobile van in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach.

chunks.title: Tire Sidewall Markings: M+S, Snowflake, Max Press and More
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- Federal rules require each sidewall to show the DOT symbol, size, maximum permissible inflation pressure and maximum load, and at least one to show cord materials, ply counts, TUBELESS and RADIAL.
- MAX PRESS is the maximum cold pressure the tire can take, not the pressure to run. Your door placard has that number.
- Michelin says M+S reflects the manufacturer's own criteria, while the three-peak mountain snowflake means the tire met a standardized winter test.
- XL, HL or Reinforced means the tire is built for higher loads than a standard tire of the same size, and Michelin says it should be replaced with an equivalent.
- A directional tire has an arrow it must roll toward; an asymmetric tire has a side marked to face out.

chunks.title: Tire Sidewall Markings: M+S, Snowflake, Max Press and More
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
What does M+S mean on a tire?
Mud and snow. Michelin explains that it indicates the tire is designed for mud and snow based on the manufacturer's criteria. It isn't the result of a standardized snow traction test, which is what the three-peak mountain snowflake symbol represents.
Should I inflate my tires to the max PSI on the sidewall?
No. The federal standard defines that number as the maximum cold inflation pressure the tire may be inflated to. The pressure to run is the one on your vehicle's door placard or in the owner's manual, set with the tires cold.
What does the arrow on my tire mean?
It marks a directional tire, which Continental describes as designed to roll forward in one direction only. The tire must be mounted so it turns the way the arrow points when the car moves forward.
What does OUTSIDE mean on a tire?

chunks.title: Tire Sidewall Markings: M+S, Snowflake, Max Press and More
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
