chunks.title: How Long Do Tires Last? Miles, Years and Warranties
chunks.text:
Tread & Wear
How Long Do Tires Last? Miles, Years and Warranties
How long do tires last? Why tread, age and damage each set a limit, how treadwear warranties differ from UTQG grades, and what Florida heat changes.
The honest answer: until the first limit
There's no single number of miles or years for every tire. A tire is done when it hits any one of three limits:
Limit
Where the line is
Who draws it
Tread
2/32 inch to replace; 4/32 inch for wet roads
NHTSA; AAA
Age
Yearly inspection from 5 years; replace at 10 years
Bridgestone, Michelin
Damage
A bulge, a cut, or a puncture that can't be repaired
Your installer's inspection
Whichever comes first is the one that counts. A low-mileage car can age out its tires with tread to spare. A commuter can wear through a set long before it's five years old.

chunks.title: How Long Do Tires Last? Miles, Years and Warranties
chunks.text:
Miles: what decides how fast tread wears
Bridgestone gives a useful starting point. It notes that people drive 12,000 to 15,000 miles a year on average, and that at that pace a good-quality all-season tire lasts roughly three to five years, depending on maintenance, driving style and conditions.
That range is wide for a reason. Goodyear's warranty terms list the things that affect tread life: tire type, tread compound, construction, the vehicle, maintenance, road and weather conditions, and driving habits. Some you choose when you buy. Others you control every month:
- Pressure. Run tires at the placard pressure, checked cold. Our guide on how to check tire pressure walks through it.
- Rotation. Rotation moves each tire through the positions on the car on a schedule; see the rotation pattern for your car.
- Alignment. Uneven wear across one tire is a clue to have it checked.

chunks.title: How Long Do Tires Last? Miles, Years and Warranties
chunks.text:
Miles: what decides how fast tread wears
- Load and driving habits. Both are on Goodyear's list. Keep loads within what the door placard allows.
The only way to know where your tires stand is to measure. Our guide on how to check tread depth shows the penny test, the quarter test and a gauge.
Treadwear warranties vs UTQG grades
Two numbers on a tire listing look like they answer "how long will it last". Only one is a promise.

chunks.title: How Long Do Tires Last? Miles, Years and Warranties
chunks.text:
A treadwear warranty is the maker's mileage promise
Many tires come with a treadwear (or tread life) limited warranty: a mileage figure the tire maker stands behind. Michelin, for example, covers its passenger and light truck replacement tires with a limited mileage warranty for treadwear.
Read the conditions, because they matter. Goodyear's tread life warranty terms, as one example, are prorated, apply to the original owner, ask for rotation records, and end when the tire wears to its wear bars (2/32) or after a set number of years from purchase, whichever comes first. Other makers' terms differ, so check the warranty for the exact tire.
What a warranty tells you: how long the maker expects the tread to last under normal use with proper care. What it doesn't: that your tires will reach that number.

chunks.title: How Long Do Tires Last? Miles, Years and Warranties
chunks.text:
UTQG treadwear is a comparison, not miles
The UTQG treadwear grade on the sidewall, like the 500 in "500 AA A", is something else. Under the federal grading rule, it compares a tire's wear with a control tire graded 100 on a government test course. The tire maker assigns it, and NHTSA's consumer guide warns that real-world results can depart significantly from the norm because of driving habits, service practices, roads and climate.
There's no formula that turns a grade into miles. Use it to compare tires within one brand; use the warranty to judge mileage. Our UTQG guide breaks down all three grades.

chunks.title: How Long Do Tires Last? Miles, Years and Warranties
chunks.text:
Years: the age limit, whatever the tread
Tires age even when they aren't wearing. NHTSA's TireWise guidance notes that some vehicle and tire makers recommend replacing tires 6 to 10 years old, regardless of treadwear. Bridgestone and Michelin set the same two markers:
- From 5 years: a professional inspection at least once a year.
- At 10 years: replace the tire, even if it looks good. Bridgestone's guidance includes the spare.
A tire's age starts at its DOT date code, not the day it went on your car. Your vehicle maker may set a shorter timeframe in the owner's manual. Our guide How Old Is Too Old for Tires? lays out the guidance side by side, and reading the tire date code shows where to find the date.

chunks.title: How Long Do Tires Last? Miles, Years and Warranties
chunks.text:
The Florida factors
South Florida is hard on tires in ways a mileage number doesn't show.
Heat. NHTSA lists excessive speed, underinflation and overloading as conditions that can cause heat build-up and possible tire failure, and it calls underinflation the leading cause of tire failure. Summer heat adds to that, so the monthly cold pressure check matters more here, not less. Our guide to Florida heat and tires covers it in detail.
Sun and aging. NHTSA lists sunlight and a warmer climate among the things that contribute to tire aging, and its research found aging is a greater concern in the southern part of the Sun Belt. Take the five-year inspection seriously.
Rain. AAA's testing found tires worn to 4/32 took an average of 87 feet longer to stop on wet roads at 60 mph than new tires. If you drive through the rainy season, 4/32 is the practical end of a tire's life, not 2/32.

chunks.title: How Long Do Tires Last? Miles, Years and Warranties
chunks.text:
The Florida factors
Cars that sit. A second car or a seasonal car can reach five years with most of its tread left. Low miles don't mean young tires.
How to make tires last their full life
- Check pressure monthly, cold, against the door placard.
- Measure tread monthly in three grooves on every tire.
- Rotate on schedule and keep the records if your tires have a tread warranty.
- Watch for uneven wear and have alignment checked if you see it.
- Read the DOT dates once a year, spare included.
- Don't overload past what the placard allows.

chunks.title: How Long Do Tires Last? Miles, Years and Warranties
chunks.text:
How to make tires last their full life
Want a quick read on tread, age and damage together? Try Do I Need Tires Yet?. When it's time, shop tires by size and check each tire's treadwear warranty with its maker. Free shipping covers the 48 contiguous states and DC; Extreme Tires installs at the Sunrise shop or by mobile van in Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach. See how installation works, or call (954) 773-1896.

chunks.title: How Long Do Tires Last? Miles, Years and Warranties
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- A tire is done when it reaches its first limit: tread depth, age or damage. Whichever comes first counts.
- Bridgestone puts a good-quality all-season tire at roughly three to five years for a driver covering 12,000 to 15,000 miles a year.
- A treadwear warranty is the maker's mileage promise, with conditions. A UTQG treadwear grade is a comparison on a test course, not miles.
- Bridgestone and Michelin recommend a yearly professional inspection from five years old and replacement at 10 years. Bridgestone's guidance includes the spare.
- Heat, low pressure and heavy loads shorten tire life, which makes the monthly check matter more in South Florida.

chunks.title: How Long Do Tires Last? Miles, Years and Warranties
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How many miles do tires last?
It depends on the tire, the car and how it's driven and maintained. Bridgestone notes that drivers average 12,000 to 15,000 miles a year and puts a good-quality all-season tire at roughly three to five years at that pace. A tire's treadwear warranty, if it has one, shows the mileage its maker stands behind.
How many years do tires last?
Bridgestone and Michelin recommend a professional inspection at least once a year from five years old and replacing tires 10 years after they were made, even if the tread looks good. NHTSA notes some vehicle and tire makers recommend replacing tires 6 to 10 years old. Your owner's manual may set a shorter timeframe.
Does a treadwear rating of 600 mean 60,000 miles?

chunks.title: How Long Do Tires Last? Miles, Years and Warranties
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
No. The UTQG treadwear grade compares a tire's wear with a control tire on a government test course. NHTSA's consumer guide says real-world results can depart significantly from the norm. A mileage warranty is the closer guide to how long the maker expects the tread to last.
Do tires wear out faster in Florida?
Heat is one factor. NHTSA says underinflation, excessive speed and overloading can cause heat build-up, and its research found tire aging is a greater concern in the southern Sun Belt. Keeping pressure at the placard number, checked cold, is the part you control.

chunks.title: How to Check Tread Depth: Penny, Quarter or Gauge
chunks.text:
Tread & Wear
How to Check Tread Depth: Penny, Quarter or Gauge
How to check tire tread depth with a penny, a quarter or a gauge: what each test shows, where the wear bars sit at 2/32 and why 4/32 matters on wet roads.
Two coins, one gauge, five minutes
You can check your tread with a penny from the cup holder. It just won't tell you everything.
There are three ways to check tread depth at home: the penny test, the quarter test and a tread depth gauge. Each one answers a different question. Here's what each shows, how to do it, and which lines matter.

chunks.title: How to Check Tread Depth: Penny, Quarter or Gauge
chunks.text:
The two lines that matter: 2/32 and 4/32
In the US, tread depth is measured in 32nds of an inch, from the top of the tread to the bottom of the main grooves.
Line
About
Who draws it
What it means
2/32
1.6 mm
NHTSA
Replace the tire. The wear bars are flush with the tread.
4/32
3.2 mm
AAA
Replace for wet roads. Stopping distances grow sharply.
The 2/32 line is the floor. The 4/32 line is where AAA recommends replacing, based on its 2018 wet-braking study: at 60 mph, tires worn to 4/32 took an average of 87 feet longer to stop a passenger car than new tires did. Consumer Reports makes the same point about worn tires in the wet. In a South Florida rainy season, 4/32 is the line to plan around.
Our tread depth chart covers every depth in between. This guide is about measuring.

chunks.title: How to Check Tread Depth: Penny, Quarter or Gauge
chunks.text:
Method 1: the penny test (checks 2/32)
NHTSA and USTMA give the same instructions:
- Hold a penny with Lincoln's head upside down, facing you.
- Push it into a main groove until the edge touches the bottom.
- Look at his head. If you can see the top of Lincoln's head, the tread is at or below 2/32, and NHTSA says to replace the tire.
If part of his head is hidden by the tread, you're above 2/32 at that spot. That's all it tells you: above the floor or not.

chunks.title: How to Check Tread Depth: Penny, Quarter or Gauge
chunks.text:
Method 2: the quarter test (checks 4/32)
Same move, bigger coin:
- Hold a quarter with Washington's head pointing down into the groove.
- Push it in until it touches the bottom.
- If you can see all of Washington's head, you're at about 4/32 or less. Time to start shopping.
Bridgestone's tread guide describes the quarter test this way, as a check for the 4/32 line on wet roads. If the tread covers part of his head, you have more than 4/32 at that spot.
Coins are quick, but they're pass-or-fail checks at one line. Treat them as a screen, not a measurement.

chunks.title: How to Check Tread Depth: Penny, Quarter or Gauge
chunks.text:
Method 3: a tread depth gauge (gives you a number)
A tread depth gauge is a small probe that reads in 32nds of an inch, and often millimeters too. It's the only one of the three methods that gives you a number you can write down and compare next month.
How to use one:
- Push the probe in so it sticks out past the base.
- Set the tip into a main groove, not a thin slit in the tread block.
- Press the base flat against the tread blocks on either side of the groove.
- Read the depth, then pull the gauge out without touching the probe.
Drag the gauge below to see what each depth looks like, with the penny and quarter overlaid:

chunks.title: How to Check Tread Depth: Penny, Quarter or Gauge
chunks.text:
The built-in check: wear bars
You don't even need a coin to spot the 2/32 line. NHTSA describes treadwear indicators: small raised bars molded across the bottom of the grooves. Every tire has them.
- Look across the tread for short, flat bridges running between the ribs.
- If the tread surface is flush with a bar anywhere, the tire is at 2/32 there and it's time to replace it.
Wear bars only show the floor. By the time they're flush, the tire is already past AAA's 4/32 line.

chunks.title: How to Check Tread Depth: Penny, Quarter or Gauge
chunks.text:
How to check tread depth, step by step
- Park on level ground and turn the front wheels fully to one side so you can see the whole tread.
- Check three grooves on every tire: inside, center and outside.
- Check at two or three spots around each tire. Roll the car a few feet if you need to.
- Go by the shallowest reading. A tire is only as deep as its most worn groove.
- Look for the wear bars while you're there.
- Write it down by position: front left, front right, rear left, rear right.
- Check the spare if it's a full-size tire that's part of your rotation.
Do it monthly, alongside the pressure check. Our guide on how to check tire pressure covers the other half of the routine.

chunks.text:
What your readings are telling you

chunks.title: How to Check Tread Depth: Penny, Quarter or Gauge
chunks.text:
Tread isn't the whole story
Deep tread doesn't clear a tire on its own. While you're down there, look for cuts, bulges and cracks in the tread and sidewalls; NHTSA's advice is to have any damage looked at by a tire professional. And check the date code, because a tire can have plenty of tread and still be old. Our guide on how long tires last covers miles and years together.

chunks.title: How to Check Tread Depth: Penny, Quarter or Gauge
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- The penny test checks the 2/32 line: if you can see the top of Lincoln's head, NHTSA says replace the tire.
- The quarter test checks the 4/32 line: if you can see all of Washington's head, start shopping. AAA recommends replacing at 4/32 for wet roads.
- A tread depth gauge gives an actual number in 32nds, so you can track wear month to month.
- Every tire has wear bars molded into the grooves at 2/32. Tread flush with the bars means it's time to replace.
- Measure the inside, center and outside grooves on every tire, and go by the shallowest reading.

chunks.title: How to Check Tread Depth: Penny, Quarter or Gauge
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How do you do the penny test on tires?
Put a penny into a tread groove with Lincoln's head upside down and facing you. NHTSA and USTMA say that if you can see the top of his head, the tread is at or below 2/32 of an inch and the tire should be replaced.
Is the quarter test better than the penny test?
It checks a different line. The quarter test shows whether you're above or below about 4/32 of an inch, the depth AAA recommends replacing at because its tests found much longer stopping distances on wet roads. The penny test only shows the 2/32 replacement line.
What are tread wear indicator bars?
Small raised bars molded across the bottom of the tread grooves. NHTSA explains that when the tread wears down level with them, the tire is at 2/32 of an inch and it's time to replace it.
How do you use a tread depth gauge?

chunks.title: How to Check Tread Depth: Penny, Quarter or Gauge
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
Push the probe into a main groove, press the gauge's base flat against the tread blocks on either side, and read the depth in 32nds of an inch or millimeters. Take readings in the inside, center and outside grooves and go by the lowest.
Need tires, or a second look at yours?

chunks.title: Tire Tread Depth Chart: When to Replace Your Tires
chunks.text:
Tread & Wear
Tire Tread Depth Chart: When to Replace Your Tires
A tire tread depth chart in 32nds and millimeters: what 2/32 and 4/32 mean, why rain changes the math, and how to measure your own tires in five minutes.
By TireDrop Team, Extreme Tires, Sunrise FL·Published Sep 30, 2026·Updated Sep 30, 2026·4 min read
Tread depth, in plain numbers
In the US, tread depth is measured in 32nds of an inch from the top of the tread to the bottom of the main grooves. Most of the world uses millimeters. The conversion is simple: divide by 32, then multiply by 25.4.
Here is the chart that matters. The two lines in bold are the ones the sources draw.

- Coin tests are approximations. A tread-depth gauge is more precise, and a tire technician can measure for you.
- Legal minimums are set by each state. For Florida, check current Florida law; this demo doesn't state a legal minimum.

chunks.title: Tire Tread Depth Chart: When to Replace Your Tires
chunks.text:
Tread depth, in plain numbers
Sources: NHTSA TireWise ; USTMA Tire Care Essentials ; Consumer Reports, worn-tire performance ; AAA, Worn Tires Put Drivers at Risk ; Tire Review, Quarter Test ; Bridgestone, The Penny Test
A tread cross-section from 10/32 inch down to 0/32 inch shows the tread-wear bars becoming flush at 2/32 inch, and when Lincoln's head (penny test, 2/32 inch) and Washington's head (quarter test, 4/32 inch) become fully visible. NHTSA and USTMA use 2/32 inch as the point to replace a tire, and Consumer Reports' testing supports considering replacement at 4/32 inch for wet roads.

chunks.title: Tire Tread Depth Chart: When to Replace Your Tires
chunks.text:
The 2/32 line: wear bars and the penny test
Every tire has a built-in warning. NHTSA describes treadwear indicators: small raised bars molded into the bottom of the grooves. When the tread wears down level with those bars, the tire is at 2/32 of an inch, and NHTSA says it's time to replace it.
You don't need a tool to spot them:
- Look across the tread for short, flat bridges running between the ribs.
- If the tread surface is flush with those bridges anywhere, you're at 2/32 there.
The coin version is the penny test. NHTSA and USTMA give the same instructions: put a penny into a groove with Lincoln's head upside down and facing you. If you can see the top of his head, the tread is at or below 2/32.
Treat 2/32 as the floor, not the goal. It's the point where the sources say you're done, not the point where it makes sense to start planning.

chunks.title: Tire Tread Depth Chart: When to Replace Your Tires
chunks.text:
The 4/32 line: why rain changes the math
Tread isn't there for looks. Grooves give water somewhere to go so the rubber can stay in contact with the road. As the grooves get shallower, they move less water.
That's why AAA and Consumer Reports both draw a second line at 4/32. AAA's 2018 study, run with the Automobile Club of Southern California's Automotive Research Center, compared new all-season tires with the same tires worn to 4/32 on wet pavement:
- At 60 mph, stopping distances rose by an average of 43 percent.
- That's an extra 87 feet for a passenger car and 86 feet for a light truck.
- When the new tires had fully stopped, the worn tires were still traveling at close to 40 mph.

chunks.title: Tire Tread Depth Chart: When to Replace Your Tires
chunks.text:
The 4/32 line: why rain changes the math
AAA's recommendation from that work is to replace tires at 4/32, not 2/32. The check for it is the quarter test: slip an upside-down quarter into a groove. If you can see all of Washington's head, you're at about 4/32 and it's time to start shopping.
For a South Florida driver who lives through a rainy season every year, this is the line that matters more. Our post on hydroplaning on Broward roads covers what to do in the moment.

chunks.title: Tire Tread Depth Chart: When to Replace Your Tires
chunks.text:
What about Florida law?
You'll find plenty of websites quoting a specific Florida minimum tread depth. We aren't going to add another one.
We could not confirm a numeric Florida minimum against the statute text itself, so check current Florida law before relying on any number. The Florida Statutes are searchable free at the Florida Senate website . If you need a legal answer for a specific situation, ask an attorney.
Either way, the legal question and the practical one aren't the same. A tire can be over any legal minimum and still be past the point AAA recommends replacing it.

chunks.title: Tire Tread Depth Chart: When to Replace Your Tires
chunks.text:
How to measure your own tires
Five minutes, and one coin or a tread depth gauge:
- Park on level ground and turn the front wheels all the way to one side so you can see the tread.
- Measure three grooves on each tire: the inside, the center and the outside.
- Go by the shallowest reading. A tire is only as deep as its most worn groove.
- Measure at more than one spot around the tire if you can roll the car a few feet.
- Write it down for each position, so next month's reading means something.
A tread depth gauge gives you an actual number. Coins give you a pass or fail at one line. Our step-by-step penny and quarter test guide covers both methods in detail.

chunks.title: Tire Tread Depth Chart: When to Replace Your Tires
chunks.text:
Uneven readings are a clue
If the inside groove reads 3/32 and the outside reads 6/32, the tire isn't just worn. Something is wearing it unevenly. Inflation, alignment and suspension are all possible causes, and new tires on the same car will wear the same way if the cause isn't found.
Extreme Tires in Sunrise does four-wheel alignments in the shop and measures tread depth at every corner during a rotation. If your readings don't match across a tire, have a technician inspect it before you buy replacements.

chunks.title: Tire Tread Depth Chart: When to Replace Your Tires
chunks.text:
Depth isn't the only thing to check
A deep tread doesn't clear a tire on its own. NHTSA's inspection advice is to check the tread and sidewalls for cuts, punctures, bulges, scrapes, cracks or bumps, and to take the vehicle to a tire service professional if you see damage.
Also check the date code. A tire can have plenty of tread and still be old. Our guide on reading the tire date code shows you where to find it.
Run your readings through the Do I Need Tires Yet? check. If the answer is "consider replacing", you can shop tires by size and have them installed in Sunrise or by mobile van across Broward.

chunks.title: Tire Tread Depth Chart: When to Replace Your Tires
chunks.text:
Key takeaways
- US tread depth is measured in 32nds of an inch. 2/32 is about 1.6 mm and 4/32 is about 3.2 mm.
- NHTSA says to replace tires at 2/32, the point where the built-in wear bars sit flush with the tread.
- AAA recommends replacing at 4/32, after its testing found much longer wet stopping distances on tires worn that far.
- Measure three grooves on every tire and go by the shallowest reading.
- For Florida's legal rules, check the current statutes rather than a blog post, this one included.

chunks.title: Tire Tread Depth Chart: When to Replace Your Tires
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How much tread should a tire have?
NHTSA says tires should be replaced at 2/32 of an inch, when the tread is level with the built-in wear bars. AAA recommends replacing earlier, at 4/32, because its tests found much longer stopping distances on wet roads with tires worn to that depth.
Should I replace my tires at 4/32?
AAA and Consumer Reports both treat 4/32 as the point to start shopping. In AAA's wet-road tests at 60 mph, tires worn to 4/32 took an average of 87 feet longer to stop than new tires. Consider replacing at that point, especially if you drive in heavy rain.
What is the legal tread depth in Florida?
Check current Florida law directly. The Florida Statutes are searchable free on the Florida Senate website. We don't quote a Florida number here because we haven't confirmed one against the statute text itself.

chunks.title: Tire Tread Depth Chart: When to Replace Your Tires
chunks.text:
Questions people ask
How do I convert tread depth from 32nds to millimeters?
Divide the 32nds by 32 and multiply by 25.4. So 4/32 inch is 0.125 inch, or about 3.2 mm, and 2/32 inch is about 1.6 mm.

chunks.text:
Free tool
Does the new tire's load index and speed rating measure up?
The number and letter after a tire size, like the 94V in 225/45R17 94V, are its load index and speed rating. Enter the ones on your current tire and on the tire you're looking at to see the load each carries, per tire and for all four, and whether the new one meets or exceeds the old. Start from what your vehicle maker specifies on the door placard.

chunks.title: Load Index and Speed Rating Check
chunks.text:
The tool
Text version of this demo
Compares a current tire's load index and speed rating with a replacement's, showing the load per tire and for four in pounds and kilograms, and whether the replacement meets or exceeds the current tire. A speed rating is the speed a tire was tested to carry its load, not a recommended driving speed.
Step by step
How to use it
- 1Find the load index and speed rating on your current tire's sidewall: the number and letter right after the size, such as 94V. The door placard or owner's manual lists what your vehicle maker specifies.
- 2Type it into “Your current tire”, or pick the load index and speed rating from the lists.
- 3Do the same for the tire you're considering.
- 4Read load and speed separately. A tire below your current one on either isn't a like-for-like replacement.

chunks.title: Load Index and Speed Rating Check
chunks.text:
Have it checked
A tool can point you in a direction. A technician looking at the car can tell you what's going on.
Book tire installation

Questions
The things people ask next
Can I use a tire with a lower load index?
Replacement tires should match or exceed the load index your vehicle maker specifies. USTMA says never to go lower. A lower index means each tire is rated to carry less weight at its proper pressure.
Is the speed rating a speed I can drive at?
No. A speed rating is the speed a tire was tested to carry its load under lab conditions, not a recommended driving speed. Match or exceed the rating your vehicle maker calls for, and drive to the posted limit and the conditions.
What does XL after the load index mean?

chunks.title: Load Index and Speed Rating Check
chunks.text:
The things people ask next
XL marks an extra-load version of the size. It carries more than a standard-load tire of the same size, at the higher pressures in the tire maker's load and inflation tables. A tire with no load marking is standard load (SL).
Why does an LT tire show two load indexes?
An LT marking such as 121/118 gives two figures. The first is for a single tire, and the second is for pairs on dual rear wheels. Compare the first one.

Heat, pressure and your Hollywood tires
Florida heat moves tire pressure: roughly 1 psi for each 10°F, according to NHTSA. A tire inflated on a cool morning therefore shows a higher number once the day warms up, and sinks back overnight. Take readings with the tires cold, before the car has been driven, and aim for the number on the door-jamb placard, never the maximum stamped into the sidewall.
A monthly gauge check is cheap protection. Underinflated tires bend more with every turn of the wheel and run hotter, and a slow leak appears as a creeping number weeks before it becomes a flat.

The things people ask next
What is plus sizing?
Fitting a larger-diameter wheel with a lower-profile tire, such as going from 205/55R16 to 225/40R18, so the overall diameter stays close to the original. One inch more on the wheel is plus one; two inches is plus two.
How much can the overall diameter change?
Fitment guides commonly work to 3% or less. That's a guideline, not an approval: load index, clearance to the body and suspension, and wheel width all matter, so have fitment confirmed before you order.
Why does my speedometer read differently with bigger tires?
The speedometer counts how often the wheels turn. A taller tire covers more ground each turn, so the car is going faster than the speedometer says, and a shorter tire does the opposite. The odometer is off by the same amount.

What we collect, why we collect it, who else touches it, and how to tell us to stop. Plain language, no dark patterns.

This document is written to be understood, not to hide anything in the fine print. It is general information about how TireDrop operates — it is not legal advice, and it does not replace the terms shown at checkout, your order confirmation, or any written agreement or invoice we give you. Where those are more specific, they govern. If something here is unclear or does not seem to match your situation, call (954) 773-1896 or use our contact form and ask. We collect what we need to sell you tires, get them to you, fit them if you want that, and follow up afterward. In practice that means:
- Contact details you give us: name, phone number and email address
- Addresses: the shipping address the order goes to — or the shop, if you chose ship-to-store — and, for a mobile install, the address where the van should come
- Vehicle information: year, make, model, tire and wheel sizes, and notes about any work performed

- Your approximate location, on the local delivery page only. When that page opens, our website host estimates your ZIP code and rough location from your internet connection, and the page uses it once to check whether you are in a local delivery zone and to show you the city it places you in. If you allow it, your browser can also share your device location for a more exact check, which is compared with the delivery zones in your browser. If you allow your device location, the page also sends your approximate coordinates, rounded to about 100 meters, once to BigDataCloud, a mapping service, to look up the name of your neighborhood or city. That name is shown only to you, and we do not store it. We use your location only to check your delivery zone and name where you are, and we do not store it.

To answer your question, price an order, place it with the distributor, get it shipped to the right address, take payment, book an install, and handle any return, claim or warranty question afterward. We also look at aggregate website statistics — which pages get visited, roughly where visitors come from, what device they use — to understand what is working and fix what is not.
If you sign up using the sign-up form in the site footer, we use that address to send you TireDrop emails: the tire tips, fitment help and news about new sizes and brands the form describes. We do not use it for anything else. Sending a form or an order request does not sign you up for these emails; only the sign-up form in the site footer does.
If you ask us to, we may send occasional service reminders — a rotation coming due, for example. You can tell us to stop at any time and we will.

chunks.title: Privacy Policy
chunks.text:
2. How we use it
That is the whole list. We do not profile you, score you, or build an audience out of you.
3. Cookies, tracking and browser storage
This website uses Google Analytics to measure how the site is used — pages viewed, how visitors arrived, general location at the city or region level, device and browser type, and steps in the shop such as a tire viewed, added to the cart or searched for by size or vehicle, a delivery option chosen, a tool used, or the fact that a form was sent (its name, never what you typed into it). Google Analytics sets its own first-party cookies (named _ga and _ga_ followed by an ID) to tell one visit from the next. We have switched off Google signals and ad personalization, so this measurement is not used to build advertising profiles or to show you ads. We see the results only as aggregate reports, not as a record of what any named person did.

chunks.title: Privacy Policy
chunks.text:
3. Cookies, tracking and browser storage
The site loads no advertising or social tracking pixels. You are welcome to check both statements in your browser's developer tools.
Separately, the site uses local storage in your own browser for three things:
- Your cart — so the tires you picked are still there if you close the tab and come back
- The comparison tray — which products you lined up side by side
- The vehicle or tire size you choose to shop for — so Shop Tires takes you straight to tires for it next time. It is never sent to us except to look up tires for it and with an order or a form you send, and clearing your site data removes it
The Ask TireDrop chat keeps your current conversation in your browser's session storage until you close the tab, so it is still there when you move to another page. It is sent only as part of your next chat message, and "Start over" clears it.

chunks.title: Privacy Policy
chunks.text:
3. Cookies, tracking and browser storage
All three stay on your device. The cart and comparison tray are not sent to us; none of the three contains a name, email address, street address or payment detail, and nobody else can read them. Clearing your browsing data deletes them, and you lose your cart.
The email sign-up form in the site footer saves nothing in your browser. An earlier version of the site had a sign-up pop-up that remembered whether you had closed it, under the name td-nl-popup. The pop-up is gone, and the site now deletes that entry if your browser still has it.

chunks.title: Privacy Policy
chunks.text:
3. Cookies, tracking and browser storage
Translating a page is optional. Nothing from Google Translate loads until you open the Language button at the top of the page. Once you do, the site loads Google Translate (or, if that is unavailable, opens the page through translate.google.com), and Google processes the page's text to translate it and may set its own cookies, such as googtrans, which remembers the language you picked. The site keeps your pick in your browser's session storage until you close the tab, and "English (original)" switches translation off.
You can block or delete the Google Analytics cookies in your browser settings, or install Google's opt-out add-on at tools.google.com/dlpage/gaoptout; the site works the same either way. If we add any other third-party script, this section gets rewritten before that ships, not after.

chunks.title: Privacy Policy
chunks.text:
4. Who else sees your information
A short list, and only where there is a reason:
- Shopify, the platform the shop's orders and online payments run through, which receives your order, contact details and address so the shop can process it, and processes card payments on its checkout page — it receives the card details, not us
- Shopify also stores what you send us through the site. An email sign-up from the sign-up form in the site footer is saved as a customer record in the shop's Shopify account, marked as agreeing to marketing email. A form message or an order request is saved on your customer record there — found by your email or phone number, or created with your name, email and phone — and Shopify emails a copy to our own inbox so someone can reply. An order request is also saved as a draft order, which is not charged until we confirm it with you

chunks.title: Privacy Policy
chunks.text:
4. Who else sees your information
- ATD (American Tire Distributors), our distributor, which receives the shipping address and order details because it packs and dispatches your tires
- Shipping carriers, for delivery and tracking
- Financing providers, if you choose to apply; your application goes to them under their own privacy policy, not ours
- Manufacturers, when a warranty claim requires it
- The company that hosts this website, which estimates a visitor's rough location from their internet connection for the local delivery page (see section 1), and keeps ordinary server logs of requests made to it — and, if an order request cannot be saved in Shopify, a copy of that request in the same logs, so it is not lost

chunks.title: Privacy Policy
chunks.text:
4. Who else sees your information
- BigDataCloud, a mapping service that looks up the name of your neighborhood or city on the local delivery page, only if you allow your device location. The page sends it your approximate coordinates, rounded to about 100 meters, once, and nothing else from us: no name, ZIP code or contact details. Like any website you contact, it also sees your device's IP address. The name it returns is shown only to you, and we do not keep it
- Google, which provides Google Analytics and receives information about how the site is used (see section 3), processed under Google's own privacy policy
- Anthropic, whose API also writes the answers in the Ask TireDrop chat. It receives the messages of the conversation you are having and the page you are on, with no name or contact details unless you type them, and we do not keep a copy

chunks.title: Privacy Policy
chunks.text:
4. Who else sees your information
- Anthropic, whose API reads a photo you choose to scan in the Tire Size Finder to find the tire size or VIN printed on it. Only the photo is sent, once, with no name or contact details, and we do not keep a copy
- NHTSA, the US Department of Transportation agency whose public vehicle database decodes a VIN you enter or scan in the Tire Size Finder. Only the VIN is sent
- Law enforcement or regulators, where we are legally required to respond
That is the complete list. No advertising network and no data broker. We do not sell your personal information, and we do not share it for cross-context behavioral advertising — Google Analytics is set up with Google signals and ad personalization switched off, so the site's measurement data is not used for advertising.

chunks.title: Privacy Policy
chunks.text:
5. How long we keep it
Order, service and transaction records are kept as long as we need them for warranty, accounting and tax purposes. Messages and requests sent through the site's forms stay on your customer record in Shopify until we delete them — when they are no longer needed, or when you ask. When information is no longer needed for a legitimate business or legal reason, we dispose of it.
An email sign-up stays on the list until you unsubscribe. Unsubscribing stops the emails; the customer record stays in Shopify, marked as unsubscribed, until you ask us to delete it.

chunks.title: Privacy Policy
chunks.text:
6. Your Privacy Choices
You have real choices here, and exercising them will not change how we treat you as a customer. Depending on the state you live in, some of these may also be rights you can enforce — we apply them to everyone rather than sorting customers by ZIP code.
- Ask what we hold. Call us and we will tell you what customer records are associated with your name, phone number, order number or vehicle.
- Ask us to correct it. If a phone number, address or vehicle detail is wrong, we will fix it.
- Ask us to delete it. Call and request deletion. We will remove what we are not required to keep for warranty, accounting or legal reasons — including an email sign-up and any form messages on your Shopify customer record — and we will tell you plainly what we had to retain and why.

chunks.title: Privacy Policy
chunks.text:
6. Your Privacy Choices
- Unsubscribe from TireDrop emails. Use the unsubscribe link in any of those emails, or email info@tiredroponline.com and ask, and we will unsubscribe you.
- Opt out of reminders. Say the word on the phone, or reply to any message asking to stop, and we will take you off the reminder list.
- Clear what the site stored on your device. Your cart, comparison tray and the vehicle or tire size you shop for live in your own browser; the sign-up form in the site footer stores nothing there. Clearing your browsing data removes them. It does not remove anything you sent us — for that, ask us to delete it.
- Opt out of analytics. Block or clear the Google Analytics cookies in your browser, or use Google's opt-out add-on (tools.google.com/dlpage/gaoptout). We do not sell personal information or share it for cross-context behavioral advertising.

chunks.title: Privacy Policy
chunks.text:
6. Your Privacy Choices
To use any of these, call (954) 773-1896 during business hours, email info@tiredroponline.com, or send a message through our contact form. We may need to confirm a couple of details — an order number, say — to be sure we are talking to the right person before we change or delete a record.
7. Security
We take sensible steps to protect customer information, and we limit access to the people who need it to do the job. Card details are never stored by us — they are handled by our payment processor. No website or business can promise perfect security, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. If something goes wrong in a way that affects you, we will tell you.

chunks.title: Privacy Policy
chunks.text:
8. Children
This site is meant for adults buying tires and arranging vehicle service. We do not knowingly collect information from children. If you believe a child has given us information, call us and we will remove it.
9. Changes to this policy
If our practices change, we will update this page and change the revision date at the top. Questions about anything here are welcome — call and ask.

chunks.title: How Shipping Works
chunks.text:
Shipping
Ordered online. Shipped to your door.
TireDrop is an online tire and wheel store, so your order ships free, direct from the distributor warehouse, to anywhere in the 48 contiguous states and DC. No storefront markup, no waiting on one shop's back room to restock.
Shop tires Ship to store instead
Ships across the 48 contiguous states and DC Free ship-to-store in South Florida Powered by Extreme Tires
The short version

chunks.title: How Shipping Works
chunks.text:
Your tires never sit in our building
TireDrop does not hold stock. When you order, the order goes to a distributor warehouse and your tires leave from there. That is what lets a small South Florida operation put a wide catalog in front of you and still get your size moving the same way a chain store would.
It also means we are honest about what we control. We control the order, the follow-up and the fix when something goes wrong. We do not control how fast a freight network moves on a given week, which is why you will not find a transit-time promise anywhere on this page — you will find a real estimate at checkout instead.

chunks.title: How Shipping Works
chunks.text:
A deeper catalog
Distributor inventory runs far wider than any single shop's rack, so odd sizes and staggered fitments are usually gettable.
Factory-fresh stock
Tires move through distribution rather than sitting on a showroom floor waiting for someone to want that size.
A real phone number
Online store, local people. Call (954) 773-1896 and someone who knows tires picks up.
At checkout

chunks.title: How Shipping Works
chunks.text:
Two ways to take delivery
You pick one at checkout. Everything else about the order stays the same.
48 contiguous states + DC
Ship to my address — free
Home, work, or the shop you already trust with your car. Tires arrive where you told us to send them, and you arrange fitting on your own schedule.
- Free to any address across the 48 contiguous states and DC
- Ships direct from the distributor warehouse
- Tracking sent as soon as it exists
Shop tires
South Florida

chunks.title: How Shipping Works
chunks.text:
Ship to the store — free
Send the order to Extreme Tires in Sunrise, then book a fitting. No shipping charge, no four tires in your garage, no second trip.
- Free ship-to-store on every order
- Installed by the people who do it daily
- Old tires taken away and recycled
How ship-to-store works
After you order
What happens next
Four stages, and you hear from us at each one. No silent stretches where you are left wondering whether the order went through.
01

chunks.title: How Shipping Works
chunks.text:
Your order is confirmed
You get an order confirmation listing every tire or wheel, the quantity, and the address it is headed to. Nothing else happens until that confirmation is in your inbox.
02
We place it with the distributor
Your order is routed to a distributor warehouse that has your size in stock. Because they stock it and we do not, nothing sits waiting on us to reorder.
03

chunks.title: How Shipping Works
chunks.text:
It ships direct to you
The warehouse picks, packs and hands off your order. It travels straight from them to your door — or to our Sunrise shop if you chose ship-to-store.
04
You get tracking
As soon as the shipment has a tracking number, it comes to you. From that point you can follow it yourself without calling anyone.
Coverage
Shipping is national. Installing is not.

Free tool
Do you actually need new tires yet?
Every tire shop on earth will tell you the answer is yes. This one checks the two things that decide it — how much tread is left and how old the rubber is — and tells you plainly if the answer is no.
Nothing here is stored, and if nothing says replace yet the page says so and stops. No countdown, no pitch.
Step one
How much tread is left?
Three ways in, depending on what you have to hand. Check three spots across each tire and use the shallowest reading — tires rarely wear evenly, and the worn edge is the one that decides.
What are you using?
Which coin?
Drag until the picture matches your tire
Coin sits on topCoin sinks in deep

chunks.title: Do I need new tires? Tread depth and tire age checker
chunks.text:
How much tread is left?
Push the coin into a groove head-first, with Lincoln's head pointing down. The tread hides part of the portrait — drag the slider until the drawing shows the same amount of head you can see on the tire. Right now the tread covers the top of the head, so you are above 2/32".
Your reading
Drag the slider to match your tire and the verdict appears here.
Step two

chunks.title: Do I need new tires? Tread depth and tire age checker
chunks.text:
How old is the rubber?
Tread wears; rubber ages on its own schedule. The DOT code stamped on the sidewall is the only honest answer to how old a tire is — the day you bought it is not the day it was built.
The last four digits of the DOT code
Paste the whole serial if it is easier — only the last four digits carry the date. The first two are the week, the last two are the year: 3421 is the 34th week of 2021.

chunks.title: Do I need new tires? Tread depth and tire age checker
chunks.text:
Where to find it
- 1Look on the sidewall for the letters DOT, followed by a run of letters and numbers. It is molded in, the same colour as the tire, so it is easier to feel than to see.
- 2This is where everyone gets stuck: the full code with the date on the end is normally only stamped on one side of the tire. If the side facing you ends after the plant and size codes, the date is on the inboard face — look from under the car, or turn the wheel to full lock to see the inside of a front tire.
- 3Four digits inside a small oval, right at the end. Three digits instead of four means the tire was built before 2000.
Age check
Type the four digits and this will tell you the week the tire was built, how old it is now, and what that means.
The answer

chunks.title: Do I need new tires? Tread depth and tire age checker
chunks.text:
So — do you need tires?
Fill in either check above — the tread, the date code, or both — and the answer lands here. Both together is the complete picture: a tire can fail on tread with plenty of age left, or on age with plenty of tread left.
Know your size? Carry it through.
It is on the sidewall in the form 215/60R16, and on the placard inside the driver's door. Enter it and every link on this page points at your size — including if you bookmark or share this result.
Your tire size
Optional. Everything above works without it.
Questions

chunks.title: Do I need new tires? Tread depth and tire age checker
chunks.text:
The things people ask next
Short answers, including the ones that mean you do not need to buy anything.
How often should I actually check?
Once a month, at the same time you check pressures, and again before any long drive. It takes under a minute per tire. Check three spots across each tire — outer shoulder, middle, inner shoulder — because a tire rarely wears evenly, and the shallowest reading is the one that counts.
Does the spare count?
Yes, and it is the one nobody checks. A full-size spare ages in the trunk at the same rate as the four doing the work, so a spare with beautiful tread can still be a ten-year-old tire. Check its date code and its pressure twice a year. A temporary compact spare is a different animal: it carries its own speed and distance limits printed on the sidewall, usually 50 mph and a short trip to a shop.
What does uneven wear tell me?

chunks.title: Do I need new tires? Tread depth and tire age checker
chunks.text:
The things people ask next
Worn down the centre with the shoulders still full means over-inflation — the tire is crowned and riding on its middle. Worn on both shoulders with the centre full means the opposite: chronic under-inflation. Worn on one shoulder only is alignment, usually camber or toe, and no new tire will survive it until the alignment is fixed. Patchy or scalloped wear that you can feel with your palm points at worn shocks, struts or a wheel that is out of balance.
There is plenty of tread. Does age really matter?

chunks.title: Do I need new tires? Tread depth and tire age checker
chunks.text:
The things people ask next
It does, and this is the part the tread check cannot see. Rubber cures and hardens over time whether the tire is driven or parked, which is why a barely-used spare or a low-mileage car on original tires can be past it with most of the tread still there. Six years is the usual point at which manufacturers ask for a yearly inspection, and ten years is the usual hard stop — but both are manufacturer guidance, not law. Heat and sunlight, which South Florida has in quantity, move it along faster.
Is 2/32" really the legal line?

chunks.title: Do I need new tires? Tread depth and tire age checker
chunks.text:
The things people ask next
In most US states, yes — it is the point at which a tire is legally worn out, and it is what the penny test finds. A handful of states word it differently or set the bar elsewhere, so treat 2/32" as the floor rather than the whole answer. Either way, well before that, wet braking has already fallen off sharply: below 4/32" the grooves can no longer move enough water out of the way.
Do I have to replace all four?

chunks.title: Do I need new tires? Tread depth and tire age checker
chunks.text:
The things people ask next
Not always. On a front- or rear-wheel-drive car, two can be enough if the other two still have real tread — and the new pair goes on the rear axle regardless of which end drives, because a car that loses grip at the back first is much harder to catch. All-wheel drive is stricter: many manufacturers require all four within a small difference in circumference, so a single replacement on a worn set can cook a differential. Check the owner's manual before buying one tire.

How much does tire pressure change with the temperature?
Air in a tire reads higher when it's warm and lower when it's cool. Enter your door-sticker pressure, the temperature when you filled the tires and the temperature now to see the estimated reading by the common rule of thumb and by the gas law. Whatever the estimate says, set pressure cold, to the door placard.

Step by step
How to use it
- 1Enter the cold pressure from the sticker in the driver's door jamb, not the maximum on the sidewall.
- 2Enter the air temperature when the tires were last set, cold.
- 3Move the temperature-now slider, or try one of the Florida days.

chunks.title: Tire Pressure Temperature Calculator
chunks.text:
The things people ask next
How much does tire pressure change per 10 degrees?
USTMA and Goodyear put it at one to two psi for every 10°F, and Bridgestone says about 1 psi. The gas-law estimate for a typical passenger tire lands a little under 1 psi per 10°F.
Should I let air out when the tires read high on a hot day?
No. NHTSA's guidance is that pressure rises as tires warm, and letting air out of a warm tire can leave it low once it cools. Recheck after the car has been parked for three hours or more.
Why did the tire pressure light come on on a cool morning?
As the air cools, so does the pressure. A tire that was already a little low can drop far enough overnight to trigger the light. Set all four to the placard pressure, cold, even if the light goes out as the day warms up.
What counts as a cold tire?

chunks.title: Tire Pressure Temperature Calculator
chunks.text:
The things people ask next
NHTSA defines cold as parked for at least three hours, so first thing in the morning is the easiest time to check.

chunks.title: Tire Rotation Pattern for Your Drivetrain
chunks.text:
The things people ask next
How often should tires be rotated?
The Tire Industry Association suggests every 5,000 to 7,000 miles. Your owner's manual's schedule comes first, and some vehicle makers set their own.
Can directional tires be rotated side to side?
Not on their own wheels. A directional tire is built to roll one way, so it moves front to back on the same side. Moving it to the other side means remounting it on the wheel.
How do you rotate staggered tires?
When the rear tires are wider than the fronts, they can't swap axles. Non-directional staggered tires can swap sides on the same axle. Staggered directional tires can't swap sides or axles without being remounted, so ask us about your setup.
Why rotate tires at all?
Tires in different positions wear at different rates. Rotating on a regular schedule spreads that wear across the set, so the four wear more evenly.

chunks.title: Tire Size Finder: what size tires does my car have?
chunks.text:
Tire size questions people ask
Short answers about the sticker, staggered sizes, VINs and your photo.
Where is the tire sticker on my car?
On most cars it is on the driver's door frame or on the edge of the driver's door, headed "Tire and Loading Information." Some cars put it inside the fuel door or the glove box. It lists the factory size for the front and rear tires, the spare, and the cold tire pressures.
What if my front and rear sizes are different?
That is a staggered setup, common on sports sedans and performance cars. The sticker lists both, and the finder keeps both: you shop 2 front tires in one size and 2 rear tires in the other. We confirm fitment before your order ships.
Why doesn't my VIN give me a tire size?

chunks.title: Tire Size Finder: what size tires does my car have?
chunks.text:
Tire size questions people ask
The VIN tells us the year, make, model and often the trim, through NHTSA's public database. NHTSA doesn't publish tire sizes, and many cars came with more than one wheel size, so the door sticker (or the size on your tires) is where the exact size comes from.
What happens to my photo?
It is shrunk on your phone, sent to our server and read once by Anthropic's AI to find the size, then dropped. We don't save the photo or your VIN. You can always type the size instead.
Which tire pressure should I use?
The pressure printed on your sticker is the carmaker's cold pressure for the factory size. The number molded on the tire's sidewall is the most that tire can hold, not a pressure to run it at. Check pressures cold, before driving.

chunks.title: Tire Size Calculator & Sidewall Decoder
chunks.text:
Three places the size is written
- 1The driver's door jamb. Open the door and look at the frame. This placard is what the car was engineered around — size, load index, speed rating and the right pressures.
- 2The tire sidewall. Tells you what is fitted right now, which is not always what the car asked for. If the two disagree, trust the placard.
- 3The owner's manual. Usually lists every size the car was offered with from the factory, including the optional wheel packages.
Every figure on this page comes from the marking itself. It cannot see your wheels, your fenders or your suspension, so it is a starting point, not a fitment approval.
How this works

chunks.title: Tire Size Calculator & Sidewall Decoder
chunks.text:
What the marking means
Every number and letter on the sidewall, explained with the real figures for your size — not a generic example. Width, sidewall height, wheel diameter, load in pounds, speed in mph.
Whether a different size works
Put a second size in and we draw both to scale, one on top of the other, and show you the diameter, width, sidewall and clearance change between them.

chunks.title: Tire Size Calculator & Sidewall Decoder
chunks.text:
What it does to your speedo
A taller tire covers more ground per turn, so the needle reads low. We tell you what you are actually doing at an indicated 60, and when the change is big enough to matter.
Questions
Tire sizes, answered properly
The questions we get asked on the phone, written out the way we would answer them.
What do the numbers on the side of a tire actually mean?
Take 215/60R16 95H. 215 is the width across the tire in millimetres. 60 is the aspect ratio — the sidewall is 60% of that width, so 129 mm tall. R means radial construction. 16 is the wheel diameter in inches, measured at the bead seat. 95 is the load index, which is 1,521 lbs per tire. H is the speed rating, certified to 130 mph. The first four have to be right for the tire to physically fit; the last two have to meet or beat what your car was built for.
Where do I find the right size for my car?

chunks.title: Tire Size Calculator & Sidewall Decoder
chunks.text:
Tire sizes, answered properly
Open the driver's door and look at the placard on the door jamb. That is the size, load index and speed rating the car was engineered around, along with the correct inflation pressures. The owner's manual repeats it. The sidewall of the tires currently on the car tells you what is fitted, which is not always the same thing — a previous owner may have changed it. When the placard and the sidewall disagree, the placard is the one to trust.
Can I fit a different size than the placard says?

chunks.title: Tire Size Calculator & Sidewall Decoder
chunks.text:
Tire sizes, answered properly
Physically, often yes. Whether you should is a different question. Most fitment guides work to within 3% of the original overall diameter, because your speedometer, odometer, ABS and traction control all read wheel speed and assume the original rolling circumference. Past that they are all reading wrong by the same margin. A replacement also has to meet or beat the original load index, and it has to clear the suspension and bodywork at full steering lock and full suspension travel — which is something no calculator can see. Check the owner's manual before you buy.
Can I mix tire sizes front and rear?

chunks.title: Tire Size Calculator & Sidewall Decoder
chunks.text:
Tire sizes, answered properly
Some cars leave the factory staggered, with a wider tire on the rear — that is fine, because it is the design. Mixing sizes that were not designed to be mixed is not. Never mix sizes across one axle. On an all-wheel-drive car, even small differences in rolling circumference between axles make the centre differential or coupling work continuously, and that gets expensive. Replace in pairs across an axle at minimum, and all four on an all-wheel-drive car.
What does plus-sizing do?

chunks.title: Tire Size Calculator & Sidewall Decoder
chunks.text:
Tire sizes, answered properly
Plus-sizing means going up in wheel diameter and down in sidewall to keep the overall diameter roughly the same — 205/55R16 to 225/45R17, for example. Less sidewall flex sharpens steering response and usually looks better. You also get a harsher ride, more road noise, more exposure to pothole and rim damage, and a more expensive tire to replace. It needs the matching wheel: the tire cannot go on the wheel you have.
Is a 60-series sidewall always the same height?
No, and this is the single most common misreading of a tire size. The aspect ratio is a percentage of that tire's own width, not a fixed measurement. A 205/60R16 has a 123 mm sidewall; a 275/60R16 has a 165 mm one. Same 60, 42 mm difference.
What about XL, reinforced, and the letters before the size?

chunks.title: Tire Size Calculator & Sidewall Decoder
chunks.text:
Tire sizes, answered properly
A letter in front — P, LT or ST — is the service type: passenger, light truck, or special trailer. XL or Reinforced after the size means the tire is built to carry more than a standard tire of the same size, and it will carry a higher load index to match. Both matter for load, neither changes the tire's dimensions.
Still not sure what you need? Look it up by vehicle or ask us — a size question takes about a minute to settle.

California's tire rules are unusually specific: a 1/32 inch tread minimum, chain controls in the mountains with a 6/32 inch rule for snow tires used instead of chains, a stud season and a $1.75 tire fee. Here they are with sources, and what they mean for the set you choose.

State rules

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to California
chunks.text:
California tire rules, with sources
A plain-English summary with a source for each line, not legal advice. Laws change: check the California DMV for current rules.
Tread depth
Passenger tires need at least 1/32 inch of tread in any two adjacent grooves at any point on the tire. Snow tires used instead of chains in a posted chain-control area need 6/32 inch.
Source:California Vehicle Code § 27465

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to California
chunks.text:
Traction and chain laws
R-1: chains required except on passenger vehicles and light trucks under 6,000 lb with snow tires on at least two drive wheels. R-2: chains or traction devices required except on 4WD/AWD vehicles with snow-tread tires on all four wheels, which must still carry traction devices. R-3: chains or traction devices required on all vehicles, no exceptions. Snow tires are marked MS, M/S, M+S or MUD AND SNOW on the sidewall.
Source:Caltrans, Chain Controls

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to California
chunks.text:
Studded tires
Studded tires are allowed from November 1 through April 30. The CHP commissioner can extend this period in bad weather.
Source:California Vehicle Code § 27454
Inspection
California's periodic vehicle test is the Smog Check, an emissions inspection run by the Bureau of Automotive Repair. It is required every other year at registration once a car is more than eight model years old.
Source:Bureau of Automotive Repair, Smog Check

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to California
chunks.text:
State tire fee
California charges a $1.75 fee per new tire. It applies to new tires sold on their own and to new tires (including the spare) sold with a new or used vehicle. CDTFA administers it with CalRecycle.
Source:CDTFA, California Tire Fee: Getting Started
Climate and tire choice
Which tire type for California
All-season at home, chain rules in the mountains
Most Californians never see snow at home. On the coast and in the valleys, an all-season or summer tire fits the year; in the desert, heat and tire age matter more than tread pattern, so check the four-digit date code on the sidewall of anything you buy.

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to California
chunks.text:
All-season at home, chain rules in the mountains
If you drive into the Sierra Nevada or other mountain areas in winter, chain controls shape the choice. Under R-1, a car with M+S snow tires on two drive wheels can skip chains; under R-2, only 4WD or AWD vehicles with snow-tread tires on all four wheels can, and they still carry traction devices. Either way, a snow tire used instead of chains needs 6/32 inch of tread, so a set bought for ski trips should start the winter well above it.
California's climate runs from some of the nation's hottest, driest deserts in the south to heavy snowfall at higher elevations.
The Pacific keeps coastal temperatures mild all year; inland areas see a much wider range.

Questions
Asked about Georgia
What's the legal minimum tread in Georgia?
2/32 inch, measurable in all major grooves, under O.C.G.A. § 40-8-74; school buses and commercial vehicles need 4/32 inch on the front tires. If you're not sure where yours stand, our Do I Need Tires Yet? tool helps you measure.
Can I run studded tires in Georgia?
Only when snow, ice or similar conditions could make the vehicle skid. The rest of the time Georgia law bans studs and other non-rubber protrusions, and with snowfall this light, few Georgia drivers buy them.
Why is there a $1 fee on tires in Georgia?
Georgia charges $1 on each new replacement tire. Since July 1, 2023, the distributor that first sells the tire in Georgia collects it. Taxes and fees are calculated at checkout.
I'm in metro Atlanta. Does my emissions test check my tires?

chunks.text:
Free shipping · NY
Tires Shipped Free to New York
Tires ship free to any street address in New York, from Long Island to Buffalo. New York looks at your tires every year at inspection, sets a stud season and adds a $2.50 tire fee, and its lake-effect snow belts are among the snowiest places in the East. Here is each rule with its source, and what it means for the tires you pick.
Shop Tires Find My Tires
State rules

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to New York
chunks.text:
New York tire rules, with sources
A plain-English summary with a source for each line, not legal advice. Laws change: check the New York DMV for current rules.
Tread depth
At inspection, cars and light trucks need at least 2/32 inch of tread, measured in two adjacent major grooves where the tire is most worn.
Source:NY DMV, Safety/Emissions Inspection Program
Studded tires
Tires with metal studs may be used only from October 16 through April 30.
Source:NY DMV Driver's Manual, Chapter 10

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to New York
chunks.text:
Inspection
Every vehicle registered in New York must be inspected at least once every 12 months. Besides tread depth, the inspection fails a tire with a cut longer than an inch that shows fabric, a visible bump, bulge or knot, or a restricted-use marking.
Source:NY DMV, Safety/Emissions Inspection Program
State tire fee
New York charges a $2.50 waste tire fee on most new tires sold at retail. Tax Department guidance names online tire retailers among the businesses that collect it. Used and recapped tires are exempt.
Source:NYS Tax Department, Waste Tire Fee
Climate and tire choice

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to New York
chunks.text:
Winter tires upstate, all-weather downstate
In the lake-effect belts downwind of Lake Erie and Lake Ontario, Buffalo included, a dedicated winter tire with the three-peak mountain snowflake symbol is the straight answer. Snow there comes in intense bands, and a winter compound keeps its grip in the cold where an all-season stiffens.
In New York City, on Long Island and along the coast, where the Atlantic takes the edge off winter, an all-weather tire carrying the same snowflake symbol handles the occasional storm with no seasonal swap. If you choose studded winter tires anywhere in the state, they come off by April 30 and can't go back on before October 16.
Northern New York often gets heavy lake-effect snow: arctic air warms and picks up moisture over Lakes Erie and Ontario, then drops intense bands of snow downwind.

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to New York
chunks.text:
Winter tires upstate, all-weather downstate
In November 2014 one lake-effect storm left more than 5 feet of snow just east of Buffalo, and a second storm right behind it added as much as 4 more feet.
The Atlantic moderates the coast, while the Great Lakes and Lake Champlain moderate the northwest and northeast of the state.

What tread depth fails a New York inspection?
Less than 2/32 inch, measured in two adjacent major grooves where the tire is most worn. A cut over an inch that shows fabric, or a bump, bulge or knot, also fails it.
When do studded tires have to come off in New York?
By April 30. Metal-studded tires are allowed only from October 16 through April 30, so plan the spring changeover around that date.

Free shipping · NC
Tires Shipped Free to North Carolina
Tires ship free to any street address in North Carolina, from the Outer Banks to the Blue Ridge. North Carolina still checks tires at its safety inspection, allows studded tires within a size limit, and figures its tire tax as a share of the price rather than a flat fee. Snowfall averages about 5 inches a year across the state and about 89 inches on Mount Mitchell.
Shop Tires Find My Tires
State rules

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to North Carolina
chunks.text:
North Carolina tire rules, with sources
A plain-English summary with a source for each line, not legal advice. Laws change: check NCDMV for current rules.
Tread depth
North Carolina's tire law fails a tire with less than 2/32 inch of tread at two or more places around it, in two adjacent major grooves. Steering-axle tires on heavy-duty vehicles need 4/32 inch.
Source:N.C.G.S. § 20-122.1

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to North Carolina
chunks.text:
Studded tires
Regular and snow tires with studs are allowed, as long as the studs stick out no more than 1/16 inch beyond the tread when compressed.
Source:N.C.G.S. § 20-122
Inspection
North Carolina's safety inspection covers tires (against the state tread law), brakes and lights. You need a passing inspection no more than 90 days before you register or renew.
Source:N.C.G.S. § 20-183.3 NCDMV, Digital Vehicle Registration

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to North Carolina
chunks.text:
State tire fee
North Carolina's scrap tire disposal tax is 2% of the price for tires under 20-inch bead diameter and 1% for 20 inches and up.
Source:NCDOR, Scrap Tire Disposal Tax
Climate and tire choice
Which tire type for North Carolina
All-season on the coast, all-weather inland
On the coastal plain, an all-season tire fits most driving. The Piedmont, from Charlotte through Greensboro to Raleigh and Durham, is the tricky part of the state: freezing rain is more likely than deep snow there, and no tire grips glaze ice well. An all-weather tire with the three-peak mountain snowflake symbol is the sensible upgrade over an all-season, with better bite in slush and cold rain and no seasonal swap.
In the mountains around Boone and Asheville, where totals climb far past the state average, a winter tire earns its place on a daily driver, and studs are an option within the 1/16 inch limit.

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to North Carolina
chunks.text:
All-season on the coast, all-weather inland
North Carolina averages about 5 inches of snow a year, and the higher Appalachian elevations can get up to 100 inches.
Mount Mitchell, the state's snowiest site, averages 89.1 inches a year. In many winter storms the Piedmont sits between cold air to the west and warm air to the east, and freezing rain is common enough there that it has been called the Ice Storm Capital of the South.
Source:NC State Climate Office

chunks.text:
Free shipping · TX
Tires Shipped Free to Texas
Tires ship free to any street address in Texas, from El Paso to Beaumont and from the Panhandle to the Rio Grande Valley. Texas changed the rules recently: most passenger cars no longer get a state safety inspection, so keeping an eye on your own tread matters more than it used to. Here is what still applies, with sources, and how to get a new set mounted near you.
Shop Tires Find My Tires
State rules

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to Texas
chunks.text:
Texas tire rules, with sources
A plain-English summary with a source for each line, not legal advice. Laws change: check the Texas DMV for current rules.
Inspection
Since January 1, 2025, non-commercial vehicles in Texas no longer need a safety inspection before registration (House Bill 3297). Owners pay a $7.50 inspection program replacement fee when they register instead. Commercial vehicles still need a passing safety inspection.
Source:Texas DPS, Inspection Program Changes

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to Texas
chunks.text:
Emissions counties
Emissions testing still applies in Collin, Dallas, Denton, Ellis, Johnson, Kaufman, Parker, Rockwall and Tarrant counties around Dallas-Fort Worth; Brazoria, Fort Bend, Galveston, Harris and Montgomery around Houston; Travis and Williamson around Austin; and El Paso County, with Bexar County starting November 1, 2026. It is an emissions test, not a tire check.
Source:TCEQ, Vehicle Emissions Inspections

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to Texas
chunks.text:
State tire fee
Texas has no state fee on new tires. Its per-tire recycling fee program ended on December 31, 1997; tire shops now set their own charges for taking old tires.
Source:TCEQ, Scrap Tire Management in Texas
Sources checked October 2026.
Climate and tire choice
Which tire type for Texas
All-season down south, all-weather up north
Texas is too big for one answer. Along the Gulf and in the Valley, where January lows sit around 50°F, an all-season or touring tire fits the whole year. Heat is the bigger enemy there: check pressures in the morning before you drive, because a hot afternoon reading runs high and hides a slow leak.

chunks.title: Tires Shipped Free to Texas
chunks.text:
All-season down south, all-weather up north
In the Panhandle and North Texas, January lows near 20°F and arctic air channeled south by the Rockies make an all-weather tire with the three-peak mountain snowflake symbol worth a look. It passes a severe-snow traction test yet stays on all year, which suits a place where winter comes in short, sharp spells rather than a long season.
Texas has hot summers and mild to cool winters. The Rocky Mountains channel arctic air south in winter, and the flat interior lets air masses move north and south easily.
Source:NOAA State Climate Summaries 2022
January low temperatures typically run from about 20°F in the northern Panhandle to about 50°F near the mouth of the Rio Grande.
Source:NOAA State Climate Summaries 2022

Does Texas still inspect my tires?
Not for most passenger vehicles. Since January 1, 2025, non-commercial vehicles skip the safety inspection and pay a $7.50 inspection program replacement fee at registration instead. Commercial vehicles are still inspected.
Why is there no state tire fee on my Texas order?
Texas doesn't have one. Its per-tire recycling fee ended at the close of 1997, according to TCEQ. Shops may charge for taking old tires, and that charge is theirs. Taxes and fees are calculated at checkout.
I'm in Harris County. Is the emissions test a tire check?
No. Harris is one of the TCEQ emissions counties, and that test is about what comes out of the tailpipe. Tread and tire condition are between you and your shop now.

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Clearance Calculator
chunks.text:
Free tool
How far does a new wheel move out or in?
Offset decides where a wheel sits between the suspension and the fender. Enter your current wheel and the one you're considering to see how far the face and inside edge move, in millimeters and inches, plus the backspacing and, with tire sizes, the tire's width and diameter. The bands are generic geometry guides, not a fitment promise: clearance also depends on your vehicle, and TireDrop confirms fitment by phone before any wheel ships.

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Clearance Calculator
chunks.text:
The tool
Compares a current wheel with a new one by width and offset, and shows how far the wheel face and inner edge move in millimeters and inches, the backspacing of both, and, when tire sizes are given, the tire's width, diameter and sidewall moves. The bands are generic geometry guides, not a fitment promise: clearance also depends on the vehicle, so have fitment confirmed before you order.
Step by step

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Clearance Calculator
chunks.text:
How to use it
- 1Find the width and offset of your current wheel. They're usually stamped on the back, as in 20x9 ET18: 20 inches across, 9 inches wide and an 18 mm offset.
- 2Type the width and offset into “Current wheel”. The diameter and tire size are optional, and the tire sizes unlock the tire results.
- 3Do the same for the new wheel, using the width and offset from its listing. Or tap an example to see how the bands read.
- 4Read each result: how far the wheel face and inside edge move, and which band the change falls in.
- 5Call us with your year, make, model and trim before you order. Brakes, struts, the fender lip, suspension and steering lock decide clearance, and the numbers here can't see them.

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Clearance Calculator
chunks.text:

Book wheel installation

Questions
The things people ask next
What is wheel offset?
Offset is the distance in millimeters from the wheel's centerline to its mounting surface, usually stamped after ET. A lower offset pushes the wheel out toward the fender, and a higher one tucks it in toward the suspension. Our offset and backspacing guide explains it in full.
What is backspacing?
Backspacing is the distance in inches from the mounting surface to the back lip of the wheel. It works out to half the wheel's width plus the offset, so a more positive offset means more backspacing.
What do the three bands mean?

chunks.title: Wheel Offset and Clearance Calculator
chunks.text:
The things people ask next
They only describe how far the numbers moved. Up to about 6 mm (a quarter inch) reads as close to your current setup, up to about 19 mm (three-quarters of an inch) as noticeably different, and more than that as a large change. Tire width and overall diameter have their own limits. They are generic geometry guides, not a fitment promise.
If the result says close to my current setup, can I order?
Not on the numbers alone. The tool measures how far the wheel and tire move, not what is around them. Clearance depends on your vehicle's brakes, struts, fender lip, suspension and steering lock. Call us with your vehicle details and we confirm fitment before any wheel ships.
